stories.Headline: Bloom Energy Sinks 16% Despite 900 MW NTT DATA Deal as Midterm Fears Hit AI Power Stocks
stories.Summary:
Bloom Energy shares fell 16% on November 6, 2026, even though NTT DATA announced before the open that it will deploy 900 megawatts of Bloom's fuel cells across data-center projects around the world. Shipments under the deal are due to start in 2027, and it is the largest international project Bloom has landed. The stock had already dropped 8% two days earlier, on November 4, after Democrats swept the elections, giving back part of a jump from a Barclays upgrade the day before. Other AI power names sold off too, with GE Vernova down 7% and Oklo down 13%.

Investors fear that a Democratic Congress could slow the buildout of data centers, the customers that Bloom, GE Vernova and Oklo all depend on. Texas's incoming governor, Gina Hinojosa, who beat Greg Abbott, has promised a moratorium on new data-center approvals. Bloom is especially exposed, since 97% of its third-quarter revenue came from the U.S., which is why the overseas order matters as a hedge. Analysts expect its normalized earnings per share to rise from $0.76 in 2025 to $8.24 in 2028, and those estimates date from October 29, before the vote. Bloom traded at about 40 times forward earnings before the drop and about 34 times after it, and its customer deposits stood at $661.4 million on September 30, up from $78.2 million at the end of 2025.

The articles, written by Bobby Sankhagowit for TIKR, attribute the selling to political worry rather than any weakness in the businesses. He argued that Bloom's drop reflects what Washington and Texas might do, leaving the stock cheaper on estimates that have not moved. He also noted that Bloom's third-quarter free cash flow was negative $180.6 million. Contractors fell even harder than Bloom on November 4, with Quanta Services down 13% and Comfort Systems USA down 17%, even though Quanta's backlog hit a record $63.7 billion and Comfort Systems' backlog nearly doubled to $17.81 billion. GE Vernova CEO Scott Strazik said on the company's third-quarter call that it is now taking gas turbine reservations for 2032 delivery.

Both articles say new rules that slow data-center approvals would lead analysts to cut their 2027 and 2028 estimates first. Bloom's fourth-quarter report in early 2027, with its backlog and 2027 guidance, is described as the next real test. Oklo reports on Friday, and observers will watch whether any of its data-center deals has become a binding power contract. The contractors' fourth-quarter reports should show whether customers start pausing projects, since their strong backlogs were reported before the election.

stories.Headline: Expedia Says Travelers Plan With AI Agents but Book Direct
stories.Summary:
Travelers are increasingly using AI assistants to plan trips, but they still tend to complete their bookings with brands they trust, according to Expedia Group. CEO Ariane Gorin made the point on the company's third-quarter earnings call, held around November 4, 2026. She said the real strength of agentic AI is in discovery, and that people want to book with a brand that will take care of them if something goes wrong. Traffic from agents is high intent, she said, and third-party data shows Expedia leading in citation share in the U.S. She told CNBC the company has not yet seen AI agents change customers' booking habits, and that travel's complexities would make it hard for AI to fully replace travel services.

On the numbers, Expedia grew gross bookings 11% and revenue 12% in the quarter, while B2B bookings rose 19%. Advertising growth slowed to 7% from 13% the prior quarter, and CFO Derek Andersen said product changes are coming to give advertisers better campaign tools. Expedia has partnered with Google in AI Mode, announced a Meta Muse integration expected to go live in the U.S., and is testing OpenAI's new ad products. Qantas is the first partner on Expedia's new agentic template, and Reserve Now, Pay Later has been rolled out across all its brands. Inside the company, an agentic voice experience on Vrbo resolved more than 15% of inbound contacts in its first two months, and travelers who used the new activity agent were twice as likely to book an activity within seven days.

Gorin said agent traffic does not appear to cut into direct traffic, and is either incremental or taken from other paid channels. She added that the volume is too small to draw conclusions, and the company said the economics of its agent partnerships are still being worked out. She also said a small team built an autonomous hotel onboarding agent in less than a quarter, work that once took multiple quarters and many more people. In the booking flow, a compare agent and a property expert agent help travelers weigh hotels, which she said pushes people deeper into the funnel and leads to larger purchases. CNBC reported that Expedia's fourth-quarter guidance came in below analysts' expectations.

Rival Booking Holdings reported a similar picture on its own earnings call on November 3, 2026. CFO Ewout Steenbergen said users of its AI assistants at Priceline and Agoda converted at about twice the rate of non-users, and Agoda assistant users had average booking values about 20% higher. Referrals from large language models still account for significantly less than 1% of Booking.com's room nights, he said, though they have accelerated in recent weeks. Booking Holdings expects a slowdown in the fourth quarter, forecasting a 1% to 3% increase in room nights and a 2% to 4% rise in gross bookings. CEO Glenn Fogel suggested regulation could slow adoption of horizontal personal AI agents in parts of the world, particularly Europe.

stories.Headline: Cathie Wood Just Sold AMD Stock and Bought This AI Chip Stock Instead
stories.Summary:
Cathie Wood's Ark Invest recently swapped one AI chip stock for another. At the end of September, its flagship Ark Innovation ETF sold shares of Advanced Micro Devices valued at roughly $111.1 million, and it used the proceeds to buy $81 million worth of Nvidia stock. Ark is known for frequent, active trading and for publishing its trades even when regulators do not require it, which is why its moves draw so much attention. The details come from a Motley Fool article published November 5, 2026.

The article ties the trade to valuation. Nvidia trades at about 22 times this year's expected earnings, while AMD is valued at roughly 63.5 times expected forward profits. That gap reflects expectations that AMD will grow earnings much faster, in part by winning share in graphics processors and by benefiting as central processing units become more important to AI inference work. AMD currently leads Nvidia in CPUs, a category the article calls a possible demand catalyst for the company. Nvidia still dominates the market for advanced GPUs used in AI computing.

The article's author, Keith Noonan, offers a reading of why Ark made the move, noting that the transactions appear to signal a view that Nvidia was the more attractively valued stock. He points to Nvidia's push into CPUs as a possible factor, noting that its new Vera Rubin server platform pairs its next-generation GPUs with its next CPU offerings. In his view, that pairing could threaten AMD's growth opportunities. The article does not quote Wood or Ark explaining the trade, so the reasoning is the writer's interpretation. Noonan has no position in any of the stocks mentioned, while The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends both AMD and Nvidia.

The trade comes during a rough stretch for AI stocks. A separate Motley Fool piece from November 3 said the group had been hit for weeks by bubble fears and worries over how data center spending is financed, with some stocks down 20% to 40% from their highs. In that article, Nvidia shares were priced at $202.06, down 1.3% on the day. The article on Ark's trade does not say whether the firm plans further changes to its holdings, and Ark's next disclosures would show whether it keeps shifting toward Nvidia.

stories.Headline: 1 in 15 adults experience AI-generated image-based abuse: study - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
A study led by RMIT University in Australia found that around one in 15 adults in Australia, Britain and the United States has experienced AI-generated image-based abuse. The survey of more than 7,200 adults found that 7 percent had experienced at least one form of such abuse since turning 18, with the rate slightly higher in Australia at 7.7 percent. The abuse included having intimate images created or altered using AI without consent, having AI-generated intimate images shared without consent, or being threatened with their release. Almost 87 percent of victim-survivors reported at least one impact on their lives, including effects on their health and well-being, relationships, work or finances. The findings were published in the International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction.

The study found that men reported experiencing the abuse at more than twice the rate of women, at 10.2 percent compared with 3.8 percent. However, women reported more negative reactions and impacts, including fear for their safety and effects on their mental and physical health. Higher rates were also reported by people under 35, people from racial and ethnic minority backgrounds, and people with disability. Lead author Professor Nicola Henry from RMIT said the findings revealed the extent of the abuse across the wider community, not just celebrities and public figures. She said the true scale may be even greater because some people may never know that AI-generated images of them have been created or shared.

Henry said the findings strengthened the case for greater responsibility on technology companies to prevent AI-generated image-based abuse before it occurs. She said Australia's proposed digital duty of care is an opportunity to shift the focus from responding to abuse after it happens to requiring online services to prevent foreseeable harm. She added that regulation and new laws are not enough, and that better education, accessible support for victim-survivors, and greater responsibility on technology companies and developers are also needed. Co-author Dr Rebecca Umbach, a staff user experience researcher at Google, said understanding who is experiencing this abuse, how it occurs and its impacts is essential for designing more effective prevention and responses. The research program was funded by Google.

The findings build on two earlier studies using the same international dataset. One earlier study found that 3.2 percent of respondents reported creating, sharing or threatening to share AI-generated sexual images without consent, and among those who shared the material the most commonly reported motivation was for fun or as a joke. Another study found that almost one in five adults had deliberately viewed AI-generated sexual images of real people, excluding those who did so solely to report or remove the material. Henry said that as generative AI becomes more widely available, there is greater potential for these tools to be misused, and that what is not yet known is how quickly that is translating into increased victimization. The international team is continuing its work to better understand and prevent AI-generated image-based abuse.

stories.Headline: SK Telecom Q3 Operating Profit Surges Elevenfold, but AI Data Center Revenue Falls 7.4%
stories.Summary:
SK Telecom reported on Nov. 4 that its third-quarter 2026 revenue was 4.4973 trillion won, operating profit was 552.3 billion won and net profit was 411.8 billion won. Revenue rose 13% from a year earlier and operating profit surged 1,040%, partly because last year's figure was low after the April 2025 hacking incident led to customer compensation and service fee discounts. Operating profit was 48.4 billion won in the third quarter of last year and 533.3 billion won in the third quarter of 2024, so this year's figure was about 3.6% higher than before the hacking incident. Compared with the previous quarter, revenue rose 3.2% but operating profit fell 2.4%.

Mobile revenue rose 21% from a year earlier to 2.5697 trillion won, and 5G subscribers reached 18.094 million, up 121,000 from the previous quarter. Average revenue per user rose 0.7% quarter-on-quarter to 29,297 won. Subsidiary SK Broadband posted revenue of 1.1728 trillion won, up 2.6%, and operating profit of 134.7 billion won, up 51%. AI data center revenue rose 6.2% from a year earlier to 126.1 billion won but fell 7.4% from 136.2 billion won in the previous quarter, which the company linked to a revenue gap in its GPU-as-a-service business during a transition to new long-term contracts. AI services for enterprises and consumers brought in 70 billion won, up 27% from a year earlier and 14% from the previous quarter, and combined AI data center and AI service revenue was 196.1 billion won, up 12% from a year earlier but down 0.7% from 197.5 billion won in the previous quarter.

SK Telecom set up SK Hyper in July to develop its AI data center business and in August announced plans to separate SK Broadband's data center and submarine cable businesses into a new company, SK Horizon. It signed agreements to secure 3.08 trillion won in investment for SK Horizon from KKR and a consortium of IMM Investment and Stonebridge, and aims to complete the separation and establish the new entity in the first quarter of 2027. During the quarter, SK Telecom and SK Broadband spent 461.4 billion won on capital expenditure, and an additional 148.6 billion won went to SK Hyper's data center business development, for a combined 610 billion won. The company plans to expand data center capacity from 137 megawatts to more than 318 megawatts after 2030 by building new data centers in Ulsan, the Seoul metropolitan area and other locations.

LG Uplus said Nov. 4 that its third-quarter revenue fell 0.7% from a year earlier to 3.9813 trillion won, while operating profit rose 84% to 297.6 billion won and net profit rose 272% to 183.1 billion won. The profit jump largely reflected 150 billion won in voluntary retirement costs in the third quarter of 2025 that cut operating profit to 161.7 billion won; excluding those costs, operating profit would have been 311.7 billion won, or 14.1 billion won higher than this year's figure. Consolidated service revenue was 3.1021 trillion won, standalone service revenue rose 0.7% to 2.912 trillion won, and cumulative consolidated service revenue for the first nine months of 2026 rose 1.6% to 9.2156 trillion won. Mobile revenue fell 0.9% to 1.6867 trillion won, while mobile service revenue excluding interconnection revenue rose 0.4% to 1.6232 trillion won.

stories.Headline: Ex-Legorans Bag $2.4m For Real Estate AI Native
stories.Summary:
Cem Ucan and Kieran John Keenan, former employees of Legora, raised a pre-seed round for their new AI-native law firm Athena, which focuses on commercial real estate. The round was led by a16z Speedrun and was announced on November 3, 2026. One article reports the amount as $2.4 million, while the other gives $2.5 million. Athena launched two months before the announcement and had already signed 22 clients.

Athena's proprietary AI agents work alongside experienced transactional attorneys at its affiliated law firm, Athena Circle, to produce complex deal documents in hours at a fraction of traditional cost. The firm advises on commercial real estate acquisitions, sales and financing, covering purchase agreements, due diligence, loan documents and closings. It charges a fixed fee per transaction, typically 30 to 50 percent less than clients paid on recent deals. On an early transaction, the team turned around a purchase agreement in under 48 hours, which the client called its fastest turnaround. In its first six weeks, Athena cut attorney review time by more than 70 percent.

Ucan said the AI works hand in hand with a law firm designed around it from day one, with experienced attorneys focused on the judgment and negotiation that move deals forward. Keenan said he measures progress by how quickly an attorney can review an AI agent's work and confidently stand behind it, noting that a draft produced in minutes can still leave a lawyer with hours of work. Troy Kirwin, partner at a16z Speedrun, said clients will still want experienced professionals who take responsibility for the work as AI becomes more capable. L. Miguel Arce, CEO at Mox, a Texas-based multifamily real estate company, said the system learns from every deal and that speed only matters if the work is quality.

The founders met at Legora, where they saw the potential of AI and the limitations of selling it to traditional law firms. Ucan had spent years in Big Law, at one point billing 3,000 hours annually, before moving into legal innovation at Baker McKenzie and Legora. Keenan studied law before building an automated legal reasoning system at his own startup, and José Braz, who developed Legora's legal research agent, joined as founding engineer. The founders expect refinancing pressure from commercial properties acquired in 2021 and 2022, whose three-to-five-year loans are now approaching maturity, to drive a new wave of transactions. Athena plans to expand across property types, geographies and eventually other areas of transactional law.

stories.Headline: UK cyber chief warns of AI attacks on critical infrastructure by 2028
stories.Summary:
Britain's cyber chief warned on Tuesday that the UK will likely face artificial intelligence attacks on its critical infrastructure by 2028, as criminals and hostile states increasingly use AI in their operations. Richard Horne, head of the National Cyber Security Centre, made the warning in a speech marking the publication of the NCSC's annual report. He said the technology will let long-tolerated vulnerabilities be found and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable. The report says ransomware gangs are highly likely to weaponise AI, and that Russia and China will routinely use it to pursue their geopolitical goals.

The report puts numbers on the current threat. Over the past year, the NCSC's incident management team received 1,831 reports of cyber attacks, of which 337 needed support and 80 were nationally significant. The centre also warned 8,500 organisations that their systems had been compromised. Malicious cyber activity costs UK organisations almost $20 billion a year, and Jaguar Land Rover suffered more than $260 million in direct losses in 2025 after a cyberattack that also hit its suppliers and dented the UK economy. The NCSC urges organisations to take basic steps, including keeping devices up to date, limiting administrator access to systems and backing up important files and data.

Horne said business leaders who have "got away with tech on the cheap" will have to explain why food is missing from shelves, lights are off and firms have gone under if they fail to invest in security or replace outdated technology. He described Chinese activity as the most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the UK, said Russia runs campaigns designed to stay below the threshold of armed conflict, and said Iran attacks the UK and targets individuals it sees as threats to its regime. Anne Keast-Butler, director of GCHQ, which includes the NCSC, called on every UK organisation to act now, saying cybersecurity is now part of the nation's front line defence. Metro reported that Horne likened the moment to a "Sliding Doors" turning point and warned of a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in incidents in the coming months, caused not by AI inventing new attacks but by AI exposing old weaknesses. Security expert Will Geddes told Metro the two-year timeline underestimates the danger, saying such attacks could come within two months.

The report stresses that AI is more likely to enhance and scale existing tactics than to discover brand new vulnerabilities. Last week, governments and companies rushed out security updates after AI helped find two critical flaws in a programming language used by 70% of websites worldwide, which could let attackers take remote control of a web server without a password. Horne pointed to the recent attacks on refrigeration systems in French supermarkets as a sign of how easily hostile actors can exploit civilian infrastructure, and noted that technology automates electricity switching, water sluice gates, dams and manufacturing lines. The UK and EU states say Russia's FSB was behind a December 2025 attack on Poland's energy grid that, had it succeeded, could have cut power to 500,000 people in winter. The articles do not describe any further official steps beyond the call for organisations to act now.

stories.Headline: AI-Generated Advertising Gets New Rule in Pennsylvania
stories.Summary:
On October 22, 2026, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, which sets disclosure rules for advertisements that use AI. The law defines "synthetic content" broadly, covering images, video, audio or text that AI has generated or significantly modified. It bars advertisers from knowingly, recklessly or willfully creating or spreading ads that use such content to give a false impression of a product's or service's nature, origin or authenticity, unless the ad carries a clear and conspicuous disclosure. Robinson & Cole attorney Roma Patel summarized the law in a November 5 analysis for the National Law Review.

The disclosure has to identify the content as AI-generated or AI-modified, and it must appear the first time a consumer encounters the content. It must come in the same format as the synthetic content itself and, where technically feasible, be permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove. It also has to be understandable in the language or interaction the consumer uses, be consistent with the ad, and be audible or readable depending on the format. Exemptions cover fictional depictions, parody, satire, commentary and criticism, and ads that consist only of text are excluded from the disclosure requirement, even if AI wrote or heavily changed the text. The Act takes effect December 21, 2026.

Enforcement falls to the Pennsylvania Attorney General or a district attorney, either of whom may seek an injunction or bring a civil action. A court may impose a civil fine of up to $3,000 per violation. Patel's analysis says the main risk for companies using AI in advertising arises when an ad could mislead consumers, for example a synthetic product image that misrepresents the offering. A disclosure can still fall short if consumers are unlikely to notice it or if it conflicts with the ad's message, and she says realistic synthetic media that could be mistaken for a genuine product, person or endorsement deserves particular review.

The law arrives as the national picture on AI and advertising rules shifts. PPC Land reported on November 4 that Democrats won the Senate and were projected to take the House in the midterm elections, which would upend Republican plans for a single federal standard that would preempt state AI and privacy laws. The outlet said the likeliest result for advertisers is not a new federal regime but the survival, and probable expansion, of the state-by-state approach the industry had hoped to replace. Pennsylvania's Act is an example of that kind of state rule, and Shapiro was among the governors re-elected on November 3. The new Congress is due to convene on January 3, 2027, and Pennsylvania's disclosure requirements begin on December 21, 2026.

stories.Headline: Seoul National University of Science and Technology Researchers Develop New AI-Assisted Pipeline to Identify Errors in Construction Design Documents
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Seoul National University of Science and Technology in South Korea have built an AI-assisted pipeline that finds human errors in structural design documents. The team was led by Associate Professor Jaewook Jeong of the Department of Safety Engineering. The system automatically pulls structural information out of different documents, organizes it, and compares it, and it does this without using building information modeling, known as BIM. The work was announced on Nov. 3, 2026, and the study was put online on Oct. 13, 2026. It is due to appear in Volume 185 of Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence on Dec. 1, 2026.

The pipeline begins by removing low-quality data and standardizing what remains. For calculation documents, it uses layout analysis and optical character recognition models to extract data on structural members. For drawings, it uses optical character recognition and computer vision to find, filter, and standardize table regions that hold member codes. It then treats member codes and directions as identifiers, cross-validates the data, detects errors, and flags duplicates. The researchers made the tool available through a web-based application, and it achieved more than 90% accuracy when extracting information from structural design documents.

In a case study of a South Korean residential project, extraction accuracy reached 95.56% for calculation documents and 90.47% for drawings. The verification step found 253 discrepancies, 29 of which were critical errors. Those 253 consisted of 224 missing entries, 18 reinforcement mismatches, eight dimensional discrepancies, and three duplicates. The researchers say this shows the framework can verify documents and cut down the burden of manual checking.

Dr. Jeong explained that the framework checks for inconsistencies between structural calculation documents and drawings that may come from human error, and that it does so without relying on BIM. He said the pipeline could help structural engineers, design consultants, contractors, and construction supervision teams catch discrepancies before they lead to construction errors, improving the reliability of buildings and infrastructure. The problem it targets is that different stakeholders use different tools and formats, which often produces mismatches between calculations and drawings that can seriously compromise building safety. BIM can help, but high costs and technical barriers leave many projects dependent on traditional document-based collaboration. The researchers say the framework could fit into routine engineering workflows, and it is meant especially for small- and medium-sized projects that cannot afford expensive digital tools.

stories.Headline: Embodied AI's Next Frontier: Integrating Intelligence with Real-World Systems
stories.Summary:
New research published on November 4, 2026, highlights the challenge of integrating intelligence, sensing, movement, computing, energy management and connectivity into embodied AI systems that can perform reliably in demanding environments. The findings come from a white paper titled From Specialized to General-Purpose: 2026 White Paper on Embodied AI Technology Evolution and Industrial Deployment. It was jointly published by Avnet, the National and Local Co-Built Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center and GYH.AI. Embodied AI combines artificial intelligence with physical systems such as robots and autonomous machines, enabling them to perceive their surroundings, make decisions and act in the physical world.

The research identifies four factors that will influence the shift from specialized embodied AI applications toward broader industrial deployment. System integration is fundamental to performance, because AI models, computing platforms, sensors, motion control, energy management and communications must function as a coordinated system. Technology selection must reflect application requirements, balancing performance, energy efficiency, reliability, scalability and cost. The path to general-purpose embodied AI will be gradual, building on specialized systems designed for defined tasks, and industrial deployment requires lifecycle planning covering testing, software compatibility, component availability, safety, maintenance and long-term support.

Edward Tsaur, VP of Avnet Design Services, Marketing & Communications for Asia Pacific, said much of the discussion around embodied AI focuses on individual technologies, but the next stage will depend on how well they work together. He said the challenge is not just making systems smarter but ensuring they perform reliably, adapt to changing conditions and deliver consistent results over time. He added that across Asia Pacific there is growing interest in intelligent systems for manufacturing, logistics, healthcare and other operational environments. He said collaboration across the technology ecosystem will be critical to translating advances into practical solutions, looking beyond individual components to how hardware, software and engineering expertise can work together.

Separately, Envision announced on November 2, 2026, the world's first commercial deployment of an integrated 800-volt direct current power system in a large-scale AI data center. The system is powering live computing workloads at Envision's Galaxy AI data center campus in Ulanqab, China, delivering power end to end from grid input to computing loads. The 800V DC architecture simplifies AI data center power systems, bringing higher power conversion and watt-to-bit efficiency, a more compact equipment footprint, and reduced cabling and copper requirements. The system combines solid-state transformers, battery energy storage and equipment that adjusts direct-current voltage for computing hardware, coordinated in real time by Envision's Dubhe Controller, supported by its Dubhe Energy Foundation Model.

Kevin Huang, Senior Vice President of Envision Energy and President of Energy Storage and AIDC Power Systems, said AI data centers need power systems that coordinate renewable energy, energy storage and the grid to meet computing demand. He said the integrated 800V DC system is now powering live computing workloads, demonstrating an end-to-end architecture that connects renewable energy supply with computing demand. The Galaxy campus began operations in August 2026 and has a planned capacity of 3GW, designed to support up to one million AI accelerators operating in parallel at full build-out, with more than 80% of its power planned to come from direct renewable electricity connections. Envision aims to scale the approach through its Mission Gobi initiative, which targets 5GW of green AI data center capacity in desert regions worldwide by 2030.

stories.Headline: AI decision models gain traction for enterprise agents
stories.Summary:
Indian AI company Sarvam AI has launched a decision-making model called Sarvam Prism, according to a report published on November 4, 2026. The model is built on the company's Sarvam 105B base model and is meant to handle fast, structured decisions such as customer support routing, document analysis and evaluation of AI agents. It arrives as decision models gain attention across the industry, following the September release of Jev, the first public model from TypeSafe AI, which was founded by Diogo Almeida, who helped develop research behind ChatGPT at OpenAI. Instead of writing paragraphs of text, such models return a label, score, probability or confidence level that another system can act on.

On its own tests, Sarvam says Prism responds in 44 milliseconds on an NVIDIA B200 GPU and averaged 71.8 across three benchmarks, the highest among the 25 decision models it tested that answered in under 100 milliseconds. On its internal Indian-language benchmark, Prism scored 82.5, against 75 for Perplexity Decider v1.2 and 70.8 for Jev 1.14. On an internal cybersecurity benchmark of 5,517 questions, it reached 89 per cent accuracy, compared with 84.5 per cent for Clef and 78.6 per cent for Jev 1.14. For answers given with at least 90 per cent confidence, Prism erred on 2.2 per cent of English responses and 4.4 per cent of Indian-language responses, which the company says is below its own predicted error rates. Its answers also stayed the same across all 2,000 questions when the order of the options was changed.

A key part of the launch is that Sarvam has released Prism's weights under the Apache 2.0 licence, so enterprises can train the model on their own data and run it on their own infrastructure. It is also available through Sarvam's API. The company named customer support routing, document intelligence, security checks and AI-agent evaluation as early applications. In its blog post, Sarvam said Prism makes fewer errors than its confidence scores predict at every threshold it tested, from 50 per cent to 95 per cent, in both English and Indian languages. All of these figures come from the company's own testing.

Prism joins a growing field. Cloudflare has introduced Clef and Clef-flash, Microsoft has released Decision-1, AWS has launched Strands Decider 2B, and OpenAI has launched a Decisions API. Other Indian builders are also active, including PurpleTalk's Sthānika lab with its Sieve models and Kerala-based ConvAI Innovations with its open-weight Laya model. Backers describe the commercial test as whether these systems improve real workflows, not just benchmark scores, and Shubham Gupta of Together Fund said a company's own record of decisions and outcomes is what cannot be copied. The articles do not say what Sarvam plans next.

stories.Headline: Soket Labs & ZenteiQ Launch Indigenous AI Models
stories.Summary:
Two Indian startups, Soket Labs and ZenteiQ AiTech Innovations, released new large language models developed under the IndiaAI Mission. Soket's EKA-1 and ZenteiQ's Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B were unveiled at an event in New Delhi on November 3, with IT secretary S Krishnan present. Both companies were picked under the mission's IndiaAI Innovation Centre pillar to build domestic foundation models. The government said subsidised AI compute and support for ancillary research expenses helped make their development possible.

EKA-1 has 26.3 billion parameters and was trained on nearly 7.5 trillion tokens, according to the IT ministry. It is described as an open, sparse hybrid language model that supports all 22 scheduled Indian languages along with English. The model is meant for mathematics, code generation, reasoning and agentic applications. ZenteiQ's Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B are open-source multilingual models that support English and 10 other Indian languages, and they can be deployed on-premise for document-grounded automation, knowledge retrieval, and government and education uses.

Soket Labs cofounder and CEO Abhishek Upperwal said the mission's support allowed the company to build a model tailored to India's banking, financial services and cybersecurity landscape. He said it is meant to meet sector-specific needs and fit the country's changing digital ecosystem. ZenteiQ CEO Sashikumar said the Dhīr models can run on GPUs and TPUs, and that their lightweight design lets them work on mobile phones without cloud connectivity. He added that this keeps data on users' devices, which improves privacy, security and access. Krishnan said homegrown models will strengthen India's technological and strategic autonomy and raise productivity across government, industry and research.

The announcement gave no benchmark results, deployment details or pricing. The two models target different needs, with EKA-1 aimed at reasoning and agentic work and the Dhīr models at small multilingual assistants for places with limited connectivity. Separately, Sarvam AI launched Prism, an open-weight decision model built on its Sarvam 105B model for enterprise tasks such as customer-support routing and security checks. Enterprise AI in India is projected to become a $71 billion market opportunity by 2030.

stories.Headline: Opting out of data brokers may still leave your family's data exposed
stories.Summary:
In early November 2026, Fox News and Medscape published articles about how data brokers can expose personal information even after people try to remove it. The Fox News article, dated November 4, described how people who submit opt-out forms to people-search sites like Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified and Intelius may still leave their family members' data exposed. The Medscape article, dated November 3, reported on patients like Chris McQueen of San Diego, who finished leukemia treatment a year and a half ago but kept seeing ads for fake cancer cures on his phone during oncologist visits and monthly bloodwork. It also cited a 2022 American Medical Association survey in which more than 92% of patients said their health data should not be available for purchase.

The articles describe what opting out does and does not change. The Federal Trade Commission warns that even after someone opts out, their information may still appear in reports about relatives, neighbors or associates, and that opting out does not remove underlying information from government public records. The Medscape article said location data from phones is not covered by HIPAA, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. It said California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, vetoed a bill on September 27 that would have blocked the sale and sharing of location and other sensitive personal data, saying it went "a step too far." A Stanford University study showed only 9% of data brokers were adhering to an existing California privacy law, and Connecticut, Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon and Virginia have already banned the sale of precise geolocation data.

The articles name several people responsible and paraphrase their views. McQueen said the ads made him feel sick to his stomach and feared patients could be harmed if they tried untested treatments instead of following their oncologists' advice. Eric Ellsworth, director of health policy and innovation at the Center for the Study of Services, said data brokers are "hoovering up data from the open web and then buying it from anybody." F. Mario Trujillo, senior staff attorney at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, said location data is sensitive and that comprehensive collection of it reveals sensitive things. Advertising trade groups said targeted advertising saves consumers time, lowers the cost of searching for products and lets websites and apps offer services without paywalls or subscriptions.

The articles give context and describe what may happen next. The Fox News article said data brokers collect information from multiple sources, including public records and other data brokers, and that information can reappear when a site obtains updated records, so the FTC recommends checking periodically for new listings. It recommended a household approach and family data removal services that submit removal requests to hundreds of sites and send recurring requests, while noting no service can guarantee complete removal. The Medscape article said the US government has begun penalizing some companies that track Americans at health facilities and places of worship, but privacy and legal experts do not think actions against a few companies will stop the industry. It said experts are calling on more states or Congress to ban advertisers from tracking Americans' locations via their phones, though progress has been fitful and digital advertisers have lobbied states to block such limits.

stories.Headline: [Sci-Tech NOW] KAIST CluSTER cuts AI training from 10 hours to 3, speeding medical and coding models
stories.Summary:
KAIST announced on November 2 that a research team in its School of Computing has developed a method called CluSTER, which speeds up the additional training of large language models. The technology picks the most useful training data and spreads it evenly across multiple GPUs, the chips that handle the heavy calculations in AI training. It targets fine-tuning, in which an AI that is already trained is taught data from a specific field such as coding or medicine. The results were presented in October 2026 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, known as EMNLP 2026, a major international conference.

The method first analyzes how each piece of data affects learning and groups together items with similar effects, even when they look different on the surface. It then selects varied data from each group and gives different groups to different GPUs, so the chips are less likely to repeat similar work. The team fine-tuned models with about 7 billion and 13 billion parameters, using three datasets from the coding and medical fields and eight performance benchmarks. In the tests, the models kept nearly the same performance while using only about 31% of the full dataset, and training time fell by up to 69.6%. At that maximum reduction, training that once took 10 hours could finish in about 3 hours.

Most experiments ran on four GPUs, and the team also confirmed better results than conventional methods in an eight-GPU setup. The research was led by a professor in the KAIST School of Computing, whom the two articles name differently, Jae-Gil Lee in one and Jaegul Choo in the other. Hyunjin Kim, a doctoral student in the School of Computing, is the first author. Co-authors are Youngeun Nam, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Toronto, and Jaemin Han and Wonhyeok Choi, both master's students at the KAIST Graduate School of Data Science. The work was supported by the Institute of Information & Communications Technology Planning & Evaluation, funded by the Ministry of Science and ICT, through its SW Star Lab project.

The lead professor said that improving training efficiency depends not only on using more GPUs but also on choosing wisely which data to train on. He added that the study shows existing GPU resources can be used more efficiently to lighten the training burden of large AI models. The team expects the method to help companies and research institutions cut the time and GPU costs of building AI for purposes such as coding assistance or medical question answering. One report says the researchers plan to widen their validation using real industrial data and larger training environments. The paper is titled "Clustering-Based Balanced Sampling and Allocation with Data Parallelism for High-Performance Fine-Tuning."

stories.Headline: Apple iOS 27.3: Everything you need to know about Siri AI, Apple Watch and Audio Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Apple has begun rolling out the iOS 27.3 update for testing, and the release leans heavily on Siri AI, which now gets deeper access to Apple's own apps. The update also brings new features for Safari, StandBy, Health and Fitness+, along with a few device-specific additions. With this update, Siri AI is set to handle more complex tasks across apps including Calendar, Mail, Notes, and Photos. Apple says Siri can now help users create playlists based on a specific suggestion in the Music app, bring tabs together in Safari, and schedule a message to friends.

Apple's AI-powered Audio Intelligence technology for the Apple Watch is now rolling out into beta testing for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company's Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes four opt-in AI features that let Apple Watch Series 12 wearers detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes. With Live Rewind, a double-press on the digital crown shows what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet on the watch face, and these snippets are deleted automatically after 30 seconds if not saved. Siri Recaps summarize a conversation with a short sentence and bullet points, and if users do nothing, the recaps delete themselves within seven days.

According to a post on Apple's developer site, the preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents. This lets people ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out custom actions such as checking a delivery, booking a reservation, or placing an order. Apple is also introducing skills that let developers teach Siri AI to combine several actions into a single experience. The blog post calls this a sneak peek and a first look, so it is not clear yet when regular users will get this experience.

Apple says Siri Recaps is designed to omit sensitive information like government-assigned identifiers, financial and authentication data, certain personal identifiers, and any language that would promote self-harm. The features rely on the S11 chip, a built-in microphone, Apple Intelligence models that run on the iPhone, and Apple's Private Cloud Compute. Developers can currently build apps using these Intents and Skills and test them with Xcode or internal TestFlight versions, but they cannot publish apps that use these features to the App Store yet. The Audio Intelligence features will later roll out to the public beta for broader testing before becoming publicly available to all.

stories.Headline: Apple's new 18+ app limits mean little for dating apps, a lot for AI companions
stories.Summary:
Apple announced on Monday, November 3, 2026, that it is changing its App Store policies to make it harder for minors to use dating apps or AI companions with sexual or romantic content. The company shared the news in an announcement to developers. The new rules follow other steps Apple has taken to protect minors, including rolling out age assurance technology globally and adding more parental controls and child safety features. Starting November 16, developers must include new content descriptors so their app's age rating reflects its features.

Under the policy, all apps offering dating or romantic relationship features must carry an 18+ rating. Apple's questionnaire asks whether an app enables dating between real people or a virtual companion that engages a user in sexual or romantic content, and whether it shares a user's real-world location with another person or group. Apps with the dating descriptor will be hidden from users under 18 on devices where a parent or guardian has turned on content restrictions, and younger users who can still see the app must prove they are adults before buying or downloading it. The location question may not affect an app's minimum rating in some regions, and Apple cites Brazil as an exception, where local rules require an A16 rating for location-sharing apps and an A18 rating for dating apps. Developers must answer both questions when submitting a new app or an update, and every app in the store must have both declarations on file by January 12, 2027.

TechCrunch reported that the change could matter most for AI companion apps such as Character.AI and Replika, which let people create AI friends, lovers and fantasy characters and are often targeted at younger people. TechCrunch also noted that xAI launched 3D animated AI companions that allowed users to unlock NSFW capabilities, and that top AI companion apps had been downloaded 220 million times globally as of last summer. Mashable reported that a 2025 survey of U.S. teens ages 13 to 17 found that 52 percent regularly use AI companions and 33 percent use them for social interaction and relationships. James P. Steyer, founder and CEO of the nonprofit Common Sense Media, said in a statement that social AI companions are not safe for kids and are designed to create emotional attachment and dependency. Replika CEO Dmytro Klochko told Mashable in 2025 that the platform is intended only for users over 18, but he acknowledged that some users try to bypass strict protocols for preventing underage access.

Mashable reported that the change is a rather incremental update for dating apps, since platforms like Tinder, Hinge and Bumble already restrict themselves to users over 18. Common Sense Media researchers found in a 2025 study that safety measures are easily circumvented, including age gates and terms of service restrictions on teen use, and the group has since published more research criticizing AI companion platforms for relying on ineffective self reporting for age assurance. Whether Apple's new policy will adequately address these concerns is yet to be determined, since all apps must complete the declarations by January 12, 2027. The global debate over age verification remains one of the major topics concerning Big Tech and teens today, along with social media bans.

stories.Headline: STM32 Summit 2026: STMicroelectronics announces its unified MCU platform, addressing technology convergence across industrial, automotive and physical AI applications
stories.Summary:
STMicroelectronics announced on November 4, 2026, from Geneva, a unified STM32 microcontroller platform that spans industrial, automotive and robotics applications. The company, listed on the NYSE as STM, said the strategy builds on more than 20 years of STM32 development and is meant to let developers reuse architectures, intellectual property, software and tools across different markets. As part of the move, it introduced a new STM32A family that extends the platform into automotive and safety-critical systems. On the same day it also revealed the STM32G5 series of mixed-signal microcontrollers, aimed at AI datacenters, robotics, photovoltaic installations, wind turbines, industrial drives and commercial drones.

The unified platform rests on Arm Cortex-M cores, the STM32Cube software ecosystem and shared process technologies, including ST's 40nm Flash and 18nm FD-SOI with embedded phase-change memory, supplemented by TSMC eNVM technologies. The first three STM32A chips are already sampling to customers, with broader availability planned for 2027. The STM32A4 targets entry-level automotive local control nodes and safety systems, while the STM32A5 serves mid-range safety-critical uses in industrial automation, robotics, energy systems and cars. The STM32A9 is meant for safety-critical multi-domain control, where real-time response, low latency, Ethernet and deterministic communication matter.

On the STM32G5 side, the chips use an Arm Cortex-M33 core running at 280MHz and deliver twice the compute performance of the STM32G4 series, with ratings of 420 DMIPS and 1136 CoreMark. They add an enhanced 12-channel high-resolution timer, a position encoder, and a programmable logic array called PLAy that lets developers build custom hardware functions on the chip. Security features include an immutable root of trust, TrustZone, tamper detection and support for post-quantum cryptography. Dual-core STM32G5 products are due in 2027, and the series is supported by the STM32CubeMX2 development tool and the new HAL2 software layer.

Remi El-Ouazzane, who leads ST's Microcontrollers, Digital ICs and RF Products Group, said developers should not have to start over with each new product and that ST wants STM32 to become the reference MCU platform across industries. Drew Henry, Executive Vice President for Physical AI at Arm, said the next frontier for computing is putting intelligence into machines that operate in the physical world, and described the two companies' Cortex-M work as part of that effort. Patrick Aidoune, a general manager at ST, said the STM32G5 makes the compute needed for physical AI accessible and embeddable. Customers also commented, with Delta Electronics' Andy Hsiao pointing to lower energy losses and higher reliability in AI and EV designs, and Ruiyan Intelligent CEO Paul Tian saying the chip can drive more motors in a robotic hand.

ST framed the G5 as a response to rising datacenter power demand, noting that rack power is heading toward 1 MW and that the largest datacenters could need over 2 GW of peak power by 2030. A robotic hand can contain as many as 20 motors, which is why precise multi-axis control matters. Arm's Cortex-M architecture is used in more than 100 billion devices, and ST describes itself as a lead partner in shaping its future. Broader STM32A availability and the dual-core STM32G5 products are both expected in 2027.

stories.Headline: Kakao Mobility, South Korean Army to Develop AI-Based Control System for Unmanned Assets
stories.Summary:
Kakao Mobility signed a memorandum of understanding with the Republic of Korea Army on November 3, 2026, at Army Headquarters in Gyeryong, South Chungcheong Province. The agreement covers cooperation on advanced technologies, including integrated control systems for manned-unmanned combined combat operations. Kakao Mobility CEO Ryu Geung-seon and Army Headquarters Policy Director Maj. Gen. Lee Kyung-jin attended the signing.

The company announced the agreement on November 3, and the Seoul Economic Daily reported it on November 4. The partnership is linked to the Army's Army TIGER+ initiative, which aims to bring civilian AI technologies into military operations. The two sides plan to combine Kakao Mobility's platform management expertise with Army operational data to research and test AI-based control systems for defense. The central goal is a single system that can operate multiple types of unmanned vehicles, supporting a one-to-many model in which one operator manages several unmanned systems. Over the longer term, they aim to lay the foundation for a defense mobility operating system that can coordinate drones, robots and other unmanned assets on the battlefield.

They will also establish testing environments around the Army's AI Transformation hubs in Pangyo and Daejeon, and the partnership covers military dispatch systems and dedicated applications. Ryu said Kakao Mobility would support innovation in future combat systems based on its technology and help the Army secure world-class competitiveness in defense physical AI. He said the results of research and demonstrations with the Army would feed back into private-sector technology, creating a cycle in which the military and the domestic physical AI ecosystem grow together. Lee said that on future battlefields what matters is a physical AI platform that analyzes a wide range of field data and connects AI judgments to the actual operation of moving vehicles. He said applying Kakao Mobility's technology to defense would upgrade future combat systems and secure technological sovereignty in defense AI.

Kakao Mobility has been expanding into defense AI, signing an MOU with Korea University's C5ISRT Convergence Research Institute on October 6. It entered the robotics control business in 2024 with its robot delivery service BRING, began late-night autonomous driving in Seoul's Gangnam district in March 2026, and increased its operating vehicles to six from two in August. The Army conducted the Army TIGER+ Future Warfare Integrated Combat Exercise on October 14 at the Yangpyeong Comprehensive Training Center in Gyeonggi Province, demonstrating reconnaissance drones, loitering attack drones, multipurpose unmanned ground vehicles and quadruped robots. The Army aims to expand manned-unmanned combined combat systems across all units by 2040.

stories.Headline: Dollar slides to one-month low as Democratic gains stoke AI regulation fears
stories.Summary:
The US dollar fell to a one-month low on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections. Investors worried that a Democratic majority could bring tougher regulation of the artificial intelligence sector, which could slow US economic growth. The dollar index dropped 0.6% to 101.27, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell nearly 5 basis points to 4.915%. Traders also scaled back bets on interest rate hikes for next year.

Democrats captured majorities in both the Senate and the House on Tuesday, November 3, with wins reaching into Republican strongholds such as Kansas and Texas. They had flipped six Republican Senate seats so far, which secures a Senate majority even if they lose their own seats in competitive Michigan and Minnesota. Analysts said the bigger concern for the dollar was what a Democratic win could mean for AI, with markets pricing in more scrutiny of the sector. The Nasdaq underperformed as a result, and the euro and sterling rose against the dollar.

Moh Siong Sim, a currency strategist at OCBC, said the market reaction reflected worry about greater AI scrutiny and its possible effect on US growth. He also said that passing federal legislation would remain hard, given the veto power held by President Donald Trump. Carol Kong, a currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, said investor focus would return to economic fundamentals once the midterms were over. She expected strong US data to support further rate hikes, and she warned that an escalation in the Middle East could push oil prices higher and lift the dollar.

The Bank of England was set to announce its policy decision on Thursday, with an expected first rate increase since August 2023. Oil prices eased to $102.9 a barrel after a roughly 1% drop on Tuesday, their lowest level in nearly four weeks. China's offshore yuan fell 0.2% to 6.6836 per dollar, extending losses after the People's Bank of China raised the foreign currency reserves that financial institutions must hold to slow the yuan's rally. Those moves left currency markets watching both Washington and the Middle East for their next direction.

stories.Headline: Pentagon chief tech officer says government will detail laws that apply to AI labs this month - CNA
stories.Summary:
The US federal government plans to publish all the laws and regulations that apply to domestic AI labs, and Pentagon Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael announced this at a Wall Street Journal technology conference in Napa, California, on Wednesday, November 4. Michael, who serves as vice chair of the government's Super Intelligence Task Force, said the group would make the regulatory landscape public within the next week or two. Reports differ on the timing: one account says the publication would come later in November, while another says it would come within weeks of the announcement. The task force is an intergovernmental body that President Donald Trump set up to shape AI policy. Michael did not give any further details about the contents of the framework.

According to Michael, the aim is to build a framework that gives the American people confidence that AI companies will act responsibly. He said the government wants to reassure the public so that companies can operate with that trust in place. Michael argued that without such a framework, the outcome could be regulation written by Congress, which he described as "535 legislators" producing rules that "could kill the industry." His remarks were made in an interview-style conference setting, and the articles do not describe any formal legal changes that the publication itself would impose. The articles also do not say whether the framework would be binding or advisory.

Michael is the speaker responsible for these statements, and he spoke on behalf of the Pentagon's technology office and the task force he co-leads. The task force operates under the authority of a presidential directive, and the reports present it as the body tasked with establishing AI policy. Michael's comments were reported by Reuters and carried by several news outlets, including CNA and The Straits Times. The articles do not quote any responses from AI companies or lawmakers to his remarks.

The statement comes as the government works to set rules for artificial intelligence while debate continues over how much oversight the industry should face. Michael's warning about legislators suggests that the administration prefers guidance it can shape over rules written by Congress. The articles do not describe what will happen after the framework is released, such as public comment periods or enforcement steps. Further details on the regulatory landscape are expected once the task force publishes its material.

stories.Headline: Tovi Announces AI-Powered Music Creation for Its Interactive Toy in Early 2027
stories.Summary:
Tovi, a screen-free, voice-interactive plush toy for children ages 3 to 10, announced on November 5, 2026 that it plans to add AI-powered music creation in early 2027. The company, based in Dover, Delaware, says the feature will let children turn their own ideas into original music through conversation and play. It will join the toy's existing personalized stories, games, riddles, and knowledge-building activities. Tovi also plans to offer access to popular songs through a third-party streaming service.

The music creation feature is described as the central addition, giving children a chance to make original musical content rather than only listening to existing songs. The toy is sold through HeyTovi.com and combines conversational artificial intelligence with a plush format meant to encourage imagination and curiosity without a screen during normal use. Tovi says it has tested thousands of conversation scenarios and interaction flows to see how the system handles requests, declines unsuitable content, and redirects personal concerns to parents or trusted adults. The company also says its platform complies with the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). Raw voice recordings are not permanently stored during normal operation, and text conversation history can be managed through the parent app.

Parents keep oversight tools under the existing setup. The companion app lets caregivers set the child's age and interests, review text conversation transcripts, and delete conversation history. An adult completes the initial setup through the app and connects the toy to Wi-Fi, after which children can talk with it directly. Tovi states that its existing stories, games, riddles, and questions are unlimited and carry no monthly subscription or required content purchases. The company says these features will remain part of the product as it prepares the music launch.

Tovi was named Best Interactive Toy in the United States for 2026 by Best of Best Review, an award the company says reflects its mix of screen-free conversation, personalized content, and parental oversight. The toy has no camera. Contact details for business inquiries were provided by Nicole at nicole@heytovi.com. The articles do not describe a specific launch date within early 2027 or the cost of the planned music feature.

stories.Headline: US tech stocks plunge on fears of tighter AI regulation by Democrats
stories.Summary:
US tech stocks fell sharply on Thursday, November 5, 2026, as investors worried that a Democratic-led Congress would tighten rules on artificial intelligence. The sell-off hit semiconductor makers hardest, since they had recently been among the largest winners of the AI boom. By mid-morning the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 had dropped 5.5% to 26,878 points, on course for one of its steepest daily losses in recent years. The broader S&P 500 slipped 3.2% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 2.2%. The decline came two days after Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate in Tuesday's elections.

Analysts and reporters pointed to specific risks for the industry. Tech firms could face stronger opposition to building the large data centres needed to run AI systems. Democrats are generally seen as more skeptical than Republicans about the fast expansion of AI, and the Republicans have mostly pushed for deregulation. In Texas, Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has already called for an immediate moratorium on new data centre construction. Critics also cite high electricity use, noise, air pollution and water shortages linked to these facilities.

By the close, the losses had deepened. The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% to 26,629.81 points, its lowest level since April, and wiped out about $2.3 trillion in market value. The S&P 500 dropped 4.36% to 7,353.73 points, its largest daily decline since April 2025, while the Dow fell 3.44%. Nvidia shares dropped 9.3%, and memory chipmakers Seagate, Western Digital and Sandisk fell as much as 22%. Tesla fell nearly 11% and SpaceX shares dropped 9%, as fears of tougher regulation spread to companies linked to Elon Musk.

Not every large tech firm fell. A day earlier, on Wednesday, November 4, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta had rallied, with Amazon up 8%, and some investors read the Democratic gains as a sign the hyperscalers might slow their AI spending. Still, the broader picture remains uncertain, and the sector has been volatile for months amid worries that AI valuations are overstretched. The articles do not say whether the Democratic majorities will pass specific AI laws, and they describe the market reaction as a reaction to fears rather than to enacted rules.

stories.Headline: Argonne’s AI STEM Education Summit: Preparing an AI-Enabled Future with Humans in the Lead
stories.Summary:
A year after its first AI STEM Education Summit, Argonne National Laboratory, a U.S. Department of Energy lab, held a second summit on September 24, 2026, drawing more than 160 Illinois educators, academic leaders and STEM partners. The first gathering had focused on basic questions about how AI works, what it can do and how it might change STEM education and the workforce. This year's theme, "AI in Action," shifted attention toward putting AI to use in classrooms and across institutions. Educators who once only knew AI in passing now wanted to know which human skills would matter most as AI grows more capable.

The summit centered on balancing what AI does well against the distinct human abilities that science depends on, such as curiosity, critical thinking, creativity and decision-making. Keynote speaker Dan Chuparkoff, a technology expert, named solving, deciding and imagining as capabilities that will stay essential. He observed that people often spend much of their time on tasks AI could ease, like communicating, processing information and investigating, which leaves less room for higher-level thinking. He urged attendees to use AI to improve their own work rather than simply hand the work over, and he described using it to translate talks and to compare his keynotes for engagement.

The same balance guides the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, which brings national laboratories, universities and industry together to use AI for scientific discovery in areas like energy, national security and science. Its premise is that AI is meant to enable scientists rather than replace them, with AI handling tasks like synthesizing data and running simulations while researchers ask the right questions and judge results. Speakers at the summit, including Argonne Deputy Director for Science and Technology Sean Jones and Purdue University College of Science dean Lucy Flesch, described how AI is expanding research and how Purdue is adapting teaching and curricula. Jones noted that Argonne researchers have run more than 6,000 experiments on chemicals for rechargeable energy storage with AI's help.

Participants then turned these ideas into practice through breakout sessions on approaches they could adopt at their own institutions, and they toured Argonne's autonomous labs to see how AI, robotics and human expertise work together. Kelly Sturner, STEM pathway lead at Argonne, said the lab's growing ecosystem connects educators with national laboratory expertise and real examples of AI in discovery. Argonne plans to bring educators, scientists and STEM organizations together throughout the year to keep sharing ideas and challenges. Officials say preparing students will mean developing skills to think critically, evaluate evidence and apply scientific knowledge, regardless of which technologies they use.

stories.Headline: Stock futures fall as Democratic wins raise concerns over AI regulation
stories.Summary:
US stock futures fell on the night of Tuesday, 3 November 2026, after Democrats won decisive victories in key midterm races. S&P 500 futures dropped more than 0.5%, Dow Jones Industrial futures fell more than 100 points, and Nasdaq 100 futures lost more than 1%, having been down as much as 2.5% during the vote count before recovering some ground. The dollar weakened, with the US dollar index falling to a one-month low while the euro and British pound strengthened, and US Treasury yields also declined. Markets reacted cautiously on Wednesday, 4 November, as investors assessed the possibility of tighter regulation of artificial intelligence and major technology companies.

Democrats who won governor's races in Georgia and Ohio, Keisha Lance Bottoms and Amy Acton, have called for a pause in data-center construction in their states. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, and Texas is a major market for data centers and a focus for AI investors. Democrats were also projected to win Senate races in Georgia, North Carolina, Michigan, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas, where data centers were a major campaign issue. Evercore's Sarah Bianchi said the wins in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, which account for a significant share of the US project pipeline, meant new pauses and restrictions on data center development, and that 2027 is shaping up to be a turbulent year as developers adapt to a shifting policy landscape. A widespread slowdown or halt in construction could put billions of dollars in investment at risk.

JPMorgan Chase analysts warned the outcome could prompt an AI sell-off on assumed higher regulation, writing that possible data-center restrictions and higher taxes on corporations and top earners could be headwinds for tech companies. They said healthcare and clean energy could be relative beneficiaries of a Democratic-controlled Congress, while CEOs with close ties to Trump could face investigation risk. Bianchi called the result a blue tsunami and wrote that it signaled a sharp rebuke of President Trump's shift of focus away from economic issues and underscored voters' insistence that Washington tackle the cost of living. Wolfe Research's Tobin Marcus wrote that the one surprise that could plausibly spook markets was Abbott losing the Texas gubernatorial election. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that data centers in space were looking pretty appealing, an idea the article notes most experts say faces significant hurdles.

The AI boom has driven much of the Nasdaq 100's 40% gain since Election Day 2024, and Amazon, Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet and smaller data-center startups have invested hundreds of billions of dollars in AI models, data centers and equipment. On Monday the Nasdaq 100 entered a correction, a 10% drop from its most recent high, and remained there early Wednesday, and on Friday the S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted their worst sessions since mid-June after Intel and Amazon reported mixed earnings. Despite the Democratic victories, President Donald Trump retains veto power, which could limit major legislative changes, and analysts suggest political gridlock could help control government spending while lower Treasury yields may support stock markets. US stock futures recovered some of their earlier losses, with investors turning their attention to economic data, interest rates and the outlook for AI investment.

stories.Headline: Goldman, Apollo seek buyers for $40 billion SpaceX AI chip deal - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs and Apollo Global Management have begun approaching investors to sell portions of a roughly $40 billion financing deal tied to SpaceX's artificial intelligence chips, Bloomberg News reported on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. The two firms are reportedly asking some potential buyers to take stakes of up to $500 million before the formal syndication process begins. The multi-tranche financing is said to keep debt off SpaceX's balance sheet and is described as the largest arrangement of its kind for graphics processing units on record. Reuters said it could not independently verify the report. Goldman Sachs declined to comment, while Apollo Global and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests.

SpaceX said in October that an affiliate of Apollo Global Management would buy AI chips and server hardware and lease them back to the company in a transaction involving about $40 billion in principal payments. The leases are set to run for a little over five years from the date the equipment is delivered. That delivery is expected in the first half of 2027. The arrangement is meant to fund the growing computing needs of SpaceX's AI business. Its structure lets the company expand its computing capacity without taking the full cost onto its own books at once.

Responsibility for structuring and marketing the financing rests with Goldman Sachs and Apollo Global Management, according to the Bloomberg account. SpaceX confirmed the lease arrangement in October but did not respond to questions about the investor solicitation. Goldman Sachs declined to comment on the report, and Apollo Global did not immediately reply. The reporting relies on people familiar with the matter, and the figures have not been independently verified by Reuters.

The deal reflects the heavy spending that major technology companies are making on computing power to build artificial intelligence products. Financing it through leases and outside investors is one way to spread that cost across several parties. The articles do not say when the formal syndication will open or how many investors will take part. The first hardware deliveries are expected in the first half of 2027, which will be the next concrete milestone.

stories.Headline: AI Productivity to Add $28 Billion to $84 Billion to India's GDP: Cognizant Study
stories.Summary:
A Cognizant study released in early November 2026 estimates that AI-enabled productivity could add between $28 billion and $84 billion a year to India's nominal GDP under realistic adoption scenarios. The same study found that most business leaders have not yet seen financial returns from the technology. The size of the gain depends on how widely AI is adopted and how much of the productivity improvement turns into economic output. Cognizant's model also sets a theoretical ceiling of $830 billion a year, which assumes AI is used across the entire workforce and that all gains become output. The company says that ceiling is not a forecast and that all the figures are modelled estimates based on self-reported survey responses.

The research surveyed 700 enterprise employees and 75 C-suite and business executives at companies with revenues from $100 million to more than $10 billion across 10 major industries. About 97 percent of the employees said AI had improved their productivity, with an average reported uplift of 15 percent. Indian employees were more prepared than their global peers, with 74 percent having completed AI training against 56 percent globally. Gains differed by sector, with 38 percent of healthcare employees reporting improvements above 20 percent, while manufacturing had the lowest share reporting any gain at 82 percent.

Business leaders said only 36 percent of employees, on average, have access to AI tools, and 84 percent had not yet seen AI lower their costs. Cognizant's India chief, Rajesh Varrier, said India has a strong foundation to capture more value from AI, but that this will require wider adoption of AI tools across enterprises, continued investment in skilling and an environment that supports responsible AI at scale. The company says organisations need to broaden access to AI tools, keep workforce skills current, extend AI into more complex and higher-value work and improve how they measure business outcomes. Its stated aim is to turn gains at the level of individual workers into broader enterprise and economic value.

A separate report from the Ayre Think Tank, published the same day, puts the potential boost at $79.1 billion to India's GDP over ten years under a moderate scenario, with a range of about $39.6 billion to $118.7 billion. That report notes that India is home to about 382 million people aged 15 to 29, and that nearly 89 percent of young Indians want to use AI for education or work within the next year. It also flags that only about two-thirds of young people own a mobile phone and that around 30 percent are outside employment, education or training. Calvin Ayre of the think tank pointed to a national plan announced in August 2026 to train ten million young people in AI skills within a year.

stories.Headline: Where US Courts Stand on AI Training
stories.Summary:
Courts in the United States have not yet settled whether AI developers may train their systems on copyrighted works without permission, and the rulings so far point in different directions. On 29 September 2026 the US Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit held that training an AI legal research tool on case summaries was not fair use, the copying exception in US copyright law. Two California judges had ruled for AI developers on training in June 2025, but on different grounds, so neither decision binds other courts. The judges weigh four factors when deciding fair use, including the purpose of the copying and its effect on the market for the original work. In AI cases the dispute centres on whether training is transformative, meaning it serves a new purpose, and whether it harms the market for the source material.

A summary judgment ruling, issued before trial when the key facts are not disputed, can settle the question for the parties in one case. The US Copyright Office's report of 9 May 2025 said some AI training may qualify as fair use and some may not, leaving the matter to courts and possibly to Congress. The question is also being argued across the Atlantic. Advocate General Maciej Szpunar gave a non-binding opinion on 3 November 2026 in case C-250/25, a Hungarian news publisher's claim against Google's Gemini chatbot. He told the EU's top court it should find the training questions inadmissible, but offered provisional views anyway.

In those views, training on copyrighted material is generally lawful in the EU if the developer avoids pirate sources, respects paywalls, bot blocks and machine-readable opt-outs, and shows it took steps to stop the model reproducing specific works. OpenAI asked a New York court on 4 September 2026 to rule that training its models is fair use, and that request remains pending. Meanwhile the Rio Times reports that Brazilian and Norwegian media groups won court orders suspending new terms from Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram. Because no court has settled the core question, developers and rights holders on both sides of the Atlantic are still waiting for a binding answer.
