stories.Headline: NTT DATA earns recognition from SAP as client-adopted AI agents create real business impact
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA, a global business and technology services provider, received two recognitions from SAP at SAP TechEd Berlin in late October 2026, as announced in a press release dated November 5, 2026. The company took part in the partner agent race at the Partner Summit and was named an SAP Business AI Platform Validated Partner. The recognitions were given for AI agents that NTT DATA has deployed with clients. The release presents them as evidence that the company can bring agentic AI into everyday business processes. The release describes several client results.

At Lemvigh-Müller, the Purchase Order Confirmation Matching Agent automates more than 90% of supplier confirmations, with approximately 98% matching accuracy. The Project Staffing Agent used by zeb has cut the time needed for individual time entries by 50%. At Synthomer, the Purchase Order Conversion Agent has reached a 98% first-time material match rate for order intake in beta tests. NTT DATA also brought 11 client-adopted agents to SAP TechEd, and all of them are available on the SAP Discovery Center. Krunal Patel, Global AI, Innovation & Software Assets Leader at NTT DATA Business Solutions, is quoted saying that the value of agentic AI begins once it moves beyond the pilot stage into daily operations.

Karl Fahrbach, Chief Partner Officer at SAP, is quoted saying that partners help bring SAP's Autonomous Enterprise to life and that success will be judged by the business value agents deliver to customers. The release does not give further details about how the recognitions were scored beyond the validation criteria it lists. The validation criteria, according to the release, include certified expertise, client go-lives, active use of SAP Joule for Consultants, and alignment with SAP's AI-Native North Star Reference Architecture. The release frames the company's goal as becoming the world's leading AI-native services company. The page also lists other recent NTT DATA and SAP partner announcements, but the release itself does not state any next steps beyond continued work with clients on the platform.

stories.Headline: SEALSQ, WISeQey, SEALCOIN and Eco Wave Power Sign Three-Year MoU and Demonstrate Trusted Energy Transactions for AI Data Centers
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, SEALSQ, its parent WISeQey, sister company SEALCOIN AG and Eco Wave Power U.S. Inc. announced a three-year Memorandum of Understanding to explore how renewable wave energy can securely connect with digital services and energy buyers. The partners have demonstrated the technology at Eco Wave Power's wave-energy installation in Jaffa Port, Israel. The demonstration linked physical energy production to an authenticated digital twin, so the origin and integrity of production data could be verified, and used that trusted data to start a secure, auditable transaction between known counterparties under predefined commercial terms. The articles say the proof of concept is shown in a video linked in the release.

The MoU sets out a framework for further development and evaluation of these capabilities, with the main aim of connecting renewable energy producers to AI data centers, industrial facilities, energy aggregators and utilities. The companies argue that as electricity demand from AI infrastructure grows, trusted digital systems could let producers share authenticated production information with qualified buyers and automate transactions. The collaboration also intends to explore integrating SEALSQ's QS7001 post-quantum secure element and quantum-resistant cryptography to support the long-term security needs of critical infrastructure. The releases state plainly that the initial demonstration is not a physical electricity supply agreement or a completed financial settlement, and that future deployments depend on technical validation, regulation and separate commercial contracts.

Carlos Moreira, Founder and CEO of SEALSQ, said the collaboration extends the WISeQey ecosystem into renewable energy, where secure connectivity and trusted transactions could support new digital services. Inna Braverman, Founder and CEO of Eco Wave Power, said wave energy aims to become part of the energy infrastructure for AI and that the demonstration suggests wave producers could eventually transact directly with data centers and other buyers. Jonathan Llamas, Chief Product & Strategy Officer of SEALCOIN, said the work moves machines from exchanging information to acting on trusted physical-world data. Eco Wave Power U.S., its AI and data center arm, will lead its side of the collaboration and has begun talks with data center developers and infrastructure partners about possible future supply.

The collaboration will be presented at Quantum Days 2026 on November 19 at Hôtel Barrière Le Majestic in Cannes, France, where a live demonstration and fireside chat with Braverman, Llamas and WISeQey representatives is scheduled for 13:45 CET. Eco Wave Power, listed on Nasdaq as WAVE, describes its onshore technology as generating power from waves at breakwaters, jetties and piers, and says it operates Israel's first grid-connected wave energy station and launched a pilot at the Port of Los Angeles with Shell Marine Renewable Energy. It also reports a project pipeline of 404.7 MW across Portugal, Taiwan and India. The articles do not say what the financial terms of the MoU are or when a commercial deployment might begin.

stories.Headline: These AI Data Center Stocks Are Rising, Bucking the Post-Election Slump
stories.Summary:
The AI data center stocks in the article have been drawing investor attention as spending on AI infrastructure continues to expand. Insider Monkey, writing on November 4, 2026, compiled a ranked list of what it calls the cheapest AI data center stocks, screening for a forward price-to-earnings ratio below 20 and quarterly revenue growth of at least 15 percent. The article notes that hyperscalers are expected to spend more than $700 billion on capital investment this year, according to an International Energy Agency report from October 2026. Its ranking of the top five names places Western Digital, Sandisk, Broadcom, Micron and NVIDIA in that order, based on their billionaire investor counts and forward P/E ratios. The data for the screen was sourced on November 2, 2026.

The article's figures show strong results across the group, though it presents them as company-reported rather than as evidence of how stocks will perform. Western Digital reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $4.38 billion, up about 55 percent, while Sandisk reported $11.03 billion in revenue, compared with $2.31 billion a year earlier. Broadcom reported quarterly revenue of $29.6 billion, up about 86 percent, and Micron reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $54.23 billion, up 379.3 percent. NVIDIA reported $96.2 billion in revenue, up about 106 percent, with Data Center revenue making up roughly 93 percent of the total. The article also cites JLL projections of roughly 100 gigawatts of added capacity between 2026 and 2030, along with cost estimates for shell-and-core construction and tenant equipment.

The article's authors state that these companies' fortunes depend on several factors, including access to electricity, construction timing, financing needs and the durability of AI demand. They caution that a low forward P/E depends on an earnings forecast that may change, and that storage pricing and memory pricing could reverse. The article also makes clear that it is promoting its own stock-selection newsletter and other related lists, and that the billionaire counts reflect hedge fund holdings rather than an independent assessment of value. It presents none of these companies as a guaranteed purchase. Readers should treat the ranking as one commentator's screen rather than a recommendation.

stories.Headline: AI PACs spent millions trying to shape Congress — here’s how they fared
stories.Summary:
Political groups on both sides of the AI debate spent millions trying to influence Tuesday's midterm elections, with mixed results. Two industry-aligned PACs, American Mission and Building the Future, together spent $4,801,981 backing South Carolina Senate candidate Darline Graham, who lost to Annie Andrews. American Mission also spent $590,428 on Montana House candidate Aaron Flint and $509,067 on North Carolina's Laurie Buckhout, and both lost. On the regulation side, Public First and its affiliated PACs backed several candidates, with its Democratic picks faring better than its Republican ones.

Overall, AI super PACs spent $79 million across 68 House and Senate seats this cycle, according to Tech Influence Watch. Leading the Future, funded in part by Andreessen Horowitz co-founders Ben Horowitz and Marc Andreessen and by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and his wife Anna, each giving $25 million, wants light regulation and a single national AI standard. It spends through Think Big for Democrats and American Mission for Republicans. Public First pushes for stronger safeguards through Jobs and Democracy for Democrats and Defending Our Values for Republicans. The biggest early fight was New York's 12th District Democratic primary, where Leading the Future spent more than $8.1 million against Assemblymember Alex Bores and Public First spent about $15 million backing him, with more than $40 million in outside money in the race; Bores lost.

Charlie Blaettler, political director of Guardrails Alliance, said he thinks Leading the Future held back in the general election because it did not want its money to become an issue. He pointed to Michigan's Senate primary, where AIPAC spent close to $30 million for Haley Stevens, who lost to Abdul El-Sayed, and said AIPAC became the story in that race. He said people distrust and are disgusted by tech industry political spending, so spending in a competitive race would make a candidate an enormous liability. Leading the Future told TechCrunch it sees primaries as a more effective use of money, having spent $27.38 million there, including $8 million against Bores, and it assesses competitiveness and whether spending could make a difference before entering general races.

The results came amid a broader Democratic wave, and most Republicans backed by either network lost, including Graham, the industry's biggest general-election bet. Exceptions included Pete Ricketts in Nebraska and Sen.-elect Harriet Hageman in Wyoming. The main fight among the PACs is whether Congress should set a national AI framework that overrides state laws or whether states keep their own safeguards. Leading the Future said it plans to keep spending in 2028, and Guardrails Alliance said it will keep opposing industry-backed candidates, with Blaettler saying its goal is to make AI money politically toxic. Bores has started a nonprofit, Who Decides, aiming to raise $30 million before 2028.

stories.Headline: What AI Leaders Can Learn from the Midterms
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections held on November 3, 2026, while Republicans kept the White House. Markets reacted on Wednesday, with U.S. stock futures falling overnight as investors weighed the chance of tighter rules on AI, cryptocurrency and data centers. Futures later recovered after President Donald Trump said he would accept the results, according to Reuters. Elon Musk, who put more than $400 million behind Republican candidates, joked on X that data centers in space looked appealing after several of his chosen candidates lost.

The biggest worry for the technology sector is possible limits on AI infrastructure, especially power-hungry data centers. In Texas, Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on keeping a moratorium on new data center construction until the state deals with their electricity and water demands. Brad Gerstner, CEO of Altimeter Capital, said fears of a broad halt to AI buildout were overblown, though new regulations could slow some projects. He estimated that 10 to 15 gigawatts of expected AI capacity could be affected, according to MarketWatch.

Other voices were more upbeat. Deborah Cunningham of Federated Hermes said a split government could act as a blockade against new legislation, and divided government has historically been viewed favorably by markets because it can limit big policy shifts. Daniela Hathorn of Capital.com said Trump's acceptance of the results eased some fears of prolonged confrontation and gridlock, though she expected major policy disagreements to continue. Continental CFO Roland Welzbacher said companies in the U.S. need stability and a reliable economic framework, and Fraport CEO Stefan Schulte suggested the outcome might ease worries about customs problems for travelers, while warning against reading too much into it. LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic donor Reid Hoffman called the results a wave against Trump and urged Democrats to build an economy that serves every American.

Away from Washington, the legal industry is also working out how to use AI, as described in a JD Supra piece by Deborah Farone about a joint webinar of the International Bar Association and the Legal Marketing Association. More than 1,200 people from 939 firms in 104 countries registered, far above her expectation of 100 to 200, and about 700 joined live. Panelists from Bowmans, Bass, Berry & Sims, Gibson Dunn and Pierson Ferdinand said firms should start from a real problem, take small steps, verify everything AI produces, and stay accountable for the final work. They also advised preparing for client conversations about who benefits from the speed AI creates, and hiring for judgment and curiosity over prompting skills.

stories.Headline: TeraWulf gets credit backstop from Google for Anthropic data-center project
stories.Summary:
TeraWulf Inc. announced on November 4, 2026 that it had executed credit support agreements with Google LLC. The agreements relate to debt financing that supports about $19 billion of contracted lease commitments with Anthropic, PBC. Those leases cover TeraWulf's Justified Data Campus in Hawesville, Kentucky. TeraWulf also announced a definitive engineering, procurement and construction agreement with Fluor Enterprises, Inc. for the development of Justified.

Under the credit support agreements, Google, a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc., provides contractual credit support for anticipated debt financing for the long-term Justified development. Alphabet's senior unsecured debt is rated AA+ by S&P Global Ratings and Aa2 by Moody's. The Fluor agreement covers engineering, procurement and construction for three data center buildings at Justified, building on a limited notice to proceed announced in March 2026. It sets defined delivery milestones, open-book cost reporting, procurement oversight and contractual performance protections, with guaranteed maximum pricing being established as engineering and procurement progress.

Paul Prager, TeraWulf's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, said the company structured its Anthropic leases from the outset to address counterparty credit, financing costs and capital requirements. He said Google's credit support strengthens TeraWulf's ability to secure competitive project financing, while Fluor's capabilities expand its capacity to execute at scale. Patrick Fleury, TeraWulf's Chief Financial Officer, said cost of capital is fundamental to infrastructure development and that strong investment-grade credit support strengthens the project's financing profile. Prager added that Fluor lets TeraWulf scale execution without building a global engineering and construction organization internally.

TeraWulf describes itself as an energy infrastructure company that pairs long-term access to power with contracted AI and high-performance computing demand. It develops and operates the underlying infrastructure rather than investing in AI compute hardware. Under the EPC milestone schedule, phased ready-for-service completions are expected to begin in late 2027 and continue through the second quarter of 2028. The Justified milestones follow TeraWulf's recent expansion of contracted power capacity to 1 GW at its Muskie Data Campus in eastern Kentucky.

stories.Headline: Supermicro taps SambaNova to power AI inference racks alongside Nvidia
stories.Summary:
SambaNova and Supermicro have announced a partnership to build and sell AI inference systems that combine SambaNova's SN50 chips with Nvidia GPUs, and Supermicro initially plans to work with 10,000 SN50 chips. The systems split inference work between the two kinds of processor. Nvidia GPUs handle prefill, which means processing incoming prompts, while SambaNova's fifth-generation reconfigurable dataflow units handle decode, which means generating responses. SambaNova says this pairing can improve performance and efficiency while extending the useful life of GPUs customers already own.

Supermicro will integrate, test, deliver and support the systems for customers, including on-site service. SambaNova engineers will get models running and tuned on the SN50 chips and help Supermicro with deployments. The companies plan to start with NeoClouds and sovereign clouds, then expand to enterprises that run AI in their own data centers. Rodrigo Liang, co-founder and CEO of SambaNova, said that agentic AI is the next wave of inference and needs to run everywhere. He said customers can now order SN50 units alongside GPUs from a partner they trust.

A separate announcement from Supermicro, dated the same day, describes a KV-cache storage solution built with IBM and Nvidia to speed up AI inference. The solution combines Supermicro Petascale storage servers, IBM Storage Scale software, Nvidia Dynamo inference software and Nvidia Spectrum-X Ethernet switches. Keeping key-value cache data outside local GPU memory is meant to raise GPU utilization and throughput, which matters more as businesses run agentic and long-context AI workflows. Charles Liang, president and CEO of Supermicro, said the approach removes bottlenecks that limit GPU efficiency for these inference workloads.

In tests run by Supermicro and Nvidia with a 120-billion-parameter model, a persistent KV cache cut time-to-first-token by up to 56 times on prompts of 130,000 tokens. When input length grew from 30,000 to 130,000 tokens, time-to-first-token rose by only 0.377 seconds with the cache, compared with 29.55 seconds without it. The companies also say the rack-level integration and on-site deployment services can shorten rollout time from weeks to days. Sam Werner, general manager of IBM Storage, and Shruti Koparkar, AI Inference Product Lead at Nvidia, both described the work as a step toward more scalable and cost-efficient enterprise inference.

stories.Headline: Could putting AI data centers in space solve an environmental problem, or create a new one?
stories.Summary:
Google has begun testing AI computing in orbit, after launching a refrigerator-sized satellite carrying AI chips in October as part of its Project Suncatcher effort. The satellite successfully generated and transmitted a haiku back to Earth, which Travis Beals, Google's senior director leading the project, described as proof that AI processors can operate in space. Google plans to test laser communication between two satellites in 2027, and SpaceX is developing much larger AI computing satellites that could eventually form a network. The reporting places these efforts against a backdrop of communities pushing back on the electricity and water demands of AI data centers.

The potential benefits are the main reason companies are pursuing the idea. Google estimates that solar panels in certain orbits could generate five to eight times as much electricity as comparable panels on Earth, and space-based computing could reduce the need for water-intensive cooling. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has argued that cooling is easier in space and that the approach would avoid building massive power plants on Earth. SpaceX has proposed a constellation that could eventually include as many as 1 million satellites, though that system has not been approved or deployed.

Dr. Arun Kannawadi, an assistant research professor of physics at Duke University, says the advantages are far from guaranteed. He notes that heat still builds up inside the circuits and must be moved to radiators and dissipated, and that without air, satellites need specialized cooling systems, while repairs could require more launches and solar radiation can damage electronics. Kannawadi, an observational astronomer, also warns that satellites already interfere with telescope images, and that an October 2026 research paper modeling a constellation near 1 million orbital data center satellites projected substantial interference with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile. He also raised concerns about wildlife affected by a brighter night sky and about collisions producing additional orbital debris.

The article notes that orbital computing would not address near-term demand in North Carolina, where Duke Energy projects data centers could account for about 10% of its electricity sales across the Carolinas by 2030. The utility is planning billions of dollars in new infrastructure, including natural gas generation, which has raised questions about residential costs and fossil fuel impacts. The technology remains experimental, with Google's next test planned for 2027. Whether it could reduce the industry's overall environmental footprint, rather than shift some impacts elsewhere, the article says, remains an open question.

stories.Headline: AI Shopping Agents on Black Friday: Who Pays for Mistakes
stories.Summary:
Visa predicted in December 2025 that millions of shoppers would use AI agents to buy things by the 2026 holiday season, but on 27 October its chief executive Ryan McInerney said such volumes were very small. Meta launched its Muse agent on 8 September, and it asks US users to approve every purchase total and pays through Stripe's Link wallet or a single-use virtual card. Amazon blocked Muse from Amazon.com in September, saying Meta never asked permission and the agent did not identify itself as AI. Black Friday falls on 27 November this year, and it is the deadline Visa set for itself.

Muse pays with a saved method at more than one million businesses that accept Link, and elsewhere Link issues a single-use virtual card limited to the approved purchase. Meta says Link's protections for lost or damaged items, price drops and returns cover eligible Muse orders, but that is a product promise and not a legal right. Mark Zuckerberg said on 21 October that Meta plans to charge businesses a fee when Muse helps close a sale, and computing costs are one reason the agent is limited to the US and Canada. Google's agentic checkout in Search has been able to buy a tracked item at a shopper's target price since November 2025, and in May Google announced Universal Cart, a cross-retailer cart that pays with Google Pay. OpenAI stepped back from Instant Checkout in March, saying the first version lacked flexibility, and its dots agent launched on 29 September with rules that require approval for chosen actions.

Regulation E caps a consumer's loss at $50 when a lost or stolen debit card is reported within two business days, but it excludes transfers by someone the consumer gave access to, and the law does not say whether an AI agent counts. Credit cards fall under the Truth in Lending Act and Regulation Z, where unauthorised use turns on whether someone had actual, implied or apparent authority over the account. Carla Sanchez-Adams of the National Consumer Law Center told Bloomberg Law in June that federal lending and transfer laws, along with network chargeback and return standards, still apply when an agent uses a person's credit card. Eric Goldberg of Davis Wright Tremaine said in the same report that debit cards give somewhat less protection and that stablecoins allow no refunds or chargebacks.

Mastercard added trust and intelligence services to its Agent Pay programme on 30 September, including a probability score now in US testing that estimates whether an agent started a transaction. Its Verifiable Intent framework records the shopper's identity, the limits given to the agent, the shopper's consent and the actions taken. Mastercard chief executive Michael Miebach said on the 29 October results call that he expects the trend to build through the holidays, though he conceded merchants vary widely in readiness. Visa's finance chief Chris Suh told Fortune in June that he was hesitant to lean into the stablecoin and agentic commerce narratives too much, noting that most of Visa's business has nothing to do with either.

stories.Headline: Whitehurst Backs Data Center Pause But Calls Anti-AI Memes ‘Hypocrisy’ - St. Johns Citizen
stories.Summary:
Three moves from St. Johns County, Florida, and Ohio, Georgia, and Texas, now show how the data center debate is spilling into the 2026 elections. On Tuesday, November 3, 2026, the St. Johns County Commission voted 5–0 to suspend applications for medium and large data centers for one year, starting November 15. The pause gives county staff time to study where such facilities could go, how they would fit with nearby development, and whether local infrastructure could support them. Commissioner Christian Whitehurst backed the pause but criticized critics who use AI-generated memes against data centers, calling it hypocrisy. In Ohio, Amy Acton's campaign announced her victory in the governor's race on November 4, 2026, after she spoke to supporters the day before.

Her platform sets conditions that projects must meet before proceeding, covering costs, union labor, transparency, environmental standards, community benefit agreements, and siting. Those conditions would require project backers, not taxpayers or surrounding communities, to bear the full cost of gas, water, and electricity. Developers would also need to invest in their own generation and show that projects would not raise electricity prices or weaken regional reliability. Acton's platform would end data center nondisclosure agreements, add clawbacks to tax incentives, and require siting on brownfields or previously developed industrial land rather than farms. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms's August 31, 2026 proposal called for a pause on new data center construction while the state reassessed its position.

Her approach would use the pause to study the issue and design a response afterward, while Acton has already set entry conditions in advance. Texas Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who declared victory, proposed an immediate moratorium until the legislature enacts protections, and Governor Greg Abbott had already ordered a permit halt on September 21, 2026. Whitehurst said he doubted that any applicant would seek a data center in St. Johns County at the scale covered by the moratorium, and he cited a Florida Power & Light staffer who said the county was unlikely to be a candidate over the next 20 years. He argued that people who want less demand for data centers should start by using less data themselves. Deputy County Attorney Kealey West said staff would consult utility providers, the St. Johns River Water Management District, and other stakeholders during the review.

Acton's campaign and Ohio's Secretary of State have said that election-night results remain unofficial until certification, which is expected about three weeks after the election. Georgia's returns, last updated at 4:19 a.m. on November 4, 2026, showed Bottoms leading Rick Jackson with 54.31 percent of the vote. Hinojosa said Abbott called to congratulate her and offer transition assistance.

Across these races, the policy approaches differ in sequence and detail, though all three use the language of a pause or moratorium. The St. Johns County county commissioners will rely on the state study that West said should be ready in July 2027, and the county expects to consider it then. Ohio's conditions and Georgia's review will determine how restrictions take shape, and Texas's durability depends on legislative action. Reporting from Unite.AI notes that the substantive differences remain open, depending on how each proposal is implemented.

stories.Headline: Sysdig AI Defense Targets Compromised Agents at the Moment They Act
stories.Summary:
Sysdig launched AI Defense on November 4, a product that applies automated runtime security and governance to AI agents, aiming to stop unauthorized actions before they finish. The launch responds to a shift in which AI systems move from answering questions to performing actions such as shipping code, changing infrastructure, and accessing production systems. Sysdig argues that the operating system kernel is the only reliable record of what actually ran, since an agent deployed in the morning may behave differently by the afternoon. Its central claim is that an agent's own explanation needs an independent check against what really happened. The timing matters because many enterprises have approved AI tools without equivalent controls over their actions.

The product monitors every action an agent takes, from its origin to completion, including underlying kernel processes that might quietly change how the agent functions. It maintains a live inventory of agents, harnesses, models, MCP servers, skills, and plugins built from runtime telemetry, and it can trace each agent to an accountable human. Risky actions can be detected, held for human review, or blocked before they complete, using policy templates whose rules are mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. Sysdig's founder and CTO, Loris Degioanni, said blocking must happen in real time, in line with the action, and before it finishes.

Actions are recorded as they occur, creating audit-quality immutable records. The company cites IBM Institute for Business Value findings that enterprises expect to deploy an average of 1,661 AI agents by 2027, a 38 per cent increase from current deployments. Sysdig presents this as a product that changes the placement of organizational authority, so that approval is checked at execution rather than left inside an agent's instructions. Degioanni frames the problem as agents gaining the speed to act faster than human teams can review.

Responsibility for setting the rules and deciding which actions are legitimate remains with the organization, since a security product can enforce a rule but cannot independently decide whether a given export belongs in an approved workflow. The company also says policies start in alert mode, reporting activity without stopping it. The vendor's own claims about product behavior have not been independently verified. The launch sits within a competitive field where NVIDIA's OpenShell emphasizes isolated execution and credentials kept outside the agent workload, while CrowdStrike has announced an integration with NVIDIA OpenShell and a planned NVIDIA Sentry integration.

These approaches place security decisions outside the model's judgment, but they differ in where they check authority. The articles do not establish which approach performs better across equivalent tasks. Buyers are advised to verify supported platforms, integrations, and enforcement points, and to test whether a blocked action is stopped before it begins or only interrupted after it starts. Whether these controls hold up in practice will depend on that testing.

stories.Headline: Conflicting With Employees' Sincerely Held Religious Beliefs- AI
stories.Summary:
Two Utah? No, let me give the paragraphs as requested. In June 2026, Erin Maus, a Unitarian Universalist software engineer in North Carolina, asked her employer, an entertainment technology company, for an exemption from AI use. She said the ethical and environmental effects of AI conflicted with her beliefs, and the company granted the request, allowing her to write code by hand instead. Later, David Durman, a Humanist research administrator at the University of Kentucky, received a similar religious accommodation exempting him from AI at work.

He argued that generative AI runs contrary to human wellbeing, pointing to its environmental impact, job losses, and what he called theft of human creativity. The university's Office of Equal Opportunity approved his request after finding that it posed no undue burden on his department. The article, written by Laura Lawless of Squire Patton Boggs and published November 5, 2026, says employers should expect more such requests as religious and ethical leaders raise concerns about AI. It draws a comparison to the COVID-19 period, when accommodation requests over masking and vaccination rose sharply.

Under Title VII, little is required to show that a belief is sincere, and employers should avoid demanding proof such as anti-AI religious texts or statements from spiritual advisors. The article also notes that Title VII does not protect social, political, or economic philosophies or personal preferences, so employers should consider whether an objection is rooted in a moral belief system or reflects a secular policy view. Under the Supreme Court's 2023 decision in Groff v. DeJoy, an employer must show substantial increased costs to deny an accommodation, and speculative hardships do not suffice.

The article advises employers to ask whether an employee objects to some AI tools or all of them, and to craft individualized accommodations where possible. It also suggests checking whether AI use is truly necessary for a role or only preferred for efficiency. Employers should update accommodation policies and train HR staff and managers to recognize requests without requiring magic words like religion or spiritual objection. The article notes that objections to AI are a new and morally complex area, and it does not describe any court decisions yet on the issue.

stories.Headline: Guidelines on artificial intelligence issued for lawyers
stories.Summary:
The New York State Bar Association issued guidelines on lawyers' use of artificial intelligence, according to a report published on November 4, 2026. The association's House of Delegates adopted a report titled "Legal Ethics Guidelines for Lawyers' Use of Artificial Intelligence." The association said the guidelines should help avoid the unauthorized practice of law, keep legal decisions in human hands and reduce bias in legal proceedings. It noted that AI systems are increasingly used in legal research, drafting, client communications, litigation and law practice management. The guidelines urge attorneys to make sure AI output is not biased because of the data it was fed or because of how it was designed and deployed.

They also say AI should not be used in ways that could affect a person's rights, access, opportunity or treatment. Attorneys may charge fees for time spent verifying an AI tool's output, but not for learning how to use it. Acquiring an AI tool is an overhead expense, so its cost may not be billed to a client unless it is for a service specially incurred for that case. The association also reminded attorneys that they must carefully supervise non-lawyers and vendors who use AI tools. Taa Grays, president of the Bar Association, said generative AI is changing the practice of law and that the guidelines give attorneys a resource to use AI responsibly and ethically.

She said the guidelines can help attorneys avoid perils such as inadvertently practicing law in a jurisdiction where they are not licensed, or failing to notify clients or the courts of AI use. The association said that while the New York Rules of Professional Conduct do not specifically address AI-generated legal work, an attorney is still responsible for ensuring that a non-lawyer's work meets standards, even if the non-lawyer is an AI tool or system. Separately, India's Computer Emergency Response Team published 107-page guidelines on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, titled "Artificial Intelligence Security Auditing Guidelines: Framework for Secure, Ethical and Auditable Artificial Intelligence Systems." The guidelines apply to all AI developers and service providers, including US companies behind ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, but they are legally binding only for cybersecurity auditors empanelled with CERT-In. Companies must report AI-related security breaches to CERT-In within six hours and keep logs of AI systems' usage and operations for 180 days.

The framework proposes four tiers of criticality, low, moderate, high and critical, based on eight identifiers including the severity of potential impact and the sensitivity of data. An official said the guidelines are for auditors to use when examining AI systems at large companies, and that discussions about turning them into law are a separate matter progressing inside Meity. Jibu Elias of the Mozilla Foundation said the guidelines are similar to work by the EU and NIST in the US and are nothing new, and that non-binding guidelines generally do not have a major impact on an industry. The EU has adopted a legally binding AI Act, the US has voluntary AI standards through NIST, and China requires generative AI services to undergo government security checks before launch.

stories.Headline: Europe set to open lower as Democratic sweep fuels AI regulation fears
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress, and European equity futures pointed to a weaker open as investors worried about tougher rules for artificial intelligence. Futures tied to the STOXX 600 were down about 0.2% at 0639 GMT, after recovering part of a 1.4% decline during Asian trading. Contracts linked to Germany's DAX slipped about 0.2%, while UK FTSE 100 futures fell 0.4%. The pan-European STOXX 600 index later closed 1.82% higher at 657.40 points, its highest since August 26 and its steepest one-day gain since June 12. Spain's lender-focused benchmark climbed 3%, the most among regional bourses.

Investors were concerned that stronger oversight of data-centre construction could restrain AI-related spending, an important source of recent gains for technology shares. Tech stocks fell 0.2%, with Infineon, ASML and Soitec slipping between 3.4% and 11.8%, while AI equipment makers Siemens Energy and Schneider Electric shed 8% and 3.4% respectively. Euro STOXX banks climbed 4.6%, the steepest one-day jump since early April. Novo Nordisk advanced 5.6% after reporting third-quarter adjusted operating profit above expectations and raising its full-year sales and profit forecasts.

Clean energy stocks also gained, with Vestas up 2.9%, Orsted up 4.6% and Nordex up 4.8%. Heidelberg Materials advanced 9.6% and Pandora gained 10.9% after upbeat results, while the oil sector fell 2.4% as Brent crude dropped 8%. Toni Meadows, head of investment at BRI Wealth Management, said the market tends to go up after the midterms in the very short term, and whether the move lasts is a different story. He said growth still looks good and oil prices have come off in recent days, so there is room for the market to move.

Michael Field, chief equity market strategist EMEA at Morningstar, said that with Congress in Democratic hands, the ability of the US administration to impose requirements or sanctions on European banks in the US is limited. Investors also took comfort after US President Donald Trump accepted the election results. On the data front, euro zone inflation rose to a three-year high last month, increasing the chance of another European Central Bank rate hike in December. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these market moves and the inflation data.

stories.Headline: trust, training, and the future of law and medicine in the AI era
stories.Summary:
Stanford University held its first Future of the Legal and Medical Professions Symposium on Oct. 26 on its campus. The event was co-hosted by Stanford Law School, Stanford School of Medicine and the Deborah L. Rhode Center on the Legal Profession. It brought together physicians, lawyers, scholars and technology leaders to compare the shared pressures facing law and medicine. George Triantis, dean of Stanford Law School, and Lloyd Minor, dean of the School of Medicine, both spoke at the public event.

The symposium focused on how artificial intelligence is reshaping education, public confidence and access to care and justice. Speakers said students now must master four to five times more content than earlier generations. Daniel Ho, a Stanford law professor, said his team tested legal AI tools marketed as free of hallucinations and found they hallucinated 17% to 33% of the time, with more than 2,000 real legal cases involving hallucinations. Nora Freeman Engstrom, a Stanford law professor, said about 75% of U.S. civil cases have at least one side without a lawyer. A December 2024 poll found only 35% of Americans expressed confidence in the justice system.

Minor said leaders at Stanford have an obligation to rebuild trust in their educational programs and professions. Triantis said the key will be to teach adaptability, how to move from one tool to another and when a human must stay in the loop. John Whyte, CEO of the American Medical Association, asked how a student who always relies on ambient listening will learn to distill a patient history. California Supreme Court Justice Goodwin Liu said he can persuade his model to give him almost anything because it is designed to please him. Arati Prabhakar, a former White House science and technology adviser, said there is no scientific and technological foundation for thorough evaluation and validation of these models.

David Freeman Engstrom, a Stanford law professor, described an AI assistant his team built to flag likely errors in debt collection cases in Los Angeles County Superior Court, where nearly half of default judgments contain errors. He said a randomized controlled trial of the tool is underway. David Studdert, Stanford's dean of research, said the interests of the patient and client come first and should not adapt too quickly. Vivian Lee of Harvard Business School said people want to feel understood and cared about. Alyce Adams, a Stanford Medicine professor, said her team works with patients who have diabetic neuropathy, a condition with no cure.

stories.Headline: Looking Past the Chips: Tuttle Capital Launches the AI Bottleneck ETF (DLAY)
stories.Summary:
Tuttle Capital Management announced on November 5, 2026 that it has launched the Tuttle Capital AI Bottleneck ETF, trading on Cboe BZX under the ticker DLAY. The fund is actively managed and spreads its holdings across nine sleeves of companies that the firm believes are industrial chokepoints in the AI buildout. Those sleeves include advanced chip packaging, memory, power and grid equipment, and nuclear fuel. The fund does not hold companies whose main business is designing or making AI chips for sale, running large cloud infrastructure, or building large language models or generative AI applications.

The fund is weighted using a proprietary AI Bottleneck Score that considers supply concentration, order backlogs, and demand inelasticity, and it is rebalanced quarterly. A company must meet at least two of three tests to be eligible: supply concentrated among few producers, extended lead times or backlogs, and demand that cannot readily be substituted. Holdings are capped at 4% for any single name and 18% for any sleeve. The fund may invest up to 35% outside the United States, and its total annual operating expense ratio is 0.75%. Companies subject to U.S. sanctions or listed on the Commerce Department's Entity List are excluded.

Matthew Tuttle, founder and CEO of Tuttle Capital Management, said the firm built the fund because many investors focus on the same handful of AI stocks. He said the fund targets parts of the buildout that receive less attention, such as packaging capacity, transformers, cooling systems, and fuel, which he believes the industry needs regardless of which chips or chatbots succeed. The firm describes itself as a leading issuer of thematic and rules-based ETFs. The release notes that the fund is newly organized, has no operating history, and is non-diversified. It also warns that the bottleneck thesis may prove wrong if constraints are resolved through added capacity, substitution, or policy changes.

The filing flags several risks, including heightened exposure to Taiwan and China, where a meaningful share of holdings may sit, and the possibility that tensions could bring sanctions, export controls, or trade restrictions. Investors are also warned about currency risk, emerging-market risk, and the chance that shares may trade at a premium or discount to net asset value. The release says investors should read the prospectus carefully and that investing involves risk, including possible loss of principal. Paralel Distributors LLC is the distributor and is not affiliated with Tuttle Capital Management. The release does not say when the fund will report its first performance results.

stories.Headline: Pathways World School Gurgaon Sets New Direction for Responsible AI in Education
stories.Summary:
Pathways World School in Gurgaon held a two-day workshop on September 25 and 26 to shape how it will use artificial intelligence in classrooms. The sessions brought together students, faculty, school leaders, its AI Advisory Group, IT teams and parents. Rita Bateson, co-founder and Director of Education at Eblana Learning and a former IB curriculum leader, led the event. The goal was to use AI to support teaching and learning while protecting independent thinking, creativity and academic integrity.

The first day covered governance, risk management and guidelines on academic integrity, data privacy and student wellbeing. The second day moved to putting these into practice, with AI literacy for administrators, resource creation, safe data handling and plans for initial classroom pilots. Under the proposed framework, students must question AI-generated answers, watch for bias and errors, protect personal information and disclose how AI helped their work. Teachers keep full professional judgement over teaching and assessment, and are expected to model the responsible technology use they ask of students. The school is now finalising its AI policy and writing age-appropriate guidance for each stage of learning.

Pranay Jain, Director of Pathways World School, said the initiative builds on the school's record of adopting new technology. He pointed out that in 2003 Pathways Gurgaon became the first school in India to offer campus-wide wireless connectivity. He said the school now wants to bring the same pioneering approach to AI while keeping critical inquiry at the centre of education. Malcolm Nicolson, School Director of Pathways Gurgaon, argued that schools must help students handle a technology that already shapes their daily lives. He said the school is setting principles, guardrails and literacy so that students use AI to think more deeply rather than less.

Initial classroom pilots will run first so the school can measure their effect on learning before any wider rollout. Students, teachers and parents will receive orientation on the technology's potential, its limits and responsible use. The school says its aim goes beyond preparing students for change, and extends to helping them use AI with curiosity, discernment and confidence. The article describes the school's position as a belief that technology should widen what students can achieve without weakening the thinking that makes learning meaningful.

stories.Headline: 3 charged in scheme to use AI to impersonate CEOs and attorneys to steal $129 million
stories.Summary:
Three people have been charged in a scheme that used artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys in order to steal about $129 million. Prosecutors announced on Thursday, November 5, 2026, that the three were indicted on charges of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. According to the indictment filed in a federal court in New York, Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, carried out the scheme. The three allegedly targeted thousands of companies around the world over more than a year and a half.

Court documents say the victims included hospital systems in Missouri and California, a bank in Rhode Island, and a financial technology company in the United Kingdom. The defendants used AI tools to mimic the voices and appearances of company leaders and lawyers, and they sent urgent requests for money to employees who believed the messages were genuine. Some of the money was reportedly moved through multiple accounts before being spread across several countries. The indictment describes the case as one of a growing number in which the technology is used to deceive people who handle payments.

The defendants did not have attorneys listed in the released court documents. Prosecutors and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York presented the charges, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation was among the agencies that investigated. Officials said the people who were impersonated were not involved in the scheme. Each of the three faces a maximum sentence of 20 years on the wire fraud counts and a mandatory two-year term on the aggravated identity theft count, if convicted.

The articles do not say whether any of the defendants has entered a plea or spoken publicly about the case. The case is part of a broader concern about how easily AI can be used to copy a person's voice and writing, and officials urged companies to verify unusual payment requests through separate channels. Investigators said the defendants' alleged methods could be used by others unless businesses improve safeguards. The articles do not report what happens next in the case, such as a trial date or any hearing schedule.

stories.Headline: AmeriLife and Palantir Announce Enterprise Partnership to Bring AI-Driven Transformation to Insurance and Retirement Distribution
stories.Summary:
AmeriLife Group, a national insurance and retirement distributor based in Clearwater and Miami, Florida, announced on November 5, 2026 a partnership with Palantir Technologies, the data analytics and artificial intelligence company. The enterprise-wide agreement brings Palantir's Foundry and Artificial Intelligence Platform into AmeriLife's Health and Wealth distribution organizations. The work begins with Crump Life Insurance Services, where Palantir-powered tools are already running in production. Rather than adding AI on top of current processes, AmeriLife says it is building an AI-driven operating model on one unified data foundation.

The company describes the change as a fundamental shift in how it runs its business. The goal is a faster and more connected experience for the agents, advisors, financial professionals and carrier partners it serves. AmeriLife also says it hopes to set a new standard for independent insurance and retirement product distribution. Over the coming months, the two companies plan to deploy AI capabilities across many workflows to speed up how business moves and to give agents and advisors better visibility. The release does not give dollar figures for the deal.

AmeriLife chairman and CEO Scott R. Perry said that much of the industry's AI discussion has centered on productivity tools and digital assistants. He argued that working with Palantir lets AmeriLife rebuild how its business operates, from the first client conversation to the placed policy. Ryan Taylor, Palantir's Chief Revenue and Legal Officer, said AmeriLife is putting AI at the center of how it works and serves professionals. He said the deployment is building a lasting operating advantage in a complex, highly regulated industry. Taylor added that the work already in production at Crump is only the beginning.

The release places AmeriLife as a long-established distributor, saying it has partnered with top carriers for more than 50 years. It says the company's network includes over 325,000 insurance agents, advisors and financial professionals, along with 160 marketing organizations and agency locations across the United States. The Crump deployment is part of the next generation of its ACE platform, which supports case management and back-office operations. The release also includes standard forward-looking statement warnings about risks, including the failure of the platforms to perform as desired and the customer's ability to modify or terminate the contract. Media and partnership contacts were listed for both companies.

stories.Headline: Ohio receiving $8 million in GM settlement over data privacy
stories.Summary:
Ohio is set to receive about $8 million from a settlement that General Motors reached with a coalition of states over allegations that it collected and sold driver data without permission. Ohio joined 34 other states and Washington, D.C. in the lawsuit, which centered on the Smart Driver program, a service that was marketed as a way for drivers to track their own driving habits. The program was run by GM subsidiary OnStar and let drivers view their data through a smartphone app. In late October, attorneys general announced that GM would pay $220 million to resolve the case. Ohio's share of that total is the roughly $8 million now flowing to the state.

The settlement also requires GM to limit and protect the driving data it gathers, and it mandates third-party data protection assessments. Those changes build on a federal requirement imposed earlier this year, when the Federal Trade Commission placed a five-year ban on GM disclosing driver location and behavior data to consumer reporting agencies. The FTC also required GM to get affirmative express consent from consumers before collecting or using their data. Consumers must also be given an easier way to opt out of data collection and to delete data already gathered. GM had discontinued the Smart Driver product in 2024.

Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson is the state official who led the state's involvement, and he said GM broke consumers' trust by selling their data without their knowledge or consent. Wilson said Ohioans should not have to fear that information collected by their own vehicles could be used against them. He added that companies must be held accountable when they put profits ahead of consumer privacy. According to the state, the OnStar app told 380,000 drivers they were not enrolled in data collection, even though they were.

The case grew out of a 2024 report by the New York Times, which revealed that GM had been sending driver behavior data to LexisNexis without consumers' permission. LexisNexis then produced reports for insurance companies, which could adjust premiums or deny coverage based on that information. The settlement and the federal restrictions together set new limits on how the automaker handles this kind of data. The articles do not say when Ohio's payment will arrive or how the third-party assessments will be carried out.

stories.Headline: UAE AI Office and Emirates NBD hold UAE Codes 2026 hackathon for Emirati bank employees
stories.Summary:
The UAE Artificial Intelligence Office reported that more than 200,000 people took part in its "AI for All and Its Vibe Coding Lab" initiative, which was launched with Microsoft as part of UAE Codes Day on 29 October 2026 under the theme "UAE Vibe Codes." The initiative lets people use artificial intelligence to turn their ideas into websites and digital applications within minutes, with no prior coding experience needed. Participants built more than 90,000 digital platforms in total. The effort drew in more than 65 government and private sector entities, academic institutions and national organisations, along with members of the wider community.

The initiative was designed as a hands-on experience, and participants used it to explore vibe coding and build their own digital ideas and solutions. Participating organisations shared it through their communication channels and digital platforms, ran practical workshops and interactive activities, and encouraged their staff and the public to try vibe coding. Among the participants were the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Justice, Emirates NBD, Etisalat, du, Emirates Airline and Dubai Municipality. Workshops were also held with partners including Google, Emirates Global Aluminium, Dell Technologies, IBM and Siemens. The office additionally worked with Emaar and cinema operators across the country to promote the experience on digital screens.

Omar Sultan Al Olama, Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, said the turnout showed the country's vision of making technology and innovation accessible to everyone. He said the engagement demonstrated that people across the community are ready to use advanced tools to turn ideas into real projects, whatever their technical background or academic field. He also credited the combined work of government bodies, private companies, universities and global partners for widening the initiative's reach. In his view, equipping people with knowledge, skills and digital tools is essential to building an innovation-driven economy and a generation able to create solutions to new challenges.

The UAE Codes Day date has a history behind it. In October 2021, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Vice President, Prime Minister and Ruler of Dubai, directed that 29 October be marked each year as UAE Codes Day. The date commemorates the launch of the region's first e-government initiative by Sheikh Mohammed on 29 October 2001. In November 2023, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation adopted the UAE's proposal to designate 29 October as the International Day of Programming, which the articles describe as recognition of the country's leadership in programming and technology.

stories.Headline: iSpecimen Expands Into AI-Powered Drug Discovery and Disease Trend Monitoring With Acquisition of Foldlab AI Products
stories.Summary:
Nasdaq-listed iSpecimen Inc. announced on November 5, 2026 that it had completed, on November 2, 2026, its acquisition of two artificial intelligence products from Foldlab AI Ltd., a British Columbia company. One product is an AI agent that identifies disease-associated proteins, and the other is an AI model that predicts and monitors disease trends. The deal, which the company describes as its entry into AI-powered disease intelligence, was made under an Asset Purchase Agreement dated September 4, 2026, and was approved by iSpecimen's stockholders on October 9, 2026. iSpecimen received the full technology stack behind both products, including software, source code, model weights, documentation, data rights and related intellectual property.

The aggregate purchase price is $4.5 million. It includes $750,000 in cash paid at closing, plus up to $1.25 million in two milestone payments of $625,000 each, due when the milestone products are delivered and accepted under the agreement's testing procedures. The remaining $2.5 million is paid in 2,907,977 shares of iSpecimen common stock, sized by the volume-weighted average price over the 10 trading days before closing. The shares went to Foldlab on November 5, 2026 in a private placement, carry a five-year trading restriction and lock-up, and are subject to a voting rights agreement with the company. The shares were not registered under the Securities Act, and the announcement states they may not be offered or sold in the United States without registration or an exemption.

Shahin Behroyan, iSpecimen's Chief Executive Officer, said the acquisition expands the company's role in research and discovery by combining its biospecimen network with AI tools. He said the tools could help researchers identify promising protein targets and understand disease trends, and could let the company deepen customer relationships, reach new markets and build software and analytics revenue. iSpecimen operates an online marketplace connecting scientists with healthcare providers that hold patient specimens, and the announcement includes forward-looking warnings about integration risk, milestone delivery, Nasdaq listing compliance and dilution. The company also flagged possible doubts about its ability to continue as a going concern and to obtain additional financing, citing risk factors in its annual report filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The announcement does not describe any next steps beyond the integration and milestone work it mentions.

stories.Headline: Longbridge Group and Cyberport announce strategic partnership to advance responsible agentic AI innovation in Hong Kong
stories.Summary:
Longbridge Group, an AI-native financial technology company, announced on November 5, 2026 that its AI arm, Longbridge AI Technologies Limited, has signed a three-year strategic partnership with Hong Kong Cyberport Management Company Limited to advance the responsible development and adoption of agentic artificial intelligence in Hong Kong. The partnership will support the establishment of a Hong Kong AI Lab that brings together fintech expertise, research talent and technology innovation. It sets out a framework for collaboration across AI research, industry engagement, talent development and innovation. The AI Lab is meant to gather financial institutions, technology companies, academic institutions and start-ups to explore practical uses of AI. Longbridge says closer ties between the fintech and research communities should foster growth and mutual trust in AI-enabled financial solutions.

Under the arrangement, Longbridge AI will contribute its fintech expertise, AI capabilities and industry experience, while Cyberport will connect the partners to its technology and innovation ecosystem. The organisations plan to explore work in four areas: responsible AI research and innovation, the Hong Kong AI Lab as a platform for research and experimentation, industry engagement through roundtables, seminars and publications, and talent development through hackathons, workshops and mentorship programmes. The partnership also aims to turn research into proof-of-concept initiatives. The partners describe these steps as a way to support Hong Kong's development as an international financial centre and AI innovation hub.

The companies have not stated in these articles a budget or any figures beyond the three-year term. Nowa Zhu, Co-founder and CEO of Longbridge, said that agentic AI could change how people interact with financial information but that realising this requires trust, accountability and close collaboration across the financial ecosystem. Ir Eric Chan, Chief Public Mission Officer of Cyberport, said that agentic AI offers significant potential for financial services and that the AI Lab should help test, validate and deploy solutions in the real world. Zhu added that Longbridge sees Hong Kong as an important market for shaping how AI is adopted responsibly.

Longbridge describes itself as a group that operates licensed financial businesses across several jurisdictions and holds 22 financial regulatory licences or qualifications, and it was founded in 2019. The announcement comes as AI systems move beyond providing insights toward supporting complex financial decisions, which raises questions about transparency and accountability, according to the release. The articles do not describe any specific next steps or timelines beyond the planned establishment of the AI Lab and the partnership's stated areas of work. A separate CIO commentary in the same period, not tied to the partnership, notes that autonomous agents require governance built in from the outset and that human oversight matters most in high-stakes areas such as financial transactions and regulatory compliance.

stories.Headline: India flags Chinese-linked AI tools in hacking campaign against financial firms
stories.Summary:
India's cybersecurity agency, CERT-In, issued an advisory on Wednesday naming a hacking group it calls "Crafty Falcon" as the operator behind a wave of AI-driven attacks on financial firms. The agency said the group has breached non-bank lenders, fintech firms and cryptocurrency exchanges, and it identified four tools the group uses: ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn and CyberStrikeAI. Security researchers have tied at least two of those tools to China. The advisory followed a series of attacks on Indian banks and non-bank lenders in recent weeks.

CERT-In said the attackers rely on publicly available AI tools to automate break-ins at what it called machine speed, and it described the threat as active and ongoing. The group surveys its targets using machine intelligence and moves money by invoking victims' own payment and disbursement systems. It times attacks around holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring periods to delay detection, and it has returned to firms that only partly fixed flaws after earlier alerts. The Reserve Bank of India has tightened cybersecurity checks in response. The articles do not say which organisations were affected or how much money was taken in the advisory itself.

CERT-In did not say who is behind the breaches or where the group operates. The cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has reported that ARTEX, a China-made tool, was used against South Korean banks from late September, and that a China-linked group used it in an espionage campaign against more than 200 organisations in at least 14 countries. The developer made ARTEX private last month after it was linked to the South Korean attacks. CERT-In also did not say the attacks were state-sponsored, and it noted that the tools it named are freely available online.

Earlier incidents are described in the reporting but were not confirmed by CERT-In as Crafty Falcon attacks. Reuters, citing a police complaint, reported that two Mumbai-based non-bank lenders lost about $2 million in more than 700 unauthorised instant transfers from ICICI Bank accounts on October 8 and 9, after hackers compromised the software links used for loan-disbursal instructions. State Bank of India disclosed a dark-web leak of 3,897 customer records last month, Spandana Sphoorty Financial reported unauthorised debits on November 1, and AU Small Finance Bank said it was probing a potential customer-data leak. The articles do not say what further steps CERT-In or regulators will take beyond the advisory and the tighter checks already described.

stories.Headline: VIEW Tech-stock rout accelerates retreat from the AI trade
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, technology stocks fell sharply in New York, with the semiconductor index briefly dropping as much as 11 percent, its worst performance since March 2020. The Nasdaq composite fell as much as 5 percent, a decline that would have confirmed a correction, or a 10 percent pullback from its high set on October 6. Advanced Micro, Sandisk, Micron, Dell and Marvell Technology were among more than a dozen large technology stocks that fell by double digits. The selloff was the latest in a string of declines for the AI sector during a difficult month.

Market observers linked the decline to changing expectations for the AI buildout. Selling in stock and bond markets has made it harder for participants in the data-center buildout to get financing, and Tuesday's US elections brought the passage of dozens of nationwide ballot initiatives that could limit building in the coming months and years. One state governor, Greg Abbott of Texas, was cited as having imposed a moratorium on new data-center permits in September. Analysts also pointed to weak earnings from Qualcomm and ARM Holdings as a reminder that fundamentals still matter, along with aggressive institutional selling and deleveraging by hedge funds.

Several strategists said the political environment is the core issue. Bruce Zaro, a managing director at Granite Wealth Management in Plymouth, Massachusetts, said the sell-off was a secondary reaction to the election results, and that data-center stocks face heavy pushback over local siting, power-grid strain and water use. Melissa Brown, global head of investment decision research at SimCorp in New York, said investors appear to recognize that newly elected members of Congress and governors want to slow AI infrastructure development, though she doubted it could be stopped altogether. Mark Hackett, chief market strategist for Nationwide in Downingtown, Pennsylvania, described the move as an emotional sell-off driven largely by institutional selling.

Some analysts saw the decline as overdone or as a repricing rather than a permanent break. One strategist argued that the sell-off was unwarranted and that investors were still sorting out how much policy will change for AI and data-center projects. Another noted that companies could simply build data centers in places such as Canada or Brazil. Sameer Samana of Wells Fargo Investment Institute said the market had priced in strong growth, and that if that growth slows, investors may shift from growth-focused buyers to value-focused ones, a transition that could take time.

stories.Headline: Emirates SkyCargo launches AI Tech to move infrastructure powering Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Emirates SkyCargo has launched AI Tech, a dedicated product for moving critical and sensitive AI infrastructure safely and on time. The launch was announced in Dubai on November 4, 2026, through a press release distributed by APO Group on behalf of The Emirates Group. The product is aimed at AI server racks, semiconductors, GPUs, capital equipment and other critical hardware. It combines priority loading, specialised handling and proactive shipment monitoring run from the airline's command centre in Dubai.

The airline says moving technology equipment has grown more complex as computing systems become more sophisticated and AI adoption speeds up. Large deployments often involve high value cargo, tight timelines and special handling needs. AI Tech responds with standardised operating procedures across the network, covering priority loading, closer shipment oversight and active coordination with customers during transit. Key features include handling procedures meant to keep equipment oriented correctly and reduce the risk of damage. Shipments also get airport-to-airport visibility with milestone updates, along with specialist project cargo support for oversized and heavy loads.

Badr Abbas, Divisional Senior Vice President of Emirates SkyCargo, said that physical infrastructure must arrive safely and on time behind every AI breakthrough. He said the product is meant to give customers confidence that their equipment will move smoothly across the network, backed by operational oversight and communication. Abbas noted that more than 700 tonnes of AI infrastructure were transported across the global network in July alone, and that demand has kept rising. He added that the airline aims to become the carrier of choice for companies across the AI ecosystem.

The product draws on the airline's experience moving AI-related hardware between manufacturing centres and key technology markets. It is available across the global network for most AI-related cargo, while highly specialised manufacturing equipment requires advance station capability assessments. The airline also says that by March 2027 it will operate 23 dedicated freighters that provide main deck capacity for tall, dense server racks often weighing more than 3.5 tonnes. Emirates SkyCargo additionally offers capacity on its wide-body passenger aircraft. The release presents AI Tech as part of the airline's effort to serve the fast-changing needs of the AI sector.

stories.Headline: The AI Boom Has an Energy Problem. Geothermal Is the Answer | Opinion
stories.Summary:
Jeff D. Kelley, a geoscientist and engineer who founded RockWise LLC, wrote a Newsweek opinion piece published on November 3, 2026, arguing that geothermal energy can meet the power needs of artificial intelligence. He said data centers run 24 hours a day and need a flat, constant load. He cited the International Energy Agency, which reported that electricity demand from data centers soared 17 percent in 2025 while global electricity demand grew 3 percent. The IEA projects global power demand to grow 3.6 percent annually through 2030, up from 2.8 percent over the past decade. Kelley said solar and wind are essential but variable, and meeting data center reliability with on-site gas-fired generation can require 30 to 70 percent more capacity than their electricity demand.

He said only nuclear and geothermal can meet flat, 24/7 demand, and he judged micro-nuclear to be years away from commercial deployment at the scale data centers need. The U.S. leads the world with just over 4 GW of installed geothermal capacity, but the Department of Energy estimates at least 300 GW of potential. Kelley called that gap a deployment problem rather than a resource problem, and he proposed reusing existing oil and gas wells and infrastructure, including in the Gulf Coast, to cut costs. Kelley said the barrier to geothermal has never been the heat but the cost of reaching it, and that reusing infrastructure changes the economics. He called for three steps: educating local governments about the geothermal resource beneath them, giving data center developers a greener alternative to gas turbines, and using existing infrastructure to lower deployment costs.

He said that if this is done, the AI boom does not have to become an energy crisis and can become an energy transition. A separate National editorial published on November 1, 2026, said Adipec opens on Monday in Abu Dhabi, where it has been held annually since 1984, with 2,260 exhibitors, 181,000 pre-registered visitors, 40 government ministers and 12,000 conference delegates. It cited research by Adnoc, XRG and Microsoft showing that 62 percent of surveyed energy leaders rank AI among their two leading corporate priorities, up from 42 percent last year, and that almost nine in 10 increased spending on it. The survey found nearly three quarters of respondents expect AI to increase energy consumption by 2030, while only 52 percent believe existing infrastructure can meet the additional demand. A separate Adipec survey found 81 percent of energy executives expect AI-related electricity requirements to exceed current forecasts, and the editorial said investment must modernize grids, expand storage and accelerate cleaner generation.

stories.Headline: Financial policymakers to monitor U.S. AI, trade policies following election
stories.Summary:
South Korea's top financial policymakers vowed on Thursday, November 5, 2026, to watch closely for shifts in U.S. policy on artificial intelligence and trade and what those shifts could mean for the South Korean economy. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il met with Bank of Korea Governor Shin Hyun-song, Financial Services Commission Chairman Lee Eog-weon and Financial Supervisory Service Governor Lee Chan-jin after the U.S. Democratic Party won a strong result in the midterm elections earlier that week. Although major stock markets in the United States and Europe had gained, worries about tighter regulation of the AI industry had pushed semiconductor shares lower. The officials said the meeting addressed the likely effects of the election on U.S. fiscal, trade and industrial policy, and the participants agreed to follow the regulatory environment closely.

The officials also said they would keep track of U.S. tariffs and developments in the Middle East war, which could affect the economy. According to the finance ministry, they agreed to step up efforts to support stable growth by coordinating closely with relevant organizations to respond to changes in the external environment. They also agreed to prepare thoroughly for a possible rise in financial market volatility. The ministry's statement described these steps as a joint response to outside pressures rather than a set of new measures. The meeting was held in Seoul, and the ministry released a photo of the four officials posing before their talks.

Responsibility for these monitoring efforts rests with the finance minister and the heads of the central bank, the financial regulator and the financial services commission, who met to coordinate the response. The finance ministry said the officials had agreed to coordinate closely and prepare for possible market swings. stories.Headline: Sentra Raises $150M to Link AI Agents, Data and Identity
stories.Summary:
Sentra, a New York startup founded in 2021 by an Israeli Military Intelligence colonel, raised $150 million in a Series C round led by Capital One Ventures on or around November 5, 2026. The money is meant to help the company understand and control the data that AI models and agents can access. According to the articles, the funding will expand Sentra's data loss prevention tools into a broader data security platform. It will also support AI governance, agentic AI capabilities, identity and access controls, and continued work on core data discovery and classification.

The articles describe the investment as a way to link data, identity and AI security together. Sentra's CEO and co-founder, Yoav Regev, said that customers increasingly want an end-to-end data security platform rather than separate tools. He argued that data context, such as what the data is, where it lives and who can reach it, makes data loss prevention decisions more effective. Regev also described an access intelligence layer that would map people and non-human identities, including AI agents, to the data they touch. That layer could allow time-limited permissions so that agents receive only the access a given task requires.

Regev is the company's CEO and has led it since its founding. He spent nearly 24 years in Israel's Unit 8200, where he ended as head of its cyber department. Sentra has 210 employees and has raised $253 million across four outside funding rounds, including a $50 million Series B led by Key1 Capital in April 2025. Regev said that his company competes with larger rivals such as Proofpoint and Cyera on its technology, its ability to keep customer data in the customer's own environment, its operating cost and its classification accuracy. He also said that the expansion broadens Sentra's buyers beyond chief information security officers to include chief information officers and chief data officers.

The articles frame the deal as part of a wider push to make the data layer central to AI adoption, since Regev said that AI is fundamentally a data problem. Regev said that Sentra's current customers use the product for data hygiene, AI readiness and fixing excessive permissions in AI workflows. Looking ahead, he said that the company will keep improving classification, widening data coverage and increasing performance, which he described as the foundation for the newer AI use cases. The articles do not give a timeline for product releases or any specific plans beyond these areas.
