stories.Headline: Mercedes Hopes to Woo Motorists With In-Car Conversational AI
stories.Summary:
Mercedes-Benz is bringing conversational artificial intelligence into its vehicles through a partnership with Liquid AI, an MIT spinout, according to a Wall Street Journal report published Thursday, November 5. The company's aim is not to have the AI drive the car but to control features such as heating and infotainment, which it hopes will attract buyers in a difficult market. The system is meant to allow more free-flowing conversation between drivers and their cars. Mercedes' U.S. division has already used conversational AI in its vehicles since 2026, but the Liquid AI tie-up is intended to make the experience faster and more intuitive.

Liquid AI, founded in 2023, builds AI models that run directly on a device instead of in the cloud, which the company says offers greater privacy and lower latency. Jason Hoff, CEO of Mercedes-Benz North America, said an AI system permitting freer conversation is something the company sees as a clear priority for customers. The report also cited Gartner projections that by 2029, on-device AI models will handle 30% of all user-initiated AI tasks in enterprise applications, up from almost zero in 2026. PYMNTS earlier covered the partnership in May as part of a broader look at AI efforts by European carmakers, including BMW and Audi.

The announcement comes as Mercedes cut its expectations for the year, warning of a cooling market in China and higher costs for the final quarter of 2026. CEO Ola Källenius said on the company's earnings call last month that new product launches and AI changes to how the company works are meant to make Mercedes-Benz faster, more efficient and more competitive. The carmaker has said it will deploy AI across the business as part of an efficiency program. Källenius's remarks, as reported, tie the technology to both product appeal and cost control.

PYMNTS argued in its own coverage that on-device design matters beyond the cabin, since it processes data locally without sending it to a server. The outlet also said AI could be applied to production systems, reading order queues, monitoring supplier lead times and assembly progress, and flagging delays before they happen. In its view, AI is becoming the coordination layer across the full order-to-delivery chain rather than a feature added to existing processes. It described European automakers such as BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Audi as competing with software-native rivals from the United States and China, and treating the window to build such infrastructure as vital.

stories.Headline: Nebius Is Up 69% in 2026. Is Its AI Bubble “Already Popping”?
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group, the AI infrastructure company ticker NBIS, has seen its stock rise about 69% in 2026, closing at $141.39 on November 2, though it remains roughly 53% below its June 22 intraday high of $299.86. The stock sold off hard in October as worries about CoreWeave's borrowing spread across AI infrastructure names, prompting questions about whether Nebius can fund its expansion without taking on too much debt or diluting shareholders. At June 30, Nebius carried far lower net borrowings than CoreWeave, roughly $504 million compared with about $29.5 billion, though newer financing and planned buildouts are adding to its obligations. Commentary from TIKR, which tracks the company, was published on November 5, 2026.

Major customer contracts continue to support the business. Microsoft's infrastructure agreement is valued at $17.4 billion and could reach $19.4 billion, while Meta's five-year deal includes $12 billion in dedicated capacity and up to $15 billion in additional commitments. In its August 12 earnings report, Nebius reported revenue growth of 454% to $582 million, a 41% adjusted EBITDA margin, and four AI cloud agreements averaging more than $1 billion each. TIKR's October 21 consensus projects revenue rising from $530 million in 2025 to $3.35 billion in 2026 and $12.24 billion in 2027. Analysts expect about $29.1 billion in capital spending and roughly $34 billion in net debt by the end of 2027, and the company has said that sequencing its financing helps optimize its long-term cost of capital.

Financing remains the central concern. On October 21, Piper Sandler cut its price target on Nebius from $237 to $185, and the following day Nebius secured a $3.5 billion financing facility from Citi to support expansion. Despite more than $9 billion in expected 2026 customer prepayments, further borrowing could raise costs and dilute existing shareholders. Nvidia holds a reported 9.3% stake in Nebius and supplies the GPUs central to its growth, while Microsoft and Meta are its anchor customers. TIKR describes the stock as potentially undervalued on sales multiples, with about 5.9x forward sales on October 30, down from roughly 13x at the end of June and a peak near 32x in October 2025, though it notes second-quarter depreciation of nearly $260 million exceeded adjusted EBITDA of about $236 million.

Nebius reports third-quarter results on November 12, with analysts expecting about $906 million in revenue, and customer prepayments, deferred revenue and capital spending are the metrics to watch. A separate commentary from MindMatters, published November 4, argues that the AI bubble question is complicated because the value chain is narrow, with chipmakers and data center operators profiting while AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI price their services below cost. That piece says Chinese models gaining market share forced price cuts after a brief period of higher pricing in 2026, and it describes continuing losses at the labs. The TIKR article itself states that a falling valuation does not necessarily mean the AI business is collapsing, and that the outcome depends on whether Nebius can fund growth without excessive debt or dilution.

stories.Headline: Crusoe unveils 3.5 MW modular data centre for Nvidia AI racks
stories.Summary:
Crusoe, an AI data centre operator, has launched its sixth-generation modular data centre platform, called Spark Liquid, which is built to support up to 3.5 MW of compute capacity. The company says the unit is designed for Nvidia GB300 NVL72 and Vera Rubin NVL72 racks, and it was announced in early November 2026. Crusoe also claims that Spark Liquid delivers five times the compute density of earlier Spark generations. Production will begin in 2027 in Brighton, Colorado, alongside the company's existing Spark line.

The platform uses a closed-loop direct liquid cooling system, which removes heat from high-density racks more efficiently than air and recirculates water with minimal ongoing use and no evaporative loss. Each unit is built in Crusoe's factory and shipped ready to deploy in clusters, and the Spark platform will also support Nvidia's recently announced DSX POD blueprint for modular infrastructure. Crusoe said that cooling efficiency will still depend on climate, so each deployment is designed around local conditions. Crusoe acquired the electrical manufacturer Easter-Owens Electric in 2022 to bring manufacturing in-house.

Crusoe is the company behind the product, and its head of Spark, Bryan Schramm, has explained the reasoning. He said that power limits, the need for predictable delivery and the pressure to bring capacity online quickly are pushing operators toward modular designs. According to him, a factory-built unit can use power that is available now in smaller blocks, which can shorten grid connection timelines, and building in a factory makes delivery dates more reliable for customers who reserve capacity in advance. He also said that Crusoe designed the platform to move variability into a controlled factory setting, which helps the company deploy next-generation GPUs faster.

The articles place the launch within a broader industry shift toward factory-built infrastructure, as AI operators look for ways around the power and construction delays that often slow conventional builds. Nvidia describes DSX POD as a partner-delivered design in which it validates the cluster while partners build and deliver the units, and Crusoe is one of eight container solution providers on its list, alongside Eaton, Schneider Electric and Vertiv. Customers still need a prepared site with power, water and network connections. Schramm said that deployments may move closer to demand, including sites in the tens of megawatts, though the articles do not describe specific customers or deployments beyond the Colorado production plan.

stories.Headline: Grimes Joins ‘AI Film Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Ahead Of December 4 Release
stories.Summary:
Grimes, the experimental pop artist Claire Boucher, has joined the AI feature film "Gods Don't Give Gifts," which is set for theatrical release on December 4. Boucher's connection to the project began when director Zack London, who makes films under the name Gossip Goblin, messaged her after she followed his X account and engaged with his videos. Her cameo, which lasts a few minutes, appears in an early sequence of the post-apocalyptic film. The Variety report describes the collaboration as the result of direct messages and a single conversation over lunch. Boucher plays Zaynith Alda, a brash, demanding aristocrat from the wealthy Halvorith family who seeks an illicit "dreamspool" experience in the world of NiiroCradle.

London and co-writer Jacob Batchelor reworked the existing role around Boucher's persona, letting her help design a mechanical-looking mask for the character and dropping the British accent used elsewhere in the film. Her lines were recorded remotely, with London in Stockholm, his editor and sound engineer in Romania, and Boucher and her producer in Los Angeles. The film has a nearly two-hour runtime and is R-rated. The film's studio, Fable, is promoting it heavily and is positioning it for the Academy Awards' best animated feature category. Fable set a Times Square campaign featuring Boucher and hosted screenings for animation voting members of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts & Sciences in New York and Los Angeles.

Fable CEO Edward Saatchi said in a statement that the film is the first AI film and deserves a nomination. Boucher declined an interview, and her spokesperson, Mitchell Jackson, said she supports independent artists using new tools and was impressed by the size of the team and the compensation of the artists involved. The article places Boucher's cameo within a wider shift in which celebrities license their likenesses for AI projects, while others remain wary of unauthorized use. Variety's Awards Circuit does not list the film among the Academy's potential contenders. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI Starts Writing Acne Prescriptions Without a Doctor's Visit in One State
stories.Summary:
Ambient AI scribes now record doctor visits in healthcare settings, and the articles describe how they work. An AI scribe captures the conversation between a doctor and a patient, drafts a note from the audio, and hands it to the doctor to review before it enters the medical record. The articles do not report that any state has allowed AI to write acne prescriptions without a doctor's visit, so the headline's central claim is not supported by this material. The coverage instead concerns recording and documentation rules for visits that still involve a clinician.

Louisiana's Act 649, effective Aug. 1, requires a licensed healthcare professional to verbally disclose any recording device, software or service before recording part of a visit for AI transcription, and a professional who skips this can face discipline from their licensing board. Rhode Island's notification act, effective on passage in June, requires providers using AI to document a visit to notify the patient and review the AI-written note for accuracy afterward, and it names no penalty. California's AB 3030, in effect since Jan. 1, 2025, requires a disclaimer on patient-clinical messages that generative AI produced unless a licensed provider reviewed them first. Each of these laws is aimed at the scribe or the message, not at prescribing.

The articles describe the scale of adoption without assigning blame for any prescription. Abridge is live in more than 300 health systems and supports upward of 100 million clinical conversations a year, according to Fortune, and Cleveland Clinic logged more than 3.5 million encounters with Ambience Healthcare's scribe in its first year. Doximity found that use of ambient listening and AI scribes rose from 20% to 29% between its two survey waves, and 47% of 3,151 surveyed physicians said their institution's AI decision-making is still evolving. Rhode Island state Sen. Pamela Lauria, the bill's sponsor, said patients want as much transparency as possible.

The articles also explain that HIPAA does not set a specific patient-notice requirement for AI scribes, so the duty to tell patients about recording comes from state laws instead. The coverage places this within a broader trend in which patients already use digital tools and portals for their care, which could make disclosure easier to deliver. The articles do not describe any pending action on AI prescribing, so nothing further is reported on that question. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Protex AI and ALL4 Partner to Turn Site Intelligence Into Action on the Industrial Floor
stories.Summary:
Protex AI, a site intelligence platform, announced a strategic partnership with ALL4, an environmental, health and safety consulting firm, on November 4, 2026, in Boston, Massachusetts. The partnership combines Protex AI's Site Intelligence platform with ALL4's EHS and industry expertise. Together they aim to help customers turn leading indicators into actionable insight across every site. Protex AI connects the cameras and systems already on a site so safety and operations leaders can see what is happening, understand why, and optimize. ALL4 helps customers act on those insights by aligning stakeholders, embedding processes and controls, and supporting the organizational change needed to reduce risk and improve performance.

The partnership comes as industrial companies are asked to do more with less, with rising costs and harder hiring. Gartner recently predicted that 60% of AI projects implemented through 2026 will be abandoned because they lack AI-ready data. Protex AI combines video with systems a site already runs to supply context, while ALL4 helps customers prioritize what to fix and build changes into safety programs and daily operations. Protex AI says Marks & Spencer reduced incidents by 80% over three months, and Bendix recovered an estimated 226 labor hours per month by identifying and addressing an operational issue. The partnership will initially focus on industrial manufacturing, food and beverage manufacturing, forest products, and waste management, and will expand with client needs.

Dan Hobbs, CEO of Protex AI, said industrial sites have a major opportunity to adopt and scale AI across safety and operations, and that in 2027 the advantage will go to sites that give AI the context of their operation and use it to fix problems, not just spot them. He said ALL4 brings deep EHS expertise across heavily regulated industries, helping teams turn insight into lasting change. Chad Morris, Chief Growth Officer of ALL4, said industrial organizations have more data than ever but data alone does not change outcomes. He said Protex AI helps clients see risk before it becomes an incident, and ALL4 helps them act on it.

To mark the partnership, the two companies will host a joint webinar on Wednesday, December 9, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. ET on improving site safety through site intelligence solutions. Speakers will discuss how site intelligence complements existing EHS programs, how privacy-first, edge-based AI fits into real industrial environments, and how to turn continuous insight into action, including the people, process and organizational change that makes improvement last. The speakers are Chris Lane, Enterprise Client Strategist at Protex AI, and Golda Sobol, Directing Consultant at ALL4, with Cyndale Post, Directing Consultant at ALL4, as moderator. ALL4 describes itself as a global environmental consulting firm with technical experts across North America, Latin America, and Europe, and Protex AI is a Y Combinator company backed by Hedosophia and Salesforce Ventures that helps companies like Amazon, Toyota and FedEx.

stories.Headline: Clemson Business welcomed top AI and consulting industry leaders for Power of Leadership Speaker Series
stories.Summary:
On October 16, the Wilbur O. and Ann Powers College of Business hosted an edition of The Power of Leadership: A Signature Speaker Series, bringing industry leaders from AI and consulting to Clemson. Panelists from Deloitte, KPMG, GXO Logistics and venture investing discussed how artificial intelligence is changing consulting work and what students can do to prepare. The recurring message was that the first question remains the same as before: what business problem needs solving? The event was reported by Clemson News on November 5, 2026.

The panelists stressed that AI should be matched to the right tasks rather than adopted for its own sake. One speaker said a predictable, well-defined task may suit traditional automation, while work involving judgment or unstructured information may be a better fit for AI. Teams were advised to weigh potential return and whether the underlying process is ready for new technology. Another panelist described a prototype built with Claude over a weekend, compared with similar work that had taken 20 weeks four years earlier. Client expectations are shifting accordingly, with clients expecting faster plans, recommendations and results.

Several panelists are named in the coverage with their roles. Shrikant Vaidyanathan, a principal in KPMG Technology and Consumer/Retail, urged consultants to start with the root cause of a problem. Daniel Csoka, principal of AI & Engineering and a Leader in the Center for Process Bionics at Deloitte, spoke about client expectations and using AI to review conversations. Karen Bomber, GXO Logistics Inc's chief commercial officer, warned against confusing intelligence with wisdom and said people must interpret AI output. Chris Hornbecker, a founder and investor at Stronghorn Venture Capital, encouraged students to use AI to solve real problems rather than simply retrieve answers.

The panel also addressed relationships and careers, with speakers saying AI can free time for interpersonal work and that clients increasingly want consultants with specialized knowledge who can deliver quickly. Dean Wendy York described consulting as work that requires asking the right questions and moving from insight to action, and she linked the discussion to the College's emphasis on experiential learning. The coverage notes that Clemson's Management Consulting Signature Program, a multi-semester, interdisciplinary program, offers students a related path through real-world client work. The panel's advice was to build AI fluency alongside subject knowledge, judgment and communication skills.

stories.Headline: Elon AI Hub launches ‘Campus Voices’ interview series
stories.Summary:
The Elon AI Hub has launched Campus Voices, a YouTube interview series in which Elon faculty and staff discuss how artificial intelligence is shaping teaching and learning on campus. The first two episodes feature Paula Patch, teaching professor of English, and Anthony Crider, professor of astrophysics, and the launch was reported on November 5, 2026. The series is hosted by Paul Nunno, a student employee at the AI Hub, who is in the class of 2027. The interviews give faculty members a chance to talk about the uses they have found for AI, where they see its limits or risks, and the questions they are still working through.

In the first episode, titled "AI as a Second Brain: Supporting Student Learning," Patch describes using ChatGPT to capture ideas for assignments, organize course planning and reflect on what worked in class. She says the tool has made her more efficient and more creative. Patch stresses that students should keep their own engagement with reading and writing, suggesting that AI can help them break a long reading into smaller sections and plan a schedule without doing the reading for them. She also warns that AI-generated text can hide a writer's individual voice, and she argues that students and faculty should talk openly about expectations and boundaries for using the technology.

In the second episode, "AI, Education, and the Future of Work," Crider explains how agentic AI, tools that can carry out multistep tasks with some independence, helped him when Elon switched learning systems from Moodle to Canvas and his course software had to be rewritten. He notes that many coding exercises he once assigned can now be completed almost instantly by AI, so he has changed his courses. Students now work through some problems by hand and check AI-generated Python code for errors before building code themselves, with the aim of understanding core concepts and judging AI outputs in their field. Crider also discusses assessing students by what they can demonstrate through activities and experiences, and he advises students to develop proficiency with AI tools and pursue coursework beyond their main discipline.

Interviews with Jonathan Su, associate professor of engineering, Erin Hone, associate teaching professor of education, and Amanda Sturgill, associate professor of journalism, are upcoming. Both released episodes are available on the Elon University AI YouTube channel. The AI Hub also points people to its website for information on campus AI resources, consultations and upcoming events. stories.Headline: Using genomics, AI to predict, prevent, and treat disease
stories.Summary:
Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health hosted its Program in Quantitative Genomics conference on October 29 and 30, 2026, at Harvard Medical School's Joseph B. Martin Conference Center. The event, organized by Xihong Lin, a professor of biostatistics, featured about 15 leading experts and drew 130 participants. Its central question was how to combine genomic, molecular, clinical, and lifestyle data into a single unified view of a patient. The aim was to let clinicians, with help from artificial intelligence, spot complex patterns, predict disease risks, and tailor treatments.

Keynote speakers described several approaches. Eric Xing of Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and Carnegie Mellon's School of Computer Science spoke about building generative AI models of a "virtual cell" that could let researchers run systematic simulations instead of relying on trial-and-error wet lab work. Sylvia Plevritis of Stanford University described pairing multiscale modeling with multimodal AI to link longitudinal clinical records, imaging, pathology, and molecular data for lung cancer. Marinka Zitnik of Harvard Medical School discussed AI agents that act as conversational research collaborators, including "AutoScientists" that work in teams on long-running experiments. She stressed that such systems need the right data, biological context, and pairing with lab experiments to remain accurate and effective.

The organizers and speakers framed these developments as ways to move biomedical research from slow manual experiments toward faster digital simulation. Other sessions addressed kidney disease using mapped genomic data, shared digital infrastructure for drug discovery, and the trustworthiness and safety of AI systems that reason over complex evidence and take actions in scientific and health settings. The reporting describes these as presentations and discussions at the conference, with no announced policy, funding, or regulatory change attached to them. Mustafa Akben, assistant professor of management and Elon's director of artificial intelligence integration, was appointed one of two directors on the Allied AI Advisory Council. The Allied AI Collaborative brings together representatives from the Alliance's 13 member institutions to share expertise, encourage interdisciplinary collaboration and develop practical AI applications.

The collaborative focuses on three areas: research and innovation, teaching, learning and assessment, and ethics and policy considerations. As an ambassador, Lashley will help facilitate collaborative meetings, deliver presentations, share research and scholarship, mentor new participants and help shape the group's priorities throughout the year. Her appointment follows her earlier recognition as a member of the Alliance's inaugural AI Technologies Champion Network, announced in February 2026, which honored faculty and staff who integrate AI responsibly into teaching, research and institutional work. Lashley holds a law degree from North Carolina Central University School of Law. Akben, who has led Elon's AI integration work since July 2024, will provide strategic guidance through the advisory council, which identifies opportunities for research development, external partnerships and future investments.

Elon University announced the appointments and credited both faculty members with advancing the responsible use of artificial intelligence through the collaborative. It also notes that Akben's role involves integrating AI across academic and administrative departments to support teaching, research and institutional practices. The CAA Academic Alliance, established in 2002, connects the academic communities of the Coastal Athletic Association's 13 member institutions and promotes collaboration among faculty, staff and students. stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence points researchers toward new disease targets hidden in mitochondria
stories.Summary:
Texas A&M AgriLife Research scientists have used an artificial intelligence tool to begin answering a long-standing question about human biology, namely what the hundreds of unexplained proteins inside mitochondria actually do. Mitochondria are the energy centers of human cells, and about 1,100 proteins are known to exist within them, yet many of their functions remain unknown. The work was reported in a study titled "The predicted interactome of the human mitochondrial proteome," published in Nature Communications, and the findings were announced in a November 2026 report from AgriLife Today. The researchers stressed that the gap matters because mutations in nearly 30% of mitochondrial proteins have been linked to human diseases.

The team, led by Abhinav Swaminathan, Ph.D., and Vishal Gohil, Ph.D., in the Texas A&M Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics, used an AI tool called AlphaFold-Multimer to screen every possible pairing of the roughly 1,100 proteins, which came to more than 630,000 combinations. Of those, the researchers cataloged 2,895 likely interactions, and more than half had never been reported before. The predictions tie many disease-associated proteins to previously unknown biological pathways, which may point to new diagnostic and therapeutic targets. The study also gave 85 previously uncharacterized proteins their first probable partners, offering clues about their roles in cells.

Swaminathan said that without knowing what individual proteins do, scientists cannot determine how to treat the diseases they may cause. The approach relies on inferring a protein's function from the other proteins it interacts with, and the researchers say traditional laboratory methods for this work are slow. The team began about three years ago by testing AlphaFold-Multimer, which Google DeepMind released in 2022 to predict the three-dimensional shapes proteins form together, on copper pathway proteins they study. After that trial worked, they applied the tool to all human mitochondrial proteins. Swaminathan described the team as a traditional biochemistry and genetics lab rather than an AI lab.

The predictions were then checked through about two years of laboratory experiments, which confirmed several of the predicted partnerships in yeast and human cells, with some work done alongside researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. The researchers released the predictions as a free online resource called MitoMatch so scientists worldwide can assign likely partners to the proteins they study. The team is continuing to examine the data with other researchers, but it notes that cures for mitochondria-linked diseases may still be far off. The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, Texas A&M High Performance Research Computing and The Welch Foundation.

stories.Headline: Dartmouth AI Conference Prompts Focus on Human Judgment
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth held a conference called AI at 70: What Must Remain Human? from Oct. 29 to Oct. 31, 2026, seventy years after the summer workshop that launched the field of artificial intelligence. The event drew leading scholars, AI executives, and students, and more than 1,000 people registered to attend. Another 24,000 watched various livestreams of the sessions. President Sian Leah Beilock moderated a panel on how universities navigate AI’s toughest questions.

Speakers said AI offers the promise of dramatic improvements in productivity and capacity. Peter DeSantis, a senior vice president at Amazon, said a team of five software engineers using AI can finish a project that once required 50 engineers, at 10 times the pace. Michael Breen, head of strategic initiatives at Anthropic, said powerful AI can make the capacity at the heart of human agency much more common. The AI at 70 Student Hackathon brought together 187 students from Dartmouth and other institutions, and 40 teams worked in five tracks. The winners, Caleb Zhou and Aditya Tripathi, created Wheelio, a campus navigation app for wheelchair users.

Beilock said anyone can get a convincing answer from AI in seconds, and the hard skill now is judgment. She said AI literacy must help students know when to pick up the technology and when to put it down. Breen said realizing AI’s potential depends on working with researchers to address risks, including dependence on AI that can weaken human capacities and a concentration of power among those who control the systems. Ezra Klein, a New York Times Opinion columnist, said he would be pretty skeptical for now about bringing AI too heavily into education. Laura Carlson, president of the University of Delaware, said writing helps her think, so the line between thinking and writing is very blurry.

Molly Crockett, a professor at Princeton University, criticized hype driven by the tech industry in collaboration with the U.S. government. She said the new model centers the values of industry, productivity, and profit, which are at odds with the goal of science. Bruce Sacerdote, a professor of economics, presented findings from the inaugural Dartmouth AI Survey of how college students use AI. He is now surveying employers about whether entry-level jobs for college students are changing because of AI, and the next student survey will be conducted in August 2027.

stories.Headline: Project to rebuild trust in AI era lands Laude’s $10M ‘moonshot’ award
stories.Summary:
A Cornell University research team has won a multi-year, $10 million "moonshot" grant from the Laude Institute to rebuild trust in online civic discourse, the Cornell Chronicle reported on November 5, 2026. The award was announced at a ceremony on October 29 in San Francisco, and the project is titled "Rebuilding Trust in Civic Discourse: An Infrastructure for Auditable AI." The team is one of four selected from eight finalists to receive moonshot awards meant to apply AI to humanity's largest problems. Its members include faculty and students with expertise in AI, conversational behavior, computational systems and human-centered design.

The grant is meant to fund tools and protocols that restore the foundations of trust online, where AI systems increasingly take part in conversations alongside people. Researchers describe the goal as a communication ecosystem in which AI strengthens public conversation rather than undermining it. The team had already received an initial $250,000 seed grant from the Laude Institute in April, which it used to build prototypes and a proposal. Over the past six months it developed several tools, including the Assistant Toolkit, ConvoCompass, ConvoArena, Simulation Factory and an Auditing Benchmark. The project also adds an auditing layer that keeps a transparent record of each AI agent's interventions so that outside parties can verify its behavior.

The project is led by Cristian Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil, professor of information science in Cornell's Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science, who said the moment offers a rare chance to shape how AI's role in conversation develops before norms become entrenched. Jon Kleinberg, co-principal investigator, said at the ceremony that the problem is urgent and that the team feels a sense of mission to have AI help with serious challenges. Co-investigators David Rand, Natalie Bazarova, Robert Kleinberg and Mor Naaman are also named in the Chronicle's report. Rand warned that AI can enable deepfakes, impersonation and manipulation, but said his team's experiments suggest AI can correct misconceptions and mediate difficult conversations.

The article places the project against a backdrop of hostile online civic discourse and rapid advances in AI that threaten public debate. Andy Konwinski, computer scientist and Laude Institute founder, urged the researchers at the ceremony to keep working on species-level problems. The Chronicle also notes that a separate moonshot team with Cornell connections, JupyterHealth, received a grant, with JP Pollak named as project co-lead. The article does not say when the grant's work will conclude or what milestones are scheduled beyond the multi-year timeline.

stories.Headline: AI adoption surges among ‘Best Law Firms’
stories.Summary:
Best Lawyers released its 2027 Best Law Firms rankings on November 5, 2026, covering 15,671 U.S. law firms across 127 practice areas and 188 geographic markets. The rankings are in their 17th edition and represent the top 3.41% of U.S. firms. The research drew on 30,024 lawyers who cast more than 3.8 million votes, 109,963 client references, and 1,053 interviews with firm and practice group leaders. Valerie Smith, senior research manager at Best Law Firms, said the results show how excellence takes shape across specialized local firms and national ones. Alongside the rankings, the third annual Best Law Firms U.S. Legal Market Report, based on survey responses from 5,753 firms in all 50 states and the District of Columbia, tracks how the profession is adopting AI.

Among firms with 20 or more lawyers, 28% reported fully implementing generative AI across multiple practice areas, up from 11% the year before. Full adoption among firms with 150 or more lawyers rose from 23% to 56%. Firms are also adding safeguards, as the share providing training on AI risks climbed from 22% to 63%, and those with clear policies for AI in client matters rose from 14% to 47%. A gap remains, since 95% of the largest firms have such policies while only 26% of solo practitioners do. Traditional billing is still widespread, with 70% of firms offering alternative fee arrangements, down slightly from 72%.

Flat fees, retainers, and contingency fees were the most common options. AI is starting to affect billing, however, as 25% of GenAI-using firms reported reduced billable hours for certain tasks, up from 19%, and another 27% reported higher efficiency without changing their hours. Smith said that makes AI a question of pricing and client value as well as technology. The report also found that smaller firms grew revenue quickly, while firms with 150 or more lawyers produced 83% of reported revenue. Average pro bono hours per lawyer fell to 25.6, a second straight year of decline and about half the American Bar Association's 50-hour benchmark.

A separate JD Supra article by Deborah Farone, a law firm business development advisor, describes a joint IBA and LMA webinar on AI and legal marketing that drew more than 1,200 registrants from 939 firms in 104 countries, with roughly 700 attending live. Panelists from Bowmans, Bass, Berry & Sims, Gibson Dunn, and Pierson Ferdinand described their experiences and emphasized treating AI as an ongoing learning process rather than a finished project. They advised starting with the problem a tool is meant to solve, using AI to speed up pitches and proposals, and keeping lawyers responsible for verifying all output. Farone wrote that the question has moved from whether firms should use AI to how they should use it well.

stories.Headline: Descope Unveils Envoy, an Identity-Aware Way For Personal AI Agents to Act on People's Behalf
stories.Summary:
Descope announced Envoy on November 4, 2026, a set of capabilities that lets personal AI agents sign in to consumer apps through a delegated path alongside existing authentication flows. The company said consumer businesses can accept agents as first-class users with their own identities, permissions and approval flows without rebuilding their identity stack. GoFundMe, You.com, GoodRx and Composio are among the launch and design partners who will work with Descope to improve Envoy in the months to come. Descope is based in Los Altos, California.

Envoy includes support for the Personal Agent Protocol, known as Poppy, so businesses do not have to implement the draft themselves. Descope handles discovery, agent identification through Client ID Metadata Documents with no pre-registration, session tokens bound to the agent's key with Demonstrated Proof of Possession, and all three Poppy sign-in types. Businesses can set granular agent permissions using Rich Authorization Requests, so a shopping agent could browse a catalog and place orders but not touch account settings or payment methods. Sensitive actions can use out-of-band approval through Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication, and every token and log entry keeps the customer and the acting agent distinct. Descope also published a zero-dependency Typescript Poppy SDK for AI agent builders.

Slavik Markovich, co-founder and CEO of Descope, said every login page was built on the assumption that a person is on the other side, and that assumption no longer holds. He said blocking agents or letting them sign in as humans will not work long term, and that Descope believes the Personal Agent Protocol is doing for consumer agents what MCP did for enterprise tools. Arnie Katz, chief product and technology officer of GoFundMe, said every donation is an act of trust, so the company needs to know who is giving and who is acting for them. Nitin Shingate, CTO of GoodRx, said people will increasingly ask agents to find the lowest prescription price and compare pharmacies, and that agents will get clear, limited permissions for pricing information while users stay in control.

The articles say personal agents have reached consumer scale quickly, with Meta's Muse passing 5 million downloads by the end of September, OpenAI's Instant Checkout running for roughly 900 million weekly active users, and Shopify activating agentic storefronts for more than a million merchants. Amazon blocked Muse in September, and JPMorgan Chase blocked outside agents including Muse and Instinct from directly accessing customer accounts in October. Meta and Sierra published the Personal Agent Protocol draft 0.1 in October. Separately, Fortune reported that running personal agents is compute-heavy, with Elon Musk calling the cost of Grok Bot unsustainably high relative to revenue and OpenAI's Adam Fry saying Dots are on the compute-heavy side.

stories.Headline: Turn Conversations into Action with AI Agents
stories.Summary:
Zoom's TechGig masterclass, "Turn Conversations into Action with AI Agents," was announced for a live online session on 30 November 2026 at 4:00 PM IST, led by Mehar Ullipalem, Zoom's Head of Solutions Engineering for India and SAARC. The course argues that meetings, calls and chats produce decisions and next steps, yet the context needed to act on them stays scattered across applications and documents. It says capturing conversations alone is not enough for AI to move work forward. The registration fee listed is ₹10,000, and the page says seats are limited for the live cohort.

The curriculum is built around six modules that trace a path from disconnected context to completed work. It explains a context layer that combines dynamic conversation intelligence from meetings, calls, chats and contact centre interactions with static business information such as company knowledge and connected systems of record. It also covers how APIs and Model Context Protocol servers can link scheduling, transcription, search and contact centre actions to other AI environments. Human review is presented as a design principle, with organisations able to set rules that require people to check certain AI-generated client-facing content before it is shared. Participants who attend receive a certificate of participation from TechGig.

Mehar Ullipalem is described as having more than twenty years of experience across unified communications, contact centre and digital workplace domains, and as leading Zoom's regional solutions engineering function. The page presents him as someone who works with customers and partners on solution adoption and enablement. The course material frames the goal as moving beyond what AI can generate toward connected systems that help finish real work, while keeping access controls and oversight in place. The page does not describe any outcome beyond the session itself.

A separate report from Wccftech, dated 4 November 2026, shows that similar concerns are being raised across the industry. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan, speaking with Hyperbolic CEO Jasper Zhang after Hyperbolic raised $30 million in a round backed by Tan's venture firm Walden Catalyst, said AI would keep growing and be even larger than the internet. He named memory, GPU and power shortages, along with financing for data center construction, as bottlenecks to growth. Tan also said he expects some correction in the sector and that safeguarding very large numbers of AI agents from acting without authorization is a challenge. The report notes that he expects millions of agents, though it attributes the figure only as "thousand millions" in his remarks.

stories.Headline: Tech policy coalition calls for new Congress to set AI safety standards
stories.Summary:
The Chamber of Progress, a center-left tech industry policy coalition, has urged the incoming Democratic Congress to set federal artificial intelligence safety standards. The group made the call in a November 4, 2026 memo to House and Senate Democratic leadership, days after Democrats won majorities in both chambers in the midterm elections. The memo lays out ten technology priorities for 2027, with a focus on consumer protection and access to technological benefits. Its top item is passing a federal AI transparency and safety standard. Reporting on the memo appeared in Nextgov/FCW on November 5, 2026.

The group's vice president of policy and government relations, Koustubh KJ Bagchi, wrote that Democrats should build a national AI framework that pairs public transparency with independent evaluation and enforceable safeguards for the most capable models. He said Congress should require developers to publish safety frameworks, report critical incidents and protect whistleblowers. The memo points to the FRONTIER Act, introduced in July by Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., as a bill Congress could build on. That measure would set a national framework for developing and deploying the most advanced AI models.

The memo also suggests a body similar to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority could combine industry funding with federal oversight of AI. Bagchi argued that strong federal protections should anchor a single national framework that reconciles overlapping state requirements. He added that states should keep their authority over fraud, discrimination, child protection and other harmful conduct. Several Democrats have made similar pledges since the midterms. Representative Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., posted on X on November 4 that a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of the industry and a ban on artificial superintelligence should top the agenda on day one.

Representative Greg Casar, D-Texas, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, called on Democrats to make AI a top priority. The pressure reflects voter attention to the issue. According to an NBC News exit poll cited in the report, 56 percent of voters said artificial intelligence and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, while 44 percent said they were a minor factor or not a factor. The memo also covers data centers, kids online safety, workforce upskilling, driverless technology and crypto rules. The articles do not say whether Democratic leaders have committed to any of these proposals or when a bill might move.

stories.Headline: The End of the Billable Hour? How AI Can Transform Models of Time and Efficiency in Law - New York State Bar Association
stories.Summary:
The New York State Bar Association's Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies issued a report, adopted by the association's governing body on Saturday, November 1, 2026, setting out guidance on how lawyers may bill for artificial intelligence. The report treats the cost of buying and maintaining AI software as overhead, which may be passed to clients as a disbursement only when it is tied to a specific client matter and the basis for the charge has been disclosed. It also says lawyers generally need not tell clients about AI use for administrative tasks such as word processing, spelling and grammar checks, calendaring or timekeeping, provided that use does not affect fees. Reporting on the guidance appeared on November 3, 2026, in the Law360 account cited by the ABA Journal.

The guidance responds to a broader concern that AI is changing the economics of legal work, particularly the reliance on billable hours. One source argues that firms have long tied revenue to the number of hours worked, and that AI can produce research, drafts and structured analysis in seconds, weakening the link between time and revenue. That source suggests firms may shift toward hybrid pricing such as flat fees and value-based arrangements, and toward distributing evaluative judgment to junior lawyers, who would check AI outputs at the start of a workflow rather than through several layers of review. The same source ties this to attorney well-being, citing a 2024 Bloomberg Law survey in which 56% of respondents reported disrupted sleep and 48% reported trouble focusing on work tasks, and it proposes that firms train lawyers to self-regulate their mental, emotional and physical states as a professional skill.

The report also raises further risks. It warns that biased training data can deepen existing inequities, and that confidentiality may be compromised if an AI tool carries one client's information into another client's matter, in which case the New York Rules of Professional Conduct apply. It cautions against automated tools that could amount to unauthorized practice, and against using AI to pass as a human with prospective clients. Supervising lawyers remain responsible for their subordinates' compliance, and the report advises that a firm-approved tool or policy does not remove the need to review work on each matter. State Bar President Taa Grays said in a statement that the guidelines are meant to help attorneys use AI responsibly and ethically and to avoid pitfalls such as practicing in a jurisdiction where they are not licensed or failing to notify clients or courts of AI use.

stories.Headline: Brazilian court blocks Meta from using news content to train AI
stories.Summary:
A Brazilian court has blocked Meta from using news content to train its artificial intelligence systems. The ruling was reported on October 28, 2026, in coverage that also described a separate Meta terms change affecting users in the UK and EU. The court action concerns news material, while the terms update covers content from business accounts and connected websites. Meta had said it could use such content to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of its products.

The terms update was originally set to take effect on October 30, but Meta moved the date to November 20 after backlash. Meta then removed the word train from a list of allowed uses and limited those uses to advertising and business products, according to Nieman Lab. The earlier wording had covered all Meta products. The articles do not give the name of the Brazilian court, the judge, or the exact scope of the order.

Users in the UK and EU can object to certain uses of their information under the General Data Protection Regulation, which became enforceable in 2018, and the AI Act, which took effect in 2024. The UK has its own version of the GDPR. Instagram users bookish.sil and jenniqueart posted walkthroughs of objecting through the privacy center, and both said Meta approved their objections. A 404 Media reporter using a VPN found the objection options only when located in London or Belgium, and one form returned an error saying it was available only in certain regions.

The European Commission says the GDPR applies to personal data about individuals and not to data about companies, though company information can count as personal data if it identifies a person. The articles do not say what Meta argued in the Brazilian case or how the company responded to the ruling. They also do not say what the court order requires beyond blocking the use of news content for training. Unless something changes before November 20, the articles say, users outside the UK and EU do not have the objection steps.

Business Council of Australia chief executive Bran Black said that people who fearmonger about AI or hype it up were doing the country a disservice. Assistant minister Andrew Charlton also cautioned against confusing volatility in technology stocks with the long-term benefits AI can bring.

The business leaders are asking for speed rather than a specific set of new rules, and the articles do not describe the details of any policy under consideration. Their concern is that delay or restrictive measures could slow Australian adoption while competitors move ahead. Charlton's remarks suggest the government is weighing short-term market swings against the longer-term economic case for the technology. The companies named in the coverage are Wesfarmers, Telstra and BHP, and the Business Council of Australia is also among those voicing the call. Black and Charlton are the two individuals quoted. The articles present their positions as a push for a timely framework that supports growth, with Black criticising commentary that exaggerates AI's risks or benefits. Other than these statements, the reporting does not record the government's formal response.

A separate report from BusinessKorea, dated November 4, 2026, shows that AI is also being discussed in regional trade forums. Korea's Minister for Trade, Park Jung-sung, proposed at the 37th APEC Ministerial Meeting on Foreign Affairs and Trade that AI be used to improve the efficiency of customs clearance, and that supply chain information be shared more quickly during disruptions. The results are expected to be presented at the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting later this month. The articles do not say what Australia's own policy timetable will be.

stories.Headline: UNESCO, Brazilian Government and ITU partner to launch green AI Climate Institute
stories.Summary:
UNESCO, the Government of Brazil and the International Telecommunication Union formed a partnership to establish the Artificial Intelligence Climate Institute, known as AICI. The institute was announced at COP30 in Belém, and its vision was unveiled there on 11 November 2025. It will be hosted by Brazil's National Telecommunications Agency, Anatel, within the ITU's Green Digital Action Hub in Brasília. An inaugural workshop was held in Manaus on 4 August 2026 to help finalise the institute's operational structure.

The partners committed to a two-year operational roadmap for 2026 to 2027 that focuses on country-led capacity development. Its activities combine training for public officials on data governance and climate policy with practical technical support for local developers and data scientists. The roadmap also envisages a shared digital learning repository with open environmental datasets, climate-specific AI model architectures and guidance for low-connectivity, resource-constrained environments. The measures aim to help developing countries keep greater control over their data and build expertise to develop and maintain their own climate models.

The institute draws on UNESCO's 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence and its Open Science framework to guide responsible AI development. Brazil's Anatel provides institutional hosting for the AICI Secretariat and steers regional cooperation. The ITU brings technical expertise in telecommunications and digital infrastructure, with links to the ITU Academy and the AI Skills Coalition. UNESCO grounds the institute's curriculum and projects in its ethics recommendation and open science framework, and it cites a joint UNESCO-UCL study showing that task-specific models and optimised prompts can cut AI energy consumption by up to 90%.

The founding partners are scheduled to launch the institute's operational phase on 16 November 2026 in Antalya, Türkiye, at COP31. The launch is expected to present the approved 2026 to 2027 work plan and showcase pilot applications, including AI-based deforestation prevention in the Amazon Basin. It will also open membership to governments, research institutions and international financing partners committed to sustainable digital transformation. The institute aims to help developing nations design, deploy and govern their own ethical, resource-efficient AI solutions for climate action.

To speed up construction, Anthropic hired data center experts and bought data center equipment. The company explored converting old coal plants and factories into data centers and considered deals for tiny amounts of computing power.

The articles do not say what happens next with the Riot deal or when it might close. They place the agreement within Anthropic's wider effort to obtain more computing power for its growing ambitions. stories.Headline: Amazon Owns a $6.2 Billion Piece of Anthropic's AI Boom — Here's What's at Stake
stories.Summary:
Amazon holds $6.2 billion in outstanding convertible notes issued to Anthropic, according to Anthropic's IPO filing, and the entire amount came from notes issued to Amazon Web Services under agreements dating back to 2023 and 2024. The filing reported the debt as of June 30, 2026. Amazon's September-quarter filing put the estimated fair value of those notes at $146.2 billion as of Sept. 30, up from $97.9 billion in June. Amazon also reported $92.5 billion in Anthropic nonvoting preferred stock, compared with $14.8 billion at the end of 2025.

The notes would convert into approximately 184 million shares of nonvoting preferred stock, before applying the ownership cap. Amazon's conversion rights come with a 12% ownership cap, which it can waive, and any notes that cannot convert without crossing that threshold can remain outstanding and convert later as room becomes available. Amazon has also invested directly in Anthropic's preferred stock, and it has made available a $15 billion financing facility tied to compute-capacity milestones, according to Anthropic's filing. Anthropic has committed to spending more than $100 billion on AWS technologies over 10 years under an expanded agreement announced in April, a deal that secures up to five gigawatts of computing capacity and includes Amazon's custom Trainium chips.

The article attributes the figures to Anthropic's IPO filing and Amazon's own SEC and quarterly filings, and it describes the fair-value numbers as accounting estimates rather than cash proceeds or guaranteed IPO gains. It says the structure means Amazon's full position may not turn into shares at once. Anthropic also said more than 100,000 customers use Claude on Amazon Bedrock. The article says the risk is that Anthropic's enormous compute needs and future financing requirements remain substantial, while Amazon has positioned itself to capture value across multiple layers of the AI boom.

stories.Headline: Lawyers offer recommendations on proposed AI ethics opinion
stories.Summary:
A Florida Bar committee that is drafting an advisory opinion on artificial intelligence asked for public comments, and eight attorneys had submitted them by November 3. The Special Committee on Artificial Intelligence Tools and Resources requested the opinion earlier this year, and the Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics posted a public notice on October 15. No draft is available yet, but the notice said the opinion may cover lawyers' use of agentic AI tools, AI tools for recording, transcribing and summarizing communications, advice to clients about their own AI use, and updates to Florida Ethics Opinion 24-1. The comments came from lawyers including Nathan Nevins of Gainesville, Ryan Enage, Arianna Mendez of Hialeah, Jason K. Castro and others.

Nevins, a partner at Sunshine State Probate who was admitted to the Bar in 2013, was the only commenter opposed to most lawyers' use of the technology. He recommended that attorney use of AI for anything other than legal research be "wholly banned," and said even research results should be double checked by each attorney. He warned that lawyers are sending AI-generated proposals to opponents and getting AI-generated responses back. Enage, a civil trial lawyer with Lloyd & McDaniel and a Bar member since 2022, pointed to this summer's Florida Supreme Court amendments to Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.515(d)(2), which state that by filing, a signer represents that the legal authorities cited exist and are accurately cited. He recommended that papers prepared with AI, whether by attorneys or unrepresented parties, indicate "Prepared with Assistance of Artificial Intelligence," similar to the "Prepared with the Assistance of Counsel" label Florida judges recommended in 2000.

Mendez, a Bar member since 2020 whose practice focuses mostly on commercial litigation, business transactions and real estate disputes, wrote that clients have brought her AI-generated legal advice and shared sensitive information with AI tools. She said this raised concerns about discovery, including what records clients are creating, what information they are disclosing and what may need to be preserved. She wrote that clients may mistakenly see their AI use as a private exchange and said she would welcome guidance on counseling clients about these risks, including requests for prompts, uploaded materials and responses. Castro, an attorney with Golden Gate Legal Center and a Bar member since 2015, observed that generative and agentic AI let lawyers research, prepare, compare and revise documents at a pace previously unimaginable, but warned the speed creates new opportunities for human error. He asked regulators not to confuse revision fatigue and version-control risks with intentional misconduct or reckless disregard, and said the circumstances, the reasonableness of the attorney's precautions and the response upon discovery should inform any assessment under the Bar's rules.

Florida Bar Ethics Counsel Jonathan Grabb said the Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics will review the comments and the proposed advisory opinion at a December 10 meeting. Grabb said the committee could proceed with the draft as proposed, modify it, withdraw it, or take other action such as forming a subcommittee. Once a draft is proposed, it will be noticed in the Bar News before the Board of Governors considers it. A separate item in an Above the Law legal ethics roundup reported that Keith Swisher won the 2026 Warren E. Burger Prize for a paper, "The Moral Gaps in Legal Machines," arguing that legal machines cannot be ethical or accountable and need close human supervision. The same roundup noted that the New York State Bar Association's House of Delegates adopted a report titled "Legal Ethics Guidelines for Lawyers' Use of Artificial Intelligence."

Articles.Title: Lawyers offer recommendations on proposed AI ethics opinion - The Florida Bar

stories.Headline: Lunchtime webinar on AI and ethics in law
stories.Summary:
The Law Society Professional Training is organising a lunchtime webinar on AI and ethics for legal practitioners. The event takes place on Wednesday 11 November from 1pm to 2pm. It is worth one CPD hour for client care and professional standards, covering accounting and AML compliance. It is part of the Regulation Matters series of webinars looking at key regulatory issues affecting solicitors.

This is the fourth webinar in the 2026 series and is focused on professional standards and ethical issues affecting the use of AI by legal professionals. Registration is still open. The event is presented by Sorcha Hayes, head of practice regulation, practice closures, and complaints and client relations at the Law Society. Her unit is responsible for distressed practice closures, practising certificates, professional indemnity insurance, practice commencements and cessations, certificates of good standing and attestation, the Register of Orders, registered European lawyers, practice names, practice notepaper, historic complaints, and guidance and ethics.

She also serves as secretary of the Law Society's Professional Indemnity Insurance Committee. The article does not say what Hayes will say in the webinar. It gives no further details on the content beyond the focus on professional standards and ethical issues affecting the use of AI. It does not say what happens after the event.

Articles.Title: Lunchtime webinar on AI and ethics in law

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s $1.5 Trillion IPO Faces Investor Doubts as AI Spending Bill Soars
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is preparing for a stock market debut that could become one of the largest technology IPOs in history, and the plan is facing investor scrutiny. The company behind the Claude AI platform is dealing with concerns about its enormous valuation, slowing revenue growth and almost US$900 billion in AI infrastructure commitments. According to reports, some investors are now considering a valuation of around US$1.5 trillion, which is approximately A$2.14 trillion, down from expectations close to US$2 trillion. The concerns follow the release of Anthropic’s latest financial figures, which showed revenue expanding rapidly but growth slowing while infrastructure costs rise.

According to Reuters, Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue rose 47% quarter-on-quarter to US$16.96 billion, a substantial slowdown from the 144% sequential growth recorded in the second quarter. The company reported a net loss of US$23.29 billion for the quarter, narrower than its US$66.3 billion loss in the previous quarter, and an operating loss of US$567 million. Anthropic has approximately US$895.4 billion in commitments tied to AI infrastructure development, including computing capacity, data centres and cloud services, and almost half of that spending is expected before the end of 2030. The company also recorded an additional US$5 billion in computing costs during the quarter.

Anthropic is planning an international retail share offer that will include Australian investors, with CommSec, Bell Potter, LGT Wealth, Macquarie, Morgans, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, Sharesies and Stake among the institutions expected to participate. The company is not planning to list on the Australian Securities Exchange and has applied to list its Class A shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the proposed ticker symbol ANT. The Australian retail offer is expected to be made under a prospectus lodged with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. Anthropic has cautioned that the participating broker list is specific to the proposed offering and advised investors to wait for the official prospectus before making any decisions.

The proposed listing could become an important test of investor confidence in the AI sector more broadly, as technology companies have committed enormous sums to AI infrastructure and investors increasingly question whether AI revenue will justify the capital expenditure. Anthropic’s dependence on major cloud infrastructure providers, including Amazon and Google’s parent company Alphabet, adds complexity, since both are investors in Anthropic but also supply computing infrastructure and compete in the AI market. Rival AI developer OpenAI is also considering a major stock market listing. Anthropic’s debut could provide an early indication of how much investors are prepared to pay for the future of the technology.

Articles.Title: Anthropic’s $1.5 Trillion IPO Faces Investor Doubts as AI Spending Bill Soars

stories.Headline: India’s AI regulation consultation paper nearing completion: Report
stories.Summary:
India's government is close to finishing a consultation paper on artificial intelligence regulation and expects to ask the public for feedback soon, according to a report by Moneycontrol cited by Storyboard18. A senior government official said the government studied regulatory frameworks used in other countries and held talks with several stakeholders, including academics, while preparing the document. Union Electronics and Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw first announced the planned consultation on October 8, saying the government intended to publish the paper within a month and naming AI safety as a key focus. On October 23 he said the document would be released in the coming weeks and that the government would invite responses from citizens, businesses and AI users.

The consultation is expected to cover AI safety, the spread of deepfakes and the possible psychological impact of the technology on users. It will also look at skilling requirements and ways to make the gains from AI accessible to a wider section of society. The paper is expected to examine accountability, copyright, data protection, deepfake detection and institutional mechanisms as India considers a broader framework for AI governance. Vaishnaw also indicated that the scale of emerging AI-related risks warranted consideration of legislative measures and additional regulations.

The exercise builds on the India AI Governance Guidelines released in November 2025, which set out seven guiding principles for developing and deploying AI, including human oversight wherever feasible, accountability in proportion to potential harm and transparency for users and regulators. The committee that drafted the guidelines found that several AI-related risks could be addressed through existing legislation, but recommended examining gaps in the legal framework, particularly around accountability when AI systems cause harm, the application of data protection requirements to AI development and copyright issues involving material used to train AI models. The guidelines also called for uniform mechanisms to establish the origin and authenticity of digital content, especially amid growing concerns over deepfakes. On the institutional side, the framework proposed an AI Governance Group to coordinate policymaking across government departments, backed by a Technology and Policy Expert Committee, and recommended an AI Safety Institute to support research and testing.

Articles.Title: India’s AI regulation consultation paper nearing completion: Report

stories.Headline: Alphabet (GOOGL) Commits $15 Billion To Malaysia As AI Lawsuit Lands
stories.Summary:
Alphabet plans to invest US$15 billion to expand Google data centers and AI infrastructure in Malaysia, the company announced. The buildout includes new facilities to support AI services in Southeast Asia, along with sustainability and workforce programs. Shareholders have also filed a lawsuit alleging that Google trained AI models, including Lyria music tools, on copyrighted material without permission. The article frames both the Malaysia data center push and the AI copyright lawsuit as only part of what matters for Alphabet today.

The Malaysia plan covers new facilities for AI services in Southeast Asia, plus sustainability and workforce programs. The article says Alphabet has also issued multiple euro denominated bonds, including notes maturing from 2028 out to 2045. It says the US$15 billion buildout points to Alphabet using its balance sheet and access to debt markets to keep pushing AI capacity without relying only on near term cash generation. The article says the lawsuit alleges Google trained AI models, including Lyria music tools, on copyrighted material without permission.

The article does not name the shareholders who filed the lawsuit or give a court or filing date for it. It says the Narrative the market trades on hinges on Alphabet turning large AI infrastructure and custom TPU investment into durable demand for Gemini and Google Cloud while managing pressure on free cash flow. It says the US$15 billion regional data center push and the copyright lawsuit both reinforce the same tension, between big AI spend on one side and mounting legal and regulatory risks on the other. It points to a US$408 fair value figure tied to how these catalysts shape Alphabet's path.

The article says the clearest sign of whether the AI story is working will be whether Google Cloud and AI related revenue, including the AI weighted backlog already referenced by analysts, keep scaling fast enough to cover rising depreciation and interest costs from bonds and data centers. It says quarterly updates on Cloud margins and group free cash flow will be the key checkpoints, especially through 2027 when capex is flagged to rise. It describes Alphabet as running global search, video, cloud and advertising platforms across regions that include the US and Asia-Pacific. It says large AI data center projects and legal disputes over training data both sit close to how its core services are built and delivered.

Articles.Title: Alphabet (GOOGL) Commits $15 Billion To Malaysia As AI Lawsuit Lands

stories.Headline: Markets overreacting to AI regulation fears after US elections, says Roundhill Investments strategist
stories.Summary:
Global markets appear to be overreacting to fears of tighter artificial intelligence regulation after a strong Democratic showing in the US elections, according to Drew Pettit, Chief Investment Strategist at Roundhill Investments. Pettit said the Democratic performance exceeded polling expectations. He argued that corporate earnings and business fundamentals, not political outcomes, will keep driving stocks. He also said the chance of sweeping policy change remains low. Pettit said Democrats do not hold the two-thirds majority in both houses of Congress needed to advance major legislative changes.

He noted that Donald Trump has indicated he will veto new bills. Pettit said markets seem to be pricing in a Democratic president after Trump, which he described as getting ahead of developments. He said he has never made money trading politics and makes money by trading fundamentals and what businesses do. Opposition to data centre expansion is not purely partisan, and both Republicans and Democrats have raised concerns about the pace of development. Moratoriums on new data centres are already in place in Texas, where the governorship is Republican-controlled.

Pettit argued that a full reversal of the AI trade based on election results alone would require a complete sweep of Congress, the Senate and the White House, which he said the current political arithmetic does not support. He noted that voters remain focused on inflation, affordability and the war in Iran. Pettit referenced historical US market behaviour, noting that rallies have occurred in the months following each of the last 19 midterm elections since World War II. He stressed that as long as business resilience and earnings revisions remain strong, the passing of the midterms should support equity performance rather than undermine it. The article says India's AI-linked technology sector and global institutional investors track US regulatory signals closely when making capital allocation decisions.

Articles.Title: Markets overreacting to AI regulation fears after US elections, says Roundhill Investments strategist

stories.Headline: Bill Gates freezes everyone: 4 jobs AI will never steal
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates, the Microsoft co-founder, published a forecast on 4 November 2026 about which jobs artificial intelligence will not take over. He named four fields: programming, biology, the energy sector and professional sports. The article was written by Carolina Vivianti for redhotcyber.com. Gates said algorithms and robots will be able to handle a significant share of the work people do today.

In programming, Gates said AI can already generate code, find bugs and automate routine tasks, but developers are still needed to configure and fine-tune the systems AI builds. They also handle infrastructure, security and integration. In biology, AI can analyze large amounts of data, find patterns and model processes, but research also means asking questions, testing hypotheses, running experiments and interpreting results. Energy workers are needed because the sector runs critical infrastructure that homes, businesses, hospitals and transport depend on, and people must inspect equipment and respond to emergencies. Professional sport is the fourth field, because its value lies in human abilities, emotions and the spectacle of competition, and Gates said spectators are unlikely to want to watch computers play baseball.

Gates is responsible for the forecast, and the article paraphrases his view that people will still be in demand in these professions even with widespread use of new technology. He said AI could take on much of the work in manufacturing, goods transportation and food production. He also said the scenario does not mean all professions outside his list will disappear. The impact will depend on specific tasks, technological capabilities and how fast companies adopt automation, which for some workers could mean less routine work and for others the need to learn new skills or change specialization.

The article sets this against AI's growing role in writing texts, analyzing data and creating images, and against concerns that algorithms could replace part of a company's workforce and that some specializations risk disappearing in their current form. It gives no date for when Gates made the forecast beyond the article's own publication. It does not say what happens next beyond the dependence on tasks, technology and the pace of automation. It ends by pointing readers to the site's Google News page and newsletter for updates.

Articles.Title: Bill Gates freezes everyone: 4 jobs AI will never steal

stories.Headline: Ansari Wants a Day-1 AI Pause; Her Bill Sets a 10^25 Line
stories.Summary:
Rep. Yassamin Ansari, the Arizona Democrat whose re-election the Associated Press called on 3 November, posted on X at 18:54 UTC on 4 November that a pause on advanced AI development should top the Democratic agenda on day 1. Her post names no bill, but she is one of ten House members named on H.R. 10538, the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026, introduced on 24 September. Rep. Greg Casar introduced that bill, and the post and the bill use the same core idea of pausing advanced AI development. Ansari's post was published the day after the Associated Press called her race, and it drew 545,297 views by 00:10 UTC on 5 November.

The bill, as introduced, would create a Department of Artificial Intelligence and set a pause on systems trained with 10^25 or more integer or floating point operations. Under its definitions, a system under the pause may not be trained, modified or fine-tuned, and no unreleased system may be deployed during that period. The pause has no fixed end date and lasts until the Secretary determines that the Department is fully staffed and has issued rules covering pre-deployment approval, monitoring and auditing. Penalties include a fine and up to 20 years in prison for policymaking individuals or rogue actors who recklessly violate it. By the reading offered in the coverage, the introduced text contains no provision on data centers.

Casar's release of 23 September describes the measure as pausing advanced AI development until a federal AI regulatory body is operating. Ansari made a similar call at a 9 September press conference in Phoenix, where she said there should be an immediate pause on further AI development by major companies because they are not regulating themselves. She also called for banning artificial superintelligence until Congress can regulate the field. Her post came as the coverage placed the pause debate alongside local ballot limits on data centers, a separate track that targets facilities rather than model training.

The coverage presents this as one of two different pauses now in the debate, local data center limits and a federal model-training pause. The bill's future is not established by the articles, which note that a post on X sets out a position rather than a party plan. Nothing in the coverage establishes which agenda the next Congress will take up or whether H.R. 10538 will advance. The articles report the race result as an Associated Press call that has not been certified.

Articles.Title: Ansari Wants a Day-1 AI Pause; Her Bill Sets a 10^25 Line

stories.Headline: IREN Shares Drop 10% Amid Fears of AI Regulation and Construction Delays
stories.Summary:
IREN Ltd. shares fell 10.06% to $22.00 on Wednesday, reaching a fresh 52-week low, according to Benzinga Pro data. The drop came amid a broader decline in AI cloud stocks after Democratic midterm gains. Democrats now hold both chambers of Congress. Traders fear tighter regulation will delay data center construction and limit AI infrastructure expansion.

In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott after promising tighter construction restrictions, starting with an immediate statewide freeze. Wells Fargo estimates Texas will account for 27% of the gigawatts planned for U.S. data centers. Georgia accounts for 7% of planned capacity, while Pennsylvania and Ohio each account for 5%. Democrats won or retained the governorships in Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio, and those states plus Texas represent about 44% of planned capacity.

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co wrote Wednesday that Democratic gains should slow U.S. data center construction in the coming years. He named Texas as a particular concern and called Hinojosa a known opponent of data centers. He wrote that Democratic control of the Senate should make AI legislation harder. However, he said President Donald Trump's veto threats may push technology executives to negotiate with Congress.

AI stocks were already under pressure before the election results, and the Nasdaq-100 entered correction territory in late October.
