The House bill would define advanced AI as systems trained with at least 10²⁵ operations, adjustable annually, and would pause covered development until the department was staffed and its rules were set. Violators could face fines, up to 20 years in prison, or a 10-year industry ban.

Neither bill has become law, and both remain in committee, the House bill with the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and the Senate bill with the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. The Trump administration has taken a different approach, with Executive Order 14409, signed on 2 June 2026, rejecting heavy regulation and mandatory pre-release licensing while still addressing national security risks from advanced AI. Supporters of stricter controls argue safeguards are needed before capabilities outpace oversight, while critics warn that slowing development could weaken US competitiveness. Ansari has not yet set out a detailed timetable or explained how a pause would be enforced.

Articles.Title: Democrat Wants AI Development Paused and Superintelligence Banned as Party Wins Congress - www.techtimes.co.uk

stories.Headline: To save Australia’s economy, Albanese must share the AI gains and budget pains
stories.Summary:
The Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates again this week, and POLITICO columnist Paul Karp argues that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese now faces a difficult bind. Governor Michele Bullock named domestic demand, rather than the Middle East war, as the reason for the increase, which undercut the government's attempt to blame inflation on outside forces. Labor holds 94 of the 150 lower house seats but won only 34 percent of the primary vote at the 2025 election, and that support has slipped further since. The federal election is due by 2028, and Karp warns that voters struggling with living costs could cost Albanese his majority.

Karp says the government has renewed its search for budget savings so that fiscal policy can help bring inflation and, eventually, interest rates down. Such savings are hard to win, however, because the Coalition, One Nation and the Greens have blocked a series of proposals, including changes to the private health insurance rebate, veterans' allied health entitlements and aged care fees. The Sydney Morning Herald reported that the mid-year economic and fiscal update in December will focus on savings that do not need Senate approval. Karp notes that this includes plans to roll out artificial intelligence in the public sector despite opposition from public sector unions.

Karp argues that the government should share the gains from artificial intelligence and data centers with the people who bear the costs. He points to New South Wales Treasurer Daniel Mookhey, who told an audience in April that AI tools in planning are a win-win if everyone can share in the added prosperity. Karp suggests that public servants could receive above-inflation wages in exchange for productivity tools that slow or shrink the public sector, and he cites the Maritime Union of Australia's acceptance of automation in return for shorter hours and voluntary redundancies as a model. He also says data centers should offer local benefits, as landowners already receive payments for transmission lines and wind farms, and he notes that government rules requiring data centers to bring their own power and contribute locally are a start.

Karp contends that reform creates losers, and that Labor has succeeded before by bringing winners and losers together to agree on how to share pain and benefits. He cites the national summits and Accords of the 1980s, which he credits with delivering 158 quarters of economic growth out of 170 since 1984. He notes that Albanese's government has tried similar tactics through reallocating tax cuts and adjusting property and income taxes in the 2026 budget. Karp says that raising the goods and services tax and cutting income tax would share gains more widely, but Labor has ruled that option out, so the government must find another route or remain stuck in its current rut. More to follow.

Articles.Title: To save Australia’s economy, Albanese must share the AI gains and budget pains

stories.Headline: AI data centers drive nuclear energy revival, $50 billion investment by 2029
stories.Summary:
Data center operators and nuclear developers are driving a revival in the nuclear energy sector, according to a report from Data Center Knowledge carried by ET Datacenters on November 5, 2026. Research firm Industrial Info Resource (IIR) estimates that new nuclear project spending will reach about $20 billion in 2026 and almost $50 billion by 2029, after investment began rising in 2024. Between late 2026 and 2029, IIR expects $68.3 billion for new nuclear plants and another $30 billion for expanding, maintaining, or revamping existing facilities. Canada, particularly Ontario and Alberta, is expected to account for roughly $40 billion of this spending, followed by Texas with $15 billion and Tennessee with $10 billion.

The Department of Energy has offered Constellation Energy a loan of up to $5 billion to support uprates and modernization at eight plants in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania, which could add over 1 GW to the grid. The department also launched a program this year to fund 2.5 GW of additional nuclear capacity by 2027 and 5 GW by 2029. Hyperscalers are taking part directly: Amazon is working with American Electric Power and X-energy on a 1 GW small modular reactor project in Indiana, Microsoft has a 20-year power purchase agreement with Constellation for output from the refurbished Three Mile Island plant, now called the Crane Clean Energy Center, and Google is working with NextEra Energy Resources to restart the Duane Arnold Energy Center, which closed in 2020. More than 100 nuclear projects are underway across North America, including 61 involving small modular reactors and 11 focused on new conventional reactors.

IIR analyst Britt Burt said investment is rising for new and existing nuclear assets during the sector's revival, and noted that nuclear offers operational reliability, zero emissions, and insulation from fuel price volatility. Cameron Hughes, an associate at the law firm Orrick, said regulatory reforms have cut key Nuclear Regulatory Commission review timelines to about 18 months, and that modularization and factory fabrication could shorten deployment schedules after the first commercial projects are built. Romi Mahajan, CEO of ExoFusion, said the nuclear renaissance depends on aligning science, engineering, capital, political will, and a skilled workforce. Fusion remains further off: Matthias Knolker of General Atomics Magnetic Fusion Energy said grid-connected commercial fusion demonstration plants may not emerge until the mid-2030s, with gigawatt-scale deployments possibly in the early 2040s. The article indicates that small modular reactors and restarts of old plants are more likely than fusion to deliver capacity for data centers in the near term.

Articles.Title: AI data centers drive nuclear energy revival, $50 billion investment by 2029 - ET Datacenters

stories.Headline: BILL Slashes Underwriting Times From 3 Hours to 12 Minutes With AI
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence agents are saving BILL's teams more than 1,400 hours per month, which is equivalent to about eight full-time employees. BILL CEO and founder René Lacerte said this on Thursday, November 5, 2026, during the company's first quarter fiscal year 2027 earnings call. The savings come from more than 100 AI agents that his risk team built over the past year to perform work around the clock across several functions. Lacerte said these agents complete defined tasks on their own, such as pulling case files, drafting credit assessments and writing model documentation.

Lacerte highlighted three agents that work together as a suite called Robin to handle underwriting cases. Robin routes each case to the right underwriter, pulls the customer's data into a summary and offers a one-click link to make a decision. Previously, an underwriter had to assemble each case through chat messages, email and separate dashboards. Lacerte said each case now takes about 12 minutes instead of three hours, which he described as faster, better and more personalized service for small and medium-sized businesses. He also said the company launched five products during the quarter and built a Visa pilot in four weeks.

Lacerte said the company's AI-powered Chat with BILL now handles 45% of customer support conversations. He also said the company's restructuring during its fiscal year 2026 was designed to accelerate its transformation into an AI-native company. Earlier, PYMNTS reported that in May Lacerte had said BILL planned to cut its workforce by 30% by the end of that quarter as it sharpened its focus on AI. Weeks later, he said the company had overhauled its leadership team as part of that transformation. Lacerte presented the first quarter progress as an early indication that the strategy is working.

Articles.Title: BILL Slashes Underwriting Times From 3 Hours to 12 Minutes With AI

stories.Headline: AIMG® Sizes AI Governance Platforms Market at $12.5 Billion by 2030; Microsoft, Databricks and Salesforce Top AI LeaderMap®
stories.Summary:
AI Markets Group published a special report on AI governance platforms on November 4, 2026. The firm estimates the market for software that approves, constrains and evidences enterprise AI use at $3.6 billion in 2027. It expects that figure to rise to $12.5 billion by 2030, a 51% compound annual growth rate. The report says the binding constraint is now enforcement rather than policy.

The report gives several numbers on adoption and gaps. It says 98% of organizations maintain AI data-access policies, and 96.5% of large US public companies have adopted AI governance policies. Yet 86% of IT leaders saw AI tools or agents access sensitive data beyond their intended scope last year, and 46.3% of senior AI executives report bypasses. Stand-alone platforms reach $1.57 billion by 2030, with the rest bought within hyperscaler, security and identity platforms. Agent governance and non-human identity grows fastest, at 81% a year.

Peyman Mestchian, the AIMG Chair, said almost every large organization has a responsible AI policy but far fewer can show it was applied to a specific agent when it acted. He said governance is becoming a control plane, and vendors that own the enforcement points will capture most of the value. The AIMG AI LeaderMap ranks 36 vendors, with Microsoft leading, followed by Databricks, Salesforce, Google, Palo Alto Networks and ServiceNow. Credo AI reaches the Frontier band.

The EU Digital Omnibus delayed high-risk deadlines to December 2027 and August 2028 but did not remove them. AIMG expects most stand-alone specialists to be acquired or merged by 2028. Spend per enterprise more than doubles, from $1.5 million in 2027 to $3.4 million by 2030 for adopting Global 2000 firms. AIMG advises buyers to link a single AI inventory to runtime guardrails and agent identity before the 2027 EU deadlines.

Articles.Title: AIMG® Sizes AI Governance Platforms Market at $12.5 Billion by 2030; Microsoft, Databricks and Salesforce Top AI LeaderMap®

stories.Headline: Family Offices Fear Risk Of Joining AI "Gold Rush" – Law Firm
stories.Summary:
Family offices have felt pressure to adopt AI tools but worry that joining an AI "gold rush" is risky without fully testing the technology, Gwen Williamson of the international law firm Faegre Drinker told Family Wealth Report in an article published on November 4, 2026. Her comments reflected on the 2026 Global Family Office Report from Citi Wealth, issued in September. Williamson leads the firm's investment structuring, compliance and regulatory management work and advises on single and multi family offices and pooled investment vehicles. She raised concerns about privacy and control over data, asking who does due diligence when family information goes into an AI tool and where that information ends up.

The Citi Wealth report said family offices are deploying AI across investment analysis, information management, reporting, workflow automation and decision support. In its survey of more than 350 family offices worldwide, 90 per cent reported positive portfolio returns since the start of 2026, and 41 per cent were still targeting annual returns of 7 to 10 per cent. Family offices avoided wholesale portfolio repositioning, choosing active money management, hedging strategies and targeted changes amid geopolitical turmoil. Williamson said AI stocks have boosted equities so far this year, but there is "extraordinary uncertainty" in policymaking, including what happens if or when a different administration takes office. Her comments came ahead of the US mid-term elections being held that day.

Williamson said large financial institutions have worked on their own internal technology systems for years, and the focus is now moving from automation to generative AI, with agentic AI fairly far advanced. She said AI regulation requires a human in the loop, and if a regulated entity must keep records, a transcript goes onto the record automatically and a human has to look at it. She noted that if humans need to monitor AI to that degree, it adds to processes. The article did not say what happens next beyond those points.

A separate article by Richard Tromans in Artificial Lawyer, published on November 2, 2026, explored whether AI will change the identity of law firm partners. It described a keynote at ClioCon in Boston in October 2026 by writer and philosopher Malcolm Gladwell, who argued that people resist new ideas when those ideas change their sense of professional self. Gladwell used examples of less invasive robotic heart bypass surgery and data-led, community-based policing in Boston, both of which worked but were largely ignored because they altered the roles of surgeons and senior police officers. The article said partners remain rainmakers with client relationships and legal expertise, but their absolute authority is diluted somewhat by AI, as associates and clients use AI too and more work becomes automated. It asked how many partners will embrace this shift and how many will refuse to adopt anything that changes their professional identity.

Articles.Title: Family Offices Fear Risk Of Joining AI "Gold Rush" – Law Firm

stories.Headline: MARA Holdings (MARA) Commits Billions To AI Power, Is It 63% Below Fair Value?
stories.Summary:
MARA Holdings has committed about US$1.5 billion to buy the Long Ridge gas plant and roughly US$600 million for Texas land, the articles say. The company is pushing into AI infrastructure while its revenue and digital asset values decline. Its share price has fallen sharply, with a 1-month return down 38.5% and a year to date return down 30.7%. The 1-year total shareholder return has fallen 59.9%.

The company is building a powered land and data center portfolio of roughly 4.8 GW, anchored by the Long Ridge campus and the planned Matagorda County site. The portfolio could support future AI and high performance computing leases that add new revenue streams. MARA closed at $6.87, while the most followed valuation view puts fair value near $18.61. That view sees the stock as 63% undervalued, and 164 investors share it.

The articles say the narrative can break if MARA keeps posting large losses tied to Bitcoin. They also say it can break if the company struggles to convert its 4.8 GW power portfolio into signed AI leases. The articles describe two important warning signs and key risks to the narrative. They present the bullish fair value story and the headwinds as a normal tension for investors to weigh.

The articles say MARA is rebranding and focusing on AI infrastructure alongside increased Bitcoin backed borrowing and recent power asset deals. They describe the gap between price and narrative as wide and rooted in how the power portfolio might translate into contracts and cash flow. They advise reviewing the underlying numbers and weighing them against the warning signs. They do not say what happens next beyond that.

Articles.Title: MARA Holdings (MARA) Commits Billions To AI Power, Is It 63% Below Fair Value?

stories.Headline: AI May Speed Up Legal Research, But That Doesn’t Automatically Shrink The Bill
stories.Summary:
A unanimous Tenth Circuit panel affirmed a $114,663.11 fee award to the law firm Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck. The ruling came after Flux Drive’s trade secrets suit was dismissed. Flux Drive had argued that the firm’s use of AI and online research tools should have reduced its fees. Judge Carolyn McHugh wrote for the panel that plaintiffs had not shown the use of AI made the hours actually expended unreasonable.

The court said Flux Drive pointed to no specific inflated billing entry. The panel acknowledged that AI may reduce research time. It also noted that lawyers still must verify their authorities and arguments. The decision was issued on 2026-11-04, according to the Above the Law article.

Brownstein partner Christopher Ottele welcomed the ruling. He said AI is not a substitute for the judgment and analysis that attorneys still must exercise in court filings. Judge McHugh’s opinion was written for a unanimous panel. The article was written by Staci Zaretsky, the managing editor of Above the Law.

The article does not say what happens next beyond the ruling itself. It frames the case as a quote of the day feature. The panel’s reasoning ties any fee reduction to specific billing entries rather than to the use of AI alone. The article gives no further dates or names beyond those above.

Articles.Title: AI May Speed Up Legal Research, But That Doesn’t Automatically Shrink The Bill

stories.Headline: AI and The Future of Law, Health, Society, and Democracy - EPIC – Electronic Privacy Information Center
stories.Summary:
A town hall on artificial intelligence and its effects on law, health, society and democracy is scheduled for 19 November at 12:00 PM EDT. The O’Neill Institute organized it with the American Constitution Society, the Feminist Majority Foundation, Ms. magazine and other organizations. It will take place at Georgetown University’s downtown Capitol Campus, near the seat of government. Featured speakers include Representative Ted Lieu, Representative Jonathan Jackson, White House Correspondent Jon Decker and EPIC Executive Director and President Alan Butler. A reception will follow.

The event brings together lawmakers, civil society leaders, tech ethicists, legal experts and community advocates. It is meant to examine artificial intelligence in relation to democracy, the rule of law and social safety. The organizers list questions about whether AI can be used for good and at what cost. They also ask whether concerns and lawsuits about AI and youth addiction are overstated and isolated, and whether fears about data centers and environmental harms can be mitigated. Other questions cover which communities face the most risk of pollution and water safety problems from data centers, and what risks hacking poses to national security and privacy.

The announcement says the town hall raises these questions while AI developers and tech ethicists ring alarm bells. It asks whether their worries are overstated or are timely warnings that should be heeded now. It also asks who benefits from AI in health and who is harmed and left behind. The stated aim is for diverse voices to help understand the benefits and risks of artificial intelligence to law, society and democracy. EPIC is promoting the event and invites people to register.

The town hall is framed against warnings from AI developers and tech ethicists about the technology. The announcement does not say what the event will produce or what steps will follow it. It describes the gathering as putting forth important and urgent questions. The only stated follow-up is a reception after the town hall.

Articles.Title: AI and The Future of Law, Health, Society, and Democracy - EPIC – Electronic Privacy Information Center

stories.Headline: Clio Wants To Bring AI to the Judiciary, But 50-State Survey Reveals Policies Differ in Whether They Allow It - LawSites
stories.Summary:
Clio, the legal technology company, is pushing into the judiciary market by developing AI tools for judges and courts, and it has trademarked the phrase "judiciary-grade AI." The company hired Pablo Arredondo, a Casetext cofounder, as senior vice president for judiciary, and Bridget M. McCormack, a former Michigan Supreme Court chief justice, as general manager for judiciary. Clio also acquired Learned Hand, a startup that already sells AI built for judges and used in several courthouses. A survey of state policies reported by Robert Ambrogi of LawSites, with the findings current as of October 30, 2026, shows that whether judges can use AI at all depends heavily on where they sit.

The rules vary widely across the country, from detailed binding policies to advisory guidance to no statewide policy at all. Massachusetts has the most restrictive approach, banning judges, clerks, interns, and other court employees and contractors from using AI for legal research, legal writing, or other legal work under interim guidelines the Supreme Judicial Court adopted in November 2025. New York takes a more permissive path, allowing approved AI tools under set conditions and, in a September 2026 ethics opinion, recognizing the use of private AI to summarize transcripts of judicial proceedings. Rhode Island's guidance on AI is advisory rather than binding. Across the states, the policies agree on one point: judges may use AI to assist their work but cannot hand their decisionmaking to it, and they remain responsible for verifying citations and facts and for applying the law themselves.

The survey's author notes that the policies frequently forbid entering nonpublic case information, sealed material, internal deliberations, or personally identifying information into public chatbots. Several states, including Arizona, New York, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Utah, and Virginia, control which tools court personnel may use, and some require training, supervisory approval, or disclosure of AI use to the judge. Arizona's Supreme Court, in August 2026, declined a proposed categorical ban on judges using AI and instead chose to let judges test the tools in a controlled way. Ambrogi says the survey does not cover policies aimed at lawyers or litigants, and he invites corrections, since "not identified" in his chart may mean only that no policy was found. With Clio and others entering the market, he argues, the distinctions between permitted and prohibited uses will matter more.

Articles.Title: Clio Wants To Bring AI to the Judiciary, But 50-State Survey Reveals Policies Differ in Whether They Allow It - LawSites

stories.Headline: CLM Provider Leah Launches Self-Service AI Tool-Building Feature
stories.Summary:
Leah, a contract lifecycle management provider, announced on Thursday the launch of Harness Builder, a new self-service feature for building AI-powered tools. The feature lets customers create their own harnesses, which are the context, tools and controls that govern how large language models act within an application. Harness Builder works inside Leah Maestro, the company's AI agent orchestration layer. The announcement was reported on November 5, 2026. Harness Builder can generate a prototype from a plain language description, and human engineers then refine it through further iterations.

The company says the feature is meant to let customers build bespoke applications that carry enterprise-grade controls. It is intended to help users replace existing point solutions with tailored tools that fit their own needs. The articles do not give pricing, availability dates or customer numbers. Leah is the party responsible for the launch, and the articles report its announcement without naming any individual spokesperson.

The article describes the feature as designed to let users build applications suited to their specific needs. Other details about the company's plans were not included in the available text. The launch comes as legal technology providers push AI products into legal workflows, a theme that other coverage on the same site touched on in the days before. The articles do not say what comes next for Harness Builder or whether further updates are planned.

Articles.Title: CLM Provider Leah Launches Self-Service AI Tool-Building Feature - Law.com

stories.Headline: The Biggest Pro-AI Super PAC Network Didn’t Really Impact the Midterms
stories.Summary:
Leading the Future, the largest network of pro-AI super PACs, spent heavily on the 2026 midterms but ended with just over $20 million still in the bank, according to WIRED. The network entered the scene in August 2025 with a war chest of around $100 million from tech billionaires including Andreessen Horowitz, Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale, and OpenAI’s Greg Brockman. It was led by major political strategists and set up as a structured ecosystem of 501(c)(4) organizations and federal and state super PACs on both sides of the aisle. American Mission largely gives to Republicans, while Think Big largely gives to Democrats.

The donations went overwhelmingly to safe candidates, and the network spent about $26 million on the primaries alone before its spending tapered off ahead of the general election. It dropped about $10 million in total while backing safe races, and it reported zero donations in the second and third quarters. In New York’s 12th congressional district, it spent millions on attack ads against Democrat Alex Bores, a former Palantir engineer running on an AI safety platform, but he came second in a crowded primary to Micah Lasher. The pro-AI safety network Public First, backed significantly by Anthropic, spent $15 million boosting Bores.

In one of its biggest bets, American Mission donated more than $2 million to Darline Graham, the sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham, in South Carolina, and she lost with 46.5 percent. In North Carolina’s 1st congressional district, American Mission backed Republican Laurie Buckhout in her primary, and Democrat Don Davis, backed by the Guardrails Alliance, won. Leading the Future also backed Aaron Flint in Montana’s first congressional district, and he conceded to Democrat Sam Forstag, though the Associated Press has yet to call the race. American Mission Florida, a state-level super PAC in the network, got $3 million in support of Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds.

Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, said the network came out saying it would spend millions to influence how lawmakers legislate and to target them in primaries and reelection. Haworth said the purpose was to bully lawmakers into acquiescence and intimidate them from sticking their necks out on AI safety or tech industry regulation. Brad Carson, co-founder of Public First Action, said the midterms marked a victory for AI safety and called the results a crushing blow to the AI industry’s anti-regulatory efforts to buy a Congress that would look the other way. Leading the Future did not respond to requests for comment.

An NBC exit poll found that 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers played a major role in their vote, and stark polling showed widespread distrust of Big Tech and cronyism in Washington, DC. Haworth described backing safe candidates as an influence play aimed at ingratiating the network with incoming members of Congress. After Tuesday night, Silicon Valley is expected to brace for a reckoning over the expansive power and freedom it has enjoyed during Trump’s second term. Democrats have vowed to bring Big Tech bosses to Capitol Hill for hearings, and Senator Ron Wyden signaled what is to come in a statement on X, writing, “Subpoenas.”

Articles.Title: The Biggest Pro-AI Super PAC Network Didn’t Really Impact the Midterms

stories.Headline: Stacey Abrams on DEI, artificial intelligence and regulation ahead of Democrat midterm wins
stories.Summary:
On October 29, 2026, Stacey Abrams spoke by phone with the UWM Post ahead of the Wisconsin gubernatorial election, while she was in Wisconsin campaigning with David Crowley and attending canvass events in Milwaukee and Oak Creek. Abrams, a voting rights activist and former Democratic minority leader in the Georgia House of Representatives, was asked about diversity, equity and inclusion, artificial intelligence and regulation. The interview was published on November 5, 2026. The article does not describe a single event or action beyond the interview itself.

On the Wisconsin ballot question concerning DEI, Abrams said the measure is written to sound benign but would remove protections against discrimination. She argued that DEI covers laws that have expanded access to rights, and that a yes vote could bar the state legislature from correcting systemic discrimination. As an example, she described a disabled student who might lose the ability to seek enforcement of an Individualized Education Program through the federal Office for Civil Rights. On artificial intelligence, she said the technology is a tool whose use depends on the people controlling it, and she pointed to its potential to improve healthcare access. She also discussed the Milwaukee Common Council's one-year pause on data center construction, saying moratoriums give communities time to address costs and environmental effects and that data center decisions should include community input.

Abrams also addressed AI regulation at the state level, citing the call by AI executive Dario Amodei to slow AI development and arguing that regulation signals caution rather than opposition to innovation. She said Wisconsin candidates including Crowley and Attorney General Josh Kaul would want public input into how AI is governed. She contrasted this approach with a federal stance she described as opposing any AI regulation, and said Democrats frame regulation as a question of how the technology should be used. The article does not report the election result, any legislative action, or any next steps beyond the campaign context.

Articles.Title: Stacey Abrams on DEI, artificial intelligence and regulation ahead of Democrat midterm wins

stories.Headline: GVSU summit to explore societal impact of artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Grand Valley State University will host "Humans in the Lead: Community AI Summit," a free, all-day event on Thursday, Nov. 5, at the DeVos Center on its City Campus in Grand Valley. The university organized the gathering to examine how artificial intelligence is reshaping everyday life across the region. The summit begins at 8:30 a.m. and invites national experts, policymakers and local leaders to take part. Organizers say the event is meant to bring together people who rarely work at the same table on the technology's future.

The day is designed to explore the opportunities and challenges AI presents in economic development, workforce readiness, civil rights and environmental sustainability. Abre' Conner, director of the NAACP Center for Environmental and Climate Justice, will give the keynote address on how expanding technology infrastructure, including data centers, affects local communities. Breakout sessions will cover AI applications in business and industry, practical AI skills for the workplace, responsible innovation in health care, and emerging surveillance technologies and their effects on public safety and privacy. Featured speakers include Tony Reames of the University of Michigan, Kevin Jones of Indiana University Columbus, Jennifer Runyan, special agent in charge of the FBI's Detroit Field Office, and Kent County Sheriff Bryan Muir. Registration and further details are available on the GVSU events webpage.

Mark Richards, a GVSU professor of political science and one of the organizers, said universities should connect academic knowledge with decisions that affect people's daily lives. He argued that no single discipline or institution can answer the questions AI raises, and that bringing researchers, policymakers, industry professionals and community members together can support more informed decisions. Kareem Scales, CEO of Scales Consulting and a summit organizer, said the future of AI is too important to be decided in silos. He added that West Michigan has an opportunity to show that technological progress and human progress can advance together.

Articles.Title: GVSU summit to explore societal impact of artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: SPONSORED: Building AI factories at enterprise scale
stories.Summary:
ASUS announced a full-stack enterprise AI offering at NVIDIA's GTC show in Berlin on October 21 and 22, 2026. The offering is called the Enterprise Agentic AI Solution and has three layers. These are the ASUS AI Server and Infrastructure, the ASUS AI Software Stack, and the ASUS AI HUB services operation. The announcement brought together existing ASUS assets for enterprise AI users along with new hardware.

The hardware includes single and full-rack systems built around the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 eight-GPU server board. The 3U hybrid-cooled XA NR11-E12L and the 2U fully liquid-cooled XA NR11-E12 both target large AI reasoning workloads. ASUS says the tool-less CPU and GPU sleds can cut maintenance time by up to 50 percent. The company also showed MGX servers, the ExpertCenter Pro ET900N G3 developer desktop with 748GB of coherent memory, the Ascent GX10, the ProArt GR1X Mini PC, the ProArt P16 and P14 laptops, the PE3000N edge computer, and the PE6000G workstation platform.

Paul Ju, senior vice president and head of infrastructure solution BG at ASUS, said the servers help enterprises build high-performance agentic AI infrastructure for complex task execution and large-scale agent deployment. He said AI servers were historically optimized around GPU compute, but agentic workloads now depend heavily on a continuous agent loop that is CPU-intensive. He named single-thread performance, memory bandwidth, multi-die latency, and a lack of hardware sandbox isolation as bottlenecks in conventional AI servers. He also said customers must match server platforms to their projected AI workload profiles.

IDC said the worldwide server market grew 30 percent in a single year to reach $122.6bn in the first quarter of 2025. IDC expects inference to account for over 70 percent of computing demand by next year and says it is growing fastest at the edge. ASUS has adopted NVIDIA's DSX AI Factory platform with a digital twin system for planning hardware and power, and its racks become simulation-ready assets inside DSX. The digital twin is meant to keep working after go-live so operators can test changes before touching hardware.

Articles.Title: SPONSORED: Building AI factories at enterprise scale

stories.Headline: AI Reads the Classics: Machine Learning Extracts Themes from Political Theory
stories.Summary:
Stephen J. DeCanio published a commentary in the journal AI Perspectives arguing that Alan Turing’s 1950 paper on machine intelligence raised a problem that is still unsolved. Turing had imagined that artificial intelligence would develop much like the education of a child, an idea that came long before modern machine learning took shape. The problem DeCanio points to is how humans might teach or shape artificial intelligences to behave in ways that match moral standards. As one small step, he applied a natural language processing technique to works of classical political theory.

The technique is called Latent Dirichlet Allocation, or LDA, and it belongs to a family of “bag-of-words” methods that count word frequencies while ignoring sentence structure. DeCanio applied it to classical political texts downloaded in machine-readable form from Project Gutenberg. The results showed that even corpora made up of only a few authors and works could be processed successfully, and that the method works on texts distant in time from the present day. All the calculations ran on a desktop PC using Mathematica 12, so no supercomputing resources were needed. The three contributors to The Federalist Papers were treated as a single author.

DeCanio is emphatic about what the results do not show, saying the findings cannot demonstrate human-level understanding of texts by an unsupervised AI. He notes that the LDA topics are not summaries of the works, and that texts with opposing political implications might show very similar topic signatures. He uses an “M” prefix before words like analysis and comprehension to mark that machines are doing the operations, which sidesteps the question of what thinking is. He concludes that we have no idea what it is like to be an AI, and that the gap between word patterns and genuine grasp of an argument remains wide.

The commentary places the demonstration within a larger argument about moral development in machines, suggesting that an emergent AI’s motivations might partly be formed by absorbing human writings on ethics and politics. It cites an estimate that raising a child in the United States cost roughly 233,610 dollars in 2015, excluding college, and that combined public and private spending on education plus childrearing comes to roughly 10 percent of U.S. national output. It also cites an estimate that even careful software engineering in industry rarely achieves an error rate better than one error per 1,000 lines of code. One cited analysis suggests reasonable accuracy from LDA sampling may often be achieved with 5,000 iterations or less. The paper makes clear that the distance between topic signatures and moral understanding is still enormous, and no current technique closes it.

Articles.Title: AI Reads the Classics: Machine Learning Extracts Themes from Political Theory

stories.Headline: New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA has added four open-weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family, aimed at interactive world simulation for robotics and autonomous driving, according to a Hugging Face article dated November 5, 2026. The four models are Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto, which generates multi-view driving data under varied weather, lighting, and time of day, and Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto, which streams synchronized camera and LiDAR observations for driving simulation. The other two are Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer, which turns simulator controls and a text prompt into photorealistic video, and Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual, which predicts video from robot or camera actions. Each is a post-trained example of Cosmos 3 Nano with 16B trainable parameters, released under the OpenMDW1.1 license for commercial and non-commercial use. The article describes the models as complementary tools for building simulated environments.

Transfer-Auto produces offline driving data across up to 11 camera views, including fisheye cameras, with joint RGB and LiDAR generation, while Sim-Auto is a distilled variant that generates small chunks of camera and LiDAR video in a few denoising steps for fast, long, interactive rollouts. Sim-Transfer renders color observations from a physics simulator's state, and Sim-Bimanual simulates two-arm robot environments for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controlled by a policy or joysticks. Developers are encouraged to post-train the models on their own sensor rigs or robot setups before using them, and the article notes that the released checkpoints give researchers a shared starting point for adapting and comparing methods. The article attributes the work to NVIDIA and lists a group of NVIDIA researchers as authors, including Pranjali Joshi, Rick Z, Yao Xu, Qianli Ma, Chen-Hsuan Lin, Ming-Yu Liu, Xiang Li, Zhengfei Kuang, Zhonghao Wang, and Jiaxiang Tang. NVIDIA's stated aim, as the article puts it, is to help researchers and developers build richer and more responsive simulated worlds.

The authors also acknowledge that these problems remain hard, and say the next work is to measure where the models support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short. The article describes the training pipeline as moving from bidirectional adaptation through teacher forcing, consistency distillation, and self-forcing, with the final stage intended to reduce error buildup from generated history. The article gives no further timeline or planned follow-up beyond the ongoing evaluation work it describes. It also points readers to the Cosmos 3 model collections and to accompanying skill documentation for running inference and post-training.

Articles.Title: New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation

stories.Headline: As Shoppers Warm to Agentic Commerce, Terms of Use Have to be Clearly Defined
stories.Summary:
Riskified, a digital fraud and risk intelligence company, released its latest Agentic Commerce Pulse report on November 4, 2026, based on a poll of more than 5,100 consumers globally. The report found that 80 percent of those surveyed have used AI for some part of the shopping process. Half of all consumers said they were more comfortable than six months ago with an AI shopping agent completing a purchase without immediate approval. The findings suggest comfort with AI shopping is running ahead of actual adoption.

The data showed a gap between using AI to browse and letting it buy. Seventy-four percent said they would allow agentic purchases in some form, and 68 percent said they were likely to use AI for holiday shopping. Yet just 11 percent had completed a purchase inside an AI tool, and only 7 percent were comfortable letting AI buy something without their approval. On control, 43 percent still want to approve every purchase, while 29 percent would allow automatic purchases within rules they set.

On responsibility, 51 percent said the AI platform should issue refunds when AI makes a mistake, even though the terms of agents like Muse and Instinct say users are responsible for their agents' actions. Asked who they would trust to run a shopping agent, one-third named a general AI platform such as ChatGPT or Gemini, 17 percent named a retailer or brand they already shop with, and 9 percent named a bank, credit card company or digital wallet. Jeff Otto, chief marketing officer at Riskified, said consumers are getting comfortable delegating shopping to AI but have not delegated the blame. He said agentic commerce only scales if merchants can tell a real customer using a legitimate agent from a hijacked account or malicious automation.

The report's authors said the findings point to issues of control and governance that still need to be addressed for confident adoption and growth. They described an emerging relationship of conditional autonomy, in which consumers give AI greater authority if they set the limits. Riskified said it is extending its identity risk intelligence to the person behind the agent, for the order and the service interactions that follow. The company said retailers and brands will need to distinguish trusted customers and legitimate AI agents from fraudsters as agentic commerce expands.

Articles.Title: As Shoppers Warm to Agentic Commerce, Terms of Use Have to be Clearly Defined

stories.Headline: Google shouldn’t be pressuring schools to use its AI
stories.Summary:
Google has been pressing schools to accept its AI tools as a condition of keeping access to its search engine, according to a New Scientist opinion piece published on 5 November 2026. The author, who attended school when Google first appeared, describes how some US school districts want to decide whether students can use AI, while Google has said that switching off its Gemini chatbot in Classroom means losing search as well. A Google representative, Chris Phillips, told The New York Times that search and AI are deeply integrated. The author argues that this is a product decision rather than a technical one, since AI Overviews do not appear on every search and can be disabled with a short code added to the URL. He points out that Google could give schools that option if it chose to.

Google's own reply to a request for comment was a link to a blog post about its Gemini AI tutoring product. Google has since said that Gemini and search will be off by default for schools, which can switch either on at their discretion, though this does not solve the problem of having search without AI Overviews. The piece places the dispute against Microsoft's bundling of Internet Explorer with Windows, which a US court in 2001 found illegally maintained a monopoly, and which led to a European Commission ruling in 2010 requiring Microsoft to offer a range of browsers. The article notes that Google is appealing a US antitrust ruling that found it illegally maintains a monopoly in online search, and that New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Google of using its monopoly power to force AI into public schools.

The author says the courts will probably decide whether Google must offer search without AI, and that there is no suggestion Google is acting illegally in its dealings with schools. The author also cites research on learning, including a study of around 10,000 adults and another of more than 26,000 students in China, which suggested that LLM use can produce shallower understanding and weaker exam results. Google has responded with its Guided Learning product, which it says walks students through homework step by step, and reported that tests with around 1,800 students in Sierra Leone produced more than a year of typical learning progress in eight weeks. The author says he is not opposed to AI in schools but believes it should not be up to tech giants to set education policy.

Articles.Title: Google shouldn’t be pressuring schools to use its AI - New Scientist

stories.Headline: Financial Stability Board sets out 12 ‘sound practices’ for FS firms’ AI adoption
stories.Summary:
The Financial Stability Board has issued a report setting out 12 "sound practices" that financial institutions should consider for responsible AI adoption. The board monitors and makes recommendations to improve governance in the global financial system. The report was covered by Compliance Week on November 4, 2026, in an article by contributor Neil Hodge. The article lists the 12 practices but does not reproduce them in the text available.

The report is addressed to banks and other major financial services firms, which the board says should follow its recommendations. The article does not give further detail on what each of the 12 practices requires. It also gives no dates for when firms would be expected to comply. No names beyond the board and the article's author appear in the text.

The Financial Stability Board is responsible for the recommendations, which it describes as practices firms should consider rather than binding rules. The article does not include any statement from the board beyond that description. It also does not quote any officials or firms responding to the report. No other responsible parties are named in the text.

The context is the board's role in monitoring the global financial system and recommending improvements to its governance. The article does not say what happens next, such as whether the practices will be consulted on or turned into standards. It also does not say how the recommendations will be monitored or enforced. The text available does not cover those points.

Articles.Title: Financial Stability Board sets out 12 ‘sound practices’ for FS firms’ AI adoption

stories.Headline: Seattle families to rally, address generative AI tech usage in schools
stories.Summary:
Seattle families rallied outside Seattle Public Schools headquarters on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, urging the state's largest school district to pause the use of generative AI and address concerns about student-facing technology. Parents said they worry the technology could be more harmful than helpful for student learning, and they want the option for their children to have a paper alternative to using an iPad or tablet. The rally was planned before the school board's informational study session about educational technology. Superintendent Ben Shuldiner and most of the school board attended the rally.

The families called on the district to form a committee to disclose ed tech products and student data collection to caregivers, get caregiver consent to use these products, allow paper-based alternatives and device opt-outs, and set grade-level screen-time limits. The district does have time limits for student use of this technology and blocks certain web content like YouTube, Minecraft and Gemini, according to a district presentation. The district describes generative AI as deep learning models that can create complex original content like long-form text, high-quality images, realistic video or audio in response to a user's prompt. Some examples used in classrooms include Magic School, Amplify Science, Emerge, SuccessMaker Math, Lexia, enVision Mathematics, Lexia Core5, Sora, Schoology, Canva and Book Creator.

Erica Shutes-David told KOMO News she was surprised when her then-kindergartener was given an iPad, and she chose to opt her son out. She said AI is currently wildly untrustworthy and that grooming kids to rely and trust on that source is dangerous and irresponsible, in her opinion. Ashley Worobec, a Salmon Bay K-8 parent, said the tools shortcut thinking and that it does not make sense to her that they are used in schools during crucial developmental years. Director Liza Rankin told KOMO she is excited to continue the conversation and wants all kids to have the opportunity to be critical thinkers, and she said there is a lot of alignment among the parents and the board.

Parents said they are frustrated with what they call too much screen time replacing hands-on learning, a lack of a districtwide cell phone policy, no clear governance over how AI is being used, and over-purchasing of digital programs. Directors are reviewing guidance for developmentally appropriate, safe and purposeful technology and AI use to support student learning. The school board presentation notes SPS is changing how it makes software decisions, aiming to have fewer overlapping applications and better support tools with help from an advisory committee. KOMO News asked the district about parents' concerns.

Articles.Title: Seattle families to rally, address generative AI tech usage in schools

stories.Headline: Junior Lawyers Aren’t Necessarily Driving In-House AI Adoption
stories.Summary:
The assumption that younger lawyers will naturally lead the legal profession's adoption of artificial intelligence, while senior lawyers stay reluctant, may be overstated, according to new research into in-house legal teams. A survey of 133 in-house legal professionals, conducted by Pinsent Masons and Crafty Counsel, examined how technology skills are distributed across teams and who is actually pushing AI use forward. The findings were reported by Tony Thompson of Law.com in a piece published on November 5, 2026. Its central result is that while 80% of respondents saw differences in technological aptitude across their teams, only 31% agreed that more junior colleagues were driving AI adoption.

The findings challenge the idea that younger lawyers are inevitably the early adopters of legal AI. The report suggests that confidence and the opportunity to experiment may matter more than age in determining who leads. Differences in technological expertise rarely caused friction, with only around a quarter of respondents reporting conflict. In other words, the gap in skill across a team was common but seldom a source of tension. The article presents these results as a reason to rethink where in-house AI leadership is likely to come from.

Pinsent Masons and Crafty Counsel conducted the survey, and the article reports their conclusions without adding independent verification. The article does not include direct statements from the researchers beyond the findings themselves. Coverage of the report also sits alongside other Law.com items about large-scale AI investment in law firms and new AI tool-building features from legal technology providers. The article does not say what further research or follow-up the researchers plan, so the implications for future adoption remain open.

Articles.Title: Junior Lawyers Aren’t Necessarily Driving In-House AI Adoption

stories.Headline: Fact-Check: AI plays a growing role in email filtering
stories.Summary:
Email providers such as Gmail and Microsoft Outlook are expanding their use of artificial intelligence and machine learning to block spam, phishing attempts and malicious attachments. The Roy Howard Community Journalism Center's "What Is True?" team, based in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, looked into a claim that these providers are increasingly using AI to filter incoming messages. The team rated the claim as true, according to the article published by WTOK on November 5, 2026. Its review found that the claim holds, but the available evidence does not show whether the added AI use has led to more filtering errors.

Modern spam filters examine message content, sender reputation, authentication records and sending patterns to decide what reaches an inbox. Messages from unfamiliar senders or from newly created accounts may face extra scrutiny, although the article notes that practices differ from one provider to another. The systems are meant to improve security, but they can wrongly flag legitimate messages as junk. The article points out that these tools carry this risk even when they work as intended.

Microsoft has acknowledged that more aggressive junk-email protection raises the chance that legitimate messages will be classified as junk. Google has warned that messages from legitimate email providers are not guaranteed to pass its spam filters. The fact-check relies on those company statements and on the sources the team reviewed, which did not establish whether greater AI use has caused more legitimate emails to be wrongly filtered. The article does not identify any individual responsible for the filtering decisions.

The article offers practical steps for users who want to avoid missing important messages. They are advised to check spam and junk folders regularly, to mark legitimate messages as "Not spam" or "Not junk," and to confirm by phone or text that important messages were received. Readers can submit questions to the "What Is True?" team through its online inquiry form or by calling 855-474-8878. The article does not describe any further action or follow-up by the team.

Articles.Title: Fact-Check: AI plays a growing role in email filtering

stories.Headline: AI Regulation Was on the Ballot In These States. Here Are The Elon Musk Stocks That Could Be Impacted.
stories.Summary:
Democrats won sweeping victories in the midterm elections on Nov. 3, reclaiming control of both the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate. Not all results are final, but Democrats appear to control 258 House seats to the Republicans' 177. In the Senate, Democrats now appear to hold 54 seats to the Republicans' 44, with two races still undecided. The results show a clear repudiation of President Donald Trump and the Republicans' agenda over the past two years. Artificial intelligence was also on the ballot in many different elections, according to the article.

Musk spent at least $474 million during the midterm election cycle, and nowhere did he spend more than in Texas. Musk and his super PAC reportedly spent $224 million on the Texas races. James Talarico became the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in Texas since 1988, and Gina Hinojosa became the first Democratic governor of Texas since 1995. Hinojosa defeated the incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, who Musk reportedly had close ties to. Tesla's policy chief used to be Abbott's deputy director for legislative affairs.

AI became an issue in many key Congressional races and state elections in Texas, Pennsylvania, Georgia, Ohio, and Virginia, among others. Democratic candidates generally leaned toward caution and favored regulation or stricter requirements for data centers, and some sought to outright ban data centers for at least a period. SpaceX has data centers in Tennessee and Mississippi, and other states of interest for both SpaceX and Tesla include Texas and Georgia, among others. Hinojosa has talked about imposing measures such as an immediate moratorium on data center development. On SpaceX's recent earnings call, Musk told analysts that the company expects to build and bring online at least an additional 10 GW of AI compute capacity in 2027 via data centers.

Tesla is currently expanding its Cortex AI training supercluster in Austin, Texas, while SpaceX has reportedly been looking to build another data center campus in Texas with an additional 1 gigawatt of compute capacity. As of 10:45 a.m. ET, the major market indexes were soaring higher, yet SpaceX and Tesla traded roughly 3% and 2.2% lower, respectively. Hinojosa's win is described as a clear blow to Musk and both of his companies. The article says the task of adding the 10 GW of AI compute capacity likely just got a lot harder.

Articles.Title: AI Regulation Was on the Ballot In These States. Here Are The Elon Musk Stocks That Could Be Impacted.

stories.Headline: LLMjacking Attacks Steal Corporate AI Access, Run Up $100,000 Daily Bills
stories.Summary:
Cybercriminals are stealing corporate credentials for large language model services to use expensive AI computing resources without authorization, an attack known as LLMjacking. They take corporate LLM application programming interface keys and authentication tokens to run their own AI services or conduct large-scale model inference. The resulting bills are charged to the victim companies. A report released November 2 by Mandiant, Google's threat intelligence unit, said fraudulent charges can exceed $100,000 a day. In some cases, cumulative charges at affected companies reached $1 million before attackers' access was revoked.

The main targets are API keys and access tokens, which prove authorization to use an API. Once attackers obtain a key, they can access cloud-based AI services and invoke models while posing as legitimate users, without account passwords or normal login. LLMjacking has increased steadily over the past two years. CrowdStrike's August 2026 Threat Hunting Report documented an attacker who used stolen tokens to generate about 200,000 API requests in just two minutes. An attack group tracked by Google as UNC6993 obtained LLM API keys, used them to generate more keys and activated services in a victim's cloud environment, with charges reaching $100,000.

In another case, an attacker enrolled a victim company's account in a Pay-As-You-Go plan to gain unauthorized access to premium AI models. According to The Register, the attacker used a "burn and rotate" strategy, sending large volumes of requests in a short period. When usage quotas or rate limits were reached, the attacker deleted existing service accounts and created new ones to get around the restrictions. Google also found an attacker who stole a third party's API keys and used them to operate an LLM routing service called Jet Night. The attacker made more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours.

Because the operator did not pay the legitimate API usage charges and shifted the costs to other companies' accounts, it offered services far below market rates. Jet Night advertised access to cutting-edge models and an unlimited token plan for about $60 a month, while Google said comparable services would typically cost consumers between $100 and $250 a month. Google expects cybercriminals to increasingly prioritize LLMjacking over cryptojacking, which involves stealing cloud computing resources to mine cryptocurrencies. The spread of agentic AI is another factor increasing the threat, because stolen credentials combined with agentic tools let attackers sustain large volumes of API calls and automated attacks with relatively little effort. Google recommends that companies strengthen identity and access management for cloud and AI services, use centralized secrets management platforms, rotate keys regularly, apply the principle of least privilege and automatically scan source code for embedded API keys and authentication credentials.

Articles.Title: LLMjacking Attacks Steal Corporate AI Access, Run Up $100,000 Daily Bills - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

stories.Headline: Big Four Hyperscalers Seek $131 Billion for AI Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Oracle all disclosed financing plans last week to raise a combined $131 billion through loans, bond offerings and equity issuance for artificial intelligence infrastructure. Amazon announced the largest facility, access to up to $80 billion in secured loans, with borrowing expected between the first quarter of 2027 and the third quarter of 2028. Microsoft plans to issue $25 billion in corporate bonds, and Oracle plans to raise $20 billion through $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes. Google is preparing a €6 billion bond offering, and Meta, which does not run an external cloud business, announced a $15 billion corporate bond offering on Nov. 3 and last month disclosed plans to raise up to $97.5 billion through equity financing.

Amazon's loan facility is part of a vendor financing arrangement for technology infrastructure purchases, carries floating interest rates and matures five years after each borrowing date. Microsoft's fixed-rate bonds carry interest rates from 4.85% to 6.35%, and the offering was expected to close on Nov. 4. Oracle's debt offering includes $2 billion in floating-rate notes and $8 billion in fixed-rate notes at annual rates of 7% to 8.65%. Google's bonds carry rates from 3.7% to 5.25%, and Meta's full-year capital expenditure forecast stands at $135 billion to $145 billion.

Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk said during the company's fiscal 2027 first-quarter earnings announcement that it had completed the $20 billion at-the-market equity offering program announced in February. At its Oct. 28 investor day, Oracle said it would limit additional capital market financing for its fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to $20 billion, split equally between equity and debt. Google's chief financial officer attributed a free cash flow deficit of $9.01 billion, against analyst forecasts of $2.7 billion, mainly to increased capital expenditures. Amazon said it expects full-year capital expenditures to remain around $220 billion, the level first projected in July.

Google spent $51.36 billion on capital expenditures in the latest quarter and maintained its full-year forecast of $195 billion to $205 billion, while expecting investment to increase significantly in 2027. Microsoft reported capital expenditures of $45.2 billion for its first fiscal 2027 quarter and lowered its full-year forecast from $175 billion to about $170 billion. Amazon spent more than $77 billion on capital expenditures in the latest quarter, and Oracle's annual spending is expected to reach $90 billion to $95 billion. Fortune reported that financing conditions have begun to deteriorate as concerns grow over rising debt among major technology companies and uncertainty around AI profitability, and OpenAI recently reduced its fundraising target from $30 billion to $20 billion.

Articles.Title: Big Four Hyperscalers Seek $131 Billion for AI Infrastructure - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

stories.Headline: The CFO’s Guide to LLMjacking: When Stolen AI Becomes a 7-Figure Cloud Bill
stories.Summary:
Cybercriminals are hijacking corporate AI credentials and reselling access to premium language models, leaving the victim companies to pay the cloud bills. Google's cyber threat intelligence division published a report on Monday, Nov. 2, documenting these attacks, which researchers call LLMjacking. The report found fraudulent AI consumption exceeding $100,000 in a single day at some organizations, with cumulative charges reaching $1 million before access was revoked. Financial services, retail, technology and transportation companies across multiple continents were affected.

The attacks exploit exposed API keys, compromised service accounts, stolen identity tokens and credentials embedded in software repositories. Attackers sometimes expanded their privileges, activated unused AI services or created new credentials, and in one case enrolled compromised accounts in pay-as-you-go agreements and used short-lived service accounts to evade rate limits. Intermediary services called LLM Mixers aggregate stolen credentials and resell access at discounted prices. One such service, Jet Night, advertised unlimited access to frontier models for about $60 per month, and Google linked it to an attacker who made more than 500,000 API calls in under eight hours, passing nearly $1 million in token costs to a victim.

Google says the problem is that a cloud platform can correctly authenticate a request and bill the account without the business ever authorizing the expense. For finance teams, this raises the accounts payable question of who may incur an expense and what stops spending beyond that authorization. Google expects the criminal marketplace for stolen AI access to expand as premium models and autonomous workloads become more widely deployed. The same infrastructure that lets businesses buy intelligence instantly lets criminals consume it just as quickly.

Articles.Title: The CFO’s Guide to LLMjacking: When Stolen AI Becomes a 7-Figure Cloud Bill

stories.Headline: The sovereign AI mandate: How Germany’s HLRS is anchoring Europe’s digital future
stories.Summary:
The High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart, known as HLRS, is at the center of a push for sovereign AI in Europe, according to a sponsored article published by CIO on November 4, 2026. The article says HLRS has built an environment for industrial enterprises and scientific researchers that keeps their data in Germany and conforms to European standards. It describes HLRS as an operational blueprint for European enterprises that want to scale out AI without giving up data sovereignty. The article was written by HPE and AMD, which supply technology to HLRS.

The article says European organizations have faced architectural lock-in, unpredictable data egress fees and compliance headaches when moving sensitive data across borders. It says HLRS uses HPE Cray Supercomputing platforms and HPE liquid-cooling technologies to support massive parallel processing and energy efficiency. It says HLRS also integrates AMD processors and accelerators to handle both traditional high-performance computing simulations and modern AI training workloads. The article says this lets users train multibillion-parameter AI models and run billions of simulation cycles, including for automotive vision models and aerodynamic simulations.

The article presents HLRS as a co-innovation partner rather than just a data center, serving both midsize enterprises and multinational corporations. It says the model offers future-proof compliance, protection of intellectual property and uncompromised performance. HPE and AMD say they are partnering to deliver the next generation of AI and supercomputing infrastructure, combining HPE system design with AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct accelerators. The article directs readers to a podcast episode, This Week in HPC Episode 400, for more on Europe's strategic investments in digital autonomy.

The article ties the shift to the EU AI Act and to European concerns about privacy laws in other jurisdictions. It says sovereign AI is no longer a niche regulatory preference but a core business strategy for CIOs. It argues that organizations building on data autonomy will be positioned to lead as AI matures. The article does not say what specific projects or customers HLRS has signed.

Articles.Title: The sovereign AI mandate: How Germany’s HLRS is anchoring Europe’s digital future

stories.Headline: USCIS Seeks Input on AI-Enabled Contact Center Recompete
stories.Summary:
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services posted a request for information on SAM.gov on Monday, according to ExecutiveGov. The notice seeks industry feedback on a cloud-based, artificial intelligence-enabled contact center to replace the agency's Enterprise Customer Experience operations. The new requirement is called Enterprise Customer Experience 2, or ECX2. USCIS described ECX2 as a recompete of an existing task order rather than a follow-on.

The current contact centers handle roughly 15 million toll-free calls a year through about 1,500 agents at 18 sites nationwide, many working remotely. An interactive voice response system resolves about 70 percent of External Affairs calls without a live agent. USCIS wants a FedRAMP Moderate platform with 99.99 percent availability and room for as many as 3,000 live agents, plus links to Salesforce and ServiceNow. The RFI asks whether AI voice systems can top 95 percent intent-matching accuracy, respond in under 700 milliseconds and keep at least 75 percent of calls from reaching an agent, with an 85 percent target.

Responses are due by 8 a.m. Eastern time on Nov. 12, emailed as PDFs to Contract Specialist Brittany Willette. In October the agency forecast a value of $50 million to $100 million for ECX2 and set March 1, 2027, as the expected solicitation release date. The forecast also shows the current arrangement under the Enterprise Infrastructure Solutions vehicle expiring July 2, 2027. Vendors must explain how their solution could run without the incumbent's proprietary tools and how the government would retain control of its data and configurations.

Articles.Title: USCIS Seeks Input on AI-Enabled Contact Center Recompete

stories.Headline: Fake AI Images Are Targeting Students and Teachers. Schools Aren’t Prepared - Education Week
stories.Summary:
A nationwide survey of 852 educators by the EdWeek Research Center this summer found that one in three educators do not know whether their school or district has a policy to address AI-generated fake images and videos. Twenty-two percent said their school or district has no such policy, and 2 percent said one is being considered. The survey was reported by Education Week on November 4, 2026. The issue is growing faster than policies to address it.

A 2024 student survey by the Center for Democracy and Technology found that one in four K-12 students know someone depicted in a nonconsensual, sexually explicit deepfake. Free AI tools let students make fake images or videos of peers or educators, many of them sexually explicit and targeting women or girls. Some fake videos show principals or other employees making racist or inappropriate remarks. In the EdWeek survey, 13 percent of educators said they did not know what a deepfake is, and nine in 10 said they had not been trained on detecting or responding to one in the last two years.

Bart Caylor, founder of the marketing firm Caylor Solutions, said little skill is needed, describing it as grabbing a video from Facebook and using a tool to change what the person is saying and doing. Erin Mote, founder and chief executive officer of InnovateEDU, said leaders need to know whether their educators understand what a deepfake is and what to do when they encounter one. Kristin Woelfel, policy counsel at the Center for Democracy and Technology, said districts do not necessarily need a new policy and can add language to existing policies on fair technology use, harassment and cyberbullying. She said the harm to a victim is the same whether an image is real or fake.

More than 20 percent of respondents said existing policies are broad enough to cover sexually explicit deepfakes, but experts say a deepfake case differs from cyberbullying, and publishing a nonconsensual, sexually explicit image of a minor is now a federal crime. Mote said schools need an incident response plan to detect and report incidents, curtail their spread and support victims with trauma-informed care. In the survey, 56 percent of schools said they would inform parents if a student made or distributed a harmful deepfake, 48 percent would use suspension, a quarter would expel the student and 33 percent would use restorative practices. Illinois is requiring public schools to update their cyberbullying policies to address AI deepfakes.

Articles.Title: Fake AI Images Are Targeting Students and Teachers. Schools Aren’t Prepared - Education Week

stories.Headline: UK Officials Said AI Would Add £400 Billion to the Economy. That Figure Mainly Came From Google
stories.Summary:
For about two years, UK government ministers told the public that AI could add £400 billion, or $538 billion, to the economy. Last week the UK AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, admitted in a parliamentary answer that this figure was far above the government's own projections. He said the £400 billion number came from a publicly available 2023 report commissioned by Google and produced by Public First, a British consultancy now called PF Global. Narayan said the government's more recent assessment put the gain from AI adoption and data investment at £55 billion to £140 billion by 2030, with a central estimate of £120 billion. He described even that estimate as hugely uncertain.

The lower estimate had been with ministers since at least November 2025, almost a year before the admission, yet the government agency Skills England was still publishing the old figure four months later. Government departments and agencies used the Google figure for almost two years, under two governments. Narayan's answer was the first recorded evidence that the government set the two numbers side by side, or said the report was commissioned by Google. The answer did not withdraw the £400 billion figure or say it had been wrong.

PF Global's head of economics, Jonathan Dupont, said the gap was partly because of what the firm saw as slow government adoption of AI. He said AI moves fast and assumptions behind models have to be updated, and that the government's numbers assume a much slower rate of adoption than seemed possible in 2023. He said the firm's central estimate for what is likely to be achieved by 2030 is now much closer to the government's number. PF Global said its work for Google continued but all research was independent and all judgments and assumptions were its own.

Dame Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, said the government is right to promote technology like AI for public services. She said the reports highlight hype as one of the central barriers to digital transformation, and that overstating benefits risks undermining the case for change. Lord Holmes of Richmond, the Conservative peer who asked ministers in January 2025 about the origins of the claim without getting a response, said it was unfortunate the figure had now been significantly adjusted. He said it would have been better to clarify sooner and more directly, and that robust data is critical.

Sumedha Deshmukh of the Ada Lovelace Institute said the revised estimates are welcome but it is concerning they come after almost two years of ministers citing research paid for by Google. She said figures about AI that look precise often have assumptions and incentives built into them, and industry often funds or shapes the research behind them. She said the government should test the numbers it is given, fund independent research, and measure whether promised gains are delivered. The Cabinet Office, the department responsible for AI in government, and Google were approached for comment.

Articles.Title: UK Officials Said AI Would Add £400 Billion to the Economy. That Figure Mainly Came From Google

stories.Headline: Baidu Releases ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base: A 280B MoE Base Model With 14B Active Parameters
stories.Summary:
Baidu has released ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base, the raw pre-training checkpoint of a new sparse Mixture-of-Experts language model. The model is a text-only system with 280 billion total parameters, of which 14 billion are active for each token. Its weights stop at the end of pre-training, with no mid-training or post-training applied, which Baidu presents as a clean starting point for teams comparing fine-tuning, instruction tuning or reinforcement learning methods. The release was reported on November 5, 2026.

The model supports a 128,000-token training context and a 1 million-token context for fine-tuning and inference. It is meant to run on multi-GPU servers, and Baidu's reference configurations use 4-way parallelism in SGLang and vLLM. The articles do not disclose the GPU model or the VRAM required, and the weights come in FP8 and BF16 formats. The architecture has 43 layers and a hidden size of 4,096, and it was pre-trained from scratch on 33.5 trillion tokens using the Muon optimizer.

Baidu is the developer and reports the benchmark results itself. According to those figures, the model scored best on 24 of 30 base-model benchmarks in Baidu's unified evaluation pipeline. Its strongest result was 78.4 on MMLU-Pro, ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base at 69.2, while its weakest was 56.2 on HELMET-Rerank, behind DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base at 60.0. Baidu also says the model loses on six tasks, where DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base and Tencent's Hy3-preview-Base lead in some cases.

The design uses a hybrid attention scheme, in which 37 layers use compressed attention and six layers use latent attention with sparse attention, so that one in seven layers keeps full-context access. Each mixture-of-experts layer has 512 routed experts, with the top 10 active, plus one shared expert. Baidu also replaces the usual multi-token prediction component with a method called ECHO, which adds 0.36 billion parameters that are excluded from the headline counts. The articles describe the design as built around the combined cost of activated compute, cache and long-context handling.

Articles.Title: Baidu Releases ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base: A 280B MoE Base Model With 14B Active Parameters

stories.Headline: M’sia acts on AI election threat
stories.Summary:
Malaysia’s Communications Minister, Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil, said existing laws will govern any action over alleged foreign interference in Malaysian elections through an artificial intelligence platform. He said the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) would also act under the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998 and other applicable laws. Fahmi said the MCMC is seeking more information and clarification from the US AI company Anthropic. This follows a report alleging that its Claude AI platform was used to run an election manipulation operation targeting users in Malaysia. He gave the reply in writing in Parliament on Wednesday, in response to Pasir Mas MP Ahmad Fadhli Shaari.

The report, titled “Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI: September 2026”, described an alleged operation that used actual census data and millions of voter records. It said the operation targeted Malaysia’s political and social fault lines, including race, religion and the royal institution, across all 222 parliamentary constituencies. Anthropic reportedly uncovered the operation after identifying an account that used its platform to manipulate elections and target Malaysian users. Fahmi said the MCMC would decide on appropriate follow-up action based on the information and evidence obtained.
