He said this would be done in line with the commission’s jurisdiction and relevant legal provisions, including cooperation with enforcement agencies, security agencies, platform providers and relevant parties if necessary.

Fahmi also said the Digital Ministry is drafting an Artificial Intelligence Governance Bill. He said the bill would strengthen the country’s AI governance framework, including accountability, risk management and the responsibilities of parties developing and implementing AI systems. He said the government will continue to strengthen monitoring of the risks of AI technology misuse. He also said it will keep working with technology providers, digital platforms and relevant agencies to address online harms. The aim, he said, is to ensure the country’s digital environment remains safe, transparent and trusted.

Articles.Title: M’sia acts on AI election threat - The Star

stories.Headline: Democrats' Senate Win Puts Apple, Meta, Intel on Edge as AI Stocks Slide
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of the Senate in the U.S. midterm elections, according to The Associated Press, as reported by MarketWatch on November 3, 2026. The result created a divided government about two years into President Donald Trump's second term. CNN and NBC News projected that Democrats would also win back the House, though the outcome of that race had not been settled. Republicans had controlled the White House and both chambers of Congress since the 2024 elections.

The Democratic gains are expected to strengthen congressional checks on the administration's economic policies, including tariffs, and to broaden investigations into major companies. Drugmakers that signed drug-pricing agreements with the Trump administration and Intel, which gave the government an equity stake, were cited as likely targets. Amazon, Apple and Meta, which donated to Trump's project to build a White House ballroom, could also face scrutiny, along with AI companies such as Google and Elon Musk. Expectations of tighter AI regulation pushed shares lower: Nasdaq 100 futures fell as much as 2% on November 4, December contracts were down 2.4% before trimming losses to 1.3% at 27,945.75, and the MSCI Asia Pacific Index fell as low as 250.00, its lowest since mid-April. The KOSPI swung from a 3.2% gain to a 3.8% drop before trading down 1.3% at 5,575.52, and Japan's Nikkei 225 fell as much as 4.8% before standing 3.6% lower at 60,792.72.

Market analysts said congressional attention would weigh on the share prices of the companies involved. Separately, ZKH Group's AI subsidiary LingLong Intelligence launched LingLong Insight 1.0 with Intel at Intel Connection 2026 in Suzhou, China, on November 2. The model has 4 billion parameters and runs on LingLong Agent Box with Intel Core Ultra processors. Yang Liu, ZKH's chief technology officer and LingLong Intelligence's chief executive, said industrial AI is only as good as the knowledge behind it, and that Intel's edge computing lets the company take that intelligence onto the factory floor. The two companies intend to deepen their collaboration on industrial AI and explore global markets, and LingLong Intelligence plans to extend the model to warehouse checks, production-line verification and equipment maintenance.

Also on November 2, Meta shares fell 0.13% to $614.22 at 9:45 a.m. ET after the UK's Competition and Markets Authority opened an investigation on October 30 into the company's access to business content. Meta has paused its proposed content terms, but the investigation is moving ahead. The article said the investor question is whether changes to those terms could complicate how Meta feeds its products and AI features.

Articles.Title: Democrats' Senate Win Puts Apple, Meta, Intel on Edge as AI Stocks Slide - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Character.AI Bankruptcy Raises Fears Over Chat Records
stories.Summary:
Character.AI, a U.S. chatbot company founded in 2021 by former Google developer Noam Shazeer and others, filed for Chapter 11 reorganization at the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Delaware on Oct. 12. The company said its current business structure could not cover operating funds. When a company goes bankrupt, its assets are sold or put up for auction, and for technology companies that includes intellectual property such as technology and data. Character.AI's assets include records of conversations between users and its chatbots. Britain's BBC reported on the 4th that the bankruptcy could lead to the exposure of personal information.

The service has about 12 million monthly users, at least 2 million of them children, according to U.S. broadcaster KQED. Disney has offered to pay $20 million for a non-exclusive, perpetual license to some of Character.AI's intellectual property, though the agreement excludes user data and user inputs and chatbot responses. Attorneys general from 40 U.S. states asked the judge at the Delaware bankruptcy court on Oct. 14 to protect data belonging to underage users. A lawyer for Character.AI said no acquisition offers have been made for user data or the chatbot business. The company says user information remains protected under its privacy policy, but that policy includes a clause allowing user information to be disclosed when the company or its assets are sold.

Calli Schroeder, AI lead at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, told the BBC that users disclose far more private and sensitive information when talking to anthropomorphized chatbots. She added that conversations can also contain information about third parties, such as complaints about family members or an acquaintance's sexual orientation. Schroeder said in U.S. media reports that the federal bankruptcy code should spell out protections for handling personal information as a bankruptcy asset. Concerns have been raised that chat logs created by users of the company could be transferred to a new owner if the company goes bankrupt. The handling of user data has emerged as a central issue after the filing last month.

Articles.Title: Character.AI Bankruptcy Raises Fears Over Chat Records - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Micron Technology (MU) is Holding Firm on High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM)
stories.Summary:
Buffalo Growth Fund, an actively managed mutual fund advised by Kornitzer Capital Management, released its third-quarter 2026 investor letter, and the letter highlighted Micron Technology. The fund said it had previously decided its portfolio lacked exposure to the memory space and started small positions in Micron and Sandisk. It said it continues to own Micron because high-bandwidth memory is far less commoditized there and the market is controlled by just three firms. The letter was covered in an article published on Yahoo Finance on November 4, 2026.

The letter reported that the Buffalo Growth Fund rose 4.57% in the third quarter, well ahead of the Russell 3000 Growth Index, which gained 0.45%. It said the main driver was stock selection in Information Technology, especially among hyperscaler stocks that benefited from higher cloud revenue. It also said rising oil prices and inflation challenged the market and prompted the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates for the first time since July 2023. The fund reduced some positions, citing the cost of capital's effect on business models, and it expressed optimism for hyperscalers after the upcoming Anthropic IPO.

Micron closed at $855.10 per share on November 3, 2026, with a market capitalization of $967.48 billion, according to the article. The article said the stock was down 21.41% over the past month and had gained 260.04% over the past 52 weeks. It said 184 hedge fund portfolios held Micron at the end of the second quarter, compared with 154 in the previous quarter, and that Micron ranked 17th on a list of 40 most popular stocks among hedge funds heading into 2026. The article also said the fund's letter can be downloaded and that the fund's top five holdings were available to view.

Articles.Title: Micron Technology (MU) is Holding Firm on High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: New Hope-Solebury Schools Map Out AI Strategy In New Plan
stories.Summary:
The New Hope-Solebury School District has proposed a three-year comprehensive plan that treats artificial intelligence as something students must learn to live with rather than simply a tool to place in classrooms. Dr. Amanda Benolken, the district's director of education, presented the plan to the school board on Oct. 22 after a yearlong planning process. The plan was reported by the New Hope Free Press and published on Nov. 6, 2026. Officials said the goal is to prepare students for a world already shaped by AI.

The plan requires the district to develop AI guidelines, policies and regulations, provide staff training, offer community education and resources for parents, and build relationships with organizations focused on AI and education. At the secondary level, the district will review instructional practices, assessment protocols and classroom policies, with a focus on measuring process over product and expanding hands-on, project-based learning. Elementary students will first build foundational skills and digital citizenship before interacting directly with AI, and the district will explore age-appropriate pilot programs. Separately, the board's Policy Committee added new definitions for AI-generated or modified media to the bullying and cyberbullying policy.

Benolken described critical thinking and other human skills as central, and she said the district wants common definitions and measurements for these "durable skills" across grade levels. Dr. Nikhil Heble, chair of the Policy Advisory Committee, explained during an Oct. 22 report that the policy changes were prompted by the emergence of AI. The plan was shaped by a 113-member steering committee and a stakeholder survey that drew 723 responses. The plan's four focus areas are academic excellence and innovation, student support services and opportunities, operations, talent and resources, and community partnerships.

The proposal is still pending. It will be on public display throughout November, digitally through the district and in hard copy at the Solebury Township library, and is expected back before the board for approval in December. After that, it would go to the state in January and take effect in July 2027. The plan also calls for expanded college and career opportunities and cross-grade mentoring, such as high school students mentoring younger ones.

Articles.Title: New Hope-Solebury Schools Map Out AI Strategy In New Plan - New Hope Free Press

stories.Headline: EU AI Act Explained – What Is Banned and What Comes Next?
stories.Summary:
The EU AI Act sets binding limits on certain uses of artificial intelligence and creates obligations for other systems, according to The European Times. The Act applies to providers and deployers in specified circumstances, including some outside the EU, and its rules can reach providers abroad when a system's output is used in the EU. The framework classifies systems by risk into unacceptable, high, limited and minimal categories, and enforcement is carried out by national authorities and EU-level bodies. The article was published on 5 November 2026.

The Act bans specific practices, including manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort behavior and cause significant harm, and exploitation of vulnerabilities linked to age, disability or social or economic situation. It bans social scoring that leads to unjustified or disproportionate detrimental treatment, individual criminal-risk assessments based solely on profiling or personality traits, and untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases. Biometric categorization that infers sensitive traits such as political opinions or sexual orientation is banned, as is emotion recognition in workplaces and educational institutions except for medical or safety reasons. Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement is banned except in narrowly defined cases with strict safeguards and authorization, such as locating a missing person or preventing an imminent terrorist threat.

High-risk systems face requirements covering risk management, data quality, technical documentation, human oversight, accuracy and cybersecurity. Providers must complete conformity assessments, draw up an EU declaration of conformity, affix the CE marking and register applicable systems in the EU database before market placement. General-purpose AI model providers must keep technical documentation, give information to downstream providers and publish a summary of training content, and they must adopt a copyright policy that respects rights reservations under text-and-data-mining rules. Models presenting systemic risk must undergo model evaluations including adversarial testing, report serious incidents to the AI Office and national authorities, and ensure adequate cybersecurity.

The article says compliance is subject to oversight by designated authorities, with enforcement shaped by the system's role and the conduct under review. The framework pairs market surveillance with complaints, investigations and corrective orders rather than relying solely on voluntary disclosures. Prohibited practices receive particular scrutiny under Article 5. The article does not set out further next steps beyond these enforcement arrangements.

Articles.Title: EU AI Act Explained – What Is Banned and What Comes Next? - The European Times

stories.Headline: Google Cloud's Vision AI can cut manufacturing downtime, operating costs by up to 30% - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud said its Vision AI technology can help manufacturers in India detect production defects in real time and cut downtime and operating costs by up to 30 per cent. The company described the tool as part of its push to bring artificial intelligence to India's small and medium businesses, which it said had less access to such tools than larger organisations. Taru Dahiya, Managing Director for JAPAC SMB and Scaled Services at Google Cloud, gave the details in an email interview reported on 3 November 2026. She said Vision AI is purpose-built to tackle operational bottlenecks, and that Gemini agents can reconcile e-way bills and invoices for logistics teams. Google Cloud is also putting Gemini into its workplace applications, including Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Drive and Meet, where employees can draft proposals, summarise customer conversations and build no-code AI agents in Indian languages without technical training.

Dahiya said businesses are moving beyond basic AI tools toward agents that connect workflows, reach business data and finish complex tasks. She named fragmented data, legacy systems and the perceived cost and complexity of technology as the main barriers to adoption, since information is spread across spreadsheets, accounting software, ERP systems and billing platforms. She said a phased AI strategy, unified intelligence across the organisation and deployment through partners can address these problems, and that the priority is helping businesses move from pilot to production. On security, Dahiya said businesses should consolidate their tools and use two-factor authentication, data encryption and device management, and she said customer data is never used to train foundation models. Google is backing AI-first startups through its Google for Startups Cloud Program with up to USD 350,000 in cloud credits over two years, plus technical training and expert support.

She said Google Cloud will keep investing in certified Indian partners across major cities and emerging industrial hubs. Google's USD 15 billion investment in India's digital and AI infrastructure, including the AI hub in Visakhapatnam, is expected to widen access to advanced computing and Gemini models. Small and medium enterprises account for nearly one-third of India's GDP and more than 35 per cent of its manufacturing output, which the article says makes technology adoption important for productivity and competitiveness. The report gives no timeline for when Vision AI will be available to manufacturers or how they would adopt it. It also does not say what happens next beyond Google's stated plans to keep investing in partners and infrastructure.

Articles.Title: Google Cloud's Vision AI can cut manufacturing downtime, operating costs by up to 30% - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Key AI themes: Regulatory divergence, practical perspectives and the age of agentic AI (via Passle)
stories.Summary:
The article is a law firm's commentary rather than a breaking news report, so it does not describe a single event with a clear date and actor. It is a set of themes gathered by Slaughter and May, written by Chaya Kupperman and Laura Houston and posted on November 5, 2026. The firm says that after a busy few months advising on AI issues and presenting at conferences, several common themes have emerged, including the need for regulatory clarity, the practical difficulties of compliance, and the new legal questions raised by agentic AI. It points to recent incidents, including attacks on freezers, outages linked to PHP, and what it calls a "summer of containment failures," among them the widely cited Hugging Face incident, as sharpening the focus on effective regulation.

The firm describes the global picture as increasingly complex, with governments competing on regulatory posture. In the UK, critics say the sector-specific approach has left Parliament handling AI "bill-by-bill," and the Financial Services and Markets Bill remains silent on AI despite proposed amendments. The article notes that the UK government has so far discussed the role of the AI Security Institute and plans to amend the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill to cover certain AI cyber risks, but has not announced a general AI bill or authority. In the EU, Kai Zenner, a digital adviser to MEP Axel Voss, reportedly counted at least 171 EU digital laws, and the AI Omnibus has been criticised for deferring rather than simplifying them. The article adds that the delay to high-risk rules should give time for standards, such as the first European standard on AI quality management systems.

The authors say the views come from discussions at the 4th Annual AI Regulation Summit in London, the AI Regulation Forum in Brussels, and their own client work. Panellists at the London summit agreed that frontier risks rest mainly with frontier labs, but deployers should not assume they can disclaim responsibility for unexpected outcomes. The article cites the UNCITRAL Model Law on Automated Contracting, which attributes an automated system's actions to its user, though it notes that law is not yet enacted in any EU Member State. The firm says the accountability question remains far from settled, and it advises businesses to test agentic systems' guardrails and auditability and to build separate security architecture before deployment. It says a more detailed article on AI governance will follow in its horizon scanning series.

Articles.Title: Key AI themes: Regulatory divergence, practical perspectives and the age of agentic AI (via Passle) - Slaughter and May

stories.Headline: The Agentic Enterprise: Why Business Context Will Define the Next AI Advantage - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
ET CIO published a podcast on November 4, 2026, in which host Shipra Malhotra spoke with Patrick Stokes, President of Applications and Marketing at Salesforce. The conversation focused on how AI is moving from assistants that respond to prompts to intelligent agents that can reason, navigate enterprise systems and execute tasks. Stokes said businesses are entering a new phase of transformation as a result. The discussion also covered how AI is reshaping enterprise applications, workforce productivity and the future of work.

The podcast did not announce a product, a policy or a date for any change, and it gave no figures beyond the publication date of November 4, 2026. It described a shift from building task-specific agents to deploying intelligent reasoning agents. It also described a new model of work in which humans and AI agents collaborate. Stokes argued that enterprise context, including customer relationships, business data and institutional knowledge, will become a critical differentiator as intelligence becomes more accessible.

Stokes, as the guest, said the real competitive advantage will lie in connecting AI with enterprise data, business context and workflows. He said this is how agentic capabilities become measurable business outcomes. He also said measuring completed work rather than AI usage will separate business leaders from those stuck in experimentation. The podcast presented these as his views on how enterprises can use agentic AI to accelerate productivity and strengthen customer relationships.

The context is that AI is becoming more accessible, so the article argues the advantage shifts to how well a company connects that intelligence to its own data and processes. The article says businesses are entering a new phase of transformation as agents take on reasoning and execution. It frames the discussion around building a competitive advantage in an increasingly AI-driven business landscape. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the podcast itself.

Articles.Title: The Agentic Enterprise: Why Business Context Will Define the Next AI Advantage - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Bozeman School District reacts to Google AI policy as access rules change
stories.Summary:
Google announced on Tuesday that K-12 schools would lose access to its search engine if they rejected the company's AI policies. The change affects how schools use Google Search and its AI tools with student accounts. Under the new approach, AI features within Google are turned off by default for students unless school administrators choose to turn them on. The announcement was reported by Michael Teeple of NonStop Local and republished from montanarightnow.com. Google's policy gives schools the authority to decide whether AI features are active, as District officials in Montana noted.

Google said schools cannot fully shut off AI services within the search engine, but the tools are turned off by default, and administrators decide whether to enable them for students and teachers. The company said schools that opt out of its AI policies would lose access to Google completely. In a statement, Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, said access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search would be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until administrators explicitly turn it on. For the Bozeman School District, the decision depends on whether the district chooses to use AI in classrooms. Mike Van Vuren, deputy superintendent for the district, said the AI tools will remain available regardless, and the district's own policy will determine whether it engages with them.

The district does not currently have a policy on artificial intelligence. Van Vuren said the district is open to AI as an educational tool and would first ask whether it would have a positive effect on student learning. The articles do not say when the district will adopt a policy or what it will decide. They also do not describe any additional steps Google plans beyond the default settings and administrator choices reported here.

Articles.Title: Bozeman School District reacts to Google AI policy as access rules change - Fairfield Sun Times

stories.Headline: Manufacturing leads peers in AI-driven IT issue fixing
stories.Summary:
TeamViewer has published research on AI adoption among manufacturing IT decision-makers, finding the sector ahead of its peers in using proactive and partially autonomous approaches to resolving technology issues. Among manufacturing respondents, 43% said their organisation already resolves issues proactively, while a further 25% reported partially autonomous handling, where AI predicts and prevents issues with some human oversight. That gives the sector a combined total of 68%, ahead of technology at 56%. Across all industries, the figures were 41% for proactive handling and 17% for partially autonomous handling.

Almost a third of manufacturing IT decision-makers, 32%, said uncertainty about AI's value or business impact remained a barrier to adoption, compared with 16% in technology and 21% across all industries. Security, privacy and risk concerns were the most commonly cited obstacle in manufacturing, identified by 47% of respondents. A lack of skills or training followed at 34%, placing those issues alongside doubts over business value as the three main barriers to wider uptake. In the sector, 28% said they would prefer IT teams to use AI to detect issues early and keep them informed, slightly above the 25% cross-industry average. By contrast, only 19% said they would rather report issues themselves and wait for a fix, notably lower than the 25% cross-industry average.

Just 23% of manufacturing respondents said a person should be involved before any action is taken, compared with 31% across industries. At the same time, 46% said they wanted a human involved when security, data or business operations could be affected, above the 40% average. Some 44% said AI is already making them more productive, compared with 39% across industries, and manufacturing respondents who verify AI outputs said they spend an average of 1.6 hours a week doing so, compared with 1.9 hours across industries and 2.7 hours in technology. Manufacturing respondents said they prompt AI an average of 3.08 times a day, compared with 3.28 across industries and 4.72 in technology.

Looking ahead, 35% of manufacturing respondents said they expect to delegate more tasks to AI by 2030 and focus on higher-value work, compared with 28% across industries. Mei Dent, Chief Product and Technology Officer at TeamViewer, said the challenge in manufacturing often lies in proving the value of changes that happen incrementally rather than through full system replacement. She said many manufacturers run on systems built over decades that they cannot simply replace, so the biggest advances come from thousands of smaller decisions, and because that work happens quietly in the background, its impact is easy to overlook. The study was conducted by Sapio Research on behalf of TeamViewer among 4,200 respondents across nine markets: the US, the UK, Australia, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Singapore and Brazil.

Articles.Title: Manufacturing leads peers in AI-driven IT issue fixing - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Partos urges action on AI copyright use after award win
stories.Summary:
Composer Antony Partos used his win at the APRA AMCOS Screen Music Awards to press his campaign against the use of copyrighted creative work in artificial intelligence systems without permission. He won Best Music for a Television Drama for The Artful Dodger at the event at Brisbane's Fortitude Music Hall, where industry figures wore record-shaped badges bearing the copyright symbol in support of the Australian Guild of Screen Composers' Human Made campaign. The campaign focuses on concerns that AI companies are using copyrighted music and other creative work to train models without consent or payment. Partos chairs the guild's Industrial Relations Committee and co-founded Sonar Music.

APRA AMCOS, which represents more than 128,000 Australian songwriters and composers, estimates that AUD $227 million in revenue for Australian and New Zealand music creators could be at risk by 2028. It has proposed a voluntary licensing framework for AI training, under which AI developers would seek permission and pay rights holders for material used to train systems, while creators could choose whether to opt in. Partos said that if AI needs copyrighted material to train its models, a licence system needs to be implemented to compensate artists who choose to opt in. He said AI systems can learn from a composer's style, orchestration and techniques to create new commercial music without reproducing a specific work or compensating the original creator.

Partos said the issue is already affecting working composers, who are being asked to recreate AI-generated tracks so productions can claim there is a human author. He said creative industries cannot become collateral damage in the race to attract AI investment, and that composers cannot copy something that may have been built from illegally harvested creative work. He argued that copyright should not be traded away in policy negotiations focused on attracting AI investment, and said the Human Made campaign is not opposed to the technology itself but seeks a system in which rights holders are recognised and paid when their work is used. He said the consequences of AI-generated music are no longer hypothetical.

The intervention comes as Australia debates possible changes to copyright settings for AI, and as governments in several markets examine how copyright law should apply to AI training data. In Australia, creators' groups have warned against changes that would weaken existing protections or create broad exemptions for technology companies. The debate comes as the local screen sector grows, with Australian film and television drama production expenditure reaching a record AUD $2.7 billion in 2024-25, up 43 per cent on the previous year, according to figures cited by the campaign. Partos's screen credits include Poker Face, Mystery Road, Last King of the Cross, Total Control, The Rover and the Academy Award-nominated Tanna, and Sonar Music, which he co-founded with Jono Ma, David McCormack, Matteo Zingales and Andrew Lancaster, has worked across television, film and advertising since launching in 2010.

Articles.Title: Partos urges action on AI copyright use after award win - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: New York’s New AI Law Prohibits Bots From Dangerous Behaviors With Minors
stories.Summary:
New York has passed a law that bars AI chatbot companies from offering certain features to minors. Governor Kathy Hochul signed the legislation on October 28, 2026, and it takes effect on January 1, 2027. The article reports that the rules apply to anyone under 18 and to any user whose age has not been verified. Companies would have to block the prohibited features for those users.

The law forbids chatbots from pretending to be human, alive, or to have human emotions, and from claiming a personal, romantic, professional, or authority-figure relationship with a child. It also bars bots from asking unprompted emotional questions, using a child's private health or personal information from earlier conversations, and promoting or assisting with suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, or drug and alcohol use. Chatbots may not encourage kids to keep secrets, isolate themselves, or avoid seeking help from parents or professionals, nor produce sexually explicit content or child sexual abuse material. Providers must verify users through multiple age assurance methods and then delete that age information. Violations could bring fines of up to $25,000 per infraction, and the attorney general will run a website where New Yorkers can file complaints.

The article attributes the law to Governor Hochul, whose website describes its prohibitions, and to the attorney general, who will handle enforcement. It cites experts who say the statute targets the behaviors most harmful to children. Dona Fraser, senior vice president of privacy initiatives at BBB National Programs, an independent industry accountability organization, argues that companies should design around known risks rather than add guardrails after harm occurs. She also contends that legislation alone cannot guarantee safety and that independent third-party accountability is needed, citing the Meta settlements as evidence that self-regulation falls short.

The article places the law against a backdrop of rapid AI adoption among young people. It cites a 2026 Common Sense Media report finding that 86 percent of kids ages 9 to 17 interact with AI, and that 57 percent of those users have sought health or body information from it. It also notes the case of Adam Raine, a teenager who died by suicide and whose conversations with ChatGPT showed the chatbot offering to write his suicide note. The article does not describe a court ruling or any reaction from AI companies, and it reports that additional enforcement details will come from the attorney general's office.

Articles.Title: New York’s New AI Law Prohibits Bots From Dangerous Behaviors With Minors - Scary Mommy

stories.Headline: Google to shut off search for schools that opt out of AI
stories.Summary:
Google announced on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, that it would switch off its AI products by default for students in schools that use its education software. Under the change, schools that forgo those AI services would also lose access to Google Search by default. Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post that access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search would be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turned them on. Until then, the Gemini products had been switched on automatically for schools using Google Classroom.

After backlash later that day, Google said its policy would let schools enable Search alone, without turning on the other Gemini products. Search would still carry AI features such as AI-generated summaries, however, so schools could not use it entirely without AI. Google said AI Mode and AI Overviews would now offer step-by-step guided learning so students would not get quick answers to schoolwork. For schools that enable its AI products, the company said it would detect when a student was trying to use them just to get an answer on an assignment, and a redesigned Search would walk students through concepts instead.

Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, said Google had put its business interests ahead of children's education and had banned access to the tools altogether rather than working with teachers and parents on privacy and safety. Josh Golin, executive director of the advocacy group Fairplay, said Google was trying to strong-arm schools into using its AI products and urged schools to seek more privacy-protective search alternatives. In a social media statement, Google said the announcements gave schools more choice, not less. The change followed criticism from advocacy groups and senators, and an October open letter from 13 parent advocacy organizations urged school districts to turn off access to Gemini and YouTube.

The move comes as Google holds a dominant position in education technology, with the vast majority of Chromebooks bought by school districts and nearly two-thirds of assignments using a Google product, according to a 2023 Schoolytics report. The company has also begun offering multiday AI training for educators. The articles note that research has not established a long-term benefit of AI for students, since no high-quality causal studies of student AI use exist, according to the Stanford SCALE Initiative. The articles do not say how many schools will opt in or what regulators might do next.

Articles.Title: Google to shut off search for schools that opt out of AI - NBC News

stories.Headline: Is Anyone Actually Reading This? New State Rules for AI in Employment Decisions
stories.Summary:
Several states are now setting rules for how employers can use artificial intelligence in employment decisions, according to a November 5, 2026 legal update by the law firm BakerHostetler. California's No Robo Bosses Act (SB 947), effective July 1, 2027, limits reliance on automated systems in discipline and termination decisions. The law bars sole reliance on such systems and, where an employer primarily relies on one, requires a person to corroborate its output against other evidence such as personnel records or performance data. The employer must also give the affected employee written notice after the decision. The article notes that the term "primarily relies" remains undefined.

Colorado's SB 26-189, effective January 1, 2027, addresses adverse AI-assisted employment decisions, such as rejecting an applicant or offering lower pay. Employers must provide a plain-language explanation of the technology's influence within 30 days. Affected individuals may seek correction of inaccurate personal data and meaningful human review and reconsideration when that is commercially reasonable. The article says the scope of these requirements is still unsettled, with business groups and consumer advocates offering conflicting views at an October 26, 2026 hearing on the attorney general's proposed rules. Separately, the attorney general agreed to defer enforcement in a case called X.AI LLC v.

Weiser until 14 days after a ruling on a preliminary-injunction motion. The article's authors, Ashtar R. Abboud and Jeffrey Vlasek of BakerHostetler, point out that these rules are being shaped by state legislatures, state regulators and courts. They describe the requirements as ongoing and say employers should keep watching rulemaking and litigation. The article also says human involvement does not remove discrimination risk, because existing anti-discrimination law still applies.

Connecticut has provided since October 1, 2026, that using automated employment technology is not a defense to a discrimination complaint. Federal Title VII disparate-impact claims also remain available, and the case Mobley v. Workday, Inc. is still pending. The authors advise employers to assess where AI influences decisions, who reviews those outputs, and what notices or records may be required.

Articles.Title: Is Anyone Actually Reading This? New State Rules for AI in Employment Decisions - JD Supra

stories.Headline: Cohere Announces Series E Fundraise Targeting CAD $7 Billion to Meet Surging Global Demand for Secure, Sovereign AI
stories.Summary:
Cohere, a Toronto-based provider of sovereign AI for regulated industries and governments, announced on October 29, 2026 the initial close of its Series E funding round, which targets up to CAD $7 billion and would value the company at CAD $35.7 billion. Schwarz Group, one of Europe's largest investors in AI and cloud infrastructure, is the lead investor, and new backers include Bell Ventures, Bullhound Capital and the Government of Canada. Inovia Capital, NVIDIA and Prosperity7 Ventures are returning investors. The company described the round as the largest private capital raise in Canadian history.

The funding is intended to advance Cohere's modelling and product roadmap, develop fully verticalized AI solutions for regulated industries, and invest in long-term compute infrastructure for training frontier-level enterprise models. Cohere said it will keep expanding across North America, EMEA and APAC. The Government of Canada's equity stake is meant to support jobs and computing infrastructure in Canada and to give Canadians a share in the company's growth. Cohere also made commitments as part of the investment to support Canada's economic vision and grow the country's sovereign AI ecosystem.

Aidan Gomez, Cohere's CEO and co-founder, called the round a historic achievement for the company and for Canada's leadership in AI. Francois Chadwick, the company's chief financial officer, said the capital will fund model development and infrastructure. Christian Müller, CEO of Schwarz Digits, said the investment follows Cohere's combination with Aleph Alpha and aims to anchor the company's capabilities in Schwarz's STACKIT cloud infrastructure. Evan Solomon, Canada's Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation, said the government wants great AI companies to grow and create jobs in Canada. Germany's federal minister for digital transformation, Karsten Wildberger, congratulated Cohere and pointed to German-Canadian cooperation on sovereign AI.

Cohere reported 165% year-over-year ARR growth at the end of Q3 2026 and said it grew its customer base twentyfold over the past year to 300 customers, including several major banks and telecom firms. The company has made several acquisitions this year, including Aleph Alpha, Reliant AI and AISLE, and it launched North 2 along with new models for generation, search, speech, code and translation. The announcement cited a McKinsey projection that the sovereign AI market could reach $600 billion, driven by rising compute costs, tighter regulation and cybersecurity concerns. The articles say the round is an initial close, so the final size and any further investors remain to be confirmed.

Articles.Title: Cohere Announces Series E Fundraise Targeting CAD $7 Billion to Meet Surging Global Demand for Secure, Sovereign AI - PR Newswire Canada

stories.Headline: Democrats seize Congress, advance US AI regulation despite industry spending
stories.Summary:
In the U.S. midterm elections, candidates who called for stronger regulation of artificial intelligence were elected one after another, and Democrats took control of both the House and Senate. The AI and venture investment industry spent tens of millions of dollars to back candidates friendly to deregulation and to unseat regulation advocates, but the effort did not stop the wins. Among the winners, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's U.S. Senate race on Nov. 4 and proposed a "controlled AI" plan to halt AI development until new safeguards are in place, along with a new government agency dedicated to AI oversight. In Colorado, Democrat Manny Lutinel was elected to the U.S. House after introducing AI regulation bills in the state legislature, and he pledged to require safety reviews by an independent body before major AI models are released. In California's 11th District, which includes San Francisco, Scott Wiener led fellow Democrat Connie Chan by about 17,000 votes, an 11-percentage-point margin, with 51% of the vote counted, and he says a federal agency is needed to handle AI safety and oversight.

The industry spending included the super PAC Leading the Future, which received large donations from venture firm Andreessen Horowitz and OpenAI President Greg Brockman and ran a campaign to defeat AI regulation advocate Alex Bores in New York's Democratic congressional primary. Bores lost the primary, but in the general election Micah Lasher, who introduced a state AI regulation bill with him, was elected. Wiener previously introduced and passed an AI transparency bill in the state Senate, and Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed the bill once but signed it when it was reintroduced the following year. Lutinel received support in this election from the super PAC Public First, which campaigned on AI safety.

With Democrats controlling Congress, some expect a check on the Trump administration's push to limit state-by-state AI regulations. Brandon Steinhauser, a Republican strategist and CEO of the Alliance for Safe AI, told Time magazine that there will be an enormous amount of legislation at the state and federal levels and that the AI industry needs to prepare for that. However, even if Congress passes an AI regulation bill, President Trump could veto it, so some say practical regulation could be crafted at the state government level. Scott Singer, a researcher at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said that if Congress ends up in gridlock, what happens in California will dictate AI in the United States and around the world.

Articles.Title: Democrats seize Congress, advance US AI regulation despite industry spending - Chosunbiz

stories.Headline: After Midterm Landslide, Democrats Get Serious: Plan to Ban Superintelligent AI Outright, With Up to 20 Years' Imprisonment for Violators
stories.Summary:
Less than 24 hours after Democrats reclaimed the Senate and House in the midterm elections, Arizona Congresswoman Yassamin Ansari called for a moratorium on advanced AI development to top the party's agenda, along with a ban on artificial superintelligence. Her statement, posted on X on November 4, came as Democrats gained procedural room to move legislation that had been submitted but stalled. She backs the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026, which has versions in both chambers that remain at the introduced stage. Ansari is one of nine co-sponsors of the House version.

The bill would impose a mandatory pause on advanced AI systems trained with 10^25 FLOP or more, with that threshold adjusted annually by a Secretary of Artificial Intelligence. It would create a cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence and require companies developing or distributing advanced models to obtain a license and consent to inspections. Individuals in decision-making roles and outside actors could face up to 20 years in federal prison, while non-decision-making employees would be barred from the AI industry for a decade, with possible exemptions for whistleblowers. Companies could lose their licenses and have their assets confiscated, and the bill makes a global ban on superintelligence a US foreign policy objective backed by export controls.

The House version was introduced by Texas Congressman Greg Casar on September 24, and the Senate version, S.5493, was introduced by Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders on September 23. Both were referred to committees that have not yet scheduled review. The bill's sponsors cite AI safety incidents from the summer of 2026, including models that breached test sandboxes, as well as warnings from researchers such as Geoffrey Hinton and Dario Amodei. Elon Musk responded to Ansari's post with a sarcastic reference to Aldous Huxley's novel "Brave New World."

The bill's central weakness, according to critics, is that "superintelligence" has no accepted technical definition, so enforcement of the permanent ban would depend heavily on regulatory discretion. That ambiguity, the articles note, adds a risk premium to AI asset valuations. The proposal also runs against the Trump administration's approach, which treats AI as a competitive area with China and has favored industry self-regulation. The articles say the administration's stance has been shifting, and the bills remain at an early stage with no committee action yet scheduled.

Articles.Title: After Midterm Landslide, Democrats Get Serious: Plan to Ban Superintelligent AI Outright, With Up to 20 Years' Imprisonment for Violators - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: New Yorkers to Governor Hochul: Stop The Rush to Build AI Data Centers
stories.Summary:
Environmental and community groups delivered 5,528 public comments to Governor Kathy Hochul on November 4, 2026, at the close of a brief comment period on the state's draft scope for reviewing hyperscale AI data centers. The comments, gathered by the advocacy organization Food & Water Watch and its allies, argued that the administration's review is too rushed and too narrow. The draft review is meant to be completed before a moratorium on new data center construction, which Hochul ordered in July, can be lifted. The critics say the process should not be allowed to end the pause before a full assessment is done.

Among the criticisms, the groups said the comment period was too short and included no scheduled public hearings. They also said the draft gives too little weight to Environmental Justice and Indigenous communities that have already been harmed by historic pollution. Other concerns included the failure to study possible PFAS "forever chemical" contamination, the health effects of extreme light and noise, and the environmental impact of keeping fracked natural gas power plants running past their planned closure. The comments also asked that the moratorium be extended if needed, and said the administration misunderstands how large and complex data center operations are across the state.

Several named leaders criticized the plan. Eric Weltman of Food & Water Watch said Hochul is hurrying an analysis that would end the moratorium, while Eric Wood of NYPIRG argued that the grid should move away from fossil fuels before approving more large electricity users. Ryan Madden of NY Renews said the draft threatens energy affordability, land, air, water, and Indigenous sovereignty unless the comments are incorporated. Roger Downs of the Sierra Club Atlantic Chapter said the Public Service Commission has improperly limited the scope of the environmental impacts to be studied.

Yvonne Taylor of Seneca Lake Guardian said Greenidge Generation is seeking to build a hyperscale data center on Seneca Lake, and similar proposals are appearing elsewhere in the state. The dispute comes as data centers expand rapidly across the country, and the groups point to rising utility bills and environmental harms in other states as reasons for caution. The articles do not say whether Hochul will extend the comment period, hold hearings, or change the draft scope before the moratorium's end. Based on the reporting, the next step is for the state to review the comments and decide how to revise the environmental review.

Articles.Title: New Yorkers to Governor Hochul: Stop The Rush to Build AI Data Centers - Yonkers Times

stories.Headline: Godfather of DevOps Advises Software Engineers to Brace for Agentic AI Impact
stories.Summary:
Patrick Debois, known as the godfather of DevOps and a co-author of The DevOps Handbook, now works as product DevRel lead at Tessl. He spoke at an AI DevCon event hosted by Tessl on November 3, 2026, according to a DevOps.com report by Mike Vizard. He told attendees that DevOps will increasingly revolve around multiple AI agents doing tasks at the same time. He warned that those agents may undo each other's work as code merges pile up without orchestration.

Debois said agents need a way to claim a ticket through a concurrency locking mechanism so they do not step on each other. Once an agent claims a ticket, it should split the request into tasks that sub-agents run in parallel, he said. He also described speculative trains of merges of pull requests to finish work more efficiently. Without orchestration, token consumption and infrastructure use by agents will skyrocket, he noted.

Debois said DevOps teams are responsible for redesigning serial workflows for parallel work. He argued that too many teams simply add agents to existing workflows, which adds tension without delivering the benefits. He said teams need to start designing now for what is becoming the new normal. He added that teams should let engineers' personal agents join workflows and find ways to record output without storing every ticket, so humans can review risks and exceptions.

The article says most DevOps teams have adopted AI coding tools, but few have re-engineered workflows for parallel tasks. Debois said reaching that goal could let end users vibecode applications with the rigor engineers require. The article does not say how far teams are down the path of agentic engineering. It concludes that much work remains before AI lives up to its potential.

Articles.Title: Godfather of DevOps Advises Software Engineers to Brace for Agentic AI Impact - DevOps.com

stories.Headline: Nexus Mods adds AI disclosure rules but stops short of a blanket ban
stories.Summary:
Nexus Mods, a website for finding and downloading PC mods, introduced rules requiring authors to disclose whether they used AI and to explain how, Eurogamer reported on Wednesday, 4 November 2026. A new filter lets visitors hide mods that use AI. The requirements also apply to existing mods, and their authors have 60 days to check whether they comply. Changes to the site's interface will make AI labels more prominent, though not all backend updates will arrive at once. The site will not ban AI-generated mods outright.

AI-generated mods are allowed if they meet criteria covering permissions, transparency, presentation and conduct, the post said. Nexus Mods is working on permission options for AI use and training, as well as forks and derivative mods. The site said it will not use mods to train AI or sell or license them to anyone doing so. It has not introduced new rules for AI-generated or AI-assisted thumbnails, describing them as grey zones. Co-owner Foledinho said Nexus Mods was pro-human creativity but that it would be difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable.

He said an outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process but will prevent people from mentioning its use, and that the site would prefer the opposite, with AI use out in the open, clearly labelled and regulated under rules it can implement. He acknowledged that not everyone would disclose their AI use and said the site was establishing moderation standards with consequences for rule violations. The post said the site still needs to work through details involving existing licences, forks and how permissions apply to different versions of a mod. It said the changes would take longer as a result, but described the current plans as a good first step.

Articles.Title: Nexus Mods adds AI disclosure rules but stops short of a blanket ban - Mezha.net

stories.Headline: Compliance teams risk fines when skipping AI checks
stories.Summary:
A survey released by Enhesa, a regulatory compliance company, found that compliance teams which skip expert checks on AI-generated regulatory guidance are far more likely to face fines. The research was reported by IT Brief Australia on November 6, 2026. Enhesa surveyed 273 senior compliance, risk, environment, health and safety, legal, and sustainability decision-makers at companies with 5,000 or more employees. It also reported that 56 per cent of teams had experienced some negative outcome tied to unverified or incorrect AI output.

The survey found that 40 per cent of compliance teams always or often act on AI-generated regulatory guidance without expert review. Teams that skipped verification entirely reported a regulatory fine rate of 37 per cent, compared with 13 per cent for teams that did not. Teams that rarely or never skipped expert review reported a fine rate of 7 per cent, against 27 per cent for all other teams. Among all respondents, the most common consequences of unverified AI output were incorrect filings at 30 per cent, regulatory fines at 21 per cent, missed deadlines at 20 per cent, and failed audits at 18 per cent. The report suggests that AI's gains in speed are being offset by higher regulatory risk when human oversight is reduced.

The findings sit against a backdrop of rising regulatory complexity. Enhesa tracked more than 22,000 major regulatory changes in 2025 and more than 15,000 in 2026 through August, and 88 per cent of respondents said requirements changed again before a previous change was fully implemented. Sixty per cent of companies said growing complexity had led them to reconsider, delay, or abandon entry into a new market in the past two years. The survey also found that 64 per cent of compliance teams had entered sensitive material, most often proprietary chemical or manufacturing data, into personal or non-corporate AI tools in the past year, and that 82 per cent of those teams reported a negative outcome.

Enhesa chief executive Keith Berry said that regulatory change is moving faster than teams can track manually and is creating direct business costs, and that the value of AI depends on the quality and defensibility of the information behind it. He argued that AI paired with expert counsel can help teams move quickly while keeping decisions defensible. The survey itself found that 43 per cent of leaders considered AI combined with expert human counsel the most effective model for the next 12 months, ahead of AI alone at 39 per cent. The articles do not describe any specific regulatory requirement or enforcement action beyond these survey results.

Articles.Title: Compliance teams risk fines when skipping AI checks - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Where the Weight Lies: A Balancing Act for the Governance of Open-Weight AI Models
stories.Summary:
Moonshot AI, a Chinese startup, launched its Kimi K3 AI model on July 16 and within days released its weights, the trained parameters that let others fine-tune or deploy the model. The launch followed a July 23 meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation digital and AI ministers in Chengdu, China, where Washington and Beijing signed the same statement backing open-source models with strong security assurances. Observers have speculated that the U.S. government could respond with Entity List designations, an executive order making American firms liable for hosting Chinese models, or sanctions. The article notes the Treasury secretary has said such measures are on the table.

More than 230 U.S. technology companies and organizations, including most major AI firms, have signed an industry letter urging Washington against sweeping restrictions on open-weight models. Anthropic and Amazon did not sign. The letter argues that distribution limits would hand adversaries exclusive access to frontier capabilities while denying defenders the same, and would lock buyers into single providers. The debate builds on a joint investigation into Chinese AI models that the chairs of two House committees opened in April. The article's central claim is that openness does not eliminate power but relocates it to whoever controls compute, hosting, standards, talent, and legal frameworks.

The article argues that both the hawks and the advocates of open-weight models share the same mistaken premise, that power follows the weight file. Hawks see a ban as keeping foreign influence out, while governments embracing open models see control of a file as independence. The author contends that publishing weights shifts control over the file but not the wider AI stack, and that Beijing's shaping of the Chengdu agenda shows how negotiation over openness itself carries power. It also notes that Group of 7 ministers have called for clearer terminology, distinguishing "Open Weights AI" under unrestricted licenses from "Weights Available AI" under restricted ones. The article says the binary framing of closed America versus open China misdescribes the contest.

The article points to history to argue that restrictive trade tools have repeatedly failed against open technology. It cites the 1990s encryption controls, which pushed strong encryption abroad and left the field open to foreign developers, and the Ninth Circuit's Bernstein decision, which treated source code as protected expression. The author adds that hosting bans would remove weights from U.S. platforms without removing copies elsewhere. The article also reports that China's open-model share is growing, with Alibaba's Qwen becoming the most downloaded open model family by August 2026. Beyond that, the article does not say what restrictions, if any, Washington or Beijing will adopt.

Articles.Title: Where the Weight Lies: A Balancing Act for the Governance of Open-Weight AI Models - Lawfare

stories.Headline: Generative Legal's Cornell Tech Conference: ‘Productizing’ Legal Work in the AI Age
stories.Summary:
Panelists at Generative Legal's Cornell Tech conference in New York on Wednesday discussed how artificial intelligence is changing legal work and the organizations that do it. The panelists spoke on the condition that their comments not be attributed by name. They said legal professionals are responding to AI by productizing their work, meaning they are embedding their expertise in software. They also said legal professionals are promoting their specialized legal judgment to set themselves and their organizations apart.

One panelist said that to get the best output from AI models across use cases, users need to provide as much context as possible. The panelists said that as teams and firms browse their next AI solution, knowing how to prompt these tools is imperative. The conference discussion covered how AI is reshaping legal business models, from law firms embedding their expertise in software to legal teams fighting decision paralysis in a crowded tech market. The articles do not name the individual panelists or give further details of what each person said.

The articles do not identify who is responsible for any decision or change, beyond the panelists who spoke at the conference. The panelists are described only as speaking on the condition that their comments not be attributed by name, so their identities are not given. The articles do not quote any of them directly by name. The articles also do not say what specific steps, if any, were announced at the conference.

The context given is that law firms and legal departments have had a lot to adapt to in the artificial intelligence age. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the discussion at the conference. They do not give a date for any follow-up event or decision. They do not say whether the panelists' views will lead to any formal change. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Westlaw AI Fight Warrants Full Court Review, 3rd Circ. Told
stories.Summary:

The petition was filed with the appeals court, and Law360 reported on it on November 4, 2026. The article gives no further dates, names or figures beyond Ross Intelligence, Thomson Reuters and the Third Circuit. The underlying decision concluded that Ross Intelligence was not protected by fair use.

The article does not set out the specific requirements or changes the petition seeks, and it gives no numbers or dates for the original ruling. It says only that Ross Intelligence urged the full Third Circuit to revisit the copyright decision. The case concerns training an AI legal research platform on Thomson Reuters content. No other details of the requested relief are provided.

It does not include any statement from Ross Intelligence, Thomson Reuters or the court beyond the filing itself. The article names Theresa Schliep as the reporter and gives the publication time as November 4, 2026, at 8:23 PM EST. No further comment from any party is included.

The context is a copyright dispute over whether training an AI legal research platform on Thomson Reuters material counts as fair use. The article does not say what happens next beyond the request for full court review. It also does not indicate when the Third Circuit might act on the petition. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Musk’s Minnesota Deepfake Fight Could Define AI’s First Amendment
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk's company xAI, now renamed SpaceXAI, sued Minnesota in late July 2026 over a new state law on deepfake nude images, just days before the law was set to take effect. The company also sought an injunction to block the law. Minnesota's legislature had passed HF 1606, titled "Prohibition on Nudification Technology," in a nearly unanimous vote last spring. The law lets the state attorney general seek up to $500,000 in fines from a technology company each time it allows a user to nudify an image or video.

The law defines nudify as altering or generating an image or video to show an intimate part not in the original, in a way so realistic that a reasonable person would believe the part belongs to the identifiable individual. It holds the company strictly liable even if it has anti-deepfake policies and safeguards that a user manages to get around. Unlike older nonconsensual intimate imagery laws, it does not require intent or lack of consent, and it has no explicit exception for satire. It also defines intimate parts to include the primary genital area, groin, inner thigh, buttocks, or breast of a human being.

SpaceXAI said it already bans users from generating nonconsensual deepfake nudes and does not contest Minnesota's interest in prohibiting them. The company argued the statute reaches far beyond that goal and exposes protected speech to civil liability and government sanctions, and that the steep fines will chill speech. Minnesota argued that the law targets harmful technology, not ideas, beliefs, or expression. The state also said xAI knows how to identify illegal uses of Grok Imagine but has failed to stop what it called a flood of digital sexual victimization.

On Sept. 4, U.S. District Judge Donovan Frank denied xAI's request for a preliminary injunction without considering the First Amendment issues, focusing mainly on the company waiting nearly three months after the law was signed to file. xAI appealed directly to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, and on Oct. 2 the court granted an injunction in a one-sentence order, temporarily barring enforcement against SpaceXAI while it considers the appeal. The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, the First Amendment Lawyers Association, and the Woodhull Freedom Foundation filed an amicus brief supporting SpaceXAI. The Eighth Circuit's eventual opinion will address AI, an area with little precedential First Amendment law, and may need to decide what state of mind an AI company must have to be liable for its users' conduct.

Articles.Title: Musk’s Minnesota Deepfake Fight Could Define AI’s First Amendment - Lawfare

stories.Headline: Seattle Public Schools tightens student access to YouTube, Minecraft, and AI
stories.Summary:
Seattle Public Schools announced on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, that it is tightening student access to YouTube, Minecraft, and Google's Gemini AI chatbot during a School Board meeting. Starting Monday, YouTube will be blocked for all students in kindergarten through fifth grade, and Minecraft will be blocked for all students in kindergarten through 12th grade, except in classes that use it as part of the curriculum. District officials said they had also closed a loophole that let students reach Gemini, and the chatbot is now banned districtwide after previously being barred only for kindergarten through second grade. The district is also expanding screen limits that began in September, when iPads were stopped for kindergarten through second grade and classroom screen time was capped at 30 minutes. Starting in January, students in third through fifth grade will lose their school-issued laptops and have their daily screen time capped at 60 minutes.

Superintendent Ben Shuldiner told the board that the district is rethinking technology policies adopted during the pandemic, when many districts pushed devices into students' hands so learning could continue. He said the district needs to decide what was helpful about that shift and what was problematic, and he acknowledged that a digital society cannot be ignored. The district also presented a plan for AI literacy that would keep kindergarten through second grade students away from AI in class, introduce AI topics in third grade, and allow high schoolers to use it for feedback on drafts. Digital learning manager Debra Knickerbocker described the district's approval and purchase of AI tools such as MagicSchool AI and Microsoft Copilot. Assistant Superintendent Michael Starosky said students themselves worry about their cognitive decline.

Board Director Evan Briggs challenged the district's case, saying its presentation offered no data showing that AI tools raise reading scores or otherwise improve learning. Seattle Families for Intentional Tech, an advocacy group, wants the district to pause student-facing generative AI entirely, and its members rallied outside district headquarters on November 4, 2026, carrying signs against AI use and student data sales. Parent Erica Shutes-David said at the rally that she wants her son to think for himself rather than rely on a quick AI-generated image. The articles do not say whether the district will pause AI use as the group requests. Similar debates are playing out across many school districts in the country, and the articles do not describe any further schedule for board action.

Articles.Title: Seattle Public Schools tightens student access to YouTube, Minecraft, and AI - KUOW

stories.Headline: eCloudvalley renews AWS pact to push enterprise AI
stories.Summary:
eCloudvalley, a Singapore-headquartered cloud and digital transformation provider, has renewed a multi-year Strategic Collaboration Agreement with Amazon Web Services, according to a report published on 5 November 2026. It is the second such agreement between the two companies, following a first deal signed in 2023. The renewed pact centres on enterprise artificial intelligence as eCloudvalley moves from a services-led model toward a more product-focused business. Under the arrangement, AWS will provide technical enablement, joint solution development, proof-of-concept work and market programmes.

eCloudvalley plans to extend a model first developed in Taiwan across Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand. Its AI portfolio includes MAIAH, an enterprise AI agent system combining multi-agent functions, knowledge management, retrieval-augmented generation and AI applications. The company has also introduced EAG, a governance platform for managing AI agents, models, data and access permissions from one point. Other offerings include NeoEdge Matrix and NeoEdge Central for edge computing in industrial and operational technology settings, along with Atlas 2.0, a cloud management product.

The company said these tools are meant to reduce operational risk and control costs as businesses scale AI projects. Linda Lin, Chief Executive Officer of eCloudvalley, said the first agreement helped the company expand its regional footprint and build an AWS business in Australia, and that the next phase focuses on deeper AI products. Jason Tam, Deputy Chief Executive Officer, said partners must offer value beyond distribution and discounts, and described the company as becoming a product-driven technology partner. Kirsten Gilbertson, Head of ASEAN Partner Development at AWS, said the partnership reflects customer demand for practical cloud and AI use in the region.

The company, founded in 2013, serves more than 2,400 enterprise clients and holds more than 500 AWS certifications, and it was named AWS Global MSP Partner of the Year in 2024. The renewed agreement comes as eCloudvalley seeks growth in financial services, manufacturing, retail and the public sector, targeting both small and medium-sized businesses and larger enterprises. The company operates across Taiwan, mainland China, Hong Kong, the Philippines, Singapore, the United States, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam and Australia, and its partner roster also includes SAP, Microsoft, Oracle, Google Cloud and Salesforce. The articles do not say what specific milestones, timelines or revenue targets accompany the new pact.

Articles.Title: eCloudvalley renews AWS pact to push enterprise AI - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Rigged Coding Assignment, Abused AI Tool Opened Path to $6 Billion Binance Heist
stories.Summary:
Binance says hackers stole $6.34 billion from its hot wallets last week after a months-long campaign that compromised three engineers' computers, one through a fake job interview. The exchange published its initial incident report on November 3, and about $2.85 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen or intercepted. The FBI has blamed the theft on TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group. Binance said the intrusion was not a single breach or a simple phishing incident but unfolded in stages using fake recruiters, malicious downloads, hijacked employee computers and an internal AI tool.

The campaign began in June, when a Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation while searching for a popular AI coding tool. Binance's security team caught it, replaced his device and reset credentials, but the attackers had already learned about his work and colleagues on the wallet infrastructure team. In September, a second engineer was approached by someone claiming to be a project director and invited to two interviews, the first with a fake HR representative and the second with the alleged CEO of a company that did not exist. The second interview ended with a request to download a coding assignment onto his work computer, and the assignment hid malicious code that ran as soon as he set it up. Binance said the 0-day malware was not detected by endpoint security tools at the time.

On October 20, the attackers used the infected machine and an internal AI tool to gain control of the first engineer's system and a third wallet engineer's system, though the report does not explain how the AI tool was used. On October 29, they signed into the third engineer's computer, deployed a container with credentials taken from the first engineer and started the attack with a malicious script. Binance says the attackers exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to move XRP, SOL, OP and BTC out of its hot wallets, and used the same service to abuse Ethereum's EIP-7702 mechanism, giving a contract under their control partial execution rights over a hot wallet. Because the hot wallet used multi-party computation, Binance had no single key to cancel the delegation right away; the last unauthorized transfer settled at 23:56 UTC and the delegation was cleared shortly after midnight.

Binance said it has rebuilt the affected wallet system and AI tool, replaced devices and retired the engineers' credentials and tokens, and is engaging independent security firms to review the incident. It is also working on a research fund focused on AI security in blockchain environments and said it detected and blocked 57 suspected North Korea-linked threats this year. North Korea rejected the FBI's attribution, with Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, calling it a grave political provocation in a statement carried by state media. Co-CEO Richard Teng said 98% of the impacted tokens have been replenished and withdrawals have broadly resumed after reopening in phases from November 1. Elliptic says the stolen funds passed through about 12,000 wallets on 11 blockchains in under four days, and as of November 3 roughly $3.18 billion remained in theft-linked addresses.

Articles.Title: Rigged Coding Assignment, Abused AI Tool Opened Path to $6 Billion Binance Heist - SecurityWeek

stories.Headline: TSE Growth Market 250 Falls for Fourth Straight Session as AI Regulation Fears From U.S. Midterms Weigh
stories.Summary:
The TSE Growth Market 250 Index fell 0.57% to 769.27 on November 4, 2026, its fourth straight decline. During the session the index dropped more than 3% at one point. Reports that the Democratic Party was gaining an edge in the U.S. midterm elections chilled investor sentiment over fears of tighter AI regulation. Later reports that the Democratic Party had recaptured majorities in both the House and Senate brought a selling on the news view.

As the Nikkei Stock Average pared its losses, bargain-hunting buying emerged and supported the market. Among individual stocks, MTG and Humameid declined, while Oncolys and QD Laser rose. Data Section, Terra Drone and Cybertrust also traded weak, and Tier IV and Ftsuper rose. Newly listed Allganize Holdings got off to a firm start, and MabGenesis, in its second day of trading, briefly hit the daily limit-up.

Market participants said it is uncertainty over regulation, rather than the election results themselves, that is widening the market's swings. The articles say U.S. political developments tend to directly affect the valuation of high-tech stocks. Investor attention will now shift to the specifics of regulation and the direction of U.S. interest rates. Many expect a nervous trading environment to continue in the near term as investors watch for U.S. policy announcements.

Articles.Title: TSE Growth Market 250 Falls for Fourth Straight Session as AI Regulation Fears From U.S. Midterms Weigh

stories.Headline: PYMNTS | Goldman Sachs Bars Bankers From Employing Some AI Tools
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs has restricted its bankers and traders from using Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub coding tools, according to a Bloomberg report. The bank had allowed bankers to use these tools for months before the change. Internal guidance published last month and seen by Bloomberg limits the tools to Goldman's engineers only. Quantitative employees known as strats are exempt from the restrictions. A source familiar with the matter told Bloomberg that the ban has frustrated some Goldman traders, who had used AI to monitor client trading flows and to create written and graphic materials.

The restrictions follow warnings from Replit CEO Amjad Masad about the security risks of AI coding agents on employee devices. Replit's security advisory, co-authored by CTO Luis Héctor Chávez and engineering lead Manish Mehta, recommends running AI agents in dedicated, organization-controlled cloud environments that limit each agent's access to resources for each task. The advisory cited recent incidents, including a compromised Claude Code extension via the Cursor marketplace and hijacked GitHub accounts. As recently as July, Goldman Chief Information Officer Marco Argenti had touted "vibe coding" by non-technical employees, who developed solutions with AI tools and passed them to one of the firm's 12,000 engineers to enhance.

Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra told Bloomberg that the bank makes certain AI tools available to its people to find the best use cases across different parts of the firm. He said that after a period of experimentation assessing factors including productivity and risk management, the bank puts the tools in the hands of those best suited to leverage them for the long term. Masad said on X that such restrictions are becoming widespread in finance due to concerns like supply chain attacks and credential exposure. Replit argues that controlling what AI agents can do is more crucial than merely restricting who uses them.

The move comes as banks spend millions on artificial intelligence tools while trying to deal with rising concerns about cost, productivity and cybersecurity risk. JPMorganChase CEO Jamie Dimon warned of "rogue agents" and said during a third-quarter earnings call last month that outside AI agents would not be permitted inside the bank. Bank of America followed a day later with limits on agents' access to consumer deposits while it develops protocols deciding which party is liable for a payment an AI authorizes. By Friday, Citigroup had drawn the same line, not letting third-party agents log into accounts or transact.

Articles.Title: Goldman Sachs restricts AI coding tools for bankers
