Eleven of the 17 named security operations, such as alert triage and the first pass of investigations, as where agents paid off, and Lusha and Orca cited automating customer security questionnaires, which Lusha's Einat Shimoni said cut turnaround from weeks to days.

Aviv Nahum, CEO of Above Security, said the rogue AI framing is mostly a distraction, and Raul Zayat Galante, CISO at Port, described the concern as a legitimate actor with legitimate credentials executing a legitimate action under the wrong context at machine speed. Einat Shimoni, CISO at Lusha, said the risk is not malice but specification failure at scale, and Nir Mishal, CISO at Orca Security, described thousands of well-intentioned agents with standing privileges, chained tools and no owner. Eli Hakimov, CISO at Immunai, called unvetted agents a shadow workforce that is autonomous, fast and invisible, and Lior Mazor, CISO at Appcharge, said his biggest concern is that autonomy will move faster than accountability. Chris Jones, chief trust and security officer at Axonius, said he has not seen a single company effectively mass-downsize its workforce and backfill those roles with AI agents, while Madsec's Doron Sivan said he has not seen an AI agent that directly improved an organization's security posture aside from security products that build in AI-agent capabilities.

The series noted that a self-selected group of 17 proves nothing statistically but does not suggest Israeli companies are dodging the problem, and several interviewees were wary of their own clean records, with Hakimov saying that in this space so far is doing a lot of work. Nahum said he would be more worried about a company claiming its agents always behave exactly as expected than one admitting they occasionally surprise them. The case that local leaders are ahead rests on discipline, with most companies building identity controls, approval committees and named owners before agents went live, while the case that they are merely closer to the risk rests on the fact that eight of the 17, Immunai, Orca, Madsec, Akamai, Axonius, Silverfort, Above Security and Imperva-Thales, sell security products themselves. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Israel’s security leaders aren’t afraid of rogue AI. They’re afraid of permissions.

stories.Headline: The crusade against AI slop in the workplace has a powerful new ally
stories.Summary:
Michelle Volberg, founder and CEO of the tech recruiting company Twill, sent her staff an email about six months ago asking them to stop talking to her like a robot. Some employees had been copying and pasting messages from Claude into Slack and email, and the messages read like pitches from outside consultants, with perfect punctuation but no client context and some made-up details. The problem started when Volberg rolled out an enterprise Claude subscription to her company of 10. Her policy now lets staff use AI to brainstorm but requires their own voice for internal communication. She says creative thinking and personal interaction returned once the rule took hold.

The term "workslop" was coined a year ago by researchers from the Stanford Social Media Lab and BetterUp Labs to describe low-quality, overly wordy AI-generated memos, documents, emails and slide decks that workers were passing to one another. The article reports that workers are now sending this material up to executives, and that some CEOs' mandates to use AI helped create the flood. Kate Niederhoffer, chief scientist at BetterUp Labs, says the problem is shaped more by workplace conditions than by individual behavior. Her survey published last fall found that more than half of respondents admitted sending workslop, and she argues that bosses should create environments where people feel safe discussing how AI can change their work.

The article also notes that tools have not delivered the productivity gains their builders promised, and that some workers have taken on longer hours and more tasks. Several companies have responded with written rules. In August, software startup Clay's cofounder Varun Anand posted the company's AI writing policy on LinkedIn, which requires workers to stand behind every idea in every sentence and says writing a document should take longer than reading it. Spellbook CEO Scott Stevenson told his team in early September that he would rather see five scrappy bullet points than five polished pages, and he asked that customer communication be handwritten.

Eric Fischgrund, who runs the public relations firm FischTank PR, bans AI-written content for reporters or clients, checks with an AI detector, and last year fired a worker who kept breaking the rule after a confrontation and a warning. ZocDoc issued guidance in August encouraging staff to never ship their slop and to keep their own ideas, and its chief communications officer, Jessica Aptman, says the approach is less punitive and more focused on preserving workers' value and trust. The article concludes that bosses may need to build cultures where people feel their input matters, since preventing slop may work better than cleaning it up. It does not report any further developments beyond these policies.

Articles.Title: The crusade against AI slop in the workplace has a powerful new ally

stories.Headline: These rare killer whales are threatened by shipping noise. AI is turning down the din
stories.Summary:
In September, 76 southern resident killer whales arrived in the Salish Sea, the last of an endangered population. Each year the few score left enter Admiralty Inlet and head toward Puget Sound, Washington, moving in and out from late summer until early winter to hunt Chinook salmon. Noise from heavy shipping traffic affects their ability to hunt, communicate and echolocate, and vessels pose a deadly collision risk. Scientists did not realize the southern resident was a genetically distinct group from the more populous Bigg's killer whale until the 1970s.

The first survey in 1974 found 71 whales, the count peaked at 97 in 1996 and declined to 79 in 2001, and the southern resident was listed as endangered in 2005. A 2024 study found that for every one decibel increase in maximum noise level, females were 58% less likely to pursue prey, and males and females were 12.5% less likely to capture prey. In 2022 Quiet Sound introduced a voluntary slow-down program for ships along a 20-mile stretch coming into Seattle, Tacoma and Everett, and Aronson said participation this season has been 73% and underwater noise has fallen by as much as 50% since it began. In July 2025, SMRU Consulting and Microsoft partnered to test whether AI on board a buoy could correctly identify killer whale and humpback whale calls, and in July the Communications Acoustics Buoy was launched in the Haro Strait.

Rachel Aronson, program director of Quiet Sound, an initiative within Maritime Blue, said underwater noise is a pervasive threat and that when it is loud underwater it gets harder for the whales to find food, so they sometimes hunt and miss or forgo hunting, which is a problem especially for a female building up to a pregnancy or nursing a baby. Cormac Booth, managing director of SMRU Consulting, a subsidiary of the University of St Andrews in the UK, said marine acoustic monitoring has been around for decades but the gap between data collection and analysis was once many months, and that the focus has moved away from an after-the-fact archival approach toward reliable insights of what is happening now. Juan Lavista Ferres, chief data scientist and corporate vice president of Microsoft and lab director of the Microsoft AI for Good Lab, said underwater monitoring produces far more audio than people can review manually and that AI helps most with processing this data in near-real time, and he said results so far are encouraging and false positives have decreased. Jason Wood, principal scientist and deputy director of technology at SMRU Consulting, said the Haro Strait offers the biggest bang for your buck for southern residents.

Washington is a trade-dependent state where 40% of jobs are tied to international commerce, so balancing maritime industries with wildlife conservation is a delicate act. SMRU Consulting has developed smart buoys since 2014, used in Scotland, the US East Coast and the Pacific Northwest, and Microsoft's Water SPARROW, an aquatic version of its wildlife monitoring AI launched in 2024, is already used in camera traps. The buoy has three hydrophones anchored underwater, with Microsoft's system floating in the buoy and SMRU's analysis system below the surface, and Wood said the two are engaged in a bake off to see which detects southern resident signals with the greatest accuracy. Wood said that due to the risk of false positives, the buoy, and the article ends there.

Articles.Title: These rare killer whales are threatened by shipping noise. AI is turning down the din

stories.Headline: European Enterprises Face Growing Pressure to Turn AI Investment into Business Value, ISG Says
stories.Summary:
Information Services Group, a technology research and advisory firm, published new research finding that European enterprises are under growing pressure to turn AI adoption into measurable business value. The research found that AI performance and adoption are exceeding expectations, but business and financial returns are lagging. ISG announced the findings in a press release on November 5, 2026. The firm said strategies for moving AI beyond isolated experiments will be explored at the 2026 ISG AI Impact Summit Paris.

The summit will take place November 9 to 10 at the Pullman Paris Tour Eiffel. Leaders from the Adecco Group, ArianeGroup, Cigref, Lagardère Travel Retail, Linxens, Pfizer, Philip Morris International, Thales and WPP will join the event. The first day will open with a keynote by Pierre Matuchet, senior vice president for IT and Digital Transformation at the Adecco Group. Sessions will cover identifying high-value use cases, governance, process redesign and measuring returns, and a panel on sovereign AI will feature Général Dominique Trinquand of DHT Conseil and Marc Valès of Terrespace.

Pierre Moulin, a director at ISG and chair of the summit, said many enterprises are struggling to translate productivity gains from AI into business outcomes. He said European organizations must work out how to capture returns from AI while keeping control of their data, managing risk and preparing their people and systems for increasingly autonomous operations. Day two will open with a keynote by Remi Tromeur of Thales Global Services on AI in vendor management. A panel on human and AI collaboration will feature Valentine Ferreol of Linxens, Ritika Rajpal of WPP and David Rudnianski of Loxam.

The summit is sponsored by DXC Technology, Tata Communications, Tata Consultancy Services, NTT DATA, Inetum, Accenture, Clocate and the TBM Council. ISG describes itself as a global AI-centered technology research and advisory firm with more than 900 clients, including 75 of the world's top 100 enterprises. The firm was founded in 2006 and has 1,500 professionals worldwide. The articles do not say what happens after the summit.

Articles.Title: European Enterprises Face Growing Pressure to Turn AI Investment into Business Value, ISG Says

stories.Headline: Pentagon Task Force Plans Public Inventory of Rules Governing US AI Labs
stories.Summary:
Pentagon Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael said on November 4, 2026, that the U.S. federal government plans to publish an overview of the laws and regulations that apply to domestic AI companies later this month, according to a Reuters report. Michael, who is vice chair of the government's Super Intelligence Task Force, made the announcement at a Wall Street Journal technology conference in Napa, California. He said the group expects to make the regulatory overview public within one or two weeks. The task force is an intergovernmental agency established by President Donald Trump to shape federal AI policy, and it intends to lay out the existing regulatory landscape for domestic AI labs.

Michael said the goal is to create a framework that gives Americans confidence that AI companies will act responsibly, according to the report. He warned that, without a coordinated approach, Congress could produce fragmented regulation that could harm the industry. Michael did not provide details about the document's scope, the agencies involved or how it would be used. The announcement signals an effort to map existing rules rather than introduce new legal requirements, and the scope, level of detail and intended use of the forthcoming document remain unclear.

For chief data officers, a clearer picture of the federal regulatory landscape could help organizations assess how existing obligations apply to their AI initiatives, particularly where data privacy, security, intellectual property and accountability intersect. However, an overview of existing laws will not replace the internal structures organizations and AI governance need to manage AI systems. Companies still need clear ownership of AI-related risks, documented approval processes, controls over data access and mechanisms for monitoring systems after deployment. As organizations align internal policies with evolving requirements, allocating responsibility across technology, legal, risk and data teams will remain important. The task force's forthcoming publication should provide a clearer indication of how the administration intends to describe the rules governing the U.S. AI companies.

Articles.Title: Pentagon Task Force Plans Public Inventory of Rules Governing US AI Labs

stories.Headline: AI disruption, geopolitics and partnerships in focus at Hong Kong business summit
stories.Summary:
About 100 business owners, executives and academics attended the fourth edition of the Family Business Summit in Hong Kong. The event was co-hosted by the South China Morning Post and Blue Pool Capital, with UBS as the presenting partner. It took place on Wednesday and Thursday, with the article published on 5 November 2026. Technology-driven disruptions, superpower rivalry and global partnerships dominated the closed-door discussions.

Attendees came from the United States, mainland China, Hong Kong, Southeast Asia and the Middle East. At a welcome dinner on Wednesday, Singapore's Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo spoke about her country's approach to AI. She discussed how the city state aims to capitalise on the technology while ensuring no one is left behind. The summit's focus reflected efforts by countries and tech giants to boost growth and lead the race in artificial intelligence.

The gathering was the fourth edition of the event, which brings together family business owners, executives and academics. Josephine Teo is the minister responsible for digital development and information in Singapore, and she addressed the dinner on Wednesday. The article paraphrases her remarks as covering how Singapore seeks to benefit from AI while making sure no one is excluded. The summit was co-hosted by the South China Morning Post and Blue Pool Capital, with UBS as presenting partner.

These organisations organised the event, which drew about 100 participants. The context is a global push by countries and technology companies to drive growth and compete for leadership in artificial intelligence. Superpower rivalry and technology-driven disruption shaped the agenda alongside global partnerships. The article does not say what follows the summit or any planned outcomes.

Articles.Title: AI disruption, geopolitics and partnerships in focus at Hong Kong business summit

stories.Headline: Friday's jobs report could be a tiebreaker for Wall Street's AI trade as inflation worries linger
stories.Summary:
The Business Insider piece, written by Joe Ciolli, reports that U.S. stocks have been caught between two competing stories. The AI trade has been weighed down by worries about heavy capital spending and high valuations, while falling oil prices have eased fears about inflation and suggested the recent sell-off might be a short-lived reset. After a Democratic sweep in the midterm elections, Brent crude dropped below $100 a barrel for the first time in months on Wednesday, and all major U.S. stock indexes rose sharply. The article says the October jobs report due Friday could settle which story wins, with economists expecting about 65,000 payroll additions.

The article lays out three possible readings of that report. A modest payroll gain, steady unemployment and tame wage growth would be a "Goldilocks" result, suggesting inflation is cooling without a broader downturn, which would give expensive AI growth stocks room to recover and let investors focus on whether AI spending turns into revenue. A weak number would stoke fears of a wider economic slowdown, which could lower Treasury yields in the short term but would likely weigh on stocks over time. A surprisingly strong number could revive inflation fears, push yields higher and pressure the AI trade, particularly companies that rely heavily on debt financing.

A Politico newsletter from the same period, written by its Morning Money team, adds a political angle. It reports that Democrats have made artificial intelligence a central issue in the midterm elections and could expand oversight of the industry if they win control of Congress. The piece quotes James Maloney, founding partner of Tiger Hill Partners, saying that Wall Street investors "are not the oversight bullseye, but could be caught in a dragnet." Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat and potential next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has warned of an AI bubble comparable to the 2008 financial crisis and asked financial firms for more information on their AI exposure. Goldman Sachs Research estimates $1 trillion will be invested in AI-related projects worldwide this year, and JPMorgan's David Kelly said Washington must first decide how to regulate the technology before legislating.

Taken together, the two pieces describe a market under pressure from several directions at once. Investors are weighing the jobs data against lingering inflation concerns, the Nasdaq Composite has fallen more than 7% over the past month, and the outcome of the midterm elections could bring added scrutiny to AI financing. The articles do not say how the jobs report actually turned out, nor how the elections were decided. Each suggests that the coming months will show whether the AI trade can hold up under this combined pressure.

Articles.Title: Friday's jobs report could be a tiebreaker for Wall Street's AI trade as inflation worries linger

stories.Headline: Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics
stories.Summary:
Axiom Math, a startup valued at $1.6 billion, announced on Wednesday that it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics written by humans. The company's fleet of AI agents translated the library's roughly 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of computer-checked code. The work was done in Lean, a programming language, and a proof assistant checks each line so that a passing proof can be trusted as logically sound. Axiom was founded in March 2025 by CEO Carina Hong, who had left a Stanford math Ph.D. program, and the company raised a $200 million Series A in March.

The Stacks Project was started in 2005 by Johan de Jong, a Columbia mathematician, as an open-source reference that others have added to over the years. Its theorems are tightly interconnected, so the team had to keep every connection intact across the entire translation. Ashvin Swaminathan, a member of Axiom's technical staff, said the agents worked in parallel, found their own tasks and were given only a loose hierarchy. Axiom also trained its own models to be strong at math, and an in-house Lean expert initially taught the agents a sense of taste before they picked it up on their own. The company says the result fills a large gap in formalized math in algebraic geometry.

Hong told TechCrunch that she was not sure vibe coding could preserve the beauty of the project, and she described the challenge as bringing together things that are big and things that are delicate. Swaminathan said that researchers working on algebraic geometry now have a verified base to build on. Terence Tao, a UCLA mathematician and Fields Medal winner, has argued that the more formalized proofs exist, the more can be made. Hong also issued an open challenge to other coding companies to work on formalization at this scale.

The effort is aimed at a wider concern about AI-generated work, as OpenAI recently released 719 manuscripts claiming solutions to hard problems and computer checks can themselves slip. Axiom's position is that verified foundations will matter for software as AI agents write more of the world's code, and that mathematics is a good place to start. Swaminathan said the agents can read, understand and build new infrastructure on top of the Lean formalization. Hong argued that agents need a reusable, well-built body of knowledge to avoid producing slop and to keep pushing the frontier.

Articles.Title: Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics

stories.Headline: OpenAI debuts new cybersecurity-focused AI model amid growing alarm about AI-driven cyber attacks
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has released GPT-6 Cyber, a new artificial intelligence model built for cybersecurity professionals, according to a November 5, 2026 report by Fortune. The company says the model performs better than its general-purpose GPT-6 Astra model on most cyber tasks. Because the model could be misused to carry out cyberattacks, OpenAI is making it available only to a small group of approved security customers for now. The release comes as AI tools grow better at finding software flaws and turning them into working attacks.

The articles describe the model's focus as advanced vulnerability research and exploit development, the kind of work that tests whether a system can be broken into. OpenAI tested it on Firefox and the Linux kernel, where the company says researchers found 81 previously unknown, high-severity Firefox vulnerabilities. The company also says researchers developed working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including 588 flaws not previously known, and some of these could let an attacker gain the highest level of control over a system. Initial access is limited to approved Daybreak Red customers, with access expanding to all Red customers over the coming weeks.

Gartner forecast in September that worldwide spending on AI cybersecurity would reach $51.3 billion this year, nearly double last year's $25.9 billion. OpenAI describes this as a market it is increasingly pursuing to grow its enterprise sales, and it has hired Dali Rajic, who comes from a cybersecurity software background, as chief revenue officer. The article notes this is OpenAI's fourth cybersecurity-focused model this year, following releases in April, June and August. Competitors Google and Anthropic are also courting security customers through vetted-access programs.

The articles note that the same techniques used to test defenses can be used in real attacks, which is why general-purpose models restrict some work that can also block legitimate security research. OpenAI has said its cyber models are trained both to improve specialized security skills and to reduce refusals on certain tasks. Fortune first reported in September that OpenAI was planning a specialized cyber model based on GPT-6. Beyond the initial rollout, the articles do not describe further planned steps.

Articles.Title: OpenAI debuts new cybersecurity-focused AI model amid growing alarm about AI-driven cyber attacks

stories.Headline: Semantic data aggregation with BigQuery and AI.AGG
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud published a blog post on November 5, 2026, by Pramod Niralakeri, a Strategic Cloud Engineer, introducing AI.AGG, a function that is currently in preview and built into BigQuery's GoogleSQL. The article explains that BigQuery has long handled structured data aggregation at petabyte scale, but it has lacked a native way to synthesize meaning across millions of rows of text and multimodal data such as logs, support transcripts, and images. Row-level AI functions like AI.GENERATE and AI.CLASSIFY already exist, yet analyzing a whole dataset at once runs into the context window limits of large language models, which can cause truncation or failure. Before this, teams had to build external map-reduce pipelines to split, process, and recombine results themselves.

AI.AGG handles that work inside the database by checking that no single row exceeds the maximum context window, which is 10 MiB, and by grouping rows into batches that fit the token limits of the chosen Gemini endpoint. The natural-language prompt is run against each batch in parallel through Vertex AI, and the intermediate summaries are then combined and passed back to the model with the same instruction until one final string remains for each GROUP BY group. The article says the function uses full-weight LLMs at every stage, unlike row-level functions that can use distilled proxy models. It also supports multimodal inputs through object tables and OBJ.GET_ACCESS_URL, and it works within VPC Service Controls. Several operating limits are listed: each group's output is capped at 10,000 tokens, each row must stay under 10 MiB, rows with fewer than 10 images are recommended, and queries should handle no more than 20 million rows and 1,000 distinct groups.

Pramod Niralakeri presents the function as a way to turn the data warehouse into an active system for semantic analysis, and the post recommends practices for production use. Those include wrapping nullable struct fields in IFNULL, because a single null field causes the whole row to be discarded, and writing prompts as strict output contracts. The article also advises using WHERE and LIMIT filters to control costs, since recursive batching sends more tokens to Gemini than the source data contains, and it suggests using AI.COUNT_TOKENS to estimate costs before running a query. Examples in the post include summarizing forum authors' comments, grouping critical logs by time window to surface root causes, and creating labels that feed into AI.CLASSIFY. The article does not report any customer adoption figures or release dates beyond the preview status.

Articles.Title: Semantic data aggregation with BigQuery and AI.AGG

stories.Headline: Oracle Database pitches one engine to tame enterprise AI data
stories.Summary:
Oracle used its Oracle AI World event to pitch a single database engine as the answer to the data problem that holds back enterprise AI agents. In a video interview recorded there and published on November 5, 2026, Hasan Rizvi, executive vice president of product and research for database engineering at Oracle, described a converged platform that stores vectors, graphs, documents and transactions in one engine. The pitch centers on giving AI agents enough knowledge of a company's own data to act on live business processes. Rizvi spoke with Dave Vellante of theCUBE Research during the conference. Rizvi argued that generic AI models can write SQL but do not know a company's orders, customers or revenue definitions, so their answers stay generic.

He offered questions such as where the stock is, how to fix a transaction and how to expedite a delivery as examples of what a business-aware assistant could handle. He said that AI has made it fast for teams to create new applications and data stores, which adds to data sprawl. Skeptics tend to prefer a specialized database for each workload, but Rizvi said new data types built inside Oracle's engine inherit its availability, security and scale. He pointed to decades of engineering investment in that engine as the basis for this claim.

Rizvi also described deployment choice as part of the offer, noting that the database runs on-premises, through Oracle Cloud@Customer and across multiple public clouds. Oracle used the event to expand Iceberg support in its Autonomous AI Lakehouse, he said. On security, he described Oracle's Deep Data Security feature, which defines access policies inside the database so a user's identity travels with each request from an agent or AI-generated app. He warned that AI has made it much easier to reverse engineer fixes for vulnerabilities, which raises the stakes for attackers.

The article does not supply further figures or dates beyond the publication date. The interview is part of SiliconANGLE and theCUBE's coverage of Oracle AI World, and the outlet disclosed that it is a paid media partner for the event. Oracle, as the event sponsor, does not have editorial control over the content. The article does not say what Oracle plans next for these products or how customers have responded to them.

Articles.Title: Oracle Database pitches one engine to tame enterprise AI data

stories.Headline: DataMEDS AI Signs MOU to Deploy Health Lives Here GLP-1 Patient Management Program with Florida-Based HMO
stories.Summary:
DataMEDS AI, Inc. signed a Memorandum of Understanding with a Florida-based health maintenance organization whose name is being withheld at its request, the company announced on November 5, 2026. The agreement covers deployment of the Health Lives Here mobile application, initially focused on helping members on GLP-1 receptor agonist medications manage their treatment. The HMO expects to have between 25,000 and 30,000 members for 2027 following open enrollment, which closes on December 8, 2026. NFL Alumni Health, a strategic marketing partner of Health Lives Here, expects to support member engagement efforts.

The program aims to improve medication adherence and HEDIS and CMS star ratings, initially in obesity and diabetes members. The HMO serves Medicare Advantage members, including Chronic Special Needs Plan and Dual Eligible Special Needs Plan beneficiaries. DataMEDS would earn revenue on a per member per month model for use of the app by all HMO members, with additional revenue from an add-on GLP-1 drug patient management program. Further opportunities may arise in pharmacy dispensing, diagnostic lab testing and medical food products, and the companies expect to execute definitive agreements in the fourth quarter of 2026 to begin rolling out the app in the first quarter of 2027. The MOU is non-binding and subject to definitive agreements.

Gerald Commissiong, Interim Co-CEO of DataMEDS, said HMOs represent a significant opportunity for the company and Health Lives Here. He said the company has been adding technologies to its platform while making sure it markets the app not only direct-to-consumer but also to organizations that manage patients. He said the agreement positions DataMEDS to add its first corporate customer and to fine-tune its offering for payors. He said the framework opens the door to giving payor groups a platform they can easily implement to improve efficiency and encourage member engagement.

DataMEDS, formerly Wellgistics Health, Inc., is headquartered in Tampa, Florida, and trades on Nasdaq under the symbol MEDS. Its retail pharmacy, Corexa Pharmacy, is in-network with the HMO's pharmacy benefits manager and Medicare, and its diagnostic laboratory, Helomics, is in-network with Medicare. The press release lists forward-looking statements covering the timing of the rollout, pricing, member uptake, NFL Alumni Health's participation and related compliance matters, among other risks. It says actual results may differ materially and that the company undertakes no obligation to update its statements except as required by law.

Articles.Title: DataMEDS AI Signs MOU to Deploy Health Lives Here GLP-1 Patient Management Program with Florida-Based HMO

stories.Headline: Google puts new limits on AI agents that hunt threats and fix vulnerabilities
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud added new controls to CodeMender, its AI tool for finding and fixing software vulnerabilities, on November 5, 2026. The updates let businesses verify vulnerabilities and simulate exploits in an operating system-level sandbox or an isolated virtual machine. They also add human checks for local writes and command execution to keep testing within defined limits. Businesses can scan an entire code repository, a specific folder, or only files modified since the last scan, which gives them more control over scanning speed and costs. CodeMender remains in preview.

Google Cloud is also extending security and governance controls across environments where AI agents run, including Gemini, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run, and the new Agent Compute Engine. Auth Manager is now generally available and centralizes credential management in a Google-managed vault governed by IAM. Agent Identity JWT support, in preview, lets agents authenticate across services including AWS, Azure, on-premises backends, and Model Context Protocol servers without static, long-lived API keys. VPC Service Controls ingress and egress rules now support IAM roles, and Workload Identity Federation for GKE is in preview. A new Model Armor custom topic detector, also in preview, lets businesses define prompt-based rules to check whether agent conversations stay within approved topics.

Ivan Fontarensky, CTO of Cybersecurity Services at Thales Group, said adversaries attack at machine speed and the Fairwind Program helps keep pace with application security. He said early evaluation of CodeMender shows the potential to reduce vulnerability discovery time by over 95%, while keeping expert validation and remediation under human oversight. Sandra Joyce, VP of Google Threat Intelligence, said Wiz and Google Cloud are combining deep autonomous application understanding, connected security context, and threat intelligence to help organizations innovate securely and stay ahead of emerging threats. Google says its approach to countering autonomous, multi-agent threats combines continuous workload monitoring, threat intelligence, and automated investigations, with agents presenting mitigation actions for human approval.

Google Threat Intelligence telemetry is incorporated into defensive models to trigger automated threat hunts that reconstruct process trees and isolate threats in real time, according to the company. Wiz AI Static Application Security Testing is now in preview and correlates code weaknesses with infrastructure context in the Wiz Security Graph. A shared data model now connects Wiz Defend and Google Security Operations, and analysts can access Wiz Blue Agent's investigation findings within Google Security Operations. Google DeepMind and Wiz also launched Scan for Good, which Google says used Gemini 4 Argon to help more than 50 public service organizations and critical infrastructure providers identify and address critical security exposures during its first month.

Articles.Title: Google puts new limits on AI agents that hunt threats and fix vulnerabilities

stories.Headline: Government uses open-weight AI to control costs and meet mission needs
stories.Summary:
At the Red Hat Government Symposium in Washington, D.C. in October 2026, public sector and cybersecurity leaders discussed how federal agencies are using open-weight AI models to control costs while still meeting mission needs. The discussion was reported by TechTarget on Nov. 5, 2026. Open-weight models have trained parameters that users can download, deploy and, depending on the license, modify or fine-tune, unlike proprietary models that are typically accessed through a vendor's hosted platform or API. Examples include models from Meta's Llama family, Alibaba's Qwen and DeepSeek. Agencies are weighing the capabilities of frontier models against the economics of open-weight alternatives.

The article describes a hybrid approach that combines frontier models for complex analysis and mission-critical reasoning with smaller, less expensive models for routine tasks. The Department of Homeland Security's January 2025 Playbook for Public Sector Generative AI Deployment recommends that agencies evaluate commercial, open-source and open-weight models, including the possibility of using multiple model types. The National Institute of Standards and Technology has sought access to open-weight model hosting and inference services for its Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The General Services Administration has pursued discounted AI agreements through its OneGov initiative, and in October 2026 it announced an expanded agreement with Anthropic providing a 40% discount on token-based usage across Claude models for government customers.

Ben Cushing, Red Hat's chief architect for health and life sciences, said a hybrid approach lets agencies control costs without sacrificing access to top-tier AI capabilities, and he described running open-weight models locally on infrastructure the agency controls as the safest way to take advantage of frontier lab capabilities. He recalled that CIOs in the federal health space told him last year they had gone through their cloud credits on tokens within a month despite planning for the whole year. Lance Jenkinson, CIO and deputy assistant inspector general for management administration at the Department of Veterans Affairs, said his agency has created 42,000 patches over the last several months, primarily using open-weight models, and that about 300 AI-driven processes exist with 85% of them today using open-weight models rather than frontier models. He said answers can be just as accurate, more often than not, at a far lower cost, and he said each agency needs to weigh whether a tool is secured and supported.

The article says open-weight models are not the only way government organizations control spending, since purpose-built proprietary AI services, government-specific pricing agreements and consumption-based contracts can also reduce costs. It notes that open-weight AI can introduce infrastructure and maintenance expenses that offset some of its apparent savings. Cushing said there is absolutely not one model that rules them all, and that every model is better at certain things than others, with cost and accuracy elements to consider. Panelists recommended that decision-makers evaluate models based on the work they need to perform.

Articles.Title: Government uses open-weight AI to control costs and meet mission needs

stories.Headline: Hedgeness CEO: Fit AI to the workflow, not the other way around
stories.Summary:
Jay Singh, co-founder and CEO of Hedgeness, said artificial intelligence and automation offer many possibilities, but new technology alone does not guarantee adoption or business value. He said technology should create value for the people using it rather than add another layer of complexity. His key insight was that AI should be fitted to the workflow, not the other way around. The article was published by Digital Insurance on November 5, 2026, and was written by Grace Crane. The article gives no further numbers, dates or names beyond Singh, Hedgeness, Crane and the publication date.

It sets out no specific requirements, policy changes or new rules. It does not describe any product, funding round or deal. The piece is a short interview item in the outlet's Meet the Insurtech series. Singh is the person responsible for the view expressed, as co-founder and CEO of Hedgeness. He said technology should create value for the people using it, not introduce another layer of complexity.

He framed the point as a key insight about AI and automation. The article presents his comments without further attribution or response. The context is the outlet's Meet the Insurtech series, which runs short profiles and interviews with insurtech leaders. The same page links to other recent items on AI in insurance, including one on insurtechs getting AI past the pilot stage and one on insurers raising AI budgets before seeing returns. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Hedgeness CEO: Fit AI to the workflow, not the other way around

stories.Headline: Shoppers will let AI browse, but they still want their hand on the wallet
stories.Summary:
Nuvei published research on November 5, 2026, on how U.S. shoppers feel about AI-assisted commerce. The study found that 58% of consumers find AI useful for researching products and comparing prices, and 39% say they are using it more while shopping than three months earlier. But 56% say they would never allow AI to spend money without their approval, and only 1% want the shopping process fully automated from start to finish. Shoppers have accepted AI as a research assistant but not as a wallet.

The research gives specific numbers on what worries consumers and what would reassure them. Seventy six percent named fraud or unauthorized charges as their biggest concern, more than double the 33% who worried about the AI buying the wrong item. Eighty four percent said the ability to cancel or reverse an AI-initiated purchase after checkout is extremely or very important, with 64% calling it extremely important. Sixty one percent pointed to spending limits and 59% pointed to a required human approval checkpoint before checkout. Fifty eight percent would still prefer to complete an AI-assisted purchase on the retailer's own site or app, compared with 12% comfortable finishing inside the AI platform itself, and 62% are not comfortable letting AI complete a purchase without a traditional checkout page at all.

The article says businesses should build visible controls into the front of the experience, such as spend caps, category limits and a checkpoint before money moves, rather than burying them in settings menus. It says reversibility should be treated as core to the experience, the way free returns became a baseline expectation in e-commerce. It also says retailers have reason to build first-party AI shopping tools on their own properties rather than ceding the checkout moment and the customer relationship to third-party agent ecosystems. The article compares this to contactless cards and mobile wallets, which earned trust gradually as issuers added visible security cues like tokenization and biometric confirmation at payment.

The research points to where agentic commerce is likely to take hold earliest: purchases that are repetitive, predictable and already low-stakes. Consumer packaged goods and household replenishment are named as a natural starting point, along with subscriptions and recurring services, and food and beverage such as grocery and restaurant reorders. Travel and booking may follow once trust in reversibility catches up, but higher price points likely mean it lags the more routine categories. The article says agentic commerce gains ground fastest wherever the financial risk is small, the decision is familiar, and the shopper can see and control the guardrails around it.

Articles.Title: Shoppers will let AI browse, but they still want their hand on the wallet

stories.Headline: ID-Pal deal arms ThirdEye against AI-fuelled financial crime
stories.Summary:
ThirdEye, an anti-money-laundering platform provider, has chosen ID-Pal to supply the identity and business verification functions within its offering across Australia and New Zealand. Under the partnership, ID-Pal’s verification technology will sit inside ThirdEye’s AML platform. The deal is designed to address mounting pressure on banks and other regulated firms in the region to tackle fraud, tighten compliance and build trust from the moment a customer signs up. It also extends ID-Pal’s presence in overseas markets. Organisations in Australia, New Zealand and the UK will now be able to use ID-Pal’s document authentication, biometric checks and address verification alongside ThirdEye’s current modules.

The combined service aims to give firms in these markets a more streamlined option that can scale as their needs grow. ID-Pal applies AI to confirm that identity documents are genuine, verify both people and companies, and help detect fraud. The company says it takes a privacy-preserving approach, shielding sensitive customer data while returning verification outcomes in real time. ThirdEye pairs automation with in-market knowledge to give banks, financial institutions and other heavily regulated businesses a secure tool for countering financial crime. Its adaptable models cover customer screening, transaction monitoring, case management and regulatory reporting, helping clients protect customers, control risk and keep pace with compliance obligations.

ThirdEye general manager Hamish Shaw identified progress in AI as a major driver behind the agreement. He said the financial crime landscape has never been static and that bad actors keep evolving new techniques, and that with AI accelerating the threats it is crucial for those on the right side to work together to stay ahead. ID-Pal CEO and founder Colum Lyons said fraud and financial crime know no borders, and increasingly neither does the technology used to commit them. He said ThirdEye has built a strong AML proposition across Australia, New Zealand and the UK, and that ID-Pal is delighted to have been chosen to power identity and business verification within it. He said the two companies can together help organisations establish trust at onboarding and manage fraud and compliance risk throughout the customer lifecycle.

Articles.Title: ID-Pal deal arms ThirdEye against AI-fuelled financial crime

stories.Headline: Before buying more AI tools, hospitals should examine their tech stacks
stories.Summary:
Hospitals are being urged to review their existing technology before buying more artificial intelligence tools, according to advice from Amy Goad, managing director of consulting at Sendero Consulting, a management consulting firm based in Dallas, Texas. Her guidance, published by Healthcare IT News on November 5, 2026, responds to years of health systems adding point solutions to address isolated problems without a plan to scale them. That pattern has produced fragmented IT environments with tangled integration layers and redundant applications, which the article says increase technical debt without delivering lasting value. Goad argues that this complexity is growing harder and more expensive to manage at a time of tight budgets and workforce shortages. Goad recommends that leaders first clearly define the problem and the clinical or operational outcome they want before investing in anything new.

She says they should assess whether existing technology can address at least 50 percent of the problem through different configurations, integrations or workflow changes. Vendor partners can help by connecting organizations with peer institutions using similar setups or by providing demo environments to test functionality. Any new investment, AI or otherwise, should align with enterprise priorities, be able to scale beyond its first use case, and come with clear success metrics and a plan to retire redundant systems. If existing tools cannot meet a clearly defined need, Goad says a new AI system may be justified, but only after a rapid, targeted pilot with predefined success metrics. She advises leaders to be willing to discontinue any system that fails those benchmarks instead of continuing to spend time and resources on it.

The article also stresses repairing the underlying IT foundation, including rationalizing application portfolios, modernizing infrastructure, establishing a clear semantic data model and enterprise-wide data governance, and strengthening cybersecurity with incident response, continuity and disaster recovery plans that are tested regularly. Goad further argues that change management matters, since staff should be involved early and supported with ongoing training so that new tools do not add burden to already stretched teams. The article is framed as guidance rather than a report on a specific event, and it does not describe enforcement, regulatory requirements or a timeline for adoption. Goad concludes that by prioritizing systems that improve how people work, supporting adoption, and phasing out tools that no longer serve a purpose, healthcare organizations can build a more resilient technology stack. The piece points readers to related Healthcare IT News coverage on enterprise technical debt, data cleanup for the AI era and a new cybersecurity guide for healthcare AI.

Articles.Title: Before buying more AI tools, hospitals should examine their tech stacks

stories.Headline: Can Salesforce Win the AI Front Door Inside Teams?
stories.Summary:
Salesforce announced on November 5, 2026, that usage of its AI product Agentforce Coworker has grown 21 times in three months, reaching more than 185,000 users. The company is now taking Coworker into Microsoft Teams, connecting it to Google Workspace and Microsoft 365, and launching a $50 per user, per month option. Coworker is Salesforce's AI teammate for employees: a worker describes a job, and Coworker plans the steps, coordinates the right agents and workflows, and returns results and recommended actions for review. Salesforce says Coworker works within existing permissions, sharing rules and access controls, with approval and audit options for supported actions. New skills let a proven workflow, such as a top rep's renewal playbook, become a one-line request anyone on the team can run.

The announcement says Fulton Bank has deployed more than 20 Coworker use cases for around 3,000 users, The Adecco Group is expanding it across 40 countries, and BACA Systems switched it on in 20 minutes in an environment with 1,300 custom objects. All three examples come from Salesforce's own announcement, and none directly cover customer outcomes. Teams, iOS, Mac, and Windows access is due in November, with scheduled tasks, a Daily Digest, and Coworker in the Field Service mobile app following in December. The announcement does not say how the flat fee compares with Agentforce's existing credit-based pricing, so buyers will need to work that out for themselves.

James Nakashima, SVP of Product Management at Salesforce, said the next era of enterprise AI is not about giving users more agents to manage but about giving them one Coworker that brings the right agents together. Zeus Kerravala, Founder and Principal Analyst at ZK Research, said the Teams move is a pragmatic departure from Salesforce's traditional walled-garden strategy, and that the real bottleneck in agentic AI has been context and fragmentation rather than model intelligence. Liz Miller, VP and Principal Analyst at Constellation Research, said uniformity and predictability matter when adopting and scaling AI, and that the flat fee is hard to ignore. She said it will not change how the rest of Agentforce is sold but gives a monetization path to what used to be considered a built-in feature.

Salesforce is not the only vendor chasing that front door. On its earnings call the previous week, Satya Nadella, Chairman and CEO of Microsoft, said the company thinks of Copilot as the new OS for work, and Microsoft is also pulling Dynamics 365 skills into Copilot. That puts Coworker in the same workspace as Copilot, where employees will decide which assistant to open first. Salesforce is seemingly betting that its customer context and governance give it the edge. Whether employees choose Coworker over Copilot in Teams, and whether customers notice, will determine whether the front-door strategy works.

Articles.Title: Can Salesforce Win the AI Front Door Inside Teams?

stories.Headline: Teaching AI to Build Better Enzymes
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of California, Santa Barbara, led by HHMI Freeman Hrabowski Scholar Yang Yang, have developed SynFit, an open-source machine learning tool that predicts enzyme variants likely to perform well on several traits at once. The work was co-developed with Yunan Luo at the Georgia Institute of Technology and was reported by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute on November 5, 2026. The tool is designed to work even when experimental data are limited. Its code and data are freely available so that other labs can try it.

Enzymes help scientists make valuable chemicals, but nature's versions do not cover every reaction a researcher might want, so engineers modify them and test the results. The difficulty is that a useful enzyme usually has to be fast, stable, productive, and correctly shaped all at once, and improving one feature can undermine another. Traditional directed evolution handles this by making and screening many variants over repeated rounds, which takes considerable time. Many computational models predict only one trait at a time, so they do little to narrow that search. SynFit instead learns several measurements together and ranks candidates by how well they balance the traits that matter.

The team tested the approach on a cytochrome c enzyme engineered to build carbon-boron bonds, which can serve as building blocks for complex molecules used in medicines and materials. After training on a small batch of lab data, the researchers used SynFit to choose new variants, and many of them achieved the high yield and high selectivity the team wanted. The group also tested the tool on public protein datasets where the same protein was measured in more than one way, and it outperformed models that handled each measurement separately. Yang said the method is not limited to a specific protein and that his team is already applying SynFit and related tools to other enzymes.

Articles.Title: Teaching AI to Build Better Enzymes

stories.Headline: Europe should beware of buying America’s increasingly unaccountable AI killing-machines
stories.Summary:
Later this month in Geneva, states will meet for the Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons and decide whether to begin negotiating binding rules on autonomous weapons. More than 70 states have already said they are ready to do so. Washington is moving in the opposite direction. On 30 September, the US department of war announced an Autonomous Warfare Command, meant to scale autonomous warfare across the US military by October 2027.

The same speech launched Project Meridian, a 120-day study of the technologies the US military will need for future wars. It will be led by Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey, the CEO of the defence firm Anduril, and the US politician Newt Gingrich, with findings due in January. Critics have noted that Musk and Luckey would be identifying needs their own companies already meet, and the announcement describes no recusal or disclosure mechanism. The Pentagon's Civilian Protection Center of Excellence fell from 40 staff to nine in 2025, and its inspector general concluded the department no longer has the personnel and capabilities to meet its legal responsibilities.

Jessica Dorsey, an assistant professor of international law at Utrecht University, wrote the article. She said Europe is in a position to answer with more than words, and that responsibility works best when designed into a system from the start. She said precautions must be built in at the design stage, with deliberate friction where speed would erode judgment, meaningful human decision-making, and sustained engagement among developers, lawyers and operators. She said European standards for testing and assurance, limits on civilian harm written into procurement contracts, and legal review from the design stage would give governments real choices about what they buy and on what terms.

Dorsey said the Group of Governmental Experts' final report softened what earlier drafts framed as obligations on responsibility and accountability into encouragement. She said European governments should back the start of negotiations on a legal instrument in Geneva. She said they should also write responsibility by design into their own procurement now, without waiting for a treaty. She said Europe should demand a different theory of responsibility from whoever supplies its autonomy.

Articles.Title: Europe should beware of buying America’s increasingly unaccountable AI killing-machines

stories.Headline: AI Data Center Liquid Cooling Market Size, Forecasts Report 2026-2035
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a market report published in November 2026 by Global Market Insights, report ID GMI16496, covering AI data center liquid cooling. The report says the market was valued at 2.79 billion dollars in 2025, is estimated at 3.37 billion dollars in 2026, and is projected to grow at a 20.6 percent compound annual growth rate from 2026 to 2035 to reach 18.21 billion dollars by 2035. North America is the largest market and Asia Pacific is the fastest growing region. Schneider Electric led with over 9.0 percent market share in 2025, and the top five players, Schneider Electric, Vertiv Holdings, Rittal GmbH, Stulz GmbH and Boyd Corporation, held 35.0 percent combined. The report also says liquid cooling supported about 2.8 gigawatts of IT load in 2025.

The report ties demand to rising power use and chip heat. It cites International Energy Agency figures showing global data center electricity use is projected to reach 945 terawatt hours by 2030, up from 415 terawatt hours in 2024, and U.S. Department of Energy figures showing U.S. data centers used 4.4 percent of total U.S. electricity in 2023. It says NVIDIA H200-class GPUs carry a thermal design power of up to 700 watts per chip, Blackwell-generation accelerators exceed 1,000 watts per GPU, and NVIDIA's DSX program sets coolant distribution unit integration requirements for Vera Rubin-generation AI factories. By component, solutions generated 2.21 billion dollars in 2025 and are projected to reach 13.84 billion dollars by 2035. Direct-to-chip cooling was 60.0 percent of solution revenue in 2025 and is projected to reach 8.72 billion dollars by 2035, immersion cooling is projected to hold a 30.0 percent share of solution revenue by 2035 at a 21.6 percent growth rate, and rear-door heat exchangers generated 309.4 million dollars in 2025 and are expected to grow at 13.2 percent.

The report names barriers and gives analyst views. It cites an Uptime Institute Cooling Systems Survey 2025 finding that 38 percent of data center operators cite cost as a primary barrier to direct liquid cooling and 39 percent identify a lack of industry standards as the leading barrier. It says retrofit work requires routing secondary fluid loops through live server infrastructure and managing coolant chemistry, leak risk and fluid compatibility across equipment from multiple vendors. GMI analysts describe a split adoption cycle, with liquid cooling becoming integral to AI infrastructure design at the high-density end while elsewhere deployment depends on justifying upfront investment and managing integration risk. The report says this favors vendors that pair thermal performance with deployment and lifecycle support.

The report says the market is moving from specialized high-performance computing deployments toward a core infrastructure layer for AI-ready facilities, with operators evaluating cooling alongside power availability, facility layout, serviceability and lifecycle energy exposure. It says demand is strongest where operators can engineer liquid loops into high-density builds, while retrofit economics, component interoperability and operational assurance determine how quickly adoption spreads to the broader installed base. It says cost sensitivity moderates growth in the enterprise and edge segments below the 20.6 percent market average, and that interoperability uncertainty keeps enterprise and brownfield adoption below technology potential through the mid-forecast period. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these forecasts.

Articles.Title: AI Data Center Liquid Cooling Market Size, Forecasts Report 2026-2035

stories.Headline: Travelers AI tool lets agents skip workers comp data entry
stories.Summary:
Travelers launched an AI workers compensation quoting tool for insurance agents who work with small businesses. The tool is called Travis Upload & Go, and it lets agents upload documents including industry forms and handwritten notes to start a quote. The company announced the tool in a press release. The launch targets a major pain point tied to manual data entry.

The tool is aimed at cutting the manual data entry that agents face when quoting workers compensation coverage for small businesses. Travelers surveyed insurance agents and found that 77 percent of them said manual data entry is one of the least valuable and most time-consuming parts of their job, according to the press release. The article gives the date of November 5, 2026, for the launch. The article names Kaitlyn Mattson as the managing editor of Digital Insurance, who covers topics related to insurance including risk, climate change, and talent and retention.

Travelers is the company behind the tool, and it built Travis Upload & Go for agents who work with small businesses. The survey of agents, cited in the press release, found that 77 percent see manual data entry as one of the least valuable and most time-consuming parts of their job. The article does not say who at Travelers led the project or give direct comments from company officials. It also does not name any individual agent who uses the tool.

The article places the launch in the context of insurance companies using AI to change how work gets done. It links to other Digital Insurance pieces on AI risks at data centers, insurers retraining AI and insourcing data, agents wanting more AI and automation, carriers fixing culture and processes first, and where insurers are cashing in on AI. The article does not say what happens next with the Travelers tool, such as a wider rollout or added features. It also gives no details on pricing or availability beyond the launch.

Articles.Title: Travelers AI tool lets agents skip workers comp data entry

stories.Headline: Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, OpenAI published two documents setting out how it plans to build and run its future compute campuses in the United States: a National Community Compact and a Compute Campus Policy Blueprint. The announcement, posted on the company's website under the headline "Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure," said the compact covers campuses that OpenAI itself owns and operates. It described the move as the next step in work the company began in January under its Stargate Community commitments, which had already included specific pledges in Georgia and Ohio. Under the compact, each future campus would have its own local agreement reflecting local priorities, with early resident engagement, a local point of contact and annual public reporting.

Common commitments include paying the full cost of the electricity and infrastructure the campus uses, and providing financial assurances before major spending so other customers are protected if a project is delayed or canceled. OpenAI also says it will develop a water plan for each site, favor closed-loop or low-water cooling, publish water and electricity use, and release construction plans and noise studies. The company says it will not use non-disclosure agreements with public officials, except for narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets or competitively sensitive data. Examples cited include a $4.8 million grant for free school meals for all 14,000 students in Effingham County, Georgia, and a joint $6 million childcare commitment with SB Energy in Pike County, Ohio.

The accompanying blueprint asks federal, state and local policymakers to set clear rules for the industry rather than relying only on voluntary pledges. It proposes that state utility commissions require large electricity customers to cover the grid costs they add and protect other customers if a project falls through, and that Congress speed up transmission upgrades and restore and expand tax incentives for clean electricity. The document also calls for public reporting on water, energy, noise and hiring, narrow limits on NDAs with officials, and public terms for tax incentives with a way to recover benefits if a developer falls short. OpenAI points to its planned Effingham County campus, where an agreement with Georgia Power would let the utility reduce power delivered by up to 1,000 megawatts during periods of high demand.

The company also suggests early sharing of purchasing plans with local suppliers and hiring forecasts that community colleges and unions can use to train residents. OpenAI is the party making these commitments, and the company frames the effort as a way to ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared. The published text does not describe any regulator's response or any enacted policy, and it does not say when the blueprint's proposals might be taken up by lawmakers. The articles provided do not indicate what happens next beyond the company's stated plan to engage residents, publish annual reports and continue its ongoing work with communities.

Articles.Title: Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure

stories.Headline: Source: Meta has decided to stop using fruit for its AI model codenames, as they didn't suit its lofty AI ambitions; its latest model was named "Watermelon" (Charles Rollet/Business Insider)
stories.Summary:
Meta has decided internally to stop naming its artificial intelligence models after fruit, a person familiar with the matter said. The change is largely a branding decision, because fruit-based codenames do not fit Meta's lofty AI ambitions, the person added. The company's latest model, Wonder Full, which Meta described as its first cutting-edge frontier model, carried the internal codename Watermelon. Meta teased that launch by posting photos of the fruit, and it declined to comment on the naming change.

Meta had dubbed its previous language and image models Avocado and Mango. On the Cheeky Pint podcast last month, CEO Mark Zuckerberg and AI chief Alexandr Wang joked that they had run out of fruit names. Zuckerberg said they were out of fruits and would have to switch to a new convention. Wang said the only fruit technically larger is the durian, and you do not want to go to the durian.

Meta is not the only tech company to name AI products after grocery store items. In 2025, OpenAI internally dubbed one model Garlic, according to The Information, and Google released its Nano Banana image generator that same year. More recently, as AI models grow more powerful, it has become trendy to give them more awe-inspiring names, such as Anthropic's Mythos or OpenAI's Astra. The articles do not say what naming convention Meta will use next.

Separately, Yahoo Finance video host Ejaaz Ahamadeen said AI is breaking the traditional search business because people no longer go to Google and scroll through links. He said they outsource searching to AI, which does not carry monetizable search revenue and belongs to Anthropic, OpenAI and other chatbot competitors. He cited Reddit, which reported record earnings yet saw its stock fall around 26% in opening trading hours, after noting that search ad revenue was not driving enough traffic to its site. Ahamadeen said Reddit is building walls around its service, requiring users to create an account and log on, because it fears AI will replace its company and moat by training on its data without paying.

Articles.Title: Source: Meta has decided to stop using fruit for its AI model codenames, as they didn't suit its lofty AI ambitions; its latest model was named "Watermelon" (Charles Rollet/Business Insider)

stories.Headline: A sweeter future? AI helps scientists discover new sugar substitutes
stories.Summary:
Researchers Shayma El-Atawneh and Amiram Goldblum at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem have used artificial intelligence and molecular modeling to identify 92 promising candidates for future sugar substitutes. They screened more than 50 million chemical compounds to find them. The study, published in the journal Food Chemistry, was reported on November 5, 2026. The work aims to speed up the search for sweeteners that avoid the bitter aftertastes that plague some current options.

The researchers used a machine-learning algorithm called Iterative Stochastic Elimination, developed by Goldblum's group, to build models that predict whether a molecule is likely to taste sweet or bitter. They applied these models to three large chemical databases holding about 50.7 million molecules and filtered out compounds predicted to taste bitter. To refine the list, they used molecular docking to simulate how candidates might bind to the human sweet-taste receptor, made of two protein subunits called T1R2 and T1R3. Combined with chemical structure filters, this narrowed the pool to 556 potential sweeteners, and further prioritization produced the final 92.

The article says many of these candidates have chemical structures unlike those of known sweeteners, which could point to entirely new classes of sweet compounds. Several previously patented sweet-receptor modulators also appeared among the candidates, which the researchers cite as support for their method. The authors say the approach could greatly reduce the laboratory testing needed to find new sugar alternatives. The findings are relevant to food and beverage makers seeking low-calorie sweeteners that taste like sugar.

The researchers stress that the 92 compounds are still computational predictions and have not been tested in a lab. Experiments will be needed to confirm their sweetness, evaluate their safety and determine whether they are suitable for use in food products. The study is presented as a framework for discovering the next generation of sweeteners. Further laboratory validation is the next step.

Articles.Title: A sweeter future? AI helps scientists discover new sugar substitutes

stories.Headline: Anthropic S-1: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) May Be "Imminent," Here Is What That Means
stories.Summary:
Anthropic submitted an amended S-1 filing to the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, as the company prepares to raise 1.5 trillion dollars on the stock market. In the risk factors, alongside 17 billion dollars in revenue, the company wrote that its internal estimates indicate it may imminently meet the definition of dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI in its own Responsible Scaling Policy. That is Anthropic's in-house wording for what the industry calls recursive self-improvement, or RSI. The filing refers to expectations about future models, not current ones, and Anthropic says none of its existing models has crossed the threshold.

Recursive self-improvement describes the point at which an AI system takes over its own development, optimizing code, training methods and architecture largely without humans, with each improvement speeding up the next. Anthropic concedes it has in the past not identified a significant acceleration and may fail to do so again, and it is considering updates to its Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development. Letting Claude fully autonomously design and build new models is something Anthropic says it does not expect to be able to do safely for the foreseeable future. As of August, Claude leads 26 percent of AI research tasks at Anthropic, up from under one percent in February, while the share of tasks it completes fully autonomously is zero in every area measured. More than 80 percent of merged lines of code at Anthropic now come from Claude, and the prospectus cites over 90 percent for September.

CEO Dario Amodei wrote in his essay We Must Pace the Frontier that RSI is starting to happen across the industry. OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki voiced a strong expectation that progress could be sustained into recursive self-improvement, and leaders at Google DeepMind and xAI joined the call for a slower pace. David Sacks, co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, called the labs' coordinated appeal for speed limits regulatory capture, meaning rules written by the biggest players that shield them from competition. Anthropic itself supplies a dated, testable claim: within six to twelve months, an agent swarm like the one at Hugging Face could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet.

In September, a cryptic post by the leaker Lyra with the hidden capital letters R, S and I and congratulations to Google DeepMind sent the industry into a frenzy. Google had previously attributed the rapid release cadence of its Gemini Flash models, four in around 106 days, to long-running agent loops that recursively evaluate and refine the models, and according to Reuters, Sergey Brin had redirected around 1,000 researchers toward self-improving systems. According to METR, Mythos Preview completes software tasks of roughly 17 hours in length half the time, a figure that has doubled roughly every four months since 2023, albeit with wide confidence intervals. OpenAI reported in September that it had met its goal of an automated research intern, though more than half of successful multi-hour tasks still needed at least one human intervention.

Articles.Title: Anthropic S-1: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) May Be "Imminent," Here Is What That Means - trendingtopics.eu

stories.Headline: Americans wary of AI in healthcare for diagnoses and insurance claims, survey finds
stories.Summary:
A new Pew Research Center survey of 3,400-plus U.S. adults, conducted in June, finds Americans are open to artificial intelligence handling routine healthcare tasks but uneasy about it making key decisions. The results were reported by CBS News in early November 2026. Most respondents said AI could translate patient notes or schedule appointments, either on its own or with some human oversight. More than half were also willing to have AI analyze medical scans and lab results, as long as a healthcare professional supervised the work.

The public's comfort falls away when AI takes on decision-making roles. Nearly half of those surveyed said they do not want an AI model deciding whether to accept or reject an insurance claim. Forty-one percent said they do not want AI making a diagnosis on its own. Overall, 60% said they are uncomfortable with doctors using AI for tasks such as diagnosis and treatment, while only 30% were comfortable and 10% were unsure. The survey also found that 46% of respondents did not know whether AI had ever been used in their care.

Galen Stocking, associate director of science and society research at Pew, said people see value in applying AI to healthcare but want to know when and how providers and administrative staff use it. He told CBS News that respondents overwhelmingly feel it is extremely important for their healthcare provider to disclose any AI use. Stocking said the public lacks clarity on the subject. He also said people are concerned about the patient-doctor relationship and the security of their personal health information.

Americans are divided on the broader effect of AI on medical care. Thirty-seven percent of respondents said the technology will improve health outcomes, and a nearly equal share said it could reduce the quality of care. The findings suggest that disclosure and human oversight will matter to patients as healthcare providers and insurers expand their use of the technology. The articles do not describe any specific regulatory or policy changes that would follow from the survey.

Articles.Title: Americans wary of AI in healthcare for diagnoses and insurance claims, survey finds

stories.Headline: How 401(k) Advisors Are Using AI—Without Losing the Human Connection
stories.Summary:
Three retirement industry professionals describe how they use artificial intelligence in their daily work, focusing on time savings rather than any replacement of the advisor relationship. The most detailed account comes from Wendy Eldridge, a retirement plan advisor with Carnegie Investment Counsel in Ohio, who says she uses AI tools every day and most often relies on Anthropic's Claude. She has used these tools to produce projections for plan sponsors weighing a change to their matching structure or a move to a safe harbor plan, comparing how different matching formulas would play out. The article does not give specific figures from those projections.

Eldridge also uses AI to summarize complex topics, such as SECURE 2.0 provisions, for plan sponsors, and to tidy the grammar and flow of fiduciary meeting minutes. She describes these gains as a way to speed decisions and cut routine administrative work. She is now looking at applying AI to back-office functions, including client onboarding, transferring data from recordkeepers into her systems, automating her customer relationship management system and prospecting for new clients. The article presents these as plans still in development rather than completed changes.

Eldridge is firm that AI will not replace her experience or her role. She says she will remain the person sitting down with plan sponsors and individuals, listening to their goals and concerns and helping them make decisions. She does not believe robo-advisors and technology will take over the advisor's job. The article frames her view as representative of advisors who see AI as a tool for capacity rather than a substitute for the human relationship, though the other two professionals featured in the series are not described in the material provided.

Articles.Title: How 401(k) Advisors Are Using AI—Without Losing the Human Connection

stories.Headline: Democrats are fired up on AI. Consensus is harder.
stories.Summary:
Democrats won a new majority in Congress in Tuesday’s election and are promising to make AI a top priority, Semafor reported on Nov 5, 2026. More than 40 AI data center-related ballot measures passed on Tuesday, and they were designed to slow or stop growth outright. Conservative groups said voters are connecting economic troubles with unchecked AI growth and with what they called an overly friendly environment for billionaire CEOs in President Donald Trump’s Washington. Divisions between the party’s progressive wing and business-friendly moderates, and between the House and the Senate, will make quick sweeping AI rules difficult.

Democrats plan renewed pushes for bills on AI safety and on curbing data center growth, and larger coalitions are forming behind banning superintelligence. Rep. Greg Stanton of Arizona, a member of the New Democrat Coalition, said Democrats know how important this is and it will be a high priority, while acknowledging plenty of intra-party debate ahead. He said the caucus has not reached agreement on a specific policy but understands the importance of cybersecurity risks, protecting kids online and worker protections. Rep. Greg Casar of Texas said Democrats will call AI CEOs to testify under oath and called AI regulation a top priority. Rep. Ted Lieu of California said there will be public hearings on AI and legislation with reasonable guardrails.

Rep. Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey, a member of the Problem Solvers Caucus, told Semafor Democrats are in surprisingly broad agreement on AI. He said they agree the technology is changing how Americans work and live and that commonsense guardrails are needed so it works for families, workers and kids.
