stories.Headline: [Opening Market] KOSPI Slumps Below 5,500 on AI Fears
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, Nov. 5, the KOSPI opened at 5,580.09, down 103.71 points, or 1.82%, from the previous day's close of 5,683.80. The index fell below 5,580 within two minutes of opening and dropped more than 3% to 5,486.94 at one point, slipping under the 5,500 mark. The KOSDAQ opened at 716.35, up 0.20% from 714.95, but reversed and fell to 697.02, down 2.51%. The selloff followed the U.S. midterm election results the previous day, which raised the possibility of stronger regulation of technology stocks and AI data centers.

As of 10:00 a.m., foreign investors had net sold about 792.3 billion won in the KOSPI, after a selloff in the 2.5 trillion won range the previous day. Individuals net bought about 480 billion to 500 billion won and institutions about 311 billion won. In the KOSDAQ, foreigners net sold about 140 billion won, while institutions and retail investors net bought around 16 billion won and 1.2 trillion won. Samsung Electronics fell more than 5% to 206,750 won from 218,000 won, and SK Hynix dropped 5.95% to 1,313,000 won.

The article attributes the decline to foreign selling concentrated in large semiconductor stocks. It says individuals and institutions absorbed the supply through bargain hunting, though this was seen as insufficient to fully offset the foreign selling. It reports that LG Energy Solution held around 1% gains on expectations of eco-friendly benefits, while Samsung Biologics fell 0.9%. Hyundai Motor and Kia fell in the 1% to 2% range.

The won/dollar exchange rate stood at 1,340.7 won at 9:20 a.m., down 0.8 won from the previous daytime close of 1,341.5 won. Experts quoted in the article described the plunge as a reflection of excessive caution over temporary sector rotation and AI-concentrated supply and demand after the U.S. midterm elections. The article says the key question is whether foreign net selling eases in the afternoon. It says whether the 5,500 mark can be retaken and whether the drop in large semiconductor stocks can be reduced will likely determine the day's closing direction.

Articles.Title: [Opening Market] KOSPI Slumps Below 5,500 on AI Fears - Businesskorea

stories.Headline: Samsung Builds Advanced Foundry Fab in Giheung
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics has decided to build a 2-nanometer and 4-nanometer class advanced foundry fab at its Giheung Campus in Yongin, Gyeonggi Province, according to industry reports on Nov. 4, 2026. The fab will sit on the site of the Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology (SR5) and the College of Engineering (CDI), which finished demolition last month. The building complex will consist of the Kairos complex building, a green building, and a substation. Samsung E&A will take charge of engineering, procurement, and construction.

The project is called Kairos, and the fab is scheduled to have four production zones, similar to the new Pyeongtaek plant. The Kairos task force also plans to convert part of Line 6 into an advanced packaging facility. The investment scale is estimated at around $19.23 billion, and the total could reach $23.08 billion when including the Line 6 conversion. Internally, Samsung has prepared purchase estimates for dozens of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines amounting to $6.15 billion to $7.69 billion.

Samsung named the task force Kairos after the god of opportunity in Greek mythology, reflecting its expectations for the reorganization. The company has not commented further in the article. The core of the project is embedding advanced process production capacity in Giheung, which has been operated mainly with mature processes. The 2-nanometer line is meant to prepare for HBM5, the 8th generation product.

The background is the expansion of HBM demand driven by rapid growth in the AI data center market. The industry expects Samsung's HBM supply on a bit basis to increase by an annual average of 52% for three years until 2028. Base dies made with a 4-nanometer foundry process are currently manufactured only on some lines in Hwaseong and Pyeongtaek. If the Giheung fab is established, base die supply capacity is expected to expand in pace with core die production at those campuses.

Articles.Title: Samsung Builds Advanced Foundry Fab in Giheung - Businesskorea

stories.Headline: The AI Readiness Gap Almost No One’s Auditing
stories.Summary:
A November 4, 2026 article by Sumanth Kumar Gadde on govtech.com describes a gap in how public agencies prepare for artificial intelligence. Agencies check vendors, security and staff skills before launching an AI tool, but far fewer audit the data the system will learn from. Gadde points to an internal state review of Michigan's automated unemployment fraud system, which examined more than 20,000 determinations and found a 93 percent error rate. That system was not today's AI, but he says the lesson carries over because speed and scale turn hidden assumptions into public harm.

Gadde proposes three audits before go-live, each answering one plain question. The source audit asks where the data came from and who answers for it, including which source wins when two conflict and who approved that rule. The target audit asks what the system is really learning, whether the data reflects the people it will act on, and whether inputs are protected characteristics such as race, age or disability or close proxies like ZIP code, first name or employment gaps. The safeguard audit asks what catches the system when it is wrong, including whether a reviewer with real authority checks high-stakes decisions and whether residents can contest outcomes. He gives the example of a county using a model trained on past violation records to send inspectors to buildings likely to have code violations, which keeps sending inspectors to the same neighborhoods while problems elsewhere stay invisible.

Gadde says guidance nobody owns gets skipped under deadline pressure, so the fix is structural. He recommends adding a data readiness gate to every AI project plan the same way a security review is added, starting with the use case where a wrong answer would hurt someone most. A named data owner should sign off and the findings should be written down, and "we don't know" should be treated as a finding rather than a failure. He says an unanswered question found before launch is cheap, while the same question found afterward costs money, public trust and sometimes someone's benefits or livelihood.

A separate report from Dun & Bradstreet, published by ET CIO on November 2, 2026, found that 69 percent of Indian businesses plan to increase AI spending over the next 12 months. Only 3 percent described their enterprise data as fully ready to support AI at scale, compared with 8 percent globally, while 42 percent said mostly ready and 44 percent partially ready. More than 60 percent of respondents had moved beyond planning, with 35 percent scaling pilots into production and 26 percent reporting AI embedded across multiple core business processes. Julian Prower, Executive Vice President at Dun & Bradstreet and Managing Director and CEO for India and Taiwan, said India has reached an inflection point and that the next chapter will be about moving from AI adoption to AI advantage. The report said businesses with fully AI-ready data were 6.3 times more likely to report broad or strong returns than those with partially ready data.

Articles.Title: The AI Readiness Gap Almost No One’s Auditing

stories.Headline: How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI
stories.Summary:
Amazon's Marketplace team has described a new system, built on Amazon SageMaker AI, for judging the quality of A+ Content, the rich media section on Amazon product detail pages. The article, published on the AWS Blogs site on November 5, 2026, explains that brands range from large companies with in-house design teams to small brands with limited resources, which produces uneven content. Selling partners that use high-quality A+ Content reportedly see sales rise by 8 to 20 percent compared with those that do not. Because A+ Content has few strict specifications for image ratio or word count, the article says content composition varies widely, and the authors argue that checking each asset separately misses how text, images, and video work together on the page.

The proposed approach renders the full product page as a single snapshot and asks a vision-language model to evaluate it holistically across four dimensions: Visual Storytelling, Feature Presentation, A+ Layout, and Conversion Optimization. Each dimension receives a score from 0 to 10, a confidence value, and a written rationale. These outputs feed a lightweight CatBoost classifier trained on consensus labels from one ecommerce marketing expert and four professional annotators, who rated 5,478 product detail pages across 10 product categories as high or low quality. The article reports that each annotator's agreement with the consensus, measured by Cohen's kappa, ranged from 0.845 to 0.915. The authors say the classifier, which is retrained on a CPU rather than fine-tuning the foundation model, reached 0.89 accuracy and a 0.90 F1 score on a 20 percent holdout set, compared with 0.80 accuracy and 0.84 F1 for a simple averaged baseline.

The article also adds optical character recognition to measure text density, character density, spacing, and overall readability, because the vision-language model is weaker on fine-grained readability issues. Combining these readability signals with the vision-language model's scores produced 0.94 accuracy and a 0.95 F1 score on the same holdout set, and the authors use SHAP explanations to show which factors drove each decision so that selling partners receive actionable recommendations. The authors present the work as a model for scoring content at scale on Amazon SageMaker AI, covering data annotation, hosting, explainability, and production monitoring. The article excerpt provided does not say whether the system has been deployed to all sellers or what changes to Amazon's listing policies will follow, so no further rollout details can be confirmed from it.

Articles.Title: How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI

stories.Headline: Outsmart Artificial Intelligence with CEDMO Game!
stories.Summary:
CEDMO, the Central European Digital Media Observatory, has released an educational game called CEDMO Game that invites players to test how well artificial intelligence models can spot disinformation. The game was developed at the Kempelen Institute of Intelligent Technologies (KInIT) as part of CEDMO consortium activities and was published on the CEDMO website on 5 November 2026. Researchers Ján Čegiň, Tomáš Matejov, Jakub Šimko, and Ivan Srba contributed to its development. The announcement asks whether AI can reliably identify false information and how it reacts when the same information is phrased slightly differently.

The game works by giving the player a short text, which they already know to be true or false, alongside the verdict of an AI model designed to detect disinformation. The player must rewrite the text so that its meaning stays the same while the model changes its estimate of whether the text is disinformation. To start, a player needs only an email address, with no account or password required. Teachers can create a session, set a time limit, choose texts from a prepared library or add their own, and students join with a numeric code or QR code.

The game is available in Czech, Slovak, Polish, and English, although the AI model itself currently works only in English. The developers say the game is meant to show how sensitive AI systems are to linguistic nuance and how small wording changes can alter a verdict even when the content is unchanged. Tomáš Matejov said players can see within minutes how a few changed words can lead the model to a different evaluation of the same information. Ján Čegiň said that understanding these limits should help people use AI more responsibly and approach information with more critical judgment.

The announcement describes the game mainly as a tool for schools and educational activities, though anyone can use it. The article frames the game as a counterpoint to uncritical trust in AI outputs, noting that models are powerful but not infallible. It does not describe any further phases of the project or any plans beyond the current release. Interested users are directed to the CEDMO website to play the game.

Articles.Title: Outsmart Artificial Intelligence with CEDMO Game!

stories.Headline: After the midterms, Big Tech’s AI data center problem is only getting bigger
stories.Summary:
Voters in several parts of the United States used the November 2026 midterm elections to push back against AI data centers, and the outcome has left Big Tech facing a harder road for its buildout. According to preliminary results from Redbud Consulting, a Washington, D.C., polling and data science firm, voters sided against data center development in all but one of 38 local ballot contests with complete counts. In Piqua, a city of about 20,000 people in west central Ohio, residents voted to recall the mayor and two city commissioners who backed a $1 billion Meta data center with a capacity of up to 1.4 gigawatts. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott after campaigning on a moratorium on data center development until lawmakers set additional protections for residents.

The election results point toward tougher rules for these facilities. Hinojosa has called for repealing data center tax breaks and requiring developers to protect household utility bills and local water supplies, while giving residents more say over new projects. Analysts at Macquarie Group Limited wrote in a note that the impact may depend less on outright restrictions than on extracting more from operators through taxes, power rates, environmental considerations, and community support. Dell'Oro Group's Baron Fung expects delays and says companies may shift projects and take on more of the financial and energy burden instead of relying on municipalities. Around 45 data center projects worth roughly $68 billion were disrupted by local opposition in the second quarter of this year, according to Data Center Watch.

Tech companies have responded with commitments aimed at winning over communities. In October, Amazon announced "Built Together," pledging more than $1 billion over five years to communities hosting its data centers, along with publishing its energy and water use and covering the power costs of its load. In January, Microsoft promised to cover the power infrastructure costs of its facilities and stop seeking local property-tax breaks. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google also dropped requirements that local officials sign nondisclosure agreements. Oracle, which has more than $125 billion in debt and other notes payable, said in September that it does not assume every project will arrive on time and that it has backup options.

Industry leaders show no sign of slowing down. Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta are projected to spend between $720 billion and $740 billion in combined capital expenditures for calendar 2026. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said the company added 24 new data centers across five continents in the last quarter, and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy expects cloud revenue growth of 40% or more in 2027 and 2028. Elon Musk wrote on X that data centers in space look appealing right now. Analysts broadly expect the facilities to remain, with the fight now shifting to who pays for them and where they are built.

Articles.Title: After the midterms, Big Tech’s AI data center problem is only getting bigger

stories.Headline: South Bend workshop examines AI’s role in housing discrimination
stories.Summary:
The South Bend Human Rights Commission hosted a free workshop on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, about artificial intelligence, housing and civil rights. The event was held because AI is increasingly used to help make housing decisions, which raises concerns about how algorithms could contribute to discrimination. The workshop was reported by WNDU, with a byline from Kennedi Humble. It brought together experts, real estate agents and others to discuss the issue.

The workshop focused on how bias in AI systems could affect people seeking housing. Katrina Lee, executive director of the South Bend Human Rights Commission, said biased information in an AI system could prevent some applicants from securing housing. Experts said bias could affect applicants before they make it through tenant screening, and could also influence people applying for a home loan if the data used is not fair or equitable. Event speaker Breagin Riley said people should ask about the quality of the data, and that if a company cannot say where the data came from or whether it has been updated within the last six months, bias is probably being introduced.

AI-based tenant screening is already used in the rental market. A 2024 survey by TechEquity of more than 1,000 renters and 400 landlords in California found nearly two-thirds of landlords received tenant-screening reports that included an AI-generated score or recommendation. There is no comparable statewide survey showing how many Indiana landlords use similar tools, but experts say concerns about bias and a lack of transparency apply anywhere these tools are used. Real estate agent Tamara Harke, who attended the workshop, said she is embracing AI and learning to use it in her business, including for marketing, and that it is important to make sure everything is in compliance.

Experts said businesses that use third-party AI systems are still responsible for checking the data and reviewing the system's results. Riley and Myra Reid said that even with third parties, businesses have to test the data and make sure it is still compliant, and that they may still be liable for the decisions they make with that data. Advocates say people should know when AI is being used in housing decisions and understand how to challenge a decision they believe is unfair. Lee encouraged anyone who believes their housing rights may have been violated to contact the South Bend Human Rights Commission for help. Humble will discuss the topic further on the next episode of her podcast, "The Data Center Debate," on Monday, Nov. 9, at 8 p.m.

Articles.Title: South Bend workshop examines AI’s role in housing discrimination

stories.Headline: Dance, engineering professors awarded grant for dance AI model
stories.Summary:
Two assistant professors at the University of Texas at Austin have been awarded more than $600,000 from a science nonprofit, according to an Oct. 21 news release. Sinclair Emoghene teaches in the Department of Theatre and Dance, and Lillian Chin teaches in the Department of Electrical and Chemical Engineering. The two met during a faculty orientation two years ago and began exploring how their fields could merge. Chin said they happened to sit next to each other, and that Emoghene had been really interested in how technology can inform dance.

The grant comes from the Humanities and AI Virtual Institute at the nonprofit Schmidt Sciences. It will let the team develop its sensor technology through August 2029 and add to its database of dance recordings from different countries and cultures. So far the team has recorded and processed 155 dance recordings from 33 countries and built an online platform to explore how the dances are organized. Dancers wear motion sensor pads that collect data as they move, and that data trains an AI model linking each dance to its cultural origins. The model is meant to help preserve traditions as knowledge of the dances' history fades.

Emoghene said in the news release that documenting and codifying these dance movements helps preserve them as traditions change and the knowledge they carry disappears. The research is supported by the Department of Arts and Technologies and the Lab for Immersive Media in the College of Fine Arts. Michael Baker, the departmental chair for Arts and Entertainment and founding director of the lab, said the lab is about combining technologies. He said it brings together people and technologies from very different disciplines and unlocks new possibilities. The team includes undergraduate and graduate researchers.

Articles.Title: Dance, engineering professors awarded grant for dance AI model

stories.Headline: Teddy Schleifer: Democrats' Sweep Turns AI's Data Center Boom Into a Local Land War
stories.Summary:
Voters in at least 38 US jurisdictions passed bans or restrictions on data centers on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and the result has begun to reshape how the AI industry views its political future. Democrats won both chambers of Congress in the midterms, and Texas elected Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor after she campaigned on a construction moratorium. Local voters across the country also rejected nearly every measure that would have supported new data center construction. Reporting from the Big Technology Podcast and other outlets points to rising costs, water use, noise, and land use as the main concerns behind these votes.

The results do not mean sweeping federal AI law is imminent. Any bill would need both chambers of Congress and the signature of President Trump, a Republican, which makes major federal legislation unlikely. The immediate effects are more practical: committee chairs and subpoena power shift to Democrats, and local land-use votes can block individual projects. Senators elected this cycle serve six-year terms, so their oversight role will extend through 2032. Teddy Schleifer of The New York Times described the period ahead as a major change from the largely unrestricted environment the industry has enjoyed.

Teddy Schleifer, speaking on the Big Technology Podcast with host Alex Kantrowitz, argued that the local votes amounted to something close to a national referendum on data centers. He noted that the margins were lopsided, with 38 jurisdictions passing restrictions and few or none rejecting them. Kantrowitz said that AI growth depends on public support for building the facilities that supply computing power, and that the industry faces a real compute shortage. The data center industry formed its first super PAC this cycle, which spent heavily in South Carolina to back a candidate who lost. Schleifer expects political spending on data centers to rise sharply before the 2028 presidential race.

Financial markets reacted in a way that surprised many observers. Shares of the largest technology companies rose after the election, on the view that a Democratic Congress might restrain the heavy capital spending on AI that has weighed on free cash flow. Schleifer said he did not have a clear explanation for this reaction. Elon Musk, who spent roughly $500 million on the midterms, saw most of his preferred candidates lose, and California's proposed billionaire tax appeared headed for defeat after opponents raised more than $330 million. Schleifer said Congress may now probe matters such as Musk's work on federal agencies through DOGE, and he expects oversight hearings to become a central feature of the next two years.

Articles.Title: Teddy Schleifer: Democrats' Sweep Turns AI's Data Center Boom Into a Local Land War - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Professional services reinvented: Certinia’s Veda AI agents
stories.Summary:
Certinia Inc. has expanded Veda, its suite of AI agents for professional services businesses, with a new offering called System of Action, which the company unveiled in September 2026. The company launched Veda in April 2026 with 10 package agents and has since grown that number to 24, with plans to finish the year with more than 40. In July 2026, Certinia acquired Moonnox, an AI-native services delivery platform built for the professional services sector. Certinia, which launched in 2009 as FinancialForce.com Inc. and rebranded in 2023, says its platform facilitates 7.1 billion professional services operations per month.

The System of Action more than doubled the Veda Intelligent Actions library from 64 to 135 and uses a three-tier architecture to bring agents into services workflows. The first tier combines structured records with unstructured project data, the second draws on more than 17 years of Certinia's services experience, and the third lets agents act inside existing workflows. The Moonnox acquisition added a contextual layer to Veda through knowledge graphs, persistent project memory and services-specific agents. The combined platform can connect a new client request with approved scope, staffing requirements and financial impact, then recommend governed actions for professional review.

Robert Cesafsky, Certinia's chief operating officer, said the services industry has probably been more disrupted by AI than the technology industry, and that clients need the right tools and control over their services business. Mimi Spier, the chief marketing officer, said AI can take away administrative tasks so customers deliver outcomes faster at a lower cost to serve, and can identify expansion opportunities and at-risk customers. Raju Malhotra, the chief product and technology officer, said the package agents are persona based and help customers, and that Certinia wants to accelerate delivery rather than just hand over a project plan. Scott Hebner, principal AI analyst at theCUBE Research, said Veda offers a glimpse of enterprise AI working alongside humans in consequential workflows, grounded in business context, governance and real operational outcomes.

Certinia has a long-standing relationship with Salesforce, having built its platform natively on Salesforce and being featured under the AI agents and tools category for Salesforce's AgentExchange. Hebner said professional services is a leading indicator of where enterprise AI is heading because it combines knowledge-intensive work, dynamic context, collaborative decisions, measurable economics and human accountability. He said that if Certinia executes well, Veda could become an important blueprint for translating digital labor into economic outcomes. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Certinia's plan to finish the year with more than 40 package agents.

Articles.Title: Professional services reinvented: Certinia’s Veda AI agents

stories.Headline: Almost no one uses AI agents to book their Uber, company says
stories.Summary:
On Uber’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, the company said very few people are using personal AI agents to order rides or food. During its busiest week in October, the week of Halloween, only four rides were ordered through an AI agent. Uber handled around 320 million trips and orders across Uber and Uber Eats that week, but only 500 Uber Eats orders were placed by an AI agent. Chief financial officer Balaji Krishnamurthy gave the figures to Wall Street analysts on the call.

CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said the traction was very, very early and very limited so far, and added that the company hopes there will be more. He pointed out that booking a ride in the Uber app takes only 50 seconds on average, and re-ordering a favorite food takes 90 seconds, which suggests an AI agent is not necessarily saving anyone time. He also said he sees agents as another opportunity to reach the platform and expects them to be a net positive for demand. He noted there are around eight major AI assistants on the market now, and he expects that number to grow to more than 10, adding that every single AI system company is talking to Uber.

The low numbers come amid growing hype for AI agents that handle tasks on users’ behalf. Instinct, a personal AI startup founded last year, raised its most recent funding round at a $10 billion valuation, and Meta’s Muse became the No. 1 app in Apple’s U.S. App Store last month, topping 10 million users per Meta’s own reporting. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and SpaceXAI (Grok) also offer their own AI agents, as do numerous smaller startups. DoorDash said on its earnings call last week that it has received only a few hundred orders from AI agents so far, as most customers still order through its app.

Articles.Title: Almost no one uses AI agents to book their Uber, company says

stories.Headline: AI and Misinformation Are Turning Migrants Into Targets
stories.Summary:
Misinformation about migrants is spreading quickly, and artificial intelligence is making it worse, the head of the UN Migration agency warned in Geneva on 2 November 2026. Speaking at the opening of the International Dialogue on Migration, IOM Director General Amy Pope said false narratives are turning public anxiety into suspicion and turning people into targets. She said economic uncertainty, conflict and climate pressures are testing governments and communities, and that public trust in migration management is under growing strain worldwide. Pope told the gathering that facts alone will not restore confidence, and that institutions must listen and act even when what they hear is uncomfortable.

The agency says false and misleading claims about migrants, spread through social media and generative AI, are deepening division and mistrust within communities. As trust erodes, governments face stronger public resistance and have less room to cooperate, while migrants face greater risks along their journeys. This is happening as development funding shrinks and international cooperation comes under pressure. The stakes are large, since more than 304 million people live outside their country of birth, including 168 million migrant workers. Money sent home by migrants reaches around one billion people, roughly one in eight people on the planet, paying for food, schooling and healthcare.

Pope set out three areas for action. First, countries along the same routes should plan together to expand regular pathways, strengthen protection, manage borders humanely and support dignified return. Second, communities hit by repeated floods and failing harvests need early investment so people can stay where possible and move safely when they must. Third, reliable data and the voices of affected people should guide decisions, with technology that protects personal information and guards against bias. Pope framed the message as one of trust built gradually, through agreements kept and people treated fairly.

The timing matters because of several upcoming milestones. In May, a record number of States and stakeholders reaffirmed their commitment to safe, orderly and regular migration at the International Migration Review Forum. The UN will review global progress on the Sustainable Development Goal target on well-managed migration in July 2027, followed by the SDG Summit in September 2027, where discussions on what follows the 2030 Agenda will begin. The IDM, marking 25 years, will feed its outcomes into the IOM Council in December, which will hold a high-level panel on strengthening political trust for migration governance.

Articles.Title: AI and Misinformation Are Turning Migrants Into Targets

stories.Headline: AI Multiplies Advisor Expertise: A Computer Nerd Comes Clean
stories.Summary:
Mark Tennenbaum, who describes himself as a computer nerd, wrote in Advisor Perspectives on November 4, 2026 about building an AI-assisted platform called FlightDeck. He began using new AI reasoning models in 2025 to turn his ideas into working code. Since February 2026 he has built FlightDeck, a market intelligence platform with live portfolio monitors, a market weather system, replays of historical crises, a regime classification history going back to 2000, and a publishing system for his firm's research. He is the chief engineer for his firm's information systems as well as its chief portfolio and investment model designer.

Tennenbaum estimates that building the platform the way he would have in 2019 would have taken roughly 3,800 hours of senior financial engineering. At the $150 to $200 an hour he would expect to pay experienced U.S. contract fintech engineers, that comes to well over half a million dollars before the first support ticket. The actual cost was a handful of AI subscriptions, cloud hosting, and his own design and engineering expertise. He says 40-plus years of knowing where data comes from, how it flows, and when a number is wrong made the design work.

He describes three cases where the AI gave confident wrong answers that he caught because he knew what the right answer should be. In one, the AI overruled his architecture and gave monitors their own calculations, which produced screens that disagreed about the same portfolio. In another, it proposed rebalancing triggers built on a research framework meant only to judge whether alpha can be measured. In a third, it misread tickers and declared a catastrophic concentration in a single issuer, then heaped praise on the same process after he corrected it. He says none of these was a classic hallucination but a failure of comprehension and context at the prompt level.

He cites research showing AI helps novices most on tasks inside its competence and can hurt users outside it. Among 5,179 customer support agents, AI raised productivity 14% on average and 34% for novices, with little gain for the most skilled. Among 758 Boston Consulting Group consultants, those using AI on a task outside its competence were 19 percentage points less likely to get it right. In an Advisor360° survey of 300 advisors released in January 2026, just 3% said they rely on AI-generated financial recommendations while 93% called retaining control over decisions and advice non-negotiable. He urges advisors to keep one source of truth, know what each tool is for, distrust both alarm and applause, and make the AI show its assumptions.

Articles.Title: AI Multiplies Advisor Expertise: A Computer Nerd Comes Clean

stories.Headline: Building On Progress In China–USA Talks On AI – Analysis
stories.Summary:
On 24 September 2026, US President Donald J. Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping for a summit in Washington, DC, where artificial intelligence was a major topic. Analysts writing for the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) describe the meeting as a break from earlier Xi–Biden summits, which had been held on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings. This time the summit was the main purpose of Xi's state visit, and Xi went to Washington even though a United Nations General Assembly session was under way in New York. The meeting followed a May 2026 summit in Beijing and produced a deadline of November 2026 for a follow-on technical dialogue, along with an agreed bilateral communication channel for reporting AI incidents, which some have called an "AI hotline."

The authors argue that the talks need trade and industry expertise to move from broad pledges to practical rules. Earlier summits were dominated by foreign ministry and state department officials, while the May and September 2026 meetings included trade officials and chief executives from major technology firms, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, OpenAI and Apple. The authors say those executives should move from the banquet table to the negotiating table. They also say both countries depend on something the other controls, namely US limits on Chinese access to advanced chips and computing power and Chinese limits on exports of critical minerals, and that this mutual dependence could give the dialogue a starting point. The article does not say whether the chip or mineral restrictions were discussed at the September summit, though both official summaries appear to have left them aside.

The authors identify several unresolved problems. The US summary uses the term "super intelligence," while China's official report continues to use "artificial intelligence," a difference they say could complicate how incidents are defined and how the hotline is framed. They also note that it is unclear which incidents would be reported, who would report them and how, since AI companies often detect anomalies first and the US has no single mandatory national reporting system for them, whereas China already operates a tiered system under its Cyberspace Administration. The authors say the coming dialogue will be a key test of whether both sides can agree on definitions of AI incidents, designated points of contact and reciprocal information sharing. They conclude that progress is more likely if technical and operational experts from trade and industry take part, since these groups drive AI development and its integration into the economy.

Articles.Title: Building On Progress In China–USA Talks On AI – Analysis

stories.Headline: Jim Cramer explains why no AI stock seems safe from the market carnage
stories.Summary:
CNBC host Jim Cramer said on Thursday that uncertainty over the future of the data center build-out has made artificial intelligence stocks increasingly difficult to value, and that this has driven steep selling over the previous two sessions. The sell-off spread across the AI trade, reaching chipmakers as well as companies that supply power and electrical equipment for data centers. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) fell 3% on Wednesday and another 10% on Thursday, while GE Vernova and Sandisk dropped 7% and 22% respectively on Thursday. Cramer's comments were published on November 5, 2026.

Investors fear that regulatory hurdles and local opposition to new data centers could slow the build-out, which would undercut the growth forecasts that support chipmakers' valuations. Cramer used Nvidia as his main example, noting that the chipmaker trades at roughly 12 times next year's earnings with an expected growth rate of 70 percent, which makes it look cheap. He warned, however, that those projections assume demand stays strong for years, and that the stock would not be a bargain if the U.S. cannot permit new data centers as quickly as it does now. Cramer also questioned Micron's long-term take-or-pay contracts, which give some revenue visibility even if customers do not take delivery, and he wondered how firm those deals would be if a customer ran into financial trouble.

Cramer praised Advanced Micro Devices' latest earnings as among the best quarters he had seen, and he cited CEO Lisa Su's projection that the broader data center market could eventually reach $1 trillion. He said the stock, which he noted was at $188 in March and is now at $404, looks expensive by that measure, and he suggested this may be the real problem. Cramer framed the central question as whether regulatory hurdles will significantly slow data center construction or only delay it. He said that until the outlook becomes clearer, even strong earnings may not justify AI stock valuations. He also disclosed that Cramer's Charitable Trust, run by the CNBC Investing Club, owns shares of Nvidia and Micron.

Articles.Title: Jim Cramer explains why no AI stock seems safe from the market carnage

stories.Headline: Putnam Career & Technical Center students explore the future of AI
stories.Summary:
The Putnam Career and Technical Center in Putnam County, West Virginia, hosted a student-led cybersecurity conference on Thursday, November 5, 2026, themed "AI: The New Digital Frontier." Marshall University professor Dr. Josh Brunty gave the keynote presentation at the event. Education and technology professionals helped students navigate an AI-driven world and gave them a sense of what their future could look like. The sessions also covered how students can protect themselves in that environment. The conference was organized as a way for students to explore how artificial intelligence is shaping their lives and careers.

Jeff Pitchford, the cybersecurity instructor at the center, said the event gave students a chance to speak one-on-one with industry leaders who work in the middle of the field. He stressed that networking is an important skill and called the day a strong opportunity to build those connections. Pitchford also said the presenters talked with students about how AI will affect the workforce. He told the station that AI is not going to take all the jobs, which he described as a stressful concern for many young people. Instead, he said, AI can take aggregated data and make work easier and faster, and it can help workers spot problems they might otherwise miss.

Presenters came from several institutions, including professors from Marshall University, West Virginia State, Glenville State and BridgeValley. The article describes the conference as a way for students to see how these schools and companies think about AI and security. It does not report any formal changes, requirements or policies that resulted from the event. The article is a local news report published by WOWK 13 News and does not describe any follow-up events. It also does not indicate whether the conference will be repeated next year.

Articles.Title: Putnam Career & Technical Center students explore the future of AI

stories.Headline: Nothing CEO says company’s mysterious AI-first device is dropping next month
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, November 4, 2026, Nothing CEO Carl Pei posted on X that the company’s first AI-native product ships in December. Nothing is the smartphone startup behind the distinctive Nothing Phone. Pei said the device is a tool built with the personality and care that define a Nothing product. He said it has no new screen and could not have been an app.

No firm release date has been announced. Pei has teased an AI-first device for some time, and the company has also said it plans to release a pair of AI-linked smart glasses and earbuds with AI integrations. He called the product a productivity tool. He seemed to downplay any link to AI wearables, writing that the whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment with the pendant, the pin, the glasses and the companion.

He said he admires the boldness but reads this moment differently. Nothing fans should know soon enough what the company has in store. Pei is the CEO of Nothing and made the announcement in his post on X. He described the device as a tool built with personality and care. He said it has no new screen and could not have been an app.

He also said he reads the industry’s hunt for a magical consumer AI device differently. The articles do not say what the device is, and they give no price or further specifications. They say only that it ships in December and that no firm release date has been announced. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that.

Articles.Title: Nothing CEO says company’s mysterious AI-first device is dropping next month

stories.Headline: AI a threat to news organizations
stories.Summary:
Meta's new terms for businesses that use Facebook have alarmed newspapers and media outlets, according to a report in the Pine County News. The terms say media companies must allow web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers and user agents into their websites so Meta can collect news content for its use. Businesses that use Facebook have no opt out option and would be forced to agree to the new terms. Newspapers and other media outlets are joining together in possible litigation against Meta unless the terms are revised to protect intellectual property.

The policy says Meta may periodically pull updates from domains, web pages or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research and maintain advertising and business products. Meta says the update only applies to its ads and business products. The terms first said the content would be used to train AI, and Meta changed the word train to develop on October 16. The new terms take effect on November 20, after Meta delayed the original October 30 date to consult with publishers and advertisers.

Sen. Martha Blackburn, a Republican, and Sen. Adam Schiff, a Democrat, are getting involved. Schiff reached out to Mark Zuckerberg directly and insisted the company withdraw the terms as written. The Norwegian Media Businesses' Association filed the first lawsuit against Meta over the terms, and the European Publishers Council signed a joint letter arguing the terms violate the Digital Markets Act. Editor & Publisher magazine argues that if Meta can build models on local journalism and use them to generate competing summaries, publishers can argue Meta is using their property to undercut them.

Editor & Publisher also states that Google pays roughly 100 publishers for AI sourced answers, while Meta is offering nothing. The article says that if outlets agree to the terms, AI could put more newspaper companies out of business, and Meta would then have nothing to draw content from. Management at the paper has said that if the terms stand, it may deliver the news the old way, through the printed paper and website, and potentially through email or other social media platforms. Traci LeBrun is the editor of the Pine City Pioneer.

Articles.Title: AI a threat to news organizations

stories.Headline: Top 100 AI Venture Capitalists 2026: K2 Global and Ozi Amanat
stories.Summary:
K2 Global and its founder, Ozi Amanat, have both been named to the 2026 Strebulaev–Jackson AI Venture Rankings, according to a press release issued through GlobeNewswire on November 5, 2026. The rankings, published by Stanford Graduate School of Business Professor Ilya Strebulaev and researcher Blake Jackson, identify leading venture capital firms and individual investors based on their investments in U.S.-based artificial intelligence companies. Amanat is listed alongside investors including Peter Thiel, Reid Hoffman, Vinod Khosla, Ben Horowitz and Marc Andreessen. K2 Global was also named among the Top 100 AI venture capital firms worldwide, and the press release says it is the only Singapore-headquartered firm on that list and one of just five firms based outside the United States.

The rankings evaluate investment value creation using valuations, dilution, net profit and investment attribution, and they cover qualifying investments in U.S.-based AI companies through August 31, 2026. The release describes K2 Global as a relatively small, independent venture capital firm that invests across artificial intelligence, robotics, neuroscience, defense technology and other frontier sectors. Its portfolio is said to include SpaceX, Neuralink and Shield AI. The announcement does not say how the rankings were weighted beyond those factors or how many investments qualified for each firm.

Amanat, in the release, described the recognition as meaningful, saying it came after years of finding exceptional founders and backing them as they build companies. He said the honor was alongside investors he had long admired and acknowledged that the work had not always been easy. He also thanked the founders and investors who had supported the firm and said the best was yet to come. The release itself was prepared by the company and its distribution through a press-release service, and the publishing outlet notes that its editorial teams were not involved in creating the post. The source of the rankings is a Substack article by Strebulaev and Jackson, which the release links to.

Articles.Title: Top 100 AI Venture Capitalists 2026: K2 Global and Ozi Amanat

stories.Headline: Canva’s big layoffs say a lot about the AI design landscape
stories.Summary:
Canva announced its first major round of layoffs in its 13-year history on November 3, 2026. The company said 1,271 people, around 22% of its overall staff, will be laid off, reassigned to new roles, or relocated to its headquarters in Sydney, Australia. The news came in a press release from cofounder and CEO Melanie Perkins. Perkins said the layoffs are part of a larger plan to make Canva's teams more agile and less siloed.

The restructuring folds product, growth, and platform teams into one unit and reduces the number of subspecialties at the company. Perkins said she had come to the difficult conclusion that small changes would not be enough. She said Canva needs to refound itself and get back to its roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions and take ownership. Canva did not give a broader business reason for the layoffs.

Perkins is responsible for the changes and explained them in her letter to staff. In an August interview with Fortune, she said demand for new AI features had significantly exceeded the company's expectations. She said this validated the demand but also showed Canva needed to reduce the cost of completing an AI task. She said Canva decided to slow the rollout while it rebuilt the architecture and strengthened the business model.

The layoffs come as Canva works through growing pains and questions about the timing of a potential IPO. In early August, Canva told investors it was downgrading its revenue growth forecast for 2026 from 30% to 20%. By the end of 2025, Canva had more than 265 million monthly active users and more than 31 million paid users. Perkins told Fortune that since launching Canva 2.0 in April, cost per task had dropped by 90%, and Canva said its October launch of Canva Brush cut cost per task by 46% compared with the previous design agent.

Articles.Title: Canva’s big layoffs say a lot about the AI design landscape

stories.Headline: I Asked AI Tools How To Build Wealth on Middle-Class Income
stories.Summary:
MoneyLion asked three AI tools, ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, how someone could build wealth on a $75,000 salary, and published the answers on November 5, 2026. The article was written by Martin Dasko and edited by Brendan McGinley. It cited a TD Bank U.S. survey finding that 69% of Americans would let bank-provided AI tools complete a financial task for them, and that 49% had used some form of AI assistant for a personal finance decision in the past year. The piece was created with the assistance of artificial intelligence and reviewed by the editorial team.

ChatGPT said a $75,000 salary can be enough for a strong financial future with strategic money management. It advised spending less than you earn, investing 15% to 20% of gross income, buying diversified low-cost index ETFs, affordable real estate and career investments, raising income through skills and negotiated raises, avoiding lifestyle inflation and building an emergency fund. Gemini recommended a conscious spending plan that sets fixed costs, savings goals and guilt-free spending in advance, automating contributions so money moves into investments before it can be spent, using employer matches and low-cost index funds, and guarding against lifestyle creep. Claude said investing about $940 a month, which is 15% of $75,000, at an average 7% a year grows to roughly $1 million in 30 years, and put after-tax pay at roughly $4,700 to $4,900 a month.

The article said chatbots will not always be accurate on personal finance, but called some tips universally accepted as excellent advice. These were setting a clear budget, automating savings and investments, choosing simple investments because time in the market beats timing it, avoiding lifestyle inflation by raising savings, and staying patient. It said following these general tips can build wealth on any salary. For detailed numbers it recommended working with a financial advisor, and it noted that AI-generated content may be inaccurate, incomplete or outdated and should be checked against reliable sources.

Articles.Title: I Asked AI Tools How To Build Wealth on Middle-Class Income

stories.Headline: UM establishes Montana’s first artificial intelligence career certificate
stories.Summary:
The University of Montana has established the Human-Centered AI Career Certificate, the first of its kind in the state, and it is being offered this year. Lee Banville, director of the School of Journalism, and Michael Cassens, an associate professor of game design and interactive media, created the nine-credit certificate together and teach its three courses, all of which are taught online. Banville said the goal is to help students understand that artificial intelligence will affect people's lives and careers, not to promote or discourage its use. He stressed that the program is not a sales pitch for the technology.

Cassens said the certificate would strengthen students' resumes and give them foundational knowledge for a changing technological landscape. He said students would be required to use AI tools for assignments, including ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini, Meta and UM's own model, Chat MT, to see how each works. A typical exercise would be entering the same prompt into several models to compare their responses. Cassens said he accepts AI use as long as students can reasonably defend their choice and explain it openly.

The first course, Creatively Exploring AI, is already taught by Cassens and covers AI's history, hallucinations, biases, terminology, ethics and effects on various disciplines. The second course, Calling Bullshit in the Age of AI, is a journalism class taught by Banville that focuses on critical thinking and recognizing when AI is wrong, and it will be renamed next semester. The third, Human-Centered Leadership in AI, is a new class that Cassens will offer in the spring, adapted from a leadership course he previously taught. Cassens said the curriculum is meant to be adaptable as the technology changes and that the program is grounded in human concerns.

Student reactions are mixed: Grace Smith, a 23-year-old graduate student in game design, said the courses promote discussion rather than either side of the debate, while Kylie Heit, a 23-year-old senior cello performance major from Helena, said the program normalizes AI and that its "Human-Centered" title is misleading. Banville acknowledged that many people fear AI and that real questions about it deserve attention, but he noted that a free one-day, one-credit AI course the School of Journalism offered last spring drew only about 15 students, far fewer than he expected. He hopes the certificate will attract more interest and that students will engage with the topic regardless of local debates over data centers. He told students that the tools are already here and will change their lives, and that his aim is for them to be prepared to decide how, when and whether to use them.

Articles.Title: UM establishes Montana’s first artificial intelligence career certificate

stories.Headline: Did IBM Just Tell the Truth About AI?
stories.Summary:
IBM reported higher revenue but its stock fell, according to a Motley Fool podcast recorded on Oct. 22, 2026 and published on Nov. 4, 2026. Host Jon Quast and contributors Matt Frankel and Lou Whiteman discussed the results alongside Lam Research's quarterly report. Lam's revenue rose 22%, with a 40% operating margin, and its service business posted $2.5 billion in sales, up 40%. The podcast did not give IBM's specific figures or explain its unique take on AI spending in the transcript provided.

The discussion covered several numbers tied to Lam and the wider chip industry. Lam expects its service business to grow about 30% this year and advanced packaging sales to grow about 70%. Equipment spending could rise from around $150 billion to more than $200 billion next year, and Lam's stock trades at about 35 times earnings, or roughly 22 times forward earnings. Frankel described advanced packaging as stacking and connecting multiple chips instead of making one giant chip. Helium matters to chipmaking because fabrication facilities blow it across the back of silicon wafers to keep temperatures precise during etching, and spot prices have cleared $100 per thousand cubic feet.

Frankel said the service side works like a razor and blades model, where every tool sold creates years of service revenue. Whiteman compared it to aerospace and said the services side helps investors see past a possible bubble. He said management's guidance suggests the up cycle is safe at least into 2028, though he still sees cyclicality and limits on how fast the company can grow. Frankel said he would nibble on the dip but would not call the stock a value stock, and Whiteman said he would wait for a better deal.

Quast said the market was down as the podcast was taped, citing comments from President Trump implying the Iran conflict would intensify after the midterm elections. Frankel said South Korea gets about 65% of its helium from Qatar, where Samsung and SK Hynix make chips, and that there is no good substitute for helium. The transcript provided does not say what IBM requires or changes, and it does not give IBM's own statements beyond the panel's discussion of its AI spending. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Did IBM Just Tell the Truth About AI?

stories.Headline: A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout
stories.Summary:
Docusign announced on Tuesday that it has acquired Suplari, an AI-powered spending analysis company based in Seattle. The deal comes five years after Microsoft bought the startup and nearly three years after Microsoft spun it back out to its founders. Financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari's technology into its contract management platform.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh Parekh, Jeff Gerber and Brian White. By 2021 it had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures. Microsoft acquired the company in July 2021, when it had about 40 employees, and said it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft keeping a minority stake, and Gerber became CEO. Suplari now has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Docusign said it will pair Suplari's analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with its Iris AI engine. The goal is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms. Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said joining Docusign allows the company to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company's spending. Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari's technology and talent will help Docusign connect what supplier agreements say with actual spending.

Parekh wrote in a blog post earlier this year that after ChatGPT arrived in November 2022, Microsoft redirected new-product investment to Copilot. He said succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers. Microsoft concluded, and the founders agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again. Parekh, who stayed at Microsoft before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn, remains a Suplari shareholder and advisor and said he is ecstatic about the second exit.

Articles.Title: A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout

stories.Headline: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?
stories.Summary:
A user posted an Ask HN thread on Hacker News on 4 November 2026 asking how people use AI day to day. The poster, eggbrain, said the thread had 161 points and 184 comments 13 hours after it went up. The post listed five questions about subscriptions, other models, coding harnesses, orchestration tools and broader agent platforms. The poster said no one needed to answer every question and that the aim was a gut feel for current use.

Commenters described a wide range of setups. One said they self-host Qwen and Gemma 4 variants and use their own harness, having moved away from Cline and VS Code to focus on review. Another pays for Claude Ultra at 200 and ChatGPT at 20, runs local models on an M4 MacBook Pro with 128GB of RAM, and drives Claude Code through Telegram with scheduled jobs and containers. A third said they dropped Cursor and Codex for the Claude IDE after Opus 5.5 arrived, set it to medium and removed their skills. Others reported using Muse and Cursor, local models on an M1 Max, Claude Opus 5.5 on a Pro plan, and Google Ultra at 100 a month with DeepSeek pay-as-you-go tokens.

Several commenters said the default tools are good enough. One argued that people using out-of-the-box Claude Code or Codex likely get the newest agent features anyway. Another said Claude and Codex desktop are innovating fast and that built-in code review has made many AI code review startups obsolete. A third said they ask Claude Code to review a pull request and it spawns a sub-agent, though it almost always finds something wrong even after fixes. One solopreneur said they avoid agent swarms because they like to do QA on what the tools generate.

Some commenters described how much work they run at once. One said five things concurrently lasts about a day, three lasts all week and leaves weekends for untangling, and two or three a day feels manageable. Another said they have paid for a 200 plan since March 2026, cycle between four or five work projects and two or three personal ones, and tell their agents at night to keep going without asking questions. One reply said that person was doing everything right. The thread gives no further details on what happens next.

Articles.Title: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence exposes antiquities trafficking: Türkiye recovers 100 historical treasures from America
stories.Summary:
Turkey has recovered 100 looted historical artifacts from the United States, a milestone the Voice of Emirates reported on November 6, 2026. The operation was carried out by Turkish authorities, who used artificial intelligence and digital analysis to locate the pieces and check their historical origins. The article describes the recovery as the latest step in an ongoing effort to bring back objects that were illegally taken out of the country. Officials were said to have used image analysis and data comparison to match the artifacts' technical features and trace how they moved between owners.

The article says the artifacts had ended up in private collections or foreign institutions after being smuggled abroad. Returning them is presented as part of a wider effort to protect historical heritage and preserve cultural identity. The technology helped with both finding the objects and gathering evidence of where they came from, which the article says strengthens the case for their return. It also notes that the work depended on documenting each piece in enough detail to prove its origin.

The article credits Turkish authorities with leading the recovery but does not name specific officials or quote any statements from them. It does not identify the American holders of the artifacts, the institutions involved, or the individuals suspected of smuggling them. The piece frames the success as an example of how modern technology is becoming a valuable tool against the illicit trade in cultural property. It stresses that the recovery reflects the importance of international cooperation in protecting human heritage.

The article calls for continued legal and technical efforts to pursue those responsible for smuggling historical objects. It also says that returning such artifacts to their countries of origin is essential. The report does not describe any further steps, charges, or timelines for the remaining cases. Readers should look to later coverage for details on the legal process and the artifacts' eventual return.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence exposes antiquities trafficking: Türkiye recovers 100 historical treasures from America

stories.Headline: Dr. Mackensie Alston Explores Artificial Intelligence as a Bias-Detection Tool
stories.Summary:
Economist Mackensie Alston, Ph.D., visited Swarthmore College last week to deliver the annual Frank C. Pierson lecture, titled "Constructing the Criminal: Race and the Perception of AI-Generated Suspects." Alston is an assistant professor in the Department of Finance at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and a faculty affiliate for the Wilson Sheehan Lab for Economic Opportunities at the University of Notre Dame. The lecture was hosted by the college's economics department and honors Frank Pierson '34, a former department chair whose work on anti-discrimination in labor economics aligns with Alston's field. Her latest research uses AI-generated images, differing only by race, to examine bias among police candidates and to improve hiring practices.

Alston said her interest in economics began with Dan Ariely's 2008 book "Predictably Irrational," which challenges the idea that people always act rationally. She described wanting to document behavior that existing theory could not explain, and she designs experiments to test such phenomena. The articles note that economists use lab, online, and field experiments, as well as observational data, and Alston said she prefers defining economics as the study of decision-making. Conclusive research, she argued, lets policymakers test ideas before wide adoption and compare predictions with real-world outcomes. Her work applies this approach to the factors behind police decisions to use potentially lethal force.

Alston drew on Gary Becker's 1968 rational criminal model, which weighs the probability and severity of punishment against the payoff from crime. She and her partner, Dr. Emily Owens, were motivated by research showing Black people face mistreatment by police in many ways. The articles report that improved anti-bias training has shown positive effects, but its impact can fade and depends on ongoing supervisor support. Alston's approach instead targets bias in new officers before they are hired. She has so far conducted two studies using AI images created with Midjourney and Gemini Proshop, and her results have not yet been published because further studies are planned.

During the question period, Alston said she is weighing ways to address social desirability bias, including asking participants how others might describe the images. When asked whether the AI origin of the images affected responses, she said about 70 percent of participants thought the images resembled AI, with 30 percent disagreeing. In an interview with The Phoenix, she stressed interdisciplinary work, noting that economists, sociologists, and psychologists each contribute distinct insight. She suggested that such cooperation can help the academic community move toward solutions.

Articles.Title: Dr. Mackensie Alston Explores Artificial Intelligence as a Bias-Detection Tool

stories.Headline: Verizon AI-RAN work rides nationwide Ericsson Intelligent Controller deployment
stories.Summary:
Verizon is working with Ericsson to integrate AI into radio access network automation, and the effort includes a nationwide rollout of Ericsson's Intelligent Controller by the end of 2026. The platform will run AI-native rApps, which are microservices-based applications that operate in non-real time and give an operator more control over open RAN environments. Verizon pointed to an already implemented method for handing over fixed-wireless access devices from its 4G LTE network to its 5G standalone network, which it says removes the need for manual intervention when handovers fail. The news was reported on November 4, 2026.

Matt Butz, Verizon's vice president of network planning, said in a statement that the work has already shown measurable results. He cited AI control of massive MIMO antennas and traffic steering that produced a near nine percent improvement in downlink data radio bearer throughput and up to an eight percent improvement in uplink user equipment throughput. The companies also plan to test and deploy new rApps, including a cell anomaly detector, a root cause explainer and an anomaly general optimizer, which Verizon said will speed its move toward level-four network autonomy. Verizon CTO Yago Tenorio said earlier this year that early work had cut tasks that once took hours down to 90 seconds, and he wanted that in production before the end of the year, starting with the radio and later moving to transport and core.

The controller is part of Ericsson's Intelligent Automation Platform, which is meant to support multi-vendor and multi-technology systems running 4G and 5G RAN, and it is also used in rival AT&T's $14 billion network overhaul. The work builds on earlier efforts between the two companies, including a pre-standard 6G field call in the 7 GHz band at a California site and Verizon Business using Ericsson for international private 5G services. Ericsson is also part of the Verizon-led 6G Innovation Forum that launched last year. Verizon has previously used Samsung and Qualcomm in a multi-vendor deployment of AI-RAN management applications on a RAN intelligent controller, including a Samsung-developed network-efficiency rApp.

Articles.Title: Verizon AI-RAN work rides nationwide Ericsson Intelligent Controller deployment

stories.Headline: Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor
stories.Summary:
Kino AI launched on Hacker News on November 4, 2026, posted by Luke Igel, who goes by lukeigel on the site. The company, part of Y Combinator's S23 batch, describes itself as an AI media manager and video editor that lets agents and teammates work on the same timeline. The post says storage of footage and assets, a rich video editor, and review links for teammates are bundled into one product. Igel wrote that colleagues and tools like Codex and Claude Code can work on the same timeline with review notes and footage all in one place.

The full editor is free, including unlimited imports and exports, real-time collaboration, and MCP access for a user's own agent. Pro costs $25 per editor per month and adds unlimited MCP tool calls, share links, more storage, YouTube search, and the ability to edit alongside a team. Kino is code-first, built on Remotion, and everything in it has a URL, including projects, clips, footage, comments, replies, a single frame, and the line of code that draws it. The company says it built custom decoders for professional codecs such as ProRes, BRAW, and R3D, and that a 250GB ProRes clip can be dragged straight into a Kino timeline. Kino is available as an Electron download for now, and a pure web browser version has not been released.

Igel said he grew up making YouTube videos and co-directed a 3.5 hour archival documentary during his undergrad at MIT. He said the first launch in 2023 was more like Palantir for Hollywood, with bespoke on-prem deployments on shows like Survivor and A24's Beef, and that in 2025 the team rebuilt Kino as a true editor and bet on coding-as-editing. In the comments he told one user about a workflow button that indexes footage from an iPhone or SD cards and lays out a quick stringout, and he pointed another user to templates at kino.ai/templates. He also said an eye contact feature had shipped and could be found by right-clicking a timeline item.

Igel described his launch video as made entirely with Kino, with more than five agents editing the timeline at once while a friend ran a separate swarm a few minutes further down. He said one agent was rotoscoping, an LLM was color grading all media through LUT support, and both he and his friend made small tweaks along the way. Commenters raised questions about templates, the choice of Remotion over other options, and whether the proxy scrub and final render stay consistent, and Igel replied that Kino renders locally and lets users scrub original footage. The post says teams are using Kino to manage a whole company's media and spin up agents to make new videos every day, and it invites people with ProRes media or legacy editor projects to try the tool and share feedback.

Articles.Title: Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor

stories.Headline: Ricursive AI Releases Ripple-65B Preview: A 65B Dense Open-Weight Model Scoring 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1
stories.Summary:
Ricursive AI released Ripple-65B Preview on November 4, 2026. It is a 65B dense open-weight model pretrained from scratch for agentic coding, and it is a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model behind Ricursive's AI chip design platform. Ricursive reports a score of 80.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, which it calls the top self-reported score among US open-weight models. The release includes three checkpoints under Apache 2.0: an instruction-tuned BF16 model, an NVFP4 version, and a BF16 base model.

The model was pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context. Ricursive says the full R&D cost was $32M, which it estimates at one-tenth the cost of the prior open-weight agentic coding leader. The model runs in BF16 on datacenter GPUs at 250 tokens per second on 2x B200, and an experimental NVFP4 build targets NVIDIA DGX Spark. Ricursive chose a dense Transformer over Mixture-of-Experts to reduce infrastructure complexity, and training held 40% MFU with simple sharding, no custom kernels and no quantization.

The architecture is thin and deep, with a d_model of 5120 across 80 layers. Ricursive says it built its post-training recipe without buying any post-training data, using its own synthetic pipelines. Its mixed RL recipe uses truncated importance sampling, score centering and a linear length penalty, and it reached 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with 1.4M rollouts, which Ricursive puts at roughly 70x fewer than Beam. On other benchmarks it scored 79.1 on SWE-bench Pro v2.0 Hard, 76.5 on SWE-bench Verified, 98.3 on AIME 2025 and 90.5 on HMMT Feb 2026.

Its weak spots include SciCode at 39.4, DeepSWE 1.1 at 44.3, MCP Atlas at 71.67 and GPQA Diamond at 85.2. Ricursive compares Ripple with larger MoE rivals: Reflection Beam at 501B total parameters scored 80.1, Meta Muse Spark Open at 816B scored 76.4, Thinking Machines Inkling at 975B scored 63.8 and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra at 550B scored 56.4. In a rerun of Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the official Terminus 2 harness at 128K, most rivals dropped, with Beam falling to 70.8 and Muse Spark Open rising to 78.7, still below Ripple's 80.5. Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face, Together AI, GMI Cloud and OpenRouter, and Fireworks goes live later today.

Articles.Title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding

stories.Headline: OpenAI Forms JPMorgan Partnership Ahead of 2027 IPO
stories.Summary:
OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, that the company could be ready for an initial public offering in 2027. He made the remarks at the WSJ Tech conference, and the same day the company said it had formed a strategic partnership with JPMorganChase to supply the bank with artificial intelligence services. The details come from a Wall Street Journal report that PYMNTS cited. Brockman's comments were made as the company faces questions about its financing.

Under the partnership, OpenAI will give the bank access to cybersecurity-focused models through its Daybreak program. According to OpenAI's website, Daybreak gives approved individuals and organizations access to its advanced cybersecurity capabilities, along with security solutions, partners and support for protecting systems. After the event, Brockman posted on X that the two companies will explore how advanced AI can help the bank's engineers, security teams, employees and customers. He wrote that he was especially excited about working together on cybersecurity to protect the financial system. Brockman also said the company wants to go public when the timing is right for it.

Brockman's remarks followed a Wall Street Journal report that OpenAI had secured about $11 billion in commitments for its current funding round, less than half of its initial $30 billion target. The report said the company plans to raise more money from family offices and high-net-worth individuals over the coming weeks to reach $20 billion. OpenAI had described this round as an "opportunistic" bridge before a potential IPO, according to a report from October 22. In June, the company said it had submitted a confidential S-1 registration statement to the Securities and Exchange Commission. At that time it said it had not decided on timing and that it may be a while, because some plans are likely easier as a private company.

Articles.Title: OpenAI Forms JPMorgan Partnership Ahead of 2027 IPO

stories.Headline: The AI Resilience map: Where’s your organisation Now?
stories.Summary:
A Dell Technologies article published on 4 November 2026 sets out a way for organisations to judge how ready they are for AI failures. It was written by Venkat Sitaram, Senior Director and Country Head of the Infrastructure Solutions Group at Dell Technologies India. He argues that there is plenty of guidance on AI resilience, but organisations must first understand their own starting point. He compares this to sailing, where a good map was useless without knowing your own position. The article cites the Dell Technologies Modern Enterprise Readiness Study 2026, conducted by Vanson Bourne.

It found that 61% of Indian organisations surveyed said security and compliance concerns had slowed or paused AI adoption. It also found that 26% reported well-established AI or generative AI solutions in production, up from 20% a year earlier. Sitaram says ambition and deployment do not automatically mean readiness. Sitaram describes two maturity curves, one for cyber resilience and one for AI adoption, which move independently. Together they create four positions: Clean Slate, Fortified Newcomer, Exposed Frontrunner and Proving Ground.

He says each position needs different priorities, such as listing dependencies, extending recovery practices to AI-specific assets, prioritising critical workloads or testing recovery under realistic conditions. He says resilience must evolve with the technology and the business processes it supports. Sitaram is responsible for the argument, and the study figures come from Vanson Bourne. He says the first step is an honest view of where an organisation stands, and that a uniform approach risks directing resources away from the most immediate vulnerabilities. The article does not say what happens next beyond that.

Articles.Title: The AI Resilience map: Where’s your organisation Now?

stories.Headline: BuzzFeed Stock in Free Fall as Pivot to AI Blows Up in Its Face
stories.Summary:
BuzzFeed's stock fell sharply on November 5, 2026, dropping from a high of $2.09 earlier that year to $0.57 in a single morning, a 38 percent decline. The fall followed the company's third-quarter earnings report, which showed earnings per share of negative $0.22, 13 cents worse than analysts had expected. Back in March, the company had warned there was "substantial doubt" about its ability to continue operating, after reporting a net loss of $57.3 million for 2025. The stock had already drawn some enthusiasm in May, when a family affiliate of TV personality Byron Allen bought a majority stake in the company.

Allen's affiliate pushed the company toward free-streaming video, audio and user-generated content, and Jonah Peretti received the title of "president of BuzzFeed AI." Allen said the company was chasing YouTube and aimed to become a free video streaming service powered by AI. BuzzFeed has since laid off 33 percent of its remaining staff, roughly two months after Allen took over. The article notes that the company's AI push began in 2023 after the launch of ChatGPT, when it published quizzes and AI-generated travel guides that drew criticism.
