stories.Headline: Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’
stories.Summary:
Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman said on the company’s quarterly earnings call on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, that most people will not want an AI agent to do their house hunting for them. He said people are happy to let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but searching for a home is different because the enjoyment is the point. He compared it to watching a movie or playing a game, which no one wants an agent to do for them. He said finding a home is a milestone people want to live themselves, not a chore to hand off to a robot.

The issue matters to Zillow because most of its money comes from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business. That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with human agents and loan officers, and an AI agent that does the searching could cut Zillow out. Wacksman said Zillow is not yet seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms, and about 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini and is now working with Anthropic.

Zillow’s AI mode, a conversational search feature, is now available to all signed-in users, and more than 2.5 million people used it from March to September, asking 8.5 million questions. Wacksman made the case in prepared remarks as personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases, raise questions for the company. Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent does not identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser, and a federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

Zillow’s Follow Up Boss software for real estate agents is getting AI that spots leads needing attention and recommends next steps, which agents can approve. Engineers at the company are using AI to ship 60% more changes to production than in 2024, Wacksman said. For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales. The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.

Articles.Title: Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’

stories.Headline: The geopolitical stakes of AI: Why leaders must watch the sovereign AI race
stories.Summary:
Governments including India, Japan, France, Canada and the United Arab Emirates are spending billions of dollars to subsidize sovereign AI, according to researchers at Bain & Company. They are investing heavily in domestic computing infrastructure and in localized AI models trained on regional data and native languages. The article, a sponsored post from HPE and AMD published on November 4, 2026, describes this as a race among nations. It says AI has moved past simple corporate optimization and is now an engine of macroeconomic power.

McKinsey & Company estimates that sovereign AI could represent a market of $600 billion by 2030. A survey of executives, investors and government offices found that 71% see sovereign AI as an existential concern or a strategic imperative for their organizational goals. McKinsey Global Institute research suggests generative AI could generate $2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion in annual economic value. Gartner says nations establishing a sovereign AI stack will need to invest at least 1% of their GDP in AI infrastructure by 2029.

The article says state leaders are hesitant to trust foreign entities, even close allies, with critical infrastructure assets. It says an adversary could cause catastrophic disruption by knocking external capabilities offline. It also says governments want governance controls that protect rights and uphold regional laws, with local languages and values embedded in the models. For CIOs, it recommends auditing infrastructure interdependencies and evaluating strategic supercomputing partners with a track record of building large-scale systems.

The article says the decisions of global superpowers today will directly affect supply chains, compliance requirements and data architectures tomorrow. It describes the tech landscape as turning into a zero-sum game as multilateral collaboration gives way to unilateral competition. It warns that standardizing on a single global public cloud provider exposes a business to regulatory penalties or abrupt service disruptions if international data laws shift. It adds that managing isolated data silos across countries raises operational complexity and total cost of ownership.

Articles.Title: The geopolitical stakes of AI: Why leaders must watch the sovereign AI race

stories.Headline: Washington’s AI experiment is flying blind
stories.Summary:
The federal government is expanding its use of artificial intelligence while the civil service shrinks at extraordinary speed, and Washington has no consistent public way to judge whether the combined changes are making services better or worse. The Government Accountability Office reported that AI use cases identified across 11 federal agencies nearly doubled from 2023 to 2024, rising from 571 to 1,110, and reported generative AI use cases rose from 32 to 282. Across 22 major agencies, nearly 378,000 employees separated during 2025 while about 127,000 were hired, leaving those agencies with more than 250,000 fewer workers in January 2026 than in December 2024. Gene Lockwood-Shabat, an independent consultant and former federal official, wrote the commentary. The article calls for Congress and the White House Office of Management and Budget to build on the FITARA scorecard model and create a unified AI and Workforce Management Scorecard.

For major AI uses, agencies would identify the work an AI-assisted tool supports and report four things together: what they spent, changes in staffing and skills, performance against service targets in annual performance plans and congressional budget justifications, and quality control data such as AI-related error rates and administrative rework. The measures would show a baseline and later reporting periods, and the primary unit of measurement would be the service affected by the AI investment. The article says agencies already publish performance plans and budget justifications, so the task is to connect staffing, AI investment and service and quality measures in one place. The article points to the Internal Revenue Service and the Department of Veterans Affairs as examples of gaps. IRS officials told GAO that the Research, Applied Analytics and Statistics Division lost 63 employees, most of whom had been directly involved in designing, developing or overseeing AI projects, and that IRS had not adequately identified the AI skills it needed.

In June 2026, VA's inspector general found that staff were using general-purpose generative AI chat tools for clinical work, but VA could not measure the breadth of that use or readily identify AI-related patient-safety events, and VA concurred with the recommendations. GAO also recommended that the Defense Department, the Department of Homeland Security, the General Services Administration and VA update their policies to require systematic collection of lessons learned from AI acquisitions. The article argues that faster is not inherently better and that fewer employees is not a guaranteed win for efficiency. It says fiscal conservatives point to a leaner bureaucracy and tech optimists point to a more modernized government, and both may have a case, but a government cannot show it is getting better just by counting positions eliminated or AI tools adopted. It says a common expectation of public, service-level reporting would make questions about what is working harder to evade, and that measures would have to be tailored to each service, since an error in a clinical workflow is not the same as a delayed tax response.

Articles.Title: Washington’s AI experiment is flying blind

stories.Headline: HCPSS Teams Up with Student Group to Drive Student Interest in and Understanding of Coding, Computer Science, and Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Julie Wray and Carrie Trudden, Howard County Public School System's then and current coordinators of Instructional Technology, began receiving emails several years ago from a student group called Howard County Hour of Code, or HocoHOC. They were unfamiliar with the group and skeptical of its offer to partner on the Hour of Code, now known as Hour of AI, an annual worldwide event. The district had historically used resources from Code.org for the event with success, but the emails kept coming. In spring 2025, Wray and Trudden followed up and met with HCPSS students and HocoHOC Co-Directors Daniel Gao of River Hill High School and Ankit Mohanty of Marriotts Ridge High School.

At that meeting, Gao and Mohanty explained that HocoHOC was student-run and had built a platform at hocohoc.org with student-generated articles on coding, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and other computer science topics. Students earned points for themselves and their schools by reading articles and could enter a raffle for prizes. Wray and Trudden agreed to work with the group to prepare the site for HCPSS's Hour of Code week in December 2025, including review for accessibility and data privacy guidelines. The work also involved aligning the site with the district's computer science curriculum and creating articles, games and daily challenges for all grade levels.

Under Gao and Mohanty's leadership, the 2025 initiative reached more than 2,500 registered users, over 28,000 article views and approximately 862 hours of student engagement. Dunloggin Middle School, the 2025 winning school, received a $300 donation, and Swansfield Elementary School received $50 for second place. Gao said feedback from students and staff was positive and that teachers reported students wanting to learn more about coding after reading the articles. Mohanty said a teacher's account of thrilled students during prize handouts made the work feel worthwhile, and Trudden said schools were enthusiastic and kids loved winning prizes for learning new things.

HCPSS and HocoHOC are working together again this year, with Mohanty returning as director and River Hill student Nicholas Chen serving as co-director now that Gao has graduated. Mohanty said student writers are producing new articles and the group is developing games and daily challenges for extra points during December. Prizes will again include $300 for the winning school and $50 each for second and third place. Students in all grades may take part in the 2026 Hour of AI activities from Dec. 8 to 15, and participating schools will share more information with students and families.

Articles.Title: HCPSS Teams Up with Student Group to Drive Student Interest in and Understanding of Coding, Computer Science, and Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Speaking a thousand pictures: How GenAI is changing the business of art
stories.Summary:
Artists and the businesses that buy their work are facing a new question: how to prove a piece was made by a human hand. Writing in Mint, reporter Samiksha Goel describes how generative AI is reshaping the art market, from commissions and pricing to galleries checking the origins of what they show. The article, published on 5 November 2026, draws on interviews with a dozen artists, gallery owners, agencies and collectors. It places the current debate within a long argument about art and mechanical reproduction, noting how the German philosopher Walter Benjamin argued in 1935 that a copy lacks the unique presence of an original.

Illustrators are already feeling the pressure. Rajyasree Sarkar says she has seen fewer commissioning enquiries despite a growing audience, and she turned down one book project because the client wanted her to supply only ideas while AI produced the pictures. Vijaya Aswani says smaller businesses began wanting attractive images rather than a specific style, and she moved towards teaching. Clients now often create AI visual references before approaching artists, which can leave a gap between the reference and what a hand-made work can achieve. Aanchal Gupta says she sometimes loses projects because her fees look high beside what AI seems to produce.

On the business side, Vinc chief executive Rudresh Upadhyaya says his company delivered a batch of shots previously quoted at one year of work in six weeks, at a cost about 35% lower. He says the industry now values creative direction and judgement more than execution alone. Akhil Nair of BigTrunk Communications says AI lets teams test several visual directions before committing to costly production. The article also notes that some online sellers offer AI-generated wall art and NFTs, and that an NFT records ownership but does not establish who made an image.

Authenticity is becoming a practical concern for galleries and collectors. Isha Praneeth reported that a gallery running an online exhibition tested her submitted painting for AI generation before approving it, though the gallery did not respond to questions about its process. Vikram Bachhawat of Aakriti Art Gallery in Kolkata says process records such as studio photos will sit alongside certificates of authenticity, and Mohit Gupta of Mukesh Art Gallery in Jaipur says such records should stay practical for artists. Amit Kumar of Mehta Art Gallery in Varanasi says the artist's concept and physical execution remain central, even as digital provenance tools are considered. The article notes that such records are not yet central to most sales, but questions about human authorship are coming up more often.

Articles.Title: Speaking a thousand pictures: How GenAI is changing the business of art

stories.Headline: Democrats' Data Center Crackdown Sends AI Stocks Reeling, $5 Trillion Wipeout Deepens
stories.Summary:
Democrats won the governor's races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, according to results reported during Asian trading hours on Wednesday, and the victories sent chip and AI shares lower from Seoul to Tokyo. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix gave up early gains, Kioxia fell 5.4% and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. slipped 1.5%, while U.S. equity futures also dropped before paring losses. Roughly $5 trillion of market value has evaporated from 47 AI and chip stocks since Oct. 6, according to Investing.com data. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott, ending three decades of Republican control of the governor's mansion, and Democrat James Talarico won a Senate seat in the same wave.

Texas and Georgia together account for about one-third of U.S. AI data center spending and projects, and GLJ Research estimates Texas alone holds about a quarter of U.S. data center capacity due online by 2030. Hinojosa wants an immediate halt to new projects until lawmakers strengthen community protections, and she opposes the tax breaks that have lured developers. Ohio Gov.-elect Amy Acton supports a data center moratorium and has promised lower energy bills and a utilities commission not beholden to utility companies, and Sherrod Brown's Senate victory over incumbent Jon Husted reinforces the shift. Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated billionaire Rick Jackson and ended more than 20 years of Republican control, but no reporting was found detailing her specific data center platform. A group called Conserve Ohio is pursuing a 2027 constitutional amendment to ban data centers above 25 MW.

Aidan Yao of the Amundi Investment Institute said the midterms were more like a referendum on AI than on Donald Trump, and that restrictions on the AI theme would make the U.S. economy, inflation and monetary policy very uncertain. Nick Ferres of Vantage Point Asset Management said the two key risks have been return on investment and financing of the boom, and both have likely become more challenging. Charu Chanana of Saxo said markets are pricing in a stronger-than-expected Democratic surge, and Jake Dollarhide of Longbow Asset Management called Democratic control of Congress a headwind for tech stocks. Katie Koch of TCW said AI providers have a PR crisis and need to define the social utility of AI and data centers to Americans.

Analysts flagged state-level authority over permits and grid connections as the more immediate risk, since a presidential veto cannot override decisions by governors and utility commissions. BNY's Kevin Shea said policy can disrupt the timing and the cost but will not derail the theme, and some analysts see scarcity value emerging as new supply is delayed. Ohio carries the highest moratorium risk, Texas the largest dollar exposure and Georgia the most room for a negotiated outcome, based on campaign positions and published reporting. The next regular Texas legislative session is likely in January 2027, though that timing is an assumption rather than a stated fact.

Articles.Title: Democrats' Data Center Crackdown Sends AI Stocks Reeling, $5 Trillion Wipeout Deepens - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: 40 of 41 Data Center Votes Go Against AI Builders [2026]
stories.Summary:
Voters in the 2026 midterms delivered a clear signal against new data centers, according to reporting from Reuters on November 4, 2026. Reuters counted 41 data-center-related ballot measures, and Ballotpedia found that all but one moved in an anti-data-center direction, meaning 40 of 41 leaned against new server farms. The same Reuters report tied the result to governor's races in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, where Democratic candidates won after promising to pause new data-center permits and tighten construction rules. CNBC also covered the ballot results that same day. The reporting does not give vote totals, company names, capacity figures or the exact wording of the permit rules, so the strength of each measure is still unclear.

The measures concerned data-center infrastructure, meaning the buildings, power hookups and permits that determine how much computing capacity exists to run AI models. Reuters did not establish that voters weighed in directly on AI research or AI software products. A campaign pledge to pause permits does not itself halt projects, since new governors still need legislatures, agencies and sometimes courts to act. Existing projects with signed agreements may continue under older rules. Even so, the pledges already shape how utilities, lenders and companies rank states for multi-year training clusters.

Reuters framed the results as a message to AI builders, while the reporting points to local worries rather than a verdict on AI itself. Survey data from Pew Research Center, published in October 2026, found that 61% of voters disliked elected officials who supported building data centers in their area, while 8% liked such officials. A separate Pew analysis from September 2026 reported that 41% to 53% of informed U.S. adults said data centers were mostly bad for home energy costs, the environment or nearby quality of life. McKinsey & Company estimated that about 14% of the $5.2 trillion in capital expenditures needed to energize AI workloads over five years would go to power and related infrastructure, roughly $720 billion.

Industry forecasts also project that around 70% of total data-center capacity demand by 2030 will come from facilities equipped for advanced AI workloads. Because permitted projects usually keep moving, any effect on model capacity would likely show up in 2027 and 2028 planning rather than in models shipping now. The reporting we reviewed does not connect any specific model release to the ballot results, and no lab has said a launch will slip because of these measures. Whether the pattern spreads beyond these states remains an open question the available sources do not answer.

Articles.Title: 40 of 41 Data Center Votes Go Against AI Builders [2026] - shattered.io

stories.Headline: 41 Data Center Ballot Measures [2026]: What AI Teams Face - tech-insider.org
stories.Summary:
Voters in the U.S. midterm elections this week considered 41 data center-related ballot measures, according to a Reuters newsletter dated November 4, 2026, which credited Ballotpedia for the count. All but one of the 41 moved in an anti-data-center direction, meaning 40 of them did. Texas, Georgia and Ohio were identified as states with plans for significant data-center capacity growth. Democrats won the governorships in all three states.

The newly elected governors in Texas, Georgia and Ohio were described as having promised to pause new data-center permits and tighten construction rules. The Reuters excerpt gives no timeline and no mechanism for how such a pause would work. A governor's promise to pause permits is not the same as a pause taking effect, and existing permits usually stay valid. The measures concerned data centers and related development, and they did not ask voters whether AI models or AI research should continue. Reuters wrote that voters could influence how quickly AI infrastructure gets built locally.

Reuters did not publish the names of the winning candidates, vote totals, exact ballot wording or locality-by-locality results in the excerpt available. The report also gave no dollar amounts, capacity figures or company investments tied to the measures. The article states that voters rejected AI itself is unconfirmed, and that voters directly decided the speed of AI research is not established. The motives behind each measure were not listed in the Reuters excerpt.

The article says the ballot results suggest the place input for AI builders just got harder to secure in at least some jurisdictions. It says capacity can move to friendlier jurisdictions and projects can be redesigned to meet stricter rules, but delay carries a cost even when a project ultimately goes ahead. The article adds that a build plan now has to clear the cost of capital and the local electorate. It says the Reuters excerpt contains no market data, so its discussion of market impact is analysis rather than a report of price moves.

Articles.Title: 41 Data Center Ballot Measures [2026]: What AI Teams Face - tech-insider.org

stories.Headline: Client demand for shorter AI deals reshapes Google's cloud market battle
stories.Summary:
Clients are now asking Google's cloud arm for shorter, more flexible AI agreements instead of long-term commitments to a single provider. Karan Bajwa, president of Asia Pacific at Google Cloud, said this in an interview with Mint published on 5 November 2026. He said enterprises want room to test the latest AI tools, because the technology moves quickly. Google is responding by signing rapid, short-term deals that it hopes will later turn into longer business centred on AI. The shift is not limited to cloud providers.

India's top IT services firms, which once relied on five-year, billion-dollar contracts, are also reporting shorter deal tenures. On 15 October, LTM chief executive Venu Lambu said most of the company's deal wins in its second quarter were AI contracts of six months to one year. In July, TCS chief K. Krithivasan said AI revenue often spans only a quarter or two and lacks the recurring annual deals of older maintenance work. Mint's report places these comments alongside Google's own growth figures. Bajwa spoke for Google, and Mint reported his claims, which the article does not independently verify.

He said Google Cloud revenue doubled year on year to $30.71 billion in the July to September quarter, up from $15.16 billion, and credited demand for its AI platform. He also said Google is the only major cloud provider offering access to every AI model suite, including those from OpenAI and Anthropic. Thomas Kurian, Google Cloud's global chief to whom Bajwa reports, had earlier said enterprises are central to how the company is pushing AI adoption. Anushree Verma of Gartner was quoted saying Google's control of the AI value chain is showing up in the enterprise deals it keeps signing. The article places Google third in the global cloud market behind Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure.

Synergy Research Group, cited on 2 November, put AWS at 26% share, Microsoft Azure at 19% and Google Cloud at 16%. In 2023, Google held 11%, and Mint describes it as the fastest-growing provider in the September quarter. India is a smaller share of Google's business, and Google Cloud India reported operating revenue of ₹2,019.3 crore in FY25. Bajwa said India is strategically important and that governments are pushing for sovereign data centres, which he expects more countries to prioritise over the next five years. Google's 1-gigawatt facility under construction in Visakhapatnam is the only expansion Bajwa described, and Kurian has said the company will invest more as demand grows.

Articles.Title: Client demand for shorter AI deals reshapes Google's cloud market battle

stories.Headline: Will Labour cave to Europe on AI?
stories.Summary:
After the American midterms, Democratic lawmakers replaced Republicans on Capitol Hill, and the article says this will likely shift US policy on artificial intelligence. Congressman Frank Pallone and Senator Maria Cantwell will be the ranking members on their respective commerce committees. Down the ballot, Republicans everywhere faced attacks over data centres. The article says the blue wave signals a potential techlash after two years in which tech figures found favour with the GOP.

The article says officials are working on plans for an EU-UK digital partnership ahead of a summit on 20 November. Under the plan, the Artificial Intelligence Act, with regards to free movement of products, and the Cyber Resilience Act would be added to Annex 2 of the Windsor Framework. In parliament, Kanishka Narayan declined to answer whether the country will statically or dynamically align with the EU AI Act. Ben Spencer, his opposite number, warns this will risk both direct compliance costs and lost opportunities.

The article says Andy Burnham has so far resisted calls from sections of the left to restrict Britain's gains in this area. It says he gave the AI minister a seat in the cabinet and took time on the night of Narayan's appointment to talk through how the state can use the technology effectively. It reports that Burnham's team in No. 10 looked at public attitudes to Brexit and concluded that, ten years on, the electorate is more open to a conversation about a much closer relationship with the EU. Eurosceptics regard the moves as the opening salvos in a war to get Britain back into the EU's orbit on AI.

The article says the UK now has the third-largest market and startup ecosystem in the world, and AI office space in London increased tenfold in a year. It says that if a Democrat Congress puts the brakes on American tech growth, talent, businesses and investment could divert to Britain instead. It adds that an EU-China trade war is gearing up and Britain's hard-won AI gains are potentially on the line. The article says Labour could struggle to justify why now is the right time to start getting closer to Europe once again.

Articles.Title: Will Labour cave to Europe on AI? - The Spectator Australia

stories.Headline: Tamil Nadu’s wildlife conservation initiatives on country-made gun surrender, AI-based elephant warning system bag awards
stories.Summary:
Tamil Nadu's forest department has won national recognition for two conservation efforts, a voluntary surrender drive for illegal country-made guns and an AI-based early-warning system for elephants near railway tracks, according to a report published by The Hindu on November 5, 2026. The gun campaign, called 'Ozhippom Thuppakkiyai, Kaapom Yanaigalai' (Eradicate Illegal Country-made Guns, Save Elephants), was launched at the Hosur Forest Division in September 2022 after two elephants died from illegal gunshot injuries in the Anchetty and Jawalagiri ranges that year. A second intensive phase followed in August 2024. The campaign relied on public outreach rather than enforcement alone, and 239 illegal guns were voluntarily surrendered.

The campaign's activities included social media and newspaper publicity, pamphlets, public announcements, motorcycle awareness rallies, door-to-door visits and meetings with panchayat presidents and village elders. The department also warned that sniffer dogs would be used in remote forest villages, and that any illegal firearm found would attract action under the Arms Act and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Separately, the AI-based system in the Madukkarai range of the Coimbatore Forest Division, introduced in February 2024, has helped around 2,800 elephants cross railway tracks safely. It generated more than 6,000 alerts, which a team of 20 track patrol staff responded to, and station masters and loco pilots were informed so trains could slow down.

The awards were presented through the Indian Forest Service Association and Indian Masterminds, with the special jury award going to K. Karthikeyani, now Thanjavur District Forest Officer, who led the Hosur campaign as the then Wildlife Warden. The article reports that she received it from Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav. S. Senbagapriya was given an eco-warrior award for community-based conservation and monitoring in the Mudumalai landscape, where she oversaw village relocation programmes covering 235 families in the first phase and 216 of 255 in the second, with a third-phase proposal of 168 families sent to the National Tiger Conservation Authority, which released ₹1,680 lakh. N. Jayaraj was recognised for the AI system as District Forest Officer. The article does not say what happens to the surrender drive or the warning system next.

Articles.Title: Tamil Nadu’s wildlife conservation initiatives on country-made gun surrender, AI-based elephant warning system bag awards

stories.Headline: AI bots cause disruptions for local libraries
stories.Summary:
Libraries in the Marmot system, a nonprofit consortium of academic, public and school libraries across Colorado, have faced a surge in bot traffic that has slowed service and caused occasional outages, according to the Littleton Independent. Adam Murray, the executive director of Marmot, said the system has seen increased bot activity since September 2026. Several weeks ago the system was seeing around 6 million bot connection attempts every 24 hours, or roughly 180 million in 30 days, and that number is now up to over 2 billion attempts in 30 days. Murray said the activity can be tied to AI, with some bots used to train AI models and others being personal AI agents doing searches. The surge dates back to early 2025, when AI began to bypass security protections, and after a plateau a new surge began in September 2026.

Marmot has added protections such as using Cloudflare to verify users and monitors traffic from foreign countries where bots are often routed. Murray said bots sometimes target all of Marmot, which impacts around 40 libraries across Colorado, and sometimes go after specific libraries, in which case Marmot works with that library to tailor its network traffic. Englewood Public Library Director Rachel Fewell said the bots test the system for a working library card number and then max out checkouts and scrape content to train AI. Fewell said the biggest impact is that humans cannot get in because they cannot compete with the bots, and that the tactics change every day and every minute. Englewood has had six full outages over the past few weeks, and when the system is down librarians cannot check books back in, so returns pile up, and books must be checked out by hand.

Dennis Quinn, director of Bemis Public Library, said outages have been intermittent but disruptive because the library gets little notice when something goes down or must be taken down for repairs, though he said Marmot was timely in fixing issues. Quinn described Marmot as doing the best it can to identify vulnerabilities before they become problems and to put in authentication measures once traffic spikes, adding that this will not stop the root problem but helps keep servers up. He said Marmot, which connects Bemis to share resources with 40 other libraries, lets the library offer a higher level of service and a broader range of resources than it could alone. Fewell called Marmot a strong partner and said other large systems are dealing with the same things.

Murray said the issues are not unique to Marmot and that many institutions across the country face similar problems as corporations use bots to train AI. He said the consortium is at the whims of these companies and that regulation would be very welcomed. Murray said AI bots find cultural institutions like libraries and museums good targets because they hold the richest content, material already created by people that could train their next models, making it an industry-wide problem across the United States. Fewell said libraries, museums and universities must adapt to a new era of the internet, and she said the goal is to keep access available to everyone who needs it.

Articles.Title: AI bots cause disruptions for local libraries - Littleton Independent

stories.Headline: Concerns about Seattle using AI on 911 calls went ignored
stories.Summary:
In 2019, Ginger Armbruster, then Seattle's chief privacy officer, warned the Fire Department in a memo that using artificial intelligence on 911 medical calls could carry equity risks, and she recommended steps including a race and social justice assessment and sharing details with the public. Those recommendations were largely not followed. Since 2023, AI from the Danish company Corti has listened to all 911 medical calls in Seattle and helped dispatchers decide which callers do not need a rapid response, prompting some to be routed to a Texas-based nurse line instead of getting aid right away. Callers were not told about the system until a Seattle Times report this June. Ambulances ordered by the nurse line are exempt from the city's response-time standards, and in one case a woman sent to the nurse line before the AI prompts began waited more than 10 hours and was later found dead.

The Fire Department says human dispatchers stay in control of all calls and are trained to handle them equitably, and spokesperson Kristin Hanson said dispatchers follow protocols overseen by the department's medical director and state policies for callers with disabilities or limited English. Officials cited a 2023 Danish study showing Corti's AI detected stroke in emergency calls better than human dispatchers across age and gender, and Hanson said UW Medicine is conducting an evaluation of the AI and nurse line, though no specifics or completion date have been shared. Mayor Katie Wilson declined an interview, and her spokesperson Ansel Herz said she is highly concerned about possible disparate impacts and promised a public update in early 2027 on all city uses of AI. Armbruster and experts including Emily Bender of the University of Washington and Shobita Parthasarathy of the University of Michigan said they still have questions, noting research showing speech technology works less well for some speakers, such as people with disabilities or accents.

Bender, Parthasarathy, Armbruster and Tee Sannon of the ACLU of Washington said Seattle should suspend the live AI prompts until a thorough public evaluation or audit is completed and shared. Bender said a best practice would be to collect demographic information from consenting participants and assess how the technology works across groups, and that residents can fairly ask the department to prove the system works fine. Hanson said public scrutiny is part of how systems improve and that the department recently asked the Information Technology Department to work on retroactive privacy reviews of its Corti platform. Corti did not comment.

Articles.Title: Concerns about Seattle using AI on 911 calls went ignored - The Seattle Times

stories.Headline: Queens candidate charged in AI fraud case asks judge to move case out of borough
stories.Summary:
Jonathan David Rinaldi, a perennial Queens political candidate, appeared in court on Wednesday in the criminal case over artificial intelligence-generated campaign materials that claimed endorsements he never received. In June, on the day of the primary election, Rinaldi was arrested and charged with fraud for social media posts he made during his 2025 campaign for the City Council. He made several computer-generated posts, some using AI, to create fake news stories and graphics touting endorsements he did not actually receive. He faces three counts of forgery in the third degree and 15 counts of criminal possession of a forged instrument in the third degree, and he faces up to two years in prison if convicted.

On Wednesday, Rinaldi's attorney told a judge he intends to file a motion to send the case to a court outside of Queens. His court-appointed attorney, Andray Cleghorn, said that since Rinaldi was running for political office in Queens, the borough was not an appropriate venue for the case, and that Queens County has a conflict of interest. Cleghorn declined to comment further because Wednesday was his first day representing Rinaldi. The Queens District Attorney's office has until mid-December to file its reply to the motion, and the DA declined to comment on Rinaldi's request on Wednesday.

Speaking with the Eagle outside the courthouse, Rinaldi openly admitted to making the ads and described the DA's case against him as lawfare. He claimed the fake endorsements were satire and said satirical commentary is one of the benchmarks of our politics and is protected. He said the case was a coordinated effort to stop him from running for office, adding that the punishment is the process and that they are trying to get him to not run. Rinaldi previously denied making the posts, telling the Eagle in 2025 that he was hacked and later claiming it was the work of his then-opponent, Councilmember Lynn Schulman, and when asked about those previous claims he responded, who cares, it literally doesn't matter.

Rinaldi's court appearance Wednesday came just hours after he received over 1,600 votes on a third-party line in the race for the 28th Assembly District. He previously lost the Democratic primary to longtime incumbent Assemblymember Andrew Hevesi, who won reelection to the seat this week. Rinaldi continued to post AI-generated ads during this year's campaign, including an AI deepfake of Hevesi. During his 2025 bid for the City Council as a Republican, Rinaldi created news articles and graphics claiming endorsements from Andrew Cuomo and then-Councilmember Bob Holden, and he made AI ads and videos claiming that Schulman endorsed Zohran Mamdani for mayor, which she had not done. Queens DA Melinda Katz said the case is the first-of-its-kind regarding the use of AI in political campaigns, and said in a June statement that enough is enough and that in today's world it is important to hold people accountable for materially misrepresenting facts.

Articles.Title: Queens candidate charged in AI fraud case asks judge to move case out of borough - Queens Daily Eagle

stories.Headline: ‘There Is No Plan’: Could Cheyenne Become A Tech Ghost Town If AI Bubble Bursts?
stories.Summary:
Tech giants are pouring billions of dollars into data centers in Cheyenne, Wyoming, as Wall Street’s biggest money managers disagree about whether the artificial intelligence boom is a bubble about to burst. An AI bubble happens when companies and investors spend money on a technology faster than it can earn that money back. A bubble bursts when investors lose faith that the payoff is coming, so they sell, stock prices drop and money for new construction gets much harder to find. If that happens, projects can be delayed, scaled back or abandoned partway through, leaving communities with huge half-built data centers, stalled construction jobs and power plans designed around them.

A 2.7-gigawatt Google data center campus is planned south of Cheyenne, and Meta, the company behind Facebook and Instagram, has a campus of more than $800 million under construction there since 2024. Betsey Hale, CEO of the economic development group Cheyenne LEADS, said she does not think Cheyenne will see a bust. She said not all of the city’s data centers, if any, are actually AI-purposed, and that the majority are part of the cloud, which is very different from artificial intelligence. She said cloud computing supports everyday technology that could continue even if investment in AI slows, and that demand, if anything, is only going to go up.

Cheyenne City Council member Larry Wolfe said there is no plan in place if the market turns. He recalled the late 1990s, when companies buried fiber-optic cables across the country expecting endless growth in internet traffic, and the dot-com crash in the early 2000s left many of those lines dormant for years. He said the impact of a data center bust would dwarf that, because today’s boom involves billions of dollars in borrowed money, massive physical campuses and extensive power grid overhauls. He said only one or two council members have been calling for decommissioning rules, so the city knows what happens when the buildings become obsolete and companies abandon them.

Fellow council member Pete Laybourn said the city’s leadership is focused almost entirely on managing the incoming wave of development rather than planning for a potential crash. He said his gut feeling is that every boom has a bust, and the city will have to try to manage that just as it is trying to manage the boom. David Bullard, senior economist with the Wyoming Department of Workforce Services, said the vast majority of labor tied to data centers right now is in early-stage construction, and much of that workforce travels in from out of state. He said relying on temporary workers is nothing new, since Wyoming’s energy and industrial booms have long pulled in outside labor to fill short-term gaps.

Articles.Title: ‘There Is No Plan’: Could Cheyenne Become A Tech Ghost Town If AI Bubble Bursts? - Cowboy State Daily

stories.Headline: How AI is perfecting the art of government obfuscation
stories.Summary:
Opinion columnist Sobhana K. Nair writes in The Hindu, published November 6, 2026, that government press notes are becoming increasingly vague and full of buzzwords. She notes that nearly every press note invokes the "Viksit Bharat 2047" vision, with phrases such as "digitally empowered society" and "knowledge economy" appearing alongside stock governance terms like "holistic," "convergence," and "citizen-centric." Nair says she turned to the Yes Minister and Yes Prime Minister novels after frustrating encounters with these releases. She describes the approach as one of evasion, in which such notes promote the government's achievements while keeping shortcomings out of view.

The column draws on a passage from the editor's note to the first volume, which blames the fictional politician James Hacker's training for his habit of using far more words than needed to blur issues so they become hard to understand. Nair argues this description fits many government press notes, which she says use evasive language to serve two aims at once: celebrating successes and hiding failures. She calls this an age-old tactic that many governments have used. Her central claim is that artificial intelligence now makes this obfuscation more powerful, though the article itself gives only a brief indication of how.

The author is Nair, the writer of this opinion piece, and the article presents her own views on the language used in official communications. The Hindu's page carries only the text of the column and related site navigation, with no statement from any government body responding to her criticism. The article does not describe any specific press note, ministry, or AI tool by name, nor does it report any official reaction. It also offers no detail on how AI is being used to produce these releases, leaving that question open for further reporting.

Articles.Title: How AI is perfecting the art of government obfuscation

stories.Headline: Artificial Analysis says Inkling 2 Small matches Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) in its index and would be the top open model outside China once its weights are out (Artificial Analysis)
stories.Summary:
Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Small, which Artificial Analysis reported on November 5, 2026. The model scores 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching Google DeepMind's Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) and surpassing Xiaomi's MiMo-V2.6-Pro. It launches as a proprietary model available first through Thinking Machines' Tinker platform and Tinker Playground, and the company plans to release its weights later, at a date not yet confirmed. Artificial Analysis said that once those weights are public, the model would be the highest-scoring open weights model developed outside China based on current rankings.

The model is a reasoning model with 594B total parameters and 17B active parameters, accepting text and image input and producing text output. It is priced at $0.30 per million input tokens, $1.00 per million output tokens and $0.03 per million cached input tokens. Its score is up 18 points from Inkling Small, and it averages about 150K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, roughly four times Inkling Small's 37K. Each task costs $1.18 on average, almost six times Inkling Small's $0.20, though still below Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) at $7.77 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (medium) at $10.02. Artificial Analysis said the gains are largest on agentic work, with AutomationBench-AA rising from 5% to 46% and FrontierCode 2.0 from 5% to 25%.

The results come from Artificial Analysis's own evaluations, and the firm congratulated the Thinking Machines team on the release. Its findings show mixed strengths: Inkling 2 Small beats Claude Sonnet 5.5 (medium) on FrontierCode 2.0 but trails it on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and it trails Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) on the CritPt v2 physics benchmark. On AA-Omniscience v1.1, the model's hallucination rate fell from 61% to 27%, but Artificial Analysis attributed this mainly to the model answering fewer questions, since accuracy rose only slightly, from 32% to 34%. The articles give no release date for the weights and do not say whether the company has responded to the rankings.

Articles.Title: Artificial Analysis says Inkling 2 Small matches Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) in its index and would be the top open model outside China once its weights are out (Artificial Analysis)

stories.Headline: OPINION: New AI policy guidelines warrant need for updated school policy
stories.Summary:
The New York City Department of Education recently issued new guidelines on artificial intelligence for teachers, according to an opinion article in The Classic, the student newspaper at Townsend Harris High School. The article, published on November 4, 2026 and written by Opinion Editor Anya Basnayake, says the guidelines permit teachers to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks. They also specify that AI should not be used for grading. The article notes that Townsend Harris has policies governing student use of AI but none for teachers.

The article says the new guidelines, together with the addition of Google Gemini to Google Classroom, suggest teachers are being encouraged to use AI more. It calls for the school to release its own rules stating how the DOE guidance will be applied at Townsend Harris, especially on how and when teachers may use AI. It points out that the DOE guide marks when to stop, proceed with caution, or use AI, but there is no clear way to hold teachers accountable. It adds that students are expected to cite their AI use and argues teachers should do the same.

The article cites a recent survey reporting that 80% of teachers do not think it is necessary to disclose AI use in lesson plans, often comparing AI models to calculators or textbooks. Basnayake argues AI is different because it draws on all textbooks, including outdated ones, and because lesson planning can be subjective. She says students should be informed when AI is used to create an entire lesson or assignment, and that a schoolwide document should spell out when disclosure is required. She compares this to the school's grading policy, which exists schoolwide and by department.

The article says vague language on AI-generated lesson plans could cause problems for the school community, asking whether an entire lesson, unit, or project can be generated by AI. It says AI is useful for brainstorming but cannot generate anything new, so relying on it could reinforce old teaching methods and reduce creativity. It acknowledges some believe teachers can decide for themselves when to use AI, but says there is little common agreement on the tool, and a document of dos and don'ts could close that gap. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: OPINION: New AI policy guidelines warrant need for updated school policy - thhsclassic.com

stories.Headline: Democratic midterm wins set stage for tougher tech and AI scrutiny
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate in the midterm elections held Tuesday, 3 Nov. 2026, according to the IAPP. Votes were still being counted in a number of races when the article was published on 4 Nov. 2026. The article says the victories were broad and deep, and Democrats also flipped governor and attorney general seats and several state legislative chambers. The wins end what the article calls a brief era of tech deregulation and point toward more oversight of AI and digital technology.

When the new Congress takes office in 2027, Democratic committee leaders will gain subpoena power, the ability to set hearing agendas, markup authority and control of oversight. Possible priorities include AI governance and accountability, federal privacy legislation, children's online safety, platform regulation and FTC oversight, along with surveillance and law enforcement access to data. Rep. Frank Pallone, D-N.J., is in line to lead the House Energy and Commerce Committee and said he aims to help lead a "bold agenda" to "rein in Big Tech." Omer Tene of Goodwin and the IAPP said to expect intense scrutiny of the FTC, including what it chooses not to do. The article also notes Democrats will still need to work with President Donald Trump or hold a veto-proof majority to pass legislation.

Tene said the "blue wave" that swept the states will ripple through Washington, with renewed momentum for AI regulation focused on safety and automated decision-making, drawing on models from California, Colorado, Illinois and New York. David Stauss of Stauss said Democrats flipped governor and attorney general positions and several state legislative chambers, so privacy and AI legislation that had stalled could get a fresh look. He said AI regulation has become a bipartisan issue, though laws in Democratic-controlled states were more far-reaching. The article says the progressive wing, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, D-Vt., and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, want to curb "super intelligence" and place a moratorium on new data centers, while moderate Rep. Scott Peters, D-Calif., told Politico the AI discussion is "pretty populist" and "devoid of fact."

The article says several major Washington law firms have started hiring lawyers to help clients manage new congressional scrutiny. It also points to Colorado's 8th District, where Manny Rutinel, a primary author of the Colorado AI Act, defeated Gabe Evans, who was on the Energy and Commerce Committee. In Texas, it is not clear how newly elected Democratic attorney general Nathan Johnson will pursue privacy settlements reached under Ken Paxton. Tene said he does not see the results significantly changing corporate behavior in the short term, because companies' approach is driven mainly by economic forces and the AI boom. He said a market correction could prompt companies to pause and recalibrate the balance between innovation and governance.

Articles.Title: Democratic midterm wins set stage for tougher tech and AI scrutiny - IAPP

stories.Headline: Google Gemini Copyright Warning: Case C-250/25 [2026] - tech-insider.org
stories.Summary:
On 3 November 2026, Advocate General Maciej Szpunar of the Court of Justice of the European Union gave an opinion in Case C-250/25, known as Like Company. He concluded that an AI chatbot can infringe a press publisher's rights when it retrieves an article from the publisher's website, reuses it to generate an answer and gives that answer to a user. The case involves Google's Gemini chatbot, a Hungarian publisher called Like Company as the claimant and Google's Irish arm as the defendant. A Hungarian court referred the questions to the EU court in Luxembourg, which will apply whatever the court eventually decides to the facts of the dispute.

The opinion sets out two conditions under which liability may arise. The first is unlawful access, for example when a chatbot gets past effective technical measures such as a paywall or anti-scraping controls. The second is when the answer reuses the article's recognisable form of expression so heavily that the user no longer needs to visit the original. Szpunar said the press publisher's right protects only the specific form of expression, not the mere facts reported. He also said that using protected works to train a large language model is, as a rule, freely permitted under the text-and-data-mining exception, and that nothing showed Like Company's articles trained Gemini.

The opinion is not binding, and it does not say Google lost. No fine, damages figure or order against Google appears in the reporting, and the court has not ruled that Gemini infringed anything. The adviser left the factual assessment to the Hungarian court after the EU court answers the legal questions. Google can argue that Gemini answers rarely reproduce enough expression to replace a visit to the source, and that argument gets easier if Gemini links prominently to the originals and summarises in fresh wording.

The reasoning applies to any chatbot that retrieves a press publication and reuses it, not just Gemini. Publishers are expected to pair the opinion with technical controls, since the unlawful-access condition depends on a real paywall or anti-scraping measure being in place. An adverse judgment could push Google toward licensing deals or stricter handling of paywalled pages. The EU court has not yet decided the case.

Articles.Title: Google Gemini Copyright Warning: Case C-250/25 [2026] - tech-insider.org

stories.Headline: All the news, none of the clicks: can AI chatbots bypass publishers?
stories.Summary:
On 3 November 2026, Advocate General Szpunar of the Court of Justice of the European Union delivered an Opinion on when AI chatbots' use of online news may infringe press publishers' rights. The case, Like Company v. Google Ireland Limited (C-250/25), concerns Gemini's use of articles published by a Hungarian news business. It is the first generative AI case before the Court. The Opinion examines press publishers' related rights under Article 15 of the Digital Single Market Directive, not a claim based on authors' copyright.

The judges have not yet decided the case. The Opinion separates training a model from retrieving an article to answer a user's question. It says the evidence does not sufficiently establish that Like Company's articles were part of the model's training data, so the Court need not decide that issue here. It also distinguishes a factual synthesis of a source from a recognisable reproduction that replaces the original expression. Facts themselves are not protected, and individual words and very short extracts are excluded.

Paraphrasing is not enough if the original expression survives, but lost traffic alone is not enough to amount to infringement. On responsibility, the Advocate General does not propose automatic provider liability whenever a user prompts an infringing answer. Pointing to the user is not enough if the service's business model facilitates reproduction or reasonably expected safeguards are missing. He doubts that the facts of the case amount to infringement, since effective access restrictions and recognisable expression appear absent, the acts do not appear inherent in Google's business model, and Google seems to have adopted appropriate safeguards.

For publishers, he suggests recording what a chatbot accessed and what it returned, with evidence of access and a sample of similar answers shifting the burden to the provider. The legal framework remains far from settled, despite studies and guidelines from various public bodies and institutions. The Court typically follows an Advocate General's Opinion, but there is no guarantee it will do so in this case. The last word on the relationship between copyright, related rights and AI has yet to be written.

Articles.Title: All the news, none of the clicks: can AI chatbots bypass publishers? - Stibbe

stories.Headline: WhatsApp’s AI-powered photo expansion tool starts rolling out on iOS
stories.Summary:
WhatsApp has begun letting some users on iPhone expand photos with an AI tool, according to a report published on November 5, 2026. The feature sits inside the app's photo editor and lets a user extend an image beyond its original borders. It is currently limited to select users, mainly those in WhatsApp's beta program through TestFlight, though some people on the public iOS version already have access. The tool works like the Extend feature that Apple Intelligence offers on iPhone, and similar functions exist in ChatGPT and Photoshop.

Users who open a photo in a chat see the drawing editor, where they can pick an AI effect and then choose an option to expand the image. Meta AI takes a few seconds to analyze the photo and generate the wider version, which the editor then displays for the user to send. The option also works for status updates. If a user does not like the result, an undo button restores the original, and the tool can be run again to produce a different version. The report from WABetaInfo describes this flow, and the tool is powered by Meta AI.

The reporting outlet is 9to5Mac, and the details come from WABetaInfo, which tracks WhatsApp's beta releases. The article does not say when the feature will be widely available, since beta features on WhatsApp typically have no fixed release date. It notes that because the tool has already reached Android beta users and some public iOS users, a broader launch may not be far off. The article also points readers to the full WABetaInfo report for further detail.

Articles.Title: WhatsApp’s AI-powered photo expansion tool starts rolling out on iOS

stories.Headline: Trump's "Use SI, Not AI" Pressure One Month In: 91% of S&P 500 Companies Still Stick With "AI"
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump began pressuring companies in late September to use the term "Super Intelligence (SI)" instead of "AI," arguing in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly that AI makes the technology seem fake. Days later he signed an executive order changing the AI designation in government documents, and last month he warned that those who do not use SI would be regarded as "enemies" of the White House. Elon Musk renamed SpaceX's AI business unit SpaceXSI and had Tesla specify SI in a securities filing, while Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said the company would rebrand its AIForce platform as SIForce. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he would keep the company's name, and Anthropic used AI throughout its 335-page IPO filing.

An analysis of 206 S&P 500 companies that used the relevant terms in earnings releases, securities filings and press releases between September 29 and November 2 found that 188, or 91.3%, used AI in at least 90% of references. Eleven companies mixed the two terms, and only seven, or 3.4%, used SI in at least 90% of references. Of 119 companies that mentioned the technology in just the past week, only five used the term superintelligence. Spelling was inconsistent, with some writing it as one word and others as two, and capitalization varied.

Microsoft president Brad Smith caught himself mid-sentence during a podcast last month, saying "AI safety, no, SI safety," and Microsoft said it uses multiple terms in parallel. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang mentioned "the future of superintelligence" on X the day after signing a technology safety pledge at the White House, but weeks later at a Berlin conference he said "every company in Europe will be an AI company." Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of the nonprofit Alliance for Safe AI, said companies are trying to keep their existing terminology while avoiding an outright confrontation with the White House, and his organization said it would not change its name. Even First Lady Melania Trump's Facebook account recently promoted a student computing competition and used the term AI as is.

Superintelligence originally refers to a hypothetical AI with cognitive abilities surpassing the most brilliant humans, and Trump is seeking to use this specialized concept as a general label encompassing all of AI. The issue is not one that will rattle near-term financial statements, but it poses a judgment burden for tech companies facing U.S. government procurement and regulatory compliance. If SI designations are required in government documents and contracts, companies may have to run dual product-name and description systems, while AI remains the standard in consumer-facing channels and investor communications. Given that a terminology change could affect brand value, search visibility and even regulatory interpretation, Silicon Valley's word choices are expected to continue for the time being.

Articles.Title: Trump's "Use SI, Not AI" Pressure One Month In: 91% of S&P 500 Companies Still Stick With "AI" - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Midterms deliver clear message: 'The AI reckoning is here'
stories.Summary:
Voters in the 2026 midterm elections made their concern about artificial intelligence clear, according to a Mashable report published on November 4, 2026. On the day of the vote, Google reportedly refused to let schools that bar AI use turn off AI search in its classroom products. Exit polling showed strong concern over AI and data centers, with NBC News finding that 65 percent of Democrats and 39 percent of Republicans called the two topics a crucial or major factor in their Congressional ballot. Voters approved more than 40 measures to slow or ban data center growth. Candidates calling for AI regulation, including Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and South Carolina senator-elect Dr. Annie Andrews, defeated Republican rivals who backed AI.

Experts quoted in the article read the results as a rebuke of Republican pro-AI policies and of Silicon Valley executives who aligned with President Donald Trump or donated hundreds of millions of dollars to the GOP. Michael Kleinman, head of US policy for the Future of Life Institute, said voters want strong and effective guardrails and are demanding accountability. The backlash had been building since May 2025, when the One Big Beautiful Bill Act included language that would have barred states from regulating AI. That measure was dropped, but in December 2025 Trump signed an executive order that would punish states with "onerous" AI laws by withholding certain federal funds.

Communities near data centers also raised concerns about public health, electricity prices, and pollution. Lawsuits alleging harm from AI chatbots added to the pressure, and New York governor Kathy Hochul signed what some advocates consider the strongest AI chatbot law in the country about a week before the election. Parent and education activists have also pushed to remove Big Tech and AI tools from classrooms. Josh Golin, executive director of the advocacy group Fairplay, said schools should turn off AI and teach students about the company's surveillance and advertising business.

New York Mayor Zohan Mamdani accused Google of using its monopoly power to force public schools to use its AI products, saying no corporation should dictate how children are taught. Alvaro Bedoya, a former Federal Trade Commission commissioner, suggested subpoenas for Google and for health insurers that use AI to deny claims. Several Democratic governor-elects, including Amy Acton in Ohio, Gina Hinojosa in Texas, and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, had backed data center moratoriums or greater accountability for developers. Virginia Senator Mark Warner said AI and data center policy is too important to be left to Trump and a few tech executives.

Articles.Title: Midterms deliver clear message: 'The AI reckoning is here' - Mashable SEA

stories.Headline: Trump Pushes Tech to Say SI Instead of AI, Leaving Big Tech Scrambling
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump is pressuring companies to stop calling artificial intelligence AI and use SI, short for super intelligence, instead. The Wall Street Journal reported on November 4 that Trump argued at the U.N. General Assembly in late September that the term AI makes the technology sound fake. Days later, he signed an executive order changing AI terminology in government documents. Last month, he also warned that people who refuse to use SI would be treated as enemies of the White House.

Some companies have changed names to match the White House. Elon Musk announced that SpaceX would rename its AI division SpaceXSI, and Tesla said in a securities filing that SI refers to its existing AI technologies and activities. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said the company would rename its AIForce platform SIForce. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the company would keep its name because brands do not change easily. Microsoft President Brad Smith referred on a podcast to AI safety, or rather, SI safety, and Microsoft said it uses several terms for the technology.

Corporate documents still overwhelmingly favor AI. Among S&P 500 companies that used related terms in earnings releases, securities filings and press releases from September 29 to November 2, 188 of 206 used AI more than 90% of the time. Eleven companies used both terms, while seven used SI more than 90% of the time. Even in the most recent week, only five of 119 companies that referred to the technology used super intelligence.

Super intelligence already has a distinct technical meaning, referring to hypothetical AI with cognitive abilities that exceed those of the most capable humans. Trump is trying to use the term as a label for the whole field, which leaves companies trying to satisfy the president while describing the technology accurately and protecting their brands. Brendan Steinhauser, chief executive of the nonprofit Alliance for Safe AI, said companies are trying to avoid appearing to oppose the White House while keeping the existing terminology. The group also said it would not change its name. Mixed usage continues even around the White House, where first lady Melania Trump’s Facebook account recently used AI in a post introducing a student computing competition.

Articles.Title: Trump Pushes Tech to Say SI Instead of AI, Leaving Big Tech Scrambling - bloomingbit

stories.Headline: Will Democrats stop Trump's 'flourishing' AI and data centre policies?
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, according to The National. The result ends a period in which President Donald Trump's administration promoted AI development with limited regulation. Trump had promised to support AI rooted in free speech and human flourishing, and he often claimed his actions drew trillions of dollars in investment from global tech companies. The Democrats will take control of key congressional committees overseeing technology, cyber security and commerce in January.

Trump keeps veto power, so sweeping regulatory legislation is unlikely, and analysts expect political gridlock rather than immediate reversals. Michael Strobaek of Lombard Odier said Democrats may push to scale back tax incentives, shift more grid costs onto developers and introduce early safety regulations. Charu Chanana of Saxo Bank said the more likely outcome is two years of political confrontation, greater congressional oversight and legislative gridlock. Mark MacCarthy of Georgetown University said a stalled Senate bill with mandatory ratepayer protection for new data centres could be reintroduced as a free-standing bill and serve as a starting point for action.

Timothy Kneeland, a political scientist at Nazareth University, said the days of wine and roses for AI and data centres without regulation are over. Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, posted that people should always be in control of the future and should not cede control to superintelligence. Elon Musk joked that data centres in space look appealing now, and he later joked that his election-interfering space lasers did not work this time. Lisa Su, chief executive of AMD, told CNBC that the election results do not change her outlook on AI and that demand for more compute is intense worldwide.

Analysts warned before the elections that AI-linked shares could be the most exposed to risk if Democrats won. Manjeet Markanda of Lunaro Markets said investors now see tougher scrutiny of Big Tech and data centres as more likely. David Meier of Julius Baer said greater regulatory scrutiny of AI would weigh on capital expenditures and related inflows, an important source of US dollar support this year. Nvidia's Jensen Huang has not made any statement on the shift in power.

Articles.Title: Will Democrats stop Trump's 'flourishing' AI and data centre policies? - The National

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence and intellectual property rights: the situation in Thailand - International Bar Association | IBA
stories.Summary:
Thailand has no AI-specific intellectual property laws, according to an article published on 3 November 2026 by the International Bar Association. The piece was written by Suebsiri Taweepon of the law firm Tilleke & Gibbins in Bangkok. It says the country's existing IP framework predates modern AI and gives limited guidance on AI-generated works, AI training practices and AI-generated inventions. The article reviews the current legal framework, the key IP issues arising from AI and practical considerations and future developments.

The article states that existing legal principles generally apply to AI-related activities, but there is limited guidance on AI model training, no text and data-mining exceptions and little judicial precedent. It notes that Thailand's Civil Court issued a regulation, effective since 17 November 2025, on the use of AI in preparing pleadings and other documents submitted to the court. The rule requires parties and their counsel to disclose any AI-generated content submitted to the Civil Court and to verify and certify its accuracy. The article adds that the Civil Court's rule is consistent with guidance issued by the President of the Supreme Court in September 2025, and that the Central IP and International Trade Court, where IP cases must be filed, has not announced similar rules as of the date of the article.

On copyright, the article says Thai law is founded on human authorship and does not expressly address works generated autonomously by AI systems. It notes that the US Copyright Office has confirmed that copyright protection generally requires human authorship, while acknowledging that AI-assisted works may qualify where sufficient human creative contribution exists. It points to Section 9 of the Thai Copyright Act B.E. 2537 (1994), under which the default rule is that an employee owns the copyright in a work created in the course of employment unless the parties have agreed otherwise in writing. The article also says that, unlike Singapore and Japan, Thailand does not provide a broad text- and data-mining exception permitting the use of copyrighted works for AI training.

The article says the Patent Act B.E. 2522 (1979) provides no clear mechanism for recognising an AI system as an inventor, and that mathematical methods and abstract ideas are generally not patentable. It notes that Thailand's Trade Secrets Act B.E. 2545 (2002) provides the statutory framework for trade secret protection, and that the Personal Data Protection Act B.E. 256 is also relevant to AI datasets containing personal data. It advises businesses to rely on contractual arrangements to allocate ownership, liability and risk, and to consider legal protections early in the AI adoption process rather than waiting for regulatory certainty. It adds that the IP&IT Court is likely to issue similar rules on AI use, but no such announcement has been made.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence and intellectual property rights: the situation in Thailand - International Bar Association | IBA

stories.Headline: Changan Auto Deploys First Vision AI Adhesive Application Robot, Boosting Line Efficiency by 8%
stories.Summary:
Changan Automobile has commissioned its first vision AI gluing robot for painting at its Liangjiang Plant, according to the company's announcement reported by Gasgoo on November 6, 2026. The robot uses AI visual recognition to pinpoint application locations and optimize its movement paths, which the company says improves both production efficiency and quality control in the coating process. The launch addresses the PVC undercoat gluing step, where the work is complicated by wide differences between vehicle models, tight working spaces and complex application paths. Traditional robots have struggled with nozzle calibration, angle adjustment and trajectory fine-tuning in this setting. Changan built an AI visual inspection system powered by deep Convolutional Neural Networks to handle these problems.

After hundreds of alignment tests, trajectory debugs and sealant validations, the system adjusts the robot's coordinates, nozzle posture and travel paths to suit the undercoat gluing needs of different models. Changan says the technology eased bottlenecks in the PVC process and raised the line's hourly output, measured as JPH, by roughly 8 percent. The AI vision system monitors the gluing state in real time with millisecond-level response times. Risk detection and reporting accuracy now exceed 99.5 percent, which the company describes as a shift from post-production inspection to active process monitoring. The article presents these figures as Changan's own claims.

Changan is the company responsible for the deployment, and the report relays its announcement without independent verification. The article does not name individual executives or quote them directly. It places the robot within a broader pattern at the Liangjiang Plant, where the company had already installed visual inspection systems for stamping and welding operations. According to the report, the painting gluing robot extends the use of AI vision across automotive manufacturing execution and quality assurance. The article does not describe plans for rolling the technology out to other plants or models.

stories.Headline: Asian markets follow US rout as AI investment jitters spread
stories.Summary:
Stock markets in Asia fell sharply on Friday, following a tech-led sell-off in the United States. Investors reacted to expectations that newly elected Democratic officials could slow an artificial intelligence investment boom that has pushed global stocks to record highs. South Korea's Kospi index dropped more than 8% after opening, which triggered a trading halt on that exchange. Japan's Nikkei 225 fell about 6%, and Taiwan's Taiex index declined about 8% in morning trading.

Asian technology companies have benefited from strong demand for components such as semiconductors, which are needed to build large AI data centers. US firms including Meta, Amazon and Google have spent heavily on new data centers to power AI, and a Columbia Business School study estimates that AI-related infrastructure investment was driving nearly all observed US GDP growth by the end of last year. Backlash over the environmental and community effects of new data centers, however, made AI spending a key issue in the US midterm elections. Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate and flipped several other contested state seats. That result has raised concern that Democratic lawmakers could block or slow new AI infrastructure spending, which would weaken a major driver of growth in both the US and Asia.

The article does not name a specific official or company responsible for the sell-off, and it attributes the market reaction to investor anticipation rather than to any enacted policy. Reporting frames the move as a response to what investors expect the new political makeup to mean for AI spending. The article describes the volatility as part of a year of sharp swings in some Asian markets, particularly the Kospi, as investors have questioned whether the AI boom is sustainable and whether such heavy investment will prove profitable. It does not say what steps, if any, the new officials will take, and it offers no outlook beyond the immediate market moves.
