stories.Headline: Connecticut’s AI Rules Take Shape: What Employers and Developers Need to Know
stories.Summary:
Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont signed SB 5, Public Act No. 26-15, on May 27, 2026. The law sets new obligations for employers that use AI in employment decisions and for the developers who build those tools. It covers automated employment-related decision technology, known as AEDT, which processes personal data and produces an output that is a substantial factor in an employment-related decision. The law also covers developers that build or substantially modify such tools for use in employment decisions.

The employer disclosure and notice duties begin October 1, 2027. Employers must tell employees and applicants in plain language when they are interacting with an AEDT, unless that is obvious to a reasonable person. Before using an AEDT in a decision, employers must give written notice of the tool's purpose, its trade name, the personal data it will analyze, the data's sources and the employer's contact information. Developers must give employers the information needed to meet these duties, and the parties may allocate obligations by binding contract. The use of an AEDT is not a defense to a discrimination claim under an amendment effective October 1, 2026, and employers serving federal WARN Act notices on the Connecticut Department of Labor must disclose whether layoffs relate to AI or another technological change.

The requirements are enforceable solely by the Connecticut attorney general under the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act, with no private right of action. For violations through December 31, 2027, the attorney general may give notice and a 60-day cure period if the violation is curable. Frontier developers may not retaliate against employees for protected whistleblowing, and large frontier developers with more than $500 million in annual gross revenues must set up an anonymous internal reporting process by January 1, 2027. The commissioner of economic and community development must develop a plan for an AI regulatory sandbox effective July 1, 2027, with legislative recommendations due by January 1, 2028.

The law adds Connecticut to a growing list of jurisdictions regulating AI in employment, with requirements that overlap with but differ from those in California, Colorado, Illinois and New York City. The article advises employers to inventory their AI tools, review vendor contracts, prepare disclosure and notice templates, and review anti-bias testing. It also advises updating WARN notice procedures and training internal teams. The article says it will continue to monitor developments in this area.

Articles.Title: Connecticut’s AI Rules Take Shape: What Employers and Developers Need to Know - JD Supra

stories.Headline: Jim Cramer says the AI trade is not going away as Nasdaq enters correction
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, stocks fell sharply as investors moved out of technology shares and into more defensive sectors. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 4.2%, entering correction territory after falling more than 10% from its record high last month. The S&P 500 lost 2.9% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 2.2%, giving back more than half of Wednesday's gains. Healthcare, consumer staples and utilities held up relatively better during the selloff.

The tech decline was driven by concerns that financing challenges and increased political scrutiny could slow the large buildout of AI data centers. Meta executive Dina Powell McCormick warned at a Wall Street Journal conference that building new data centers is going to be harder. Jim Cramer, host of the CNBC Investing Club, agreed that construction will likely slow but said the trade is certainly not going away. The pressure reached semiconductor and cybersecurity stocks, and even strong earnings from AMD and Qnity offered little protection.

Cramer said the weakness reinforced the Club's decision to exit Broadcom, Corning and Arm to reduce its AI exposure, while keeping positions in Micron and Qnity to preserve exposure to the theme's long-term growth. Elsewhere, Cardinal Health rose 5% after strong fiscal first-quarter results and a raised full-year outlook, and Cramer said the Club trimmed its position after the sharp rally. Kimberly-Clark also reported better-than-feared results and reaffirmed its full-year outlook despite continued sales pressure in China. Cramer warned Wednesday that Wall Street's post-election enthusiasm could prove short-lived, and the articles do not say what comes next for the market.

stories.Headline: Nasdaq sees worst day in 18 months as investors bet on AI slowdown after Democrats’ election triumph
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq composite index fell 5.5% on Thursday, its worst day in 18 months, as investors sold off technology and chip stocks. The index tumbled into what the article calls "correction territory," more than 10% below its recent record high, and more than $2tn was wiped from its value by the close of trading. It was the index's biggest one-day fall since Donald Trump announced his "liberation day" tariffs in April 2025. The losses spread to other markets worldwide, with Japan's Nikkei 225 sinking 6% and South Korea's Kospi falling more than 8% in early trading on Friday.

The sell-off was driven by worries about the artificial intelligence industry facing tougher rules after the midterm election results. Investors expect Democratic governors, who won a series of gubernatorial races, to restrict the rollout of new datacentres, and US voters also rejected datacentres in several local ballots. Chip stocks led the decline: memory maker SanDisk fell by about 19 to 22 percent, depending on the figure cited, and hard drive maker Western Digital dropped roughly 16.5 to 17 percent. Nvidia, the chipmaker at the heart of the AI boom, was the biggest faller on the Dow Jones industrial average, down 9.2%. The Dow closed more than 1,800 points lower, down 3.4% at 51,868, while the S&P 500 fell 4.3%.

Analysts placed the blame on the election outcome. Saxo UK investor strategist Neil Wilson described a "complete capitulation-level event" in tech stocks, saying the fear was a total momentum unwind as Democrats move to slow the datacentre buildout, though he thought the sell-off looked overdone. Tech analyst Dan Ives warned that Democrats taking control, especially of the Senate, would create major hurdles for AI and tech legislation over the next two years. Ted Parkhill of Incline Investment Management said the market was moving from the promise of AI to the price of AI, and that more turmoil should be expected. The article also notes that the drop reversed Wednesday's rally, when Wall Street had its biggest daily gain in months, and that Trump had boasted about record highs on Truth Social that same day.

Articles.Title: Nasdaq sees worst day in 18 months as investors bet on AI slowdown after Democrats’ election triumph

stories.Headline: AI meltdown: Nvidia and Qualcomm drop more than 9%, pushing Nasdaq to worst day since April 2025
stories.Summary:
Chipmakers and other companies tied to the artificial intelligence buildout sold off sharply on Thursday, with Nvidia and Qualcomm each falling more than 9%. The Nasdaq dropped 5.5%, its worst day since April 2025. Advanced Micro Devices, Micron and Applied Materials all lost double-digit percentages, and neoclouds such as CoreWeave fell for a second straight day. The selloff followed the midterm election results, which raised fears on Wall Street that the AI infrastructure build will slow.

Nvidia alone lost almost $450 billion in market value. Qualcomm added to the decline after issuing a disappointing earnings forecast for the current quarter. The article describes a worsening climate for firms closely linked to AI infrastructure, driven by rising interest rates, heavy capital needs and the Democratic sweep in Congress. Investors fear that much of the market could be weighed down by too much debt and too little revenue.

Several states with the most ambitious AI data center plans voted Democratic on Tuesday, including Texas, Ohio and Georgia. Of 41 local ballot measures in 10 states that would restrict data center construction, voters sided against data centers in every case except one in Harwood, North Dakota. At the Wall Street Journal Tech conference, Meta President Dina Powell McCormick said building data centers would be harder after the elections. Elon Musk's public companies, SpaceX and Tesla, each fell more than 9%.

Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners, said the technology will keep developing, but a slowdown in buildings and infrastructure is what stocks are trading on. Qualcomm's CEO, Cristiano Amon, said demand was not the problem, since supply was constrained. Analysts pointed to a global memory shortage raising prices and making key supplies harder to get. Richard Clode of Janus Henderson said the knee-jerk reaction could cause delays, and that answers would not come soon.

Articles.Title: AI meltdown: Nvidia and Qualcomm drop more than 9%, pushing Nasdaq to worst day since April 2025

stories.Headline: Asia's Tech Giants Are Getting Crushed in the AI Trade Rout
stories.Summary:
Asia's technology stocks fell sharply on Friday, November 6, 2026, as a steep sell-off in the AI trade spread across the region. South Korea's benchmark Kospi index dropped 9% in early trading, which triggered a trading halt, while Japan's Nikkei 225 sank 7%. Memory chip makers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix were among the hardest hit, with Samsung falling as much as 11% and SK Hynix losing nearly 14%. Other losers included Japan's Kioxia, down 15%, Advantest, down about 16%, and SoftBank Group, down 15%, while Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company fell as much as 10%.

The decline followed a rough session on Wall Street on Thursday, when the Nasdaq 100 entered an official correction. The article ties the selling to the US midterm elections, in which Democrats won, and says investors fear the result could lead to tighter rules for data centers and AI development. Such rules could slow the spending boom that has driven the stock market rally and helped propel US economic growth. Asia is especially exposed because South Korea, Taiwan and Japan supply many of the chips, memory and equipment that power the technology, and the region had enjoyed a year of large stock gains fueled by enthusiasm for AI.

Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said in a note on Friday that the sharp correction partly reflects a reassessment of future US infrastructure demand, and also reflects how heavily investors had bet on the same AI beneficiaries. She described the move as a repricing of future expectations rather than a sudden collapse in current demand. Chanana also wrote that investors increasingly want proof that huge AI spending will pay off, which could favor well-financed companies with established customers over those dependent on outside funding. In her view, this may not be the end of the AI trade, but it could mark the end of rewarding every company linked to AI equally.

Articles.Title: Asia's Tech Giants Are Getting Crushed in the AI Trade Rout

stories.Headline: Journalist Admits She Used AI to Edit Photo Smearing Democrat Voters
stories.Summary:
Olivia Reingold, a staff writer for The Free Press, a conservative outlet, drew sharp criticism after posting a photo on X on November 4, 2026, from an election night event for Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who won the state's Senate race. Her post singled out a woman at the party in designer items, including Valentino heels, a Chanel bag and a Moncler jacket, to argue that Michigan Democrats are wealthy and disconnected from working-class voters. Observers noticed the image had an unusually glossy look typical of AI generation, and some image detectors flagged it as AI-generated or edited, with watermark data pointing to an OpenAI model. Critics also said details such as the handbag's texture and the shoes' proportions did not match authentic designs.

Reingold then admitted on X that she had used ChatGPT to brighten and sharpen the image, and she posted what she said was the unaltered original. She argued that the processed photo still showed the same designer items worn by a real woman, so her point still held. Many users rejected that defense, noting that the AI tool added details not present in the original and changed the lighting, making the subject appear more gleaming and opulent than she looked in the shadowed source photo. The episode has raised the question of why an AI tool was needed for a basic touch up and whether such a change is acceptable for a journalist at all.

Max Spero, chief executive of the image detection company Pangram, said there is no such thing as a faithful AI upscale, warning that AI can invent details that do not reflect reality and that presenting such an image as fact puts a journalist's integrity at risk. Bruce Arthur, a columnist, was harsher, writing that actual journalists do not do this and should never do this. Reingold stood by her underlying observation in her response. The articles do not say whether The Free Press or Reingold has taken any further action or whether the post has been removed.

Articles.Title: Journalist Admits She Used AI to Edit Photo Smearing Democrat Voters

stories.Headline: Nikkei 225 falls more than 7% following AI-related declines on Wall Street
stories.Summary:
The Nikkei 225 stock average fell more than 7% on Friday morning, dropping below 60,000 for the first time since May. The decline followed heavy losses on Wall Street on Thursday, which were driven by concerns over data center and artificial intelligence investments after the Democratic Party won the U.S. midterm elections. By 10:25 a.m., the index was down 7.09%. Japanese stocks tied to AI, chips and data centers were hit hardest, with Rohm sliding 20%, Furukawa Electric falling more than 19%, Resonac dropping 15%, Kioxia losing more than 12% and SoftBank Group declining 11%.

The Topix also lost more than 6% in Friday morning trading. In the United States overnight, the Nasdaq composite fell 5.5%, its largest drop since April 2025. The S&P 500 declined 4.4%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the 30 largest U.S. semiconductor-related stocks, plunged 12.3%. The selloff spread quickly from American technology shares to Asian markets that rely on the same supply chains. The articles describe the moves as a sharp reaction to the investment outlook rather than a single company's problems.

The report was written by Kazuaki Nagata, a staff writer at The Japan Times, and the figures come from market trading data. The articles do not name a specific official or company that made a statement about the decline. They also do not say how long the selloff will last or whether investors expect a recovery. stories.Headline: Tech Rout Wipes Out $2.5 Trillion, With AI Investors Anticipating Heavier Scrutiny From Dems
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5 percent on Thursday, wiping out an estimated $2.5 trillion in market value and pushing the index into correction territory. The Wall Street Journal reported that the selloff followed weak earnings reports in the AI sector and Democratic gains in the 2026 midterm elections held on Tuesday. Shares fell across Asian chip makers, Texas power producers, New Jersey compute providers, Silicon Valley software makers, contractors and data-center developers. Leveraged traders who had bet against AI stocks were hit hard as well, and every sector in the S&P 500 finished in the red.

The Magnificent Seven group of Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla collectively lost about $1 trillion, according to the Journal. The PHLX Semiconductor index posted its worst day since the depths of the global coronavirus pandemic. The biggest AI hyperscalers, Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft, largely avoided the worst losses, while SpaceX fell more than 9 percent along with Tesla. The Nasdaq's drop was its largest single-day percentage decline since April 2025's "Liberation Day" tariff announcement, and the largest ever in dollar terms, per the Journal. Analysts quoted by the outlets said the market looks fragile, though the sell-off has not yet become a broader AI bubble panic.

Investors appear to be anticipating heavier scrutiny from incoming Democrats, who are expected to use congressional investigative powers to examine AI firms' ties to the White House. Tech executives have publicly aligned with Republicans and the White House in recent years, which has strained their relations with the party. Commentators noted it remains unclear whether Democrats will pursue aggressive oversight or settle for smaller changes, since Trump remains in office. Reuters reported that UBS estimates around 30 percent of expected U.S. data center capacity expansion in 2028 may face construction pauses. Michael O'Rourke of JonesTrading said the slowdown of the data center buildout is the key theme likely to persist after Democrats won many governorships.

Strategists also pointed to local resistance as a growing obstacle for data center projects. Bruce Zaro of Granite Wealth Management said opposition will focus on facilities located near residents, along with strain on power grids and water systems. Zaro said projects still lacking permits face a difficult road, while those already locked in should proceed. Former New York Federal Reserve president Bill Dudley has estimated the sector may need $3 trillion in annual revenue to deliver adequate returns on its heavy spending. The articles do not say how far the sell-off will extend or what Democrats will ultimately do.

Articles.Title: Tech Rout Wipes Out $2.5 Trillion, With AI Investors Anticipating Heavier Scrutiny From Dems

stories.Headline: Applied Optoelectronics Stock Earnings Beat Puts AI Demand In Focus

stories.Headline: AI stock sell-off sends the S&P 500 down 4.4% in worst day since April 2025
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, a sharp sell-off swept through Wall Street, led by stocks tied to the buildout of AI data centres. The S&P 500 fell 4.4 per cent, erasing the previous day's gain, which had been its best in three months. It was the index's worst day since U.S. President Donald Trump shook markets worldwide in April 2025 with his "Liberation Day" tariffs. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833 points, or 3.4 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5 per cent.

The Nasdaq now sits 11.9 per cent below the all-time high it set last month, and a decline of that size is what analysts call a correction. Canada's main stock index lost 736.13 points to close at 35,605.27, weighed down by technology stocks. Markets elsewhere also struggled, with South Korea's Kospi index falling 5.3 per cent. Investors have been worried for months that AI data centre construction may slow because borrowing has become expensive, and critics have argued AI stock prices were in a bubble.

Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections added to the pressure. Democrats' nationwide victories raised the possibility that governments could force pauses on new data centre construction, and voters across parties have voiced concern about AI and higher power bills. A slowdown would mean fewer purchases of AI chips and less demand for electricity and other products tied to the boom, which is driving much of the U.S. economy's growth. Nvidia fell 9.3 per cent and was the heaviest drag on the S&P 500, while Advanced Micro Devices dropped 17.3 per cent.

Not every company fell, as AppLovin jumped 31 per cent after reporting revenue and profit above analysts' expectations. Its board also approved buybacks of up to $3.2 billion US, bringing the program's total potential value to $3.6 billion US. Tapestry, the company behind the Coach and Kate Spade brands, rose 7.1 per cent after posting a stronger profit than expected and raising its forecasts. By the close, the S&P 500 stood at 7,353.73, the Dow at 51,523.06 and the Nasdaq at 24,315.00. Treasury yields kept falling, which may signal investors moving into safer U.S. government bonds.

Articles.Title: AI stock sell-off sends the S&P 500 down 4.4% in worst day since April 2025

stories.Headline: Affirm CEO Expects AI Shopping Agents to Favor Interest-Free Installments
stories.Summary:
Affirm CEO Max Levchin said on November 5, 2026, during the fiscal first quarter earnings call on Thursday, that he expects more purchases to be financed with interest-free installment loans as consumers hand shopping to artificial intelligence agents. He said agents comparing payment options could steer shoppers toward loans that spread the purchase price out without adding interest. Those interest-free plans made up 28% of Affirm's gross merchandise volume in the September quarter, while interest-bearing loans made up 72%. Levchin told analysts he expects zero-percent volume to grow a lot in agentic commerce. Affirm shares fell more than 9% in extended trading after losing nearly 8% during the regular session.

The earnings report also showed rising borrower strain alongside strong growth. Revenue rose 35% to $1.3 billion, above analyst estimates, but the share of U.S. loan balances at least 30 days past due reached 2.9% in September, up 35 basis points from June and nine basis points from a year earlier, excluding short-term Pay in X and Peloton loans. Spending on the Affirm Card more than doubled to $3.3 billion, and active cardholders doubled to 6 million. Transactions and gross merchandise volume each rose 34%, with volume reaching $14.4 billion, and the average order fell to $258 after lower minimum purchase amounts helped lift transaction counts. Active consumers rose 19% to 28.7 million, and active merchants rose 48% to about 621,000.

Levchin attributed much of the quarterly rise in delinquencies to seasonality and said short loan terms limit how long Affirm stays exposed if underwriting goes wrong. Chief Financial Officer Rob O'Hare said a September test of loan approvals and originations increased the company's provision for credit losses, and Affirm kept the test loans on its balance sheet. Levchin said about 1 million SKUs in the Affirm app carry brand-funded promotions, and that Affirm is building tools that could let a seller's AI agent make a financing offer to a shopper's agent. He also acknowledged that agentic commerce would be messy, pointing to agents making unwanted purchases and to fraud risk, and he left open who would bear liability for fraud involving an AI agent. O'Hare said fiscal 2027 outlook calls for at least 30% growth in gross merchandise volume.

Affirm plans to introduce card-specific financing offers this quarter and is preparing to pilot Edge, which would make its installment loans available through other issuers' debit cards. Levchin said some borrowers on tight budgets could still prefer a longer, interest-bearing loan if it brings the monthly payment within reach. O'Hare noted that more than 80% of Affirm Card loans have historically carried interest. Whether the interest-free model captures the agent-driven shopping Levchin expects remains to be seen, as the articles do not report results from those planned launches.

Articles.Title: Affirm CEO Expects AI Shopping Agents to Favor Interest-Free Installments

stories.Headline: 'They're shooting the generals': AI trade stocks drop as hedge funds rush to protect 2026 gains

stories.Headline: AI agents can trade stocks for you—here are the risks and benefits, according to experts
stories.Summary:
Online brokerages are rolling out agentic trading, a form of AI that performs parts of portfolio management for investors. Unlike robo-advisors, which build portfolios from preferences such as risk tolerance, these agents can turn plain-language prompts into investment strategies and execute trades on a user's behalf as market conditions shift. Robinhood rolled out agentic trading in May 2026, allowing investors to link a third-party large language model to their account for tasks like portfolio rebalancing and market analysis. The company announced AI agents integrated natively in its app in September, but those are not yet available to all customers. Users of platforms such as Robinhood and Webull can use AI to monitor markets, build strategies and automate certain approved tasks.

The tools mainly help with execution rather than prediction, and investors still need their own hypothesis about how an investment could pay off. Robinhood's vice president of brokerage product, Abhishek Fatehpuria, said the product is meant to help individuals test assumptions and vet hypotheses, not to replace having one. Shridhar Rathore, a 45-year-old self-taught investor from Charlotte, North Carolina, began experimenting with agentic trading in March 2026 after his portfolio grew too time-consuming to manage. He said agents streamline tasks such as options analysis and risk assessment, but he still makes the decisions and relies on his own experience and a paid investment newsletter. Blake Anderson, director of portfolio management at Carson Group, said AI may reduce trading delays but is unlikely to change the long-term earnings potential of a business for a fundamental investor.

The experts described several risks. Rathore warned that agents can malfunction or make decisions that do not match an investor's goals, and that inexperienced users could lose money because language models can hallucinate, meaning they invent or misread information. Robinhood's safeguards include limiting agents to a separate, dedicated brokerage account and, on default settings, requiring the investor to approve every trade, though that approval requirement can be turned off and some trades may still need approval. Anderson suggested a possible benefit is gathering information and perspectives that differ from the prevailing narrative, but he cautioned that investors should make sure the AI draws on trusted sources rather than confirming their own biases. The article does not say what further regulation or product changes are planned.

Articles.Title: AI agents can trade stocks for you—here are the risks and benefits, according to experts

stories.Headline: I’ve Finally Started Incorporating AI Into My Work ⭐
stories.Summary:
Paul Thurrott, a longtime technology journalist, wrote on November 5, 2026 that he had finally begun using AI in his own work after months of struggling to get local AI running on his RTX Spark system. He said that turning to cloud-based AI helped him confirm that his earlier problems were tied to local AI rather than AI in general. Earlier in the year, he had used Clairvoyance and Anthropic Claude to finish a WinUI programming project that had taken most of a year. He described cloud AI coding as having improved sharply over the past several months.

He also described a shift in his thinking after hearing from his wife, Stephanie, about the ways she has built AI into her own workflow. Thurrott said he had long been unwilling to use AI for writing, and he admitted that his failure to see uses that might save time and money was mostly a lack of imagination. When Stephanie told him she was building a Spanish language tutor app with Google Gemini, he said his first reaction was skeptical but that he then felt he needed to step up. He decided to write down his small frustrations and try to solve them with AI. Over two or three hours that afternoon, he said, he made real progress on four of them.

Among the problems he targeted was a native Markdown editor for Windows, tied to a short Markdown book he is writing. He said he had hoped to finish the book in under a month but kept running into perfectionist delays, and he had considered building his own editor so he could recommend a tool that suited the many variants of Markdown. He noted that some of his projects overlap with Stephanie's, including updates they both want to make to the book. The article is a personal column, and it does not describe any broader industry change, product launch, or regulatory requirement. It also does not say what, if anything, comes next beyond his stated plan to keep working through his projects before the end of the year.

Articles.Title: I’ve Finally Started Incorporating AI Into My Work ⭐

stories.Headline: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle returned just 9.3% of cash to shareholders in the first three quarters of 2026, a 15-year low amid AI spending (Patturaja Murugaboopathy/Reuters)
stories.Summary:
Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle returned just 9.3% of their cash to shareholders in the first three quarters of 2026, according to Reuters. That figure marked a 15-year low for the five companies. The report was published on October 30, 2026, and was written by Patturaja Murugaboopathy. The low share of returned cash came amid heavy spending on artificial intelligence.

The same five companies have collective AI spending commitments of more than $3 trillion over the coming years, according to Bloomberg. Alphabet alone accounts for $1 trillion of that total, and Meta accounts for $800 billion. The spending figures were reported by Brody Ford of Bloomberg. The commitments cover the years ahead and sit alongside the reduced cash returns to shareholders.

The shareholder return figure and the spending commitments were reported by Reuters and Bloomberg respectively. Murugaboopathy wrote the Reuters report, and Ford wrote the Bloomberg report. Both reports were carried on Techmeme on October 30, 2026. The articles do not say who at the companies is responsible for the spending plans or what executives said about them.

The articles do not describe any next steps or future plans beyond the spending commitments already listed. They give no timetable for when the AI spending will be completed. They also do not say whether the low rate of cash returned to shareholders is expected to continue. No further context on the companies' plans appears in the two reports.

Articles.Title: The 13 AI Giants, from Alphabet to Oracle, Sit on $1.13 Trillion in Cash. They Can Keep Spending on AI even if Markets Get Ugly
