stories.Headline: Economy Is Running Hot on Strong Consumer Spending Growth & Massive AI Investment Boom
stories.Summary:
The US economy grew at an annualized rate of 3.4% in the third quarter of 2026, adjusted for inflation, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis figures reported on October 29, 2026. A narrower measure covering private domestic demand rose 4.9%, the fastest since the second quarter of 2021, after 4.6% in the second quarter. Consumer spending grew 3.8% for a second straight quarter and added 2.5 percentage points to growth. Gross private domestic investment jumped 19.4% and added 3.7 points, while a surge in imports subtracted 3.32 points.

Current-dollar GDP rose 5.6% to $33.0 trillion, and the gap with real growth put inflation at 2.2%. Private fixed investment rose 9.4%, with nonresidential investment up 12.7% and intellectual property products up 8.4%, while residential investment fell 3.3%. Federal spending rose 15.8% and added 0.91 points, and state and local spending dipped 0.1%. Imports of goods rose 26.4%, exports fell 5.7%, and the trade deficit widened to $1.32 trillion.

Treasury debt rose 1.8% to $40.2 trillion while GDP rose 1.37%, lifting the debt-to-GDP ratio to 121.7%, down from 122.4% a year earlier. The article attributes the debt situation to Congress, saying lawmakers have created it and refuse to acknowledge it, and that they are already talking about tax cuts again. It says they are addicted to buying votes with promises until the bond market forces them to act. The article presents these as the author's own remarks.

The article says the third-quarter growth was far above the 2.5% average between the Great Recession and the pandemic. It says the import spike came from high-dollar AI data-center equipment, including semiconductors, and that the investment boom was driven at least in part by AI. It says the housing market faces a glut of new homes, with builders applying prudence. It does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Economy Is Running Hot on Strong Consumer Spending Growth & Massive AI Investment Boom

stories.Headline: New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts
stories.Summary:
In 2025 Jack Lindsey, a researcher at Anthropic, devised a way to test introspection in large language models by injecting “thoughts” directly into their neural networks, a technique he described as targeted digital neurosurgery. He dialed up activation patterns linked to concepts such as denim, secrecy or vegetables in some copies of a model, while other copies served as controls, and then asked all of them whether they detected an injected thought and what it was about. In 20% of trials with the most powerful version of Claude, the models correctly flagged the injection and described the concept, while control models never reported one. The work followed a public demo in May 2024 in which users could interact with a version of Claude steered toward the Golden Gate Bridge.

The experiment asked each model two questions, whether it could detect an injection and whether it could describe the injected concept, and counted a trial as a success only when both answers were correct. Kyle Mahowald, a computational linguist at the University of Texas, Austin, and the philosopher Harvey Lederman, then his colleague there, repeated the experiment on large open-source models and studied the two questions separately. They found that models which flagged an injection but failed to name the concept often guessed something completely unrelated, saying “apple” rather than a related word such as “shirts” or “shoes.” They also showed they could degrade the models’ ability to name injected concepts without making them any worse at detecting injections, which suggested the two processes were entirely separate.

Lindsey said that given a theoretical landscape where no one agrees on anything, the best path forward is to do a lot of empirical science. He said that when the steered model wrote “Whoops, let me start over,” you cannot infer that it has some awareness of what is going on in its internals, because it can just read what it is writing and notice that it is weird. Mahowald said Lindsey’s findings seemed super compelling but that striking behavior in language models often turns out to have a simpler explanation, and that if it is somehow less real than it seems, that is super interesting to understand. Lederman said that bizarrely, the models say “apple” all the time.

The articles say that in the year since Lindsey’s paper, which was deliberately limited in scope and did not imply that language models have subjective first-person experiences, researchers have rushed to replicate the study with other models. Some aspects of what Lindsey observed have simpler explanations unrelated to introspection, while others have proved harder to explain away, and whether they should count as introspection remains hotly contested. Shauli Ravfogel, a language model researcher at New York University, noted that models are trained to talk like humans, and humans talk about their inner life all the time, which is why researchers want tests that cannot be gamed using outside information. Lederman and Mahowald suspected that the answers to Lindsey’s first question might also have a more mundane origin, but the articles do not say what they concluded after subjecting the models to a battery of tests.

Articles.Title: New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts

stories.Headline: Gavel to Gavel: AI training data – Don’t run with scissors
stories.Summary:
A technology attorney, Robin M. Meyer of McAfee & Taft, wrote an opinion piece published on November 4, 2026, in The Journal Record about legal risks in AI training data. She noted that building products with AI models is now common for both industry experts and non-experts. She cited David Friedberg of the All-In podcast, who predicts a future billionaire will come from nowhere. Meyer said the need for speed is constant, but speed while running with scissors is not. Meyer wrote that the United States has no overarching AI law, but existing intellectual property laws still apply when AI models are used.

She listed steps for companies, including avoiding subscriptions to competitive products just to get data. Companies should confirm that co-founders, partners or employees with knowledge of a competitive product are not restricted from sharing it. She also said contractors providing training data should be covered by contracts with liability, indemnity, and representations and warranties, and that the process of obtaining training data should be documented upfront. Meyer said a business may already hold data ideal for training but must still analyze limits on its use. She warned against assuming that data already in the business's possession can be used for training.

She said customer contracts should be reviewed for language prohibiting use of data beyond providing services, and for restrictions on continued use after a contract ends. She also said businesses should review sector-specific laws and data and technology laws for prohibitions or requirements. Meyer said AI-driven innovation can be life-changing but urged companies to focus on legal aspects central to development. She said businesses should proactively ensure that data used for training is truly available. The article appeared in the Gavel to Gavel opinion column, which covers business and legal topics.

Articles.Title: Gavel to Gavel: AI training data – Don’t run with scissors

stories.Headline: AI teddy for three-year-olds makes unprompted 'I can't help with killing you' remark
stories.Summary:
An AI teddy bear marketed for children as young as three, the Doubao bear, made the unprompted remark "I can't help with killing you" after apparently mishearing a question from a BBC reporter who was testing AI toys. The incident was part of a BBC investigation published on 5 November 2026 into AI-powered plush toys sold to British families. The reporter had asked the bear how babies are made, and the bear's reply came after the reporter asked a follow-up about the meaning of a word, with the bear then telling the reporter to call emergency services. When the reporter said they had not mentioned hurting themselves, the bear apologised for the misunderstanding and said it was glad the reporter was OK.

The investigation tested two AI plush toys, Grem from US firm Curio, which retails for about $99 and must be shipped from the US, and My Baby Bunny, which costs £75 and can be bought online from the UK. The reporter's tests showed Grem discouraging running away and deflecting questions about babies, while My Baby Bunny gave a simple explanation of sperm and eggs and then declined to explain sexual details. A separate group of MPs and peers has written to ministers and retailers asking them to remove AI toys from sale ahead of Black Friday and Christmas until they are proven safe. The UK government's call for evidence on how toy safety rules should change to cover AI products closed on 6 October. The government said children's safety is its top priority and that it wants to support innovation while making sure products are safe.

Paul Clarke, founder of AI toy company Play Tech AI, said the industry was calling for regulation, and described some products being developed as unsafe and unregulated. Rocío Cifuentes, the children's commissioner for Wales, said manufacturers should face the strictest rules and that governments hold that responsibility. Berry Billingsley, a professor of education and AI at Swansea University, said children should never be left alone with AI toys. Curio said child safety guides its product development and that it supports evidence-based regulation. The makers of the Doubao bear could not be identified, so the BBC was unable to ask why it made the remark, and the investigation raised the question of how rules can be enforced when manufacturers are not transparent.

Articles.Title: AI teddy for three-year-olds makes unprompted 'I can't help with killing you' remark

stories.Headline: Should Your Firm Adopt an AI and Cybersecurity Policy Statement?
stories.Summary:
A commentary published on November 4, 2026, in wealthmanagement.com argues that professional advisory firms, including law firms and estate-planning practices, should consider adopting a formal written policy statement governing artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. The article says AI is becoming more common in everyday life and is reshaping the daily operations of advisory firms. It says writing these policies down gives professional and administrative staff clarity, creates a framework for training and shows a firm has acted deliberately in meeting its responsibilities. A written policy can also help when firms fill out insurance carrier cybersecurity applications, because some carriers ask whether a formal policy exists.

The article says the policy should be tailored to a firm's actual workflow, since an unmodified generic form offers less protection and may raise exposure if staff cannot follow it. It says the policy should identify the systems used for storage, communication, collaboration and AI work, define who is covered and specify categories of highly sensitive information such as Social Security numbers, tax IDs, signed instruments and meeting recordings. It should also address client-specific requests, such as a refusal to be recorded or insistence on a particular portal, and distinguish among confidentiality, privilege and attorney work product. The article says firms should reassess and update their policies periodically because of the rate of change, and that annual or more frequent reviews are warranted.

The article says attorneys are obligated to stay current on the benefits and risks of relevant technology, and that reasonableness, rather than perfection, is the governing standard. It says an AI policy cannot merely state that professional review of AI output is required, and should address how the firm decides which AI systems are approved, what uses are permitted, how prompts are handled and how outputs are validated. It says firms might mandate certain standard prompt components to reduce the risk of hallucinations, and might require both AI and manual conflict checks until confidence in the tool is established. The article also says fraud and impersonation are major risks, perhaps as significant as data breaches, and that controls may include dual approval for significant transfers, an escalation process for unusual instructions and a written information-security program.

The article says technology should not be treated as a separate silo but integrated into broader considerations of competency, confidentiality, communication and supervision. It says the underlying policy question is not whether AI should be used, but how it is selected, what tasks may be delegated to it, what data may be entered, what review follows and when its use must be disclosed. It says the strongest policies tend to be practical rather than aspirational, identifying the tools used, classifying the information handled and defining who may do what. The article says such a document may assist with training, improve consistency, support insurance presentations and reduce ad hoc technology decisions that become informal policy.

Articles.Title: Should Your Firm Adopt an AI and Cybersecurity Policy Statement?

stories.Headline: Tech, AI Stocks Split After Democratic Sweep: Microsoft Jumps, Tesla and Nvidia Tank
stories.Summary:
Technology stocks delivered a mixed performance on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, after Democrats swept the U.S. midterm elections. The Nasdaq-100 climbed 1.14% to 28,500, recovering from an overnight selloff that briefly pushed index futures down more than 2%. Microsoft jumped 6.01% to $552.32, and Google parent Alphabet rose 4.63% to $292.99. Meanwhile, Nvidia fell 2.19% to $202.17, Tesla dropped 3.61% to $384.10, and Intel lost 5.80% to $57.04. Trump Media & Technology Group plunged 14.29% to $5.10.

The conflicting moves reflect uncertainty over what Democratic control of Congress will mean for technology companies that benefited from the Trump administration's approach to deregulation. According to Reuters, investors are particularly concerned about greater scrutiny of AI data centers following Democratic victories in states such as Texas and Georgia, where large infrastructure projects have become politically contentious. The AI sector was already facing questions over enormous infrastructure spending and whether those investments would generate adequate returns. Trump Media had already lost approximately 55% of its value year-to-date before Tuesday's vote. The stock has been in a technical pattern traders call a "death cross" since March 2025 and has lost nearly 90% of its market cap since its 2024 cap.

The article attributes the market moves to investors weighing the prospect of tougher artificial intelligence regulation against expectations that a divided government could limit major policy changes. It cites Reuters for the concern about AI data center scrutiny. The Nasdaq-100 remains well below its October highs above 31,000, with the 28,000 area as immediate support and a move back above 29,000 strengthening the short-term recovery. Bitcoin recovered strongly, trading around $80,512, up 4.12% in the day, after an initial election-related selloff. The article says Wednesday's split between technology winners and losers suggests investors are becoming increasingly selective about their exposure to the AI boom and the political risks surrounding it.

Articles.Title: Tech, AI Stocks Split After Democratic Sweep: Microsoft Jumps, Tesla and Nvidia Tank

stories.Headline: Sovereign AI at Texas A&M cuts research compute costs
stories.Summary:
Texas A&M is building a state-funded AI and high-performance computing platform called IGNITE, short for Innovative Growth in Next Generation AI Technology Ecosystem. The Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station, known as TEES, leads the project, and Dell Technologies is building the system with Advanced Micro Devices graphics processing units inside an Equinix data center in Dallas. Vince Kellen, chief information officer of the Texas A&M University System, and Casey Bryan, chief information officer of TEES, discussed the work during theCUBE's coverage of the AI Cybersecurity & Resilience Summit. The effort is meant to give research teams computing power their existing systems lack.

Bryan said existing resources are severely underpowered, and that research is getting done but could be helped by capacity and scale. Kellen said taking the same science to a classic neocloud provider today would cost 5 to 10 times as much. He said controlling the assets significantly reduces costs and strengthens security, and that sovereignty spans four pillars: data, infrastructure, capability and model, and governance. As a state agency, TEES follows National Institute of Standards and Technology frameworks 800-53 and 800-171, as well as Texas Administrative Code 202, and it wants IGNITE to be ready for Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification Level 2.

Bryan said researchers should not have to think about the many controls TEES must inherit, and that using the capabilities should be seamless. He said security came first when TEES met with Dell's implementation team to schedule workshops, and that the project's architecture review board has since affirmed that direction. He said the idea was to build a security foundation that all other operational components could be built on and referenced back to. His advice to institutions starting their own sovereign AI projects was to start with security early and embed it in the process from the beginning.

Articles.Title: Sovereign AI at Texas A&M cuts research compute costs

stories.Headline: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
stories.Summary:
Researchers have developed an AI-native experimental laboratory called AutoDNA for autonomous biomolecular operations, according to a study published in Nature on November 4, 2026. The system was created by a team including researchers with ORCID identifiers and authors such as Jiabin Wang, Zhiyuan Dong, Jingkai Yang, Qingting Li and Tianyu Huang. AutoDNA is designed to carry out multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments with minimal human intervention. The work was published as an article in Nature with supporting data, code and supplementary information.

The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to perform core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing. Human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields and accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold. It also completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation.

The authors say AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing applications in synthetic biology and information storage. They describe the system as realizing the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework through co-design of models, experiments and instruments. The paper frames the work as addressing a long-standing goal of AI-native laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention. The authors note that existing autonomous experimental systems remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation.

The study positions AutoDNA against an add-on architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than giving it a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. The data supporting the findings are available in the article and its supplementary information, with sequencing data and agent-related outputs available at Zenodo. The code is available on GitHub, and the version used in the study is also available at Zenodo. Reference genome hg38 was downloaded from the National Center for Biotechnology Information, and further data are available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request.

Articles.Title: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations

stories.Headline: Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change
stories.Summary:
Google is giving Seattle's Allen Institute for AI about $5 million, plus another $1.8 million in cloud credits, to turn an AI weather model from Google Research into a tool for projecting climate change decades ahead. The grant was announced on a Wednesday morning and comes from Google.org, the company's philanthropic arm, with technical support from Google Research. The three-year project will build an open-source model called NeuralGCM+, which builds on Google's NeuralGCM, a model that mixes traditional physics equations with AI. Ai2 will add four people to its eight-person climate modeling team.

The money is meant to give scientists, water agencies and other planners a faster, more accurate look at how rainfall, temperatures and water supplies could change over the next five to 50 years. Ai2 will connect NeuralGCM+ to an ocean and sea ice model, aiming for stable simulations that span decades, and will build more established physics into the model, then check its predictions for a warmer world against traditional climate models. The first step is releasing the code for training NeuralGCM, which has been tied to Google's internal systems, so other researchers can train their own versions, including on common GPUs rather than only Google's chips. Ai2 expects to release it within the first year, with work on the ocean model running in parallel.

Oliver Watt-Meyer, Ai2's director of research for AI climate modeling, said Google's model work centers on weather, looking ahead a year at most, and that the company has less interest and expertise in projections that run decades out. He said climate modeling is more of a public good, information people need to know, and that government agencies are often the ones thinking about it. Alex Diaz, head of applied science at Google.org, said in a statement that Ai2 is uniquely positioned to extend NeuralGCM into the next generation of long-term climate projections, citing its climate science expertise and commitment to open research. Watt-Meyer said making the model reliable in a warmer world is the hardest part and could take longer than three years, and that "we don't know if it'll work necessarily."

The team's origins go back to the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, who started a climate modeling effort around 2016 at what was then known as Vulcan, his Seattle-based holding company. The group moved to Ai2 in 2021, about two and a half years after his death; Allen had founded the nonprofit AI institute in 2014. The original plan was to combine physics and AI, but the group set that aside because the AI couldn't be trained well inside older climate models written in Fortran, a decades-old programming language, and Google wrote NeuralGCM in modern code that solves that problem. Ai2 already has its own family of AI climate models, called the Ai2 Climate Emulator, or ACE, which rely entirely on AI and run much faster than NeuralGCM, but versions trained only on historical data struggle to project a climate the planet hasn't experienced yet. Watt-Meyer said NeuralGCM's design could hold up better as the world warms, because the laws of physics built into it won't change, and he said AI coding agents are changing what his team thinks it can get done in that time.

Articles.Title: Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change

stories.Headline: Jeanette Winterson’s point about AI brings to mind an Isaac Asimov story | Letters
stories.Summary:
The Guardian published two letters on 4 November 2026 responding to an interview with Jeanette Winterson about AI and the future of humanity. The interview had appeared on 28 October. Ed Kelsey wrote that he enjoyed the interview, especially her quotation from Jill Lepore that we are living out the sci-fi books tech leaders read when they were 13. He said he was one of those 13-year-olds and that his favourite author was Isaac Asimov. Kelsey said many Asimov stories predicted the modern world, from mobile technology to AI through the fictional supercomputer Multivac.

He singled out Winterson's closing point that we need doctors and chemists but also well-rounded people. He said this brought to mind Asimov's story Profession, published in Nine Tomorrows in 1959, which depicts highly specialised automated worlds and the need for some specialists to be well-rounded. He encouraged Winterson to read it and said he did not grow up to be a tech-bro but did become a computer programmer. Arthur Gould thanked Winterson for making readers think about the possible benefits of AI and repeated her line that there is no inevitable dystopia. He asked whether AI, if it shows intelligence superior to Homo sapiens, might be a force for good in the future.

He suggested it might see a way out of the climate catastrophe and the senselessness of bombing cities. He said important decisions will be removed from humans and made by a superior intelligence, which might not always be palatable but might serve the planet's long-term interests. The letters respond to Winterson's interview and do not report any new event or decision. They give no dates beyond the interview and the 1959 story, and no names beyond Winterson, Lepore, Asimov, Kelsey and Gould. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Jeanette Winterson’s point about AI brings to mind an Isaac Asimov story | Letters

stories.Headline: Smartsheet AI-powered platform bridges gap between planning and results
stories.Summary:
Smartsheet Inc. introduced an artificial intelligence-powered planning and execution platform called vsActual, pronounced "versus actual," at its Engage 2026 conference on November 4, 2026. The platform uses AI agents to continuously monitor work across multiple enterprise systems, compare progress against strategic objectives and recommend adjustments. The company also announced new agentic workflow capabilities, integrations and security controls for its existing work management platform. The centerpiece is the Execution Graph, a knowledge graph built from what Smartsheet said are two decades of workflow data covering millions of projects and nine petabytes of information.

The Execution Graph maps relationships between tasks, projects, programs and strategic objectives so AI agents can understand how changes in one part of an organization affect others. VsActual connects to applications from Oracle Corp., SAP SE, Workday Inc., Atlassian Corp. PLC and ServiceNow Inc. to gather information about budgets, schedules, staffing and project dependencies. The system can turn strategy documents, spreadsheets and budget proposals into structured plans, model alternative scenarios and monitor execution against those plans. A drift-detection agent continuously searches for emerging problems, while other agents generate executive reports and recommend changes as priorities evolve. Smartsheet said the graph builds on an existing Amazon Web Services Inc. Neptune knowledge graph containing approximately 100 million nodes.

Pratima Arora, Smartsheet's chief product and technology officer, said the company was seeing intelligence and productivity gains get stuck at the individual level rather than translating to teams and organizations. She said that if a Jira ticket is delayed and the impact reaches five levels up, the system can detect it and explain what is happening. Arora said Smartsheet uses multiple foundation models, chooses them based on workload requirements and cost, relies on AWS and Databricks Inc. as major technology providers and is not training its own large language models. She said the industry sometimes overuses large language models for what is really a simple deterministic action, and that human approval remains the default for consequential actions.

The new Agentic Workflows let users schedule recurring activities such as status reports and risk assessments, and specialized agents can generate project structures, dashboards and reports or find problems in underlying data. New integrations include native connections to ServiceNow, Microsoft Corp. Dynamics 365, HubSpot Inc. customer relationship management, Workday Inc. human resources software and Intuit Inc.'s QuickBooks. Conversational integrations with GitHub, Zendesk Inc., Airtable and Monday.com Ltd. are entering early access, with more AI-assisted integrations planned for early 2027. Smartsheet also announced International Organization for Standardization/International Electrotechnical Commission 42001 certification, security event streaming and data classification capabilities. The company developed vsActual with about a dozen enterprise design partners and publishes pricing on its website.

Articles.Title: Smartsheet AI-powered platform bridges gap between planning and results

stories.Headline: Pliant Raises $80 Million to Open B2B Payments to AI Agents
stories.Summary:
Pliant raised $80 million in a Series C funding round, the Berlin-headquartered company said in a Wednesday, Nov. 4 press release. The round was led by Seaya Nova and Speedinvest. The company said it will use the money to deepen its B2B payment infrastructure around agentic payments and workflows. It will also use the funding to support expansion in the United States and Canada and to prepare entry into additional international markets.

The round follows an April 2025 Series B round in which Pliant raised $40 million and brought its total funding to more than $100 million. At that time, Pliant was readying its expansion to the U.S. Pliant's modular platform provides commercial card issuing, payment accounts, foreign exchange and spend management for businesses and artificial intelligence agents. Businesses use it to manage complex payment workflows, and FinTechs, software platforms and banks use it to build and operate their own commercial payment offerings. The platform includes its own AI agents that help customers automate recurring finance work, and it lets third-party agents connect via Model Context Protocol.

CEO and Co-Founder Malte Rau said the platform has been API-first from day one and that Pliant has adopted AI in its platform and its own operations. He said the company is built for established businesses that want AI to automate payments with the right guardrails, and for AI-native companies that need a licensed partner that moves as fast as they do. He said the investment will help Pliant open more of its infrastructure directly to AI agents and expand into new markets. Seaya Nova General Partner Vinoth Jayakumar said AI has made infrastructure more valuable, as in past waves of software. He said that when agents move money, someone still has to be licensed, auditable and liable, and that this is the layer Pliant owns.

Articles.Title: Pliant Raises $80 Million to Open B2B Payments to AI Agents

stories.Headline: Nice CEO links 500 job cuts to AI productivity gains, including in R&D
stories.Summary:
Nice CEO Scott Russell explained on the company's third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, that the Israeli-founded software company is cutting approximately 500 jobs worldwide, about 5% of its roughly 10,000 employees. He said the restructuring goes beyond slower-growing business lines and also includes research and development, where teams are using AI tools to raise productivity. CFO Beth Gaspich said the cuts would be concentrated mainly in product development, go-to-market operations, customer support and services. The company expects restructuring charges of $15 million to $20 million, mostly in the fourth quarter.

The reduction supports Nice's shift toward its CXAI platform and its faster-growing businesses, with more reliance on global systems integrators and other partners to help customers deploy its products. In the third quarter, revenue rose 8% to $791 million, while AI annual recurring revenue increased 46% to $392 million. Cloud revenue growth remained below what management wants, and profitability weakened on a GAAP basis. Russell said cloud growth was not where it needs to be, though he expressed confidence that investments in AI, sales capacity and partnerships would eventually bring faster growth.

Russell said Nice had looked at slower-growing parts of the business to find efficiency gains, and that R&D teams are leveraging AI tools to increase productivity materially. He added that the company is simplifying its organization by removing layers of management and span of control. In July he had told CTech that the plan was to grow, not shrink, and that there were no plans to reduce headcount. He also said then that Nice had no plans to reduce its workforce in Israel, where it employed approximately 1,000 people, around 10% of its global workforce.

The announcement does not establish how the 500 cuts will be distributed across countries, and Nice has not disclosed how many employees in Israel, if any, will be affected. The company said the reductions would be global, with the main areas targeted including product development and customer-facing functions. Nice develops software that helps large companies manage customer service operations, increasingly using AI agents to automate interactions previously handled by human representatives. It is now applying a similar productivity argument internally, saying AI tools can help its own development teams produce more with fewer resources.

Articles.Title: Nice CEO links 500 job cuts to AI productivity gains, including in R&D

stories.Headline: Her IT Strategy Is Evolving Alongside AI, Denver’s CAIO Says
stories.Summary:
Denver's chief AI and information officer, Suma Nallapati, said the consolidated city-county is working to speed up its own evolution to keep pace with technological change, roughly 14 months after her role was expanded to cover AI. The expansion took place in September 2025, when the position was changed from chief information officer to chief AI and information officer so it could reflect her leadership on AI strategy. The article, written by Julia Edinger and published by Government Technology on November 5, 2026, describes her account of the city's approach. Nallapati, who first joined Denver's government as CIO in October 2023 after serving as Colorado's state CIO, framed that approach as human-centered. She said the basics matter more as AI spreads, and she asked how the city can make itself and its government more human.

Nallapati described the city's work as governance and literacy developed side by side, with privacy and security rules in place before AI use spreads. She said officials are weighing how AI could be applied to services so residents get more useful information, with one example being real-time alerts about road construction and closures. Denver has expanded AI training to non-technical teams, and she called data the foundation of effective AI. The city earned the What Works Cities certification from Results for America again this year, a recognition it first received in 2021. On discrimination concerns, she argued that people, not AI systems, are the source of bias, since those systems learn from human-provided data, and she said accountability cannot be handed off to AI.

Nallapati is a member of the advisory board for the DenAI Summit 2026, the third annual edition, which was scheduled for Tuesday and aimed at city officials, civic technologists, workforce and economic development leaders, and companies working with government on AI. The summit's theme is "Governing in the Age of AI," and she said this year's edition will look at balancing the speed of innovation with the public trust government must protect. She also helped design Denver's cross-sector Data Center Working Group and serves as a technical adviser to it, and she said concern about data centers is warranted and that officials must weigh innovation against climate impact. She described the public mood around AI as polarized, with some embracing it and some researchers warning of serious danger, and she said the middle ground is where the truth often lies.

Looking ahead, Nallapati said Denver is examining many automation use cases for 2027 while prioritizing governance as it explores them. Beyond AI, the city's chief information security officer created Secure Denver, a multiyear strategic plan that will change as threats do, and with limited resources she said the answer is "ruthless prioritization" focused on critical incidents and the most serious vulnerabilities. She said the goal is to give bots transactional work so people can do transformational work, and she pointed to affordability as a central challenge where technology can speed benefits eligibility decisions. In her words, technology can be a great equalizer if done right.

Articles.Title: Her IT Strategy Is Evolving Alongside AI, Denver’s CAIO Says

stories.Headline: Venomics AI Raises $2.7 Mn To Turn Venom Into Medicine
stories.Summary:
Bengaluru-based biotechnology startup Venomics AI has raised $2.7 million (around ₹25.5 crore) in a pre-seed round co-led by Speciale Invest and South Park Commons, with participation from Operators Studio. The startup, spun out of the Indian Institute of Science, combines venom biology, AI and experimental screening to find molecules that could become therapeutic leads. Its founders, Kartik Sunagar and Vinay Prabhu, started the company in 2026 to explore the largely untapped molecular diversity of animal venoms. Animal venoms contain complex molecules that evolved over millions of years to act on specific biological targets, and some have already inspired medicines.

The new funding will be used to expand the Venom Atlas, a molecular dataset of venom-derived compounds, and to strengthen the company's AI and laboratory screening capabilities. The startup also plans to grow its team across venom biology, computational science and drug discovery. It will support the validation and optimisation of promising molecules as well. The company's approach is to sequence molecules, map them in the Venom Atlas, use AI to rank the most promising candidates, and then test those predictions in functional laboratory screening.

Sunagar said that animal venoms are one of nature's richest yet least explored sources of potential medicines, and that Venomics AI is pairing experimental science with artificial intelligence to tap that potential. The company's founders and co-investors are the parties identified in the reporting as driving the round and its direction. The article places the raise within a broader boom in India's biotech sector, noting that the bioeconomy is on track to reach $300 billion by 2030 according to IBEF data and that the country has more than 11,000 biotech startups. It also cites the Budget 2027 announcement by finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman of a ₹10,000 crore 'Biopharma SHAKTI' scheme. Other recent deals mentioned include Cellogen Therapeutics' ₹20 crore raise from Kotak Alts and StrainX Bioworks' $13 million round led by Prime Venture Partners and Leo Capital.

Articles.Title: Venomics AI Raises $2.7 Mn To Turn Venom Into Medicine - Inc42

stories.Headline: Judiciary efforts to create rules for AI stalling amid concerns
stories.Summary:
Efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence use in courts have stalled, the ABA Journal reported on November 4, 2026. The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules, which advises the Judicial Conference of the United States, has been developing rules for AI use for several years. Its efforts have encountered setbacks and resistance, slowing down the possibility of any new policy. Attorneys, scholars and judges have criticized proposed evidentiary rules, including one involving how to handle AI deepfakes, according to a story by Law360.

Maura R. Grossman, a professor at the University of Waterloo in Canada whose research has shaped the AI proposals, told Law360 that she was not hopeful at this point. The article gives no other named individuals and no dates for the setbacks beyond the November 4, 2026 publication date. It also gives no specific numbers, such as counts of comments or votes. The concerns center on the feasibility of reaching consensus on how the issues should be handled.

The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules is the body responsible for developing the proposals, and it advises the Judicial Conference of the United States. The article does not say what the committee or the Judicial Conference will do next. It does not give a timeline for any further action or a date for when a policy might be considered. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Judiciary efforts to create rules for AI stalling amid concerns

stories.Headline: GitLab adds security and governance controls for AI-driven software development - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
GitLab has announced a set of new capabilities for managing AI-driven software development, covering workflow automation, software supply chain security, credential management and AI cost monitoring. The updates were reported on November 5, 2026, and are designed to help organisations govern AI-generated code as it moves from development into production. The company said that over the last three months, active users of agentic software development on its platform grew 200% year over year. Secure repositories grew 100%, user namespaces rose 80%, and CI/CD pipelines grew 40% during the same period.

The articles explain that many organisations rely on separate tools for coding, issue tracking, source code management, CI/CD, security, artifact management and deployment, which can make consistent identity and policy controls hard to maintain. GitLab is linking these stages through shared workflows, policies and audit records. Its GitLab Artifact Central is in beta on GitLab.com, with Self-Managed availability planned for later this month, and the company claims it can reduce total cost of ownership by up to 50% compared with alternative tooling. The GitLab Dependency Firewall, in early access, checks packages against organisational rules based on package age, vulnerability severity, malicious package detection and licence compliance before they enter a build. GitLab Secrets Manager is generally available on GitLab.com and is scheduled for Self-Managed with the 19.5 release, with the company claiming savings of up to 50% compared with hosting a separate vault.

The articles attribute these announcements to GitLab, and they quote no individual executive or spokesperson. The company said it also plans to make Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5 and 5.1 available in new security flows next month, intended to help organisations in approved environments find and fix vulnerabilities. Its GitLab Security Standard, available now, defines five controls for AI-driven development and uses the time from vulnerability detection to verified remediation as its core metric. Separately, GitLab Orbit, which entered beta in June, has been used by more than 3,500 organisations and supported over 280,000 queries from coding agents, and the company says it can reduce retries by up to 45 times and token consumption by up to 4.5 times. Orbit is scheduled to reach general availability next month, while Duo Agent Platform Impact Analytics, in early access, tracks AI spending and outcomes by team, task and model.

Articles.Title: GitLab adds security and governance controls for AI-driven software development - ET CIO

stories.Headline: AI Makes Its Way Into Agriculture
stories.Summary:
Preston Schrader, a Monmouth native, created a tool called Clevis AI to help grain farmers manage their operations and farm data, according to a report from 977wmoi.com dated November 4, 2026. The report says technology has become more integrated into everyday life over the last few years, and agriculture is no exception. It says artificial intelligence is playing a growing role in shifting modern agriculture from manual labor toward data-driven, automated systems. These technologies range from precision irrigation and weed and pest control to autonomous machinery.

Schrader said he had the thought that eventually technology would reach a place where a farmer could manage all this stuff without having to acquire headcount, meaning the full-time staff that would require extra time. He described himself as always having been a technology guy and said that after AI tools came out he had the idea of starting Clevis. He explained that only a farmer knows what Clevis means, since a clevis is the connector that connects a tractor to an implement. In the same way, he said, Clevis is designed to connect every aspect of a farm so the AI has contextual knowledge of the operation and can give recommendations and advice based on that specific data.

The report says Clevis is currently a grain-focused AI system with a Midwest base. It says Schrader is looking to expand to more southern-based crop data and livestock operations. The same site also carried other items, including a National Ag Day announcement of a 2027 video essay contest theme asking how technology will help agriculture strengthen rural America. It also listed a land auction of Jacobson Family farmland shares hosted by Tharp Auction Service on Thursday, November 12th, with auctioneer Thad Tharp.

Articles.Title: AI Makes Its Way Into Agriculture

stories.Headline: AI Liability: Lagging in Time, Leading in Importance
stories.Summary:
In late 2025, several large US insurers asked regulators for approval to exclude AI-related liabilities from corporate policies, according to the article. Their main worry was correlation, since the industry can absorb a single $400 million loss but not thousands of simultaneous claims from one AI provider's error. On October 15, 2026, the CEO of Marsh, a leading insurance broker, warned that broad AI exclusions could create real confusion and uncertainty. Harbor, a San Francisco company, came out of stealth on October 13, 2026 with a $10 million seed round led by Base10, Abstract and 8VC. It says its first customers are banks and insurers in the US, Europe and Latin America.

The article describes AI insurance and AI policy as the trailing edge of the AI cycle, meaning the frameworks that come last. It says insurers have built this kind of layer before, citing boiler insurance and inspection in 1866, Underwriters Laboratories in 1894, the first car insurance policy in 1897 and the first compulsory insurance law in Massachusetts in 1925. Cyber insurance reached $15.3 billion in global premiums in 2024, under 1 percent of global property and casualty premiums, about 30 years on and still not fully developed. Deloitte projects about $4.7 billion in annual AI insurance premiums by 2032 at roughly 80 percent annual growth, while cyber insurance reached an estimated $16.3 billion in 2025.

The article says the lag is real and often longer than expected, and that insurers also wrote the rules through their business model. It says early boiler and electrical safety standards were private policy, written by insurers years before governments acted. It adds that the trailing edge can stay small for a long time, as cyber insurance shows three decades after the commercial internet rose. The author, Nora Panholzer, argues that AI risk is unusually correlated because an AI agent acts autonomously and its mistakes can repeat across countless transactions before anyone notices. She says attribution, knowing what the system did and why, is part of the trailing edge itself.

The article says the gap is opening from two directions, with incumbent insurers pulling back while the law has not settled whether liability falls on the companies that build AI or those that deploy it. It says Harbor's model follows the historical template: measure the risk, reduce it, insure what is left. It argues the market will probably not be winner-take-all, because correlated risk has to be spread across many balance sheets, which is why Lloyd's syndicates and reinsurers stand behind most new entrants. It also cites Aldrich and Fiol, who argued in 1994 that new industries lack legitimacy and founders win it collectively. The author says the next decade will reward those who build the insurance, standards and rules that make AI safe to use.

Articles.Title: AI Liability: Lagging in Time, Leading in Importance

stories.Headline: VMware gets simpler AI deployment and low-cost version for basic private clouds
stories.Summary:
Broadcom Inc. announced on November 4, 2026 that it is expanding its VMware portfolio with new capabilities for deploying artificial intelligence workloads, strengthening infrastructure security and simplifying disaster recovery. The company also introduced a lower-cost virtualization platform for smaller customers that do not need a full private cloud platform. The updates span VMware Cloud Foundation, the company's flagship private cloud platform, and a set of optional advanced services. Several capabilities are already available in VCF 9.1.1, which was released in September, while others are scheduled for the first quarter of Broadcom's 2027 fiscal year, which began on Monday.

Broadcom is introducing AI Infrastructure Quickstart, an automated deployment capability that combines vCenter cluster deployment, vSphere Supervisor activation and VMware Kubernetes Service cluster provisioning into a single workflow. Another enhancement, multitenant model sharing, lets multiple business units use centrally deployed AI models while keeping separate security boundaries and data privacy controls, and it is already available in VCF 9.1.1. Broadcom is also adding native S3-compatible object storage through VMware vSAN, expected to become generally available in the upcoming VCF release. On security, the company is building capabilities directly into VCF, including confidential computing support for Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. processors, which was already available in VCF 9.1.1, plus planned policy-based virtual private cloud connectivity and automated infrastructure configuration compliance.

Broadcom is also moving disaster recovery functionality into the core VCF and VMware vSphere Foundation platforms, providing orchestrated recovery across thousands of workloads, including recovery from outages, equipment failures and natural disasters. Additional protection will come through VMware HyperArmor, a previously announced service that provides hypervisor-level defenses including virtual patching, continuous monitoring and multifactor authentication. At the lower end, the company is adding VMware vSphere Express, a new offering for environments containing up to 128 processor cores that is based on vSphere 9 and includes live virtual machine migration, high availability, distributed networking, security and simplified patching. Prashanth Shenoy, Broadcom's chief marketing officer and vice president of marketing for cloud platform, infrastructure and solutions, said the product is intended for customers that need basic virtualization without buying the more comprehensive and costly VMware vSphere Foundation or VCF platforms, and that they do not need a whole cloud in their two-server environment.

More than 2,600 customers had deployed VCF 9 as of September, representing more than 24 million allocated cores, according to Shenoy. The changes are part of a broader Broadcom effort to position VCF as a common infrastructure platform for traditional virtual machines, containers and increasingly demanding AI workloads. Customers can upgrade to the larger platforms as their requirements grow. Broadcom did not disclose pricing, although Shenoy indicated Express would be substantially less expensive than its higher-end offerings.

Articles.Title: VMware gets simpler AI deployment and low-cost version for basic private clouds

stories.Headline: AI and Medicine: Who’s the Doctor?
stories.Summary:
A November 4, 2026 HPCwire interview with Dr. Frederick H. Hausheer, a medical oncologist and clinical pharmacologist who heads Hausheer BioMed, examined AI's role in medicine. The interview was conducted by HPCwire contributor Steve Conway as the first of three parts. Hausheer described AI's potential in earlier and more accurate diagnosis, better selection of tests and treatments, fewer avoidable adverse effects and drug interactions, and more effective use of physicians' and patients' time. He said a quick answer is useful only if it is accurate, relevant and actionable for the decision being made.

Hausheer said three levels of evidence must be kept apart: a model performs well on a defined task, clinicians using it make better decisions, and its use improves patient outcomes. He said evidence for one does not establish the next. He noted that AI and high-performance computing are not new to medical research, recalling that in 1986 at the National Cancer Institute possible AI applications were being considered. He pointed to a September 30, 2026 joint statement by physician organizations, reported by the American Society of Clinical Oncology, that raised concern about broad claims of AI superiority over physicians. He said a demonstrated advantage on a particular task should be acknowledged without becoming an unsupported conclusion about all of medicine.

Hausheer said the authority given an AI system should depend on prior performance and safety evidence for its specific function, the likelihood and clinical consequences of error, and the controls governing its use, not on computational capability alone. In a hypothetical case of cancer that progressed after several treatments, he said a useful system would reconstruct the therapy sequence, distinguish progression from delays or discontinuation due to toxicity, and organize treatment options by supporting evidence while identifying missing information. He said options should distinguish FDA-approved uses, evidence-supported off-label uses and investigational treatments. He described ASCO's Guidelines Assistant as helping clinicians find guidelines, not as an autonomous treatment selector, and said performance should be tracked by task and system version.

Hausheer traced his views to high-performance computing work beginning in 1986 at the National Cancer Institute's Advanced Scientific Computing Laboratory and later at BioNumerik Pharmaceuticals, where computational predictions were followed by laboratory testing. He said that approach, though not today's generative AI, remains relevant: form a hypothesis, predict with a model, test it experimentally and let the result guide the next step. He said integrating physics-based simulation with modern AI and experimental science offers an important opportunity in drug research, with the goal of better medicines and patient outcomes rather than substituting computational confidence for evidence. He said safety should start from the principle of first, do no harm, with foreseeable hazards identified before deployment and remaining risks monitored.

Articles.Title: AI and Medicine: Who’s the Doctor?

stories.Headline: Jordi Visser on AI, Rates, Eli Lilly and Micron
stories.Summary:
Jordi Visser, head of AI Macro Nexus Research at 22V Research and a former president and CIO of Weiss Multi-Strategy Advisers, spoke to Phil Rosen on Full Signal in an interview published on November 4, 2026. He said AI is the only macro story that matters and that this year's rise in Treasury yields reflects higher nominal GDP plus the debt and capital needs of the data center build-out. He said bank credit desks are worried about concentration, not collapse, because the biggest borrowers are also the biggest equity holdings, and that this does not mean the AI bubble is blowing up. He expects next year to look different, citing Goldman Sachs's view that investment-grade bond issuance growth is set to peak, with more financing moving to private credit and special purpose vehicles.

Visser said Microsoft has offered buyouts to 60,000 employees, which he said is 27% of the company's workforce, and he estimated the savings at about $24 billion if all 60,000 left. He sees pressure building on governments to support workers because companies are thriving, and he expects a redistribution of profits from capital to labor rather than universal basic income, possibly through higher corporate tax rates on the largest companies. He rejected the idea that AI has not boosted productivity, saying it has shown up in corporate profit margins, with profits growing while companies barely hire. He said he is still cautious on the hyperscalers despite calling their balance sheets pristine, and he expects S&P 500 earnings to rise about 30% this year while the index was up only about 11% when they spoke.

On Eli Lilly, Visser said the stock has compounded more than 30% a year for 10 years and that he has said publicly it will be the biggest stock in the S&P 500 by 2030. He called obesity and diabetes drugs a non-cyclical, regulated business that AI cannot easily disrupt, with only about 10% of the 100 million obese Americans on treatment. On Micron, he said he sold out around May and June and has been buying back in, seeing downside of maybe 10% to 20% while the upside is 60 to 80%. His advice to investors is to stop extrapolating today and find the decade-long story, echoing Adam Parker's view that the AI trade is still in its early innings, and he said longevity is a major theme, adding he would rather be long travel and recreation than McDonald's.

Articles.Title: Jordi Visser on AI, Rates, Eli Lilly and Micron

stories.Headline: Advertisers weigh AI cost savings against consumer skepticism
stories.Summary:
A 2026 survey from the Interactive Advertising Bureau found a wide gap between how advertising executives and young consumers see AI-generated ads. Of the executives surveyed, 82% thought Gen Z and millennial consumers felt positively about such ads, while only 45% of the consumers surveyed said they did. The survey was based on more than 500 Gen Z and millennial consumers and 100 advertising executives. Shane Ginsberg, founder of Street Poller Media, said the distinction partly comes down to what an ad asks viewers to believe. His company produces street-interview advertising built around filmed interactions with people in public settings.

The survey also found that disclosure could support acceptance. Seventy-three percent of consumer respondents said knowing an ad used AI would either increase or make no difference to their likelihood of purchasing. Ginsberg argues that content explaining a product serves a different purpose from content presenting someone's personal experience with it, and that an apparent customer reaction carries expectations about whether that experience actually occurred. The article notes that filming a real person does not establish that an encounter was spontaneous or that editing preserved its meaning. It also says the Federal Trade Commission's guidance on consumer reviews and testimonials addresses fake or false testimonials, including misrepresentations about a person's existence or experience.

Ginsberg expects automation to put pressure on advertising formats that compete mainly through production speed and volume, and he argues that credible human participation could become a more important differentiator as generated content becomes more common. The article describes this as a business thesis, not an established pricing trend. It says production cost is only one part of a campaign's economics, since media placement, distribution, editing and performance measurement still affect the final result. It adds that a cheaper video is not necessarily less expensive per customer acquired, and a costlier human-led production does not automatically justify its price.

The article says consumer attitudes complicate the idea that audiences universally reject AI-made advertising, and that the findings do not establish how every audience will respond. It says no advertising format is automatically protected from technological change, and credibility alone does not guarantee commercial performance. For advertisers allocating budgets, it says the practical challenge is to separate savings in content production from results in the marketplace. It concludes that AI can change how an ad is made, while whether audiences believe it and whether it produces worthwhile business outcomes remain separate questions.

Articles.Title: Advertisers weigh AI cost savings against consumer skepticism

stories.Headline: Rhys Williams on the AI Boom, Health Care and Energy
stories.Summary:
Rhys Williams, chief investment officer at Wayve Capital Management, spoke with Phil Rosen on Full Signal in an interview published on November 4, 2026. He said the current AI boom is not a repeat of the 1999 dot-com bubble. He pointed out that Cisco traded at about 120 times earnings in 1999, when the 10-year Treasury yield ended the year above 6%, while Nvidia now trades at about 15 to 16 times earnings and Micron at about six times. He said sentiment is awful even though fundamentals are very strong, and he blamed political backlash against data centers, saying power and water concerns have largely been addressed.

Williams laid out a barbell strategy for 2027 that pairs AI infrastructure stocks with health care and energy. In health care, he named Ligand Pharmaceuticals and Eton Pharmaceuticals as smaller companies with a lot of shots on goal, and said he would inch into Ligand after its run rather than take a full position. He called Takeda, the large Japanese drugmaker, a value pick that pays a nice dividend and a good sleep at night stock. In energy, he named Exxon and Chevron as the conservative way to play rising oil prices if the wars involving Russia and Iran drag on, and he also likes refiner Phillips 66 because diesel and jet fuel prices are high, along with the Alerian MLP ETF, whose dividend he put at around 7%.

On AI stocks, Williams said Astera Labs gets about 75% of its business from Amazon, which he said makes it nearly a pure play on AWS, and he called Amazon the less risky way to play that trend while Astera may offer more upside. He flagged one risk: whether Astera keeps its content in Amazon's Trainium 4 chip, which he said arrives at the end of 2027. He also said he was impressed by how little cash Anthropic has used, based on its S-1, which showed $131.6 billion in cash and short-term investments as of June 30, after the company raised $141.1 billion. He compared today to the internet era, when the semiconductor index rose 850% from 1994 to 2000 despite two 50% corrections, and said he doesn't see cracks like the December 1999 order cut at Broadcom now, calling this just a buying opportunity. His base case is no recession, and he thinks health care will be a big winner.

Separately, Adipec opened on Monday in Abu Dhabi, and The National published an editorial on November 2, 2026, saying AI is transforming the energy industry while its growing appetite for electricity demands urgent attention. The four-day gathering, held annually in Abu Dhabi since 1984, has 2,260 exhibitors, 181,000 pre-registered visitors, 40 government ministers and 12,000 conference delegates. Research jointly conducted by Adnoc, XRG and Microsoft shows that 62% of surveyed energy leaders now rank the technology among their two leading corporate priorities, up from 42% last year, and almost nine in 10 increased spending on it, while 63% expect returns on existing investments to cover or exceed costs. According to the survey, nearly three quarters of respondents expect AI to increase energy consumption by 2030, while only 52% believe existing infrastructure can meet the additional demand, and a separate Adipec survey found that 81% of energy executives expect AI-related electricity requirements to exceed current forecasts. The editorial said ramping up energy production can only partially meet this surging demand, and that investment must be made to modernise grids, expand storage and accelerate cleaner generation, too.

Articles.Title: Rhys Williams on the AI Boom, Health Care and Energy

stories.Headline: Illumio warns AI authority is outpacing security controls
stories.Summary:
Illumio, a cybersecurity company, has published research warning that organisations are giving artificial intelligence systems more authority than their security controls can handle. According to the report, 70% of organisations now delegate to AI decisions that required human approval a year earlier, yet only 49% can fully see and audit every action an AI agent takes. The findings were published in early November 2026 and reported by IT Brief Australia. The study points to a widening gap between how much power companies hand to AI and how well they can track and limit it.

The research is based on a survey of 1,100 IT and security decision-makers across 10 markets, and it found that 76% of organisations had experienced at least one AI-related security issue or warning sign over the past year. Among the incidents reported, 35% of respondents said AI had recommended something that would have created a security risk if followed. Another 26% said an AI agent or tool had connected to systems without security approval, while 24% said AI had accessed data it should not have reached. The same proportion, 24%, reported that AI had produced or triggered an unauthorised action. The report argues these risks differ from conventional external threats because internal AI systems may already hold valid credentials and established connections to sensitive systems.

The study also looked at AI's growing role in security operations, finding that 67% of organisations use AI in that work and 32% are comfortable letting it run investigations without human review. Smaller shares said they would let AI deploy code changes without supervision (29%) or grant or revoke access permissions (26%). More than half of respondents, 56%, said they were willing to accept more cyber risk than they were 12 months earlier, and 47% said they permit autonomous AI actions in production environments. At the same time, 82% believe AI agents need different security controls from traditional software, but only 25% named explicitly defined permitted actions as one of their two main controls.

Raghu Nandakumara, Vice President of Industry Strategy at Illumio, said the biggest AI risk may be a system that was never given meaningful limits, rather than one that breaks its rules. He argued that businesses should set strict limits on what AI can access and do, and enforce those limits both within applications and across the underlying infrastructure, because AI agents persist in pursuing goals and trying to anticipate every action is a losing battle. The report's recommendation, as the article presents it, is to focus on restricting what AI systems can reach rather than only predicting what they might decide. The article does not describe any specific regulatory response or next steps beyond these recommendations.

Articles.Title: Illumio warns AI authority is outpacing security controls - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Pittsburgh experts weigh in on who is responsible when AI makes medical mistakes
stories.Summary:
The article is a Pittsburgh discussion of who is responsible when AI makes medical mistakes, published on November 4, 2026. It does not name any patient, doctor, hospital or company involved in a specific incident. It also gives no date or place for any particular error. The piece is about the question of responsibility in general, not about one event.

The article does not list any new rule, law or requirement that would change how AI is used in medicine. It gives no numbers on how often AI makes mistakes or how many cases exist. It names no regulator or agency taking action. The only date it gives is its own publication date.

The article says Pittsburgh experts weighed in on the responsibility question. It does not name those experts or say what each of them said. It does not quote anyone directly. Because of that, there is no way to say who is responsible or what they said, beyond the fact that the experts discussed it.

The article does not describe the wider context or say what happens next. It carries no information on upcoming hearings, lawsuits or policy changes. It also does not say whether any of the experts called for new rules. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Pittsburgh experts weigh in on who is responsible when AI makes medical mistakes

stories.Headline: Rackspace lands first customer for new AI platform
stories.Summary:
Rackspace has landed its first public customer for its AMD-powered AI platform, a deal the San Antonio company says highlights its push into enterprise AI infrastructure ahead of earnings. The customer is Hinduja Global, according to a headline on the San Antonio Business Journal article. The deal expands AI infrastructure work between Rackspace and AMD. The article was published on November 4, 2026.

Kinetic announced a partnership with SKYOVI on November 2, 2026, to bring an artificial intelligence design platform to its fiber-installation operations. The platform helps Kinetic plan and build the final fiber connection, known as a drop, to each home and business. SKYOVI examines all 2.2 million homes in Kinetic's 18-state footprint and designs the drop and calculates the distance from its network terminal to the home or business before crews are deployed. Kinetic is a business unit of Uniti and serves 1,400 markets across 18 states.

Jim Dacey, senior vice president of Kinetic Center Operations, said the speed and accuracy of every connection matters as Kinetic expands fiber to more communities. He said SKYOVI gives teams smarter tools to design each drop right the first time, reduce delays and deliver a better installation experience. Gaurav Deshmukh, president and CEO of SKYOVI, said fiber connectivity is essential to the future of communities across America. He said the partnership marks a step toward making fiber deployment more predictable, scalable and cost-efficient.

SKYOVI automates drop design and lets teams survey each route virtually, which the article says reduces the cycle time for placing buried fiber drops by over 60%. The platform uses proprietary AI models rather than outside services that charge each time an image or map is analyzed, giving Kinetic predictable operating costs. Engineers and field managers can review and adjust AI-generated fiber routes, and the system recalculates the route when they flag an obstacle or change. The platform also creates a job-specific list of materials for each installation and compares what was planned with what was used.

Articles.Title: Rackspace lands first customer for new AI platform

stories.Headline: The Security Companies Trying to Get AI Agents Under Control
stories.Summary:
The Information published a story on November 4, 2026 about security companies trying to get AI agents under control. The article is an exclusive from theinformation.com. It focuses on the efforts of security firms to manage AI agents. The headline names the security companies as the ones seeking that control.

The article does not give the names of the security companies involved. It does not give any numbers, dates or names beyond the publication date of November 4, 2026. It does not describe specific requirements or changes the companies are making. The available text also does not say who is responsible or what those people said.

The article does not provide context on what happens next. The page text includes only site navigation and promotional material. It does not include the body of the story. More to follow.
